items.title: [Bug]: Wrong timestamps if audio > 30s
items.author: dr75
items.body_excerpt:
### Your current environment


NA

### 🐛 Describe the bug

**Segment level timestamps are incrementally offset by ~0.5s per segment.**

When transcribing long audio with vLLM Whisper, segment-level timestamps are increasingly inaccurate. Chunking uses by default a 1s window to find low-energy (quiet) regions for splitting, so the next chunk may start up to 1s earlier than the nominal chunk length. This offset is not compensated for when generating segment timestamps, resulting in an average delay of ~0.5s per segment, which accumulates (e.g., 5s after 10 segments).

Clients can workaround by subtracting 0.5s per segment, but that's obviously not accurate.

Also, the [related documentation](https://github.com/vllm-project/vllm/blob/e83b7e379c11bf136c1b96bc6a67b6d2207cfde4/docs/contributing/model/transcription.md#audio-preprocessing-and-chunking) is not correct: there are no overlapping chunks, but just a window for searching the best split point. Maybe this confusion is the cause of the issue.

### Before submitting a new issue...

- [x] Make sure you already searched for relevant issues, and asked the chatbot living at the bottom right corner of the [documentation page](https://docs.vllm.ai/en/latest/), which can answer lots of frequently asked questions.

* How `null-blocks` in the request block list are handled.

items.title: [RFC] Extending MP coordinator as the control plane for distributed KV Cache management.
items.author: ruizhang0101
items.body_excerpt:
## Summary Extending the MP coordinator to LMCache's distributed KV-cache control plane, including two components: - **metadata**: a key directory (key → placements across nodes and tiers), some indexes for efficient lookup. All of them will be built from events emitted by MP servers and only guarantee **eventual consistent**. - **management API**: instance registry/heartbeat, quota, cache control (delete/move/prefetch), pins etc. Durable state are backed using **etcd** with periodical **snapshot**. Adding a new light L1 coordination interface for handling multi-l1 media(native DRAM, CXL, GDS, Device-DAX etc), which will take care of the memory allocation and eviction. The media should bring their own L1 coordinator (CXL coordinator, GDS coordinator, etc.) ## Motivation More and more use cases require a centralized service that has a “global view” of all the objects and memory allocation status, including (but not limited to) the following: - Manage objects in multi-tier/share L1 (CXL, GDS, etc) - Manage objects in a shared L2 - External management in a distributed KV cache setup (delete, move, pin, prefetch etc.) - Quota management for in different storage tier - Segmented matching (non-prefix matching) - KV cache discovery and configuration persistence - Intelligent KV cache load and store planning The coordinator we have today is a simple python-based FastAPI server with a L2-only view doing: - External management like KV cache deletion, pin/unpin, prefetch etc. - Manage objects in a shared L2 - L2 quota management - Cacheblend non-prefix matching - Discover KV cache in L2. However, the current version fails to: - Handle multi-tier/share L1 like CXL and GDS because it doesn't have L1 KV cache view. - Have a good performance under load - Have consistency across the crash of the system components. - Have intelligent KV cache load and store planning. Extending the current MP coordinator will unlock these things. ## System Overview Ownership model: | owner | owns | consistency | | --------------------------------------------------------- | -------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- | ------------------------------ | | MP server | • local memory safety: `L1Manager` locks/TTLs
• local allocation (native L1)
• L2 adapter ops
• transfers
• local delete/evict execution | strong, node-local | | L1 medium coordinator (via the L1 coordination interface) | • allocation for one byte-addressable medium (native / CXL / GDS / …)
• eviction for that medium
• shared media: arbitration across nodes | strong, medium-local | | MP coordinator | • key directory
• content index
• token store
• registry
• quota accounting
• cache-control orchestration
| **eventual** | ## Key Components **MP server** Keeps everything it has today. New or extended duties: - Event emission. Every cache-state change produces an event: L1/L2 store commit, evict, delete etc. (Finish read/write) - Potential Event Schema: ``` CacheEvent { instance_id str # emitting MP server incarnation u32 # bumped every MP-server restart (We can use start time) seq u64 # per-instance monotonic counter type STORE | DELETE | ACCESS | TOKEN tier l1 | l2 backend_id dram | cxl | gds | devdax | raw_block | fs | valkey | ... entries [ {key_hash, size, cache_salt, model_name...} | token_ids] ts u64 } ``` **Key Directory** Global key directory that has the kv cache location info. - Need snapshot and persistent event bus(e.g. Kafka) for failover - Potential schema: ``` key_hash (16B) → KeyRecord { model_name, cache_salt, kv_rank content_hash placements list[PlacementRecord] last_seq, last_access } PlacementRecord { instance_id, incarnation, tier (l1|l2), backend, size, state (might be deleting or pinned) } # Blend Index (hash_version, content_hash) → [key_hash] # token store + inverted index content_hash → { token_ids u32[chunk] (compressed)} ``` **Management API** - Registry/heartbeat/health - Quota: config should be persisted; usage aggregated from events; eviction directives to owner MP servers, confirmed by EVICT/DELETE events - Cache control: pins, token/key-based lookup, delete, move, warm prefetch (existing cache_api + #3978 /#3990), generalized tier-aware (l1 | l2 | all). All ops are directives to owners: the coordinator selects targets from the directory; the owner executes under its local locks and reports the result event. **L1 coordinator interface** A light contract for allocation and eviction over one byte-addressable L1 medium. It delegates the allocation and eviction to the specific L1 component(CXL, GDS etc) instead of a central place in LMCache. Potential Interface: ```python class L1CoordinatorInterface: """Allocation & eviction authority for one byte-addressable medium.""" def query_init_metadata(): def reserve_read(): def reserve_write(): def finish_read(): def finish_write(): def finish_write_and_reserve_read(): ``` ## Related PRs - #4025 #3488 #3630 #3662 #3597 #3708 #4172 #3584 #3947 #3972 #4010 #4052 ## Possible Implementation Plan **M1: Generalized cache events + key directory to l1** - Extend the existing L2 event reporting into the CacheEvent schema - Build I1 + the instance index - Extend startup resync to L1 placements. - Generalize cache management API across l1

items.title: [Bug][CLI] trace replay percentiles are one sample too high at whole ranks, so p90/p99 report the max
items.author: bharadwaj-pendyala
items.body_excerpt:
**Label**

`bug`, `cli`

**Describe the bug**

`_percentile()` in `lmcache/cli/commands/trace/_stats.py` treats the nearest-rank rank as a 0-based index, so it returns one sample too high whenever `pct/100 * N` lands on a whole number.

The docstring on the function says the p-th percentile is the sample at index `ceil(p/100 * N) - 1`. The code drops the `- 1`:

https://github.com/LMCache/LMCache/blob/3b8093cf8860a39d05937af915adfb5db493a047/lmcache/cli/commands/trace/_stats.py#L88-L95

`ceil(p/100 * N)` is a 1-based rank. Using it directly as a list index skips to the next sample.

The practical effect is that `lmcache trace replay` reports the slowest single sample as p90 or p99 at the sample counts you are most likely to hit. With 10 replayed calls for a qualname, p90 equals max. With 100, p99 equals max. Fractional ranks are unaffected, so the numbers look plausible and only the tail is wrong.

There is a second, smaller error in the same expression. `pct / 100.0` is inexact for most integer percentiles, so `(7 / 100.0) * 100` is `7.000000000000001` and `ceil()` picks rank 8. Multiplying before dividing keeps the product exact.

**To Reproduce**

Tested against `origin/dev` at commit `3b8093cf8860a39d05937af915adfb5db493a047`.

```python
from lmcache.cli.commands.trace._stats import ReplayStatsCollector, _percentile

vals = [float(i) for i in range(1, 101)]
print(_percentile(vals, 50))   # 51.0, want 50.0
print(_percentile(vals, 99))   # 100.0, want 99.0  (this is max)
print(_percentile(vals, 7))    # 8.0,   want 7.0   (the float rounding case)

s = ReplayStatsCollector()
for latency_ms in range(1, 11):
    s.record("op.foo", latency_ms / 1000.0)
stats = s.summary()["op.foo"]
print(stats.p90_ms, stats.max_ms)   # 10.0 10.0, want 9.0 10.0
```

Output on `dev`:

```
51.0
100.0
8.0
10.0 10.0
```

**Expected behavior**

Nearest-rank as documented: rank `ceil(p/100 * N)`, 1-based, so index `rank - 1`. p50 of 1..100 is 50, p99 is 99, p90 of ten samples is the ninth.

**Additional context**

The existing unit test encodes the off-by-one rather than catching it. `tests/cli/commands/trace/test_stats.py::TestPercentile::test_p50_on_100_values` asserts `51.0` with the comment `nearest-rank with floor((50/100)*100)=50 → index 50 → value 51`, which is where the 1-based rank got read as a 0-based index. That test needs updating alongside the fix.

Scope check on the two other percentile helpers in the CLI, neither of which should change here:

- `lmcache/cli/commands/bench/engine_bench/stats.py::_percentile` uses linear interpolation on purpose and is documented as such. Not the same method, not affected.
- `lmcache/cli/commands/bench/l2_adapter_bench/result.py` uses a `+0.999999` ceiling approximation. Different code, worth a separate look, out of scope for this.

The changed values are user visible: terminal output from `lmcache trace replay`, plus the `p50_ms`/`p90_ms`/`p99_ms` columns in the CSV and JSON exports.

I have a fix with regression tests ready and will open a PR against `dev` shortly. Happy to change direction if you would rather keep the current numbers and correct the docstring instead, though the tail numbers are wrong either way.

**Label**

RFC, Feature Request

**Summary**

Integration of UL-SMF (Unified Latent-State Memory Fabric) for extreme, linear-complexity KV-cache compression (up to 768x reduction).

**Details**

Following recent work on long-context memory bottlenecks, I have open-sourced **UL-SMF (Unified Latent-State Memory Fabric)**—a hardware-software co-designed compression layer that tackles the HBM memory wall during high-throughput inference.

Because LMCache focuses on managing, offloading, and sharing KV-caches, integrating UL-SMF could exponentially increase storage density by drastically shrinking raw cache footprints before they hit your storage connectors or transit layers.

**Key Architectural Highlights:**

* **Dynamic Orthogonal Projection:** Automatically maps varying model hidden dimensions (e.g., Llama, Mistral, Gemma, Qwen) on the fly without retraining or hardcoded weight matrices.
* **Linear Complexity:** Scales compression ratios upward as batch workloads grow.
* **Telemetry Benchmarks:** Tested on enterprise workloads, such as compressing a heavy Qwen-2.5 (72B) batch from 1.53 GB down to 2.00 MB (768x reduction) with high fidelity in under 600 ms on a single CUDA node.

**Steps / Reproduction (if applicable)**

The package is fully open-source and installable via pip for immediate evaluation in existing stacks:

1. Install the package via pip:
`pip install git+https://github.com/liventruth/UL-SMF-Cache-Compression.git`

reconstructed_cache, latents = bridge(kv_cache_tensor)

To discuss how the `UniversalLatentBridge` can be routed as an optional native compression backend or plugin within the LMCache ecosystem to maximize storage density and accelerate KV-cache transit.

items.title: [Bug] L2 benchmark loses timeout accounting after warmup filtering
items.author: mohan-zeyu
items.body_excerpt:
**Describe the bug**

In commit `1fde7bec`, `_strip_warmup()` in `lmcache/cli/commands/bench/l2_adapter_bench/command.py` has two bugs:

1. **The `BenchResult` constructor omits `timed_out_rounds` (lines 615–624).** It defaults to `0`, discarding measurement timeout counts. Since `attempted_rounds = len(round_durations) + timed_out_rounds`, attempted rounds and total keys are undercounted, even with `warmup=0`.
2. **`round_durations[warmup:]` uses the wrong offset (line 620).** Durations contain only completed rounds. A warmup timeout adds no duration, so slicing by the number of warmup attempts removes a measurement duration. `success_counts[warmup:]` is correct because success counts include every attempt.

**To reproduce**

Run these two reproductions against the affected commit, `1fde7bec`.

**1. One timed-out attempt is reported as zero rounds**

```bash
lmcache bench l2 \
  --l2-adapter '{"type":"mock","max_size_gb":0.01,"mock_bandwidth_gb":0.000001}' \
  --only store \
  --num-keys 1 \
  --in-flight 1 \
  --data-size-kb 1024 \
  --rounds 1 \
  --warmup-rounds 0
```

The store times out after approximately 120 seconds. The summary drops that attempt:

| Field | Actual | Expected |
|---|---:|---:|
| Rounds | 0 | 1 |
| Rounds timed out | 0 | 1 |
| Total keys | 0 | 1 |

**2. A warmup timeout produces a 200% lookup hit rate**

This Python reproduction runs three lookup attempts: one warmup timeout, then two successful measurements. Completion notifications are mocked to avoid waiting for a real timeout.

```python
from unittest.mock import Mock, patch

from lmcache.cli.commands.bench.l2_adapter_bench.command import _strip_warmup
from lmcache.cli.commands.bench.l2_adapter_bench.data import make_object_keys
from lmcache.cli.commands.bench.l2_adapter_bench.runner import bench_lookup

adapter = Mock()
adapter.get_lookup_and_lock_event_fd.return_value = 0
adapter.submit_lookup_and_lock_task.side_effect = [0, 1, 2]
adapter.query_lookup_and_lock_result.side_effect = [
    Mock(popcount=Mock(return_value=1)),
    Mock(popcount=Mock(return_value=1)),
]

with patch(
    "lmcache.cli.commands.bench.l2_adapter_bench.runner.wait_eventfd",
    side_effect=[False, True, True],
):
    raw = bench_lookup(
        adapter,
        in_flight=1,
        num_keys=1,
        rounds=3,
        keys_for_round=lambda r: [make_object_keys(1, key_offset=r)],
        log=lambda message: None,
    )

result = _strip_warmup(raw, warmup=1)
print(result.total_success, result.total_keys, result.actual_hit_rate)
assert result.actual_hit_rate == 1.0
```

Actual output: `2 1 2.0` (200%); the assertion fails. Expected output: `2 2 1.0` (100%). The slice drops the first measurement duration but retains both measurement hit counts.

**Expected behavior**

Preserve measurement timeout counts in the returned `BenchResult`. Remove duration samples only for completed warmup rounds. Retain all measurement attempts and partial successes.

**Environment**

- OS: macOS 26.6.2, Apple Silicon (arm64)
- Python: 3.12.13
- PyTorch: 2.14.1; CUDA unavailable
- Affected LMCache commit: `1fde7bec`

items.title: convert_hf_to_gguf.py: very large models need either the full model in RAM or 2x its size on disk (streaming two-pass mode?)
items.author: ZhiyangK
items.body_excerpt:
## Problem

Converting very large models (e.g. `DeepSeek-V4-Flash-0731-reap-150b`, 79.2 GiB as MXFP4) with `convert_hf_to_gguf.py` requires either:

| mode | requirement |
|---|---|
| default | **~85 GB RAM** — every tensor is retained in memory until the very end |
| `--use-temp-file` | **~170 GB disk** — temp copy (85 GB) + final output (85 GB) |

and `--use-temp-file` is mutually exclusive with `--split` (`convert_hf_to_gguf.py` raises `ValueError`), so sharding cannot be used as a workaround.

On a 32 GB RAM / 103 GB free-disk machine both modes fail. Default mode dies after ~24 routed-expert tensors with:

```
numpy._core._exceptions._ArrayMemoryError: Unable to allocate 561. MiB for an array
with shape (132, 2048, 2176) and data type uint8
```

Root cause is in `gguf_writer.add_tensor()`:

```python
if self.temp_file is None:
    self.tensors[-1][name].tensor = tensor   # every tensor is retained in RAM
```

## Proposal: streaming two-pass mode

Pass 1 records tensor metadata only (payload dropped); pass 2 regenerates each payload **in metadata order** and streams it straight into the output file. Sketch of the local patch I wrote to test this:

- **`gguf-py/gguf/gguf_writer.py`**: add `two_pass` flag + `pass2_registry: dict[str, Callable[[], np.ndarray]]`. In `add_tensor`, when `two_pass` and `state is WriterState.NO_FILE` and the tensor name is registered, call `add_tensor_info()` only. In `write_tensors_to_file()`, when `two_pass`, walk tensors **in metadata order**: write in-memory payloads directly, call the registered generator for dropped payloads (asserting written bytes == `ti.nbytes`), then set `state = WriterState.WEIGHTS`.
- **`conversion/base.py`**: enable `two_pass` in `write()`, and make `get_tensors()` skip names that were already emitted directly (otherwise the regenerated experts get converted twice).
- **`conversion/deepseek.py`**: for DeepSeek-V4 MXFP4 routed experts, pass 1 reads a single expert to derive the packed shape and registers a per-layer generator; pass 2 lazy-regenerates from the safetensors already on disk. `generate_extra_tensors()` must not `del self.model_tensors[name]` in two-pass mode, since pass 2 needs the sources.

## Measured result

- Peak RSS: **13.5 GB → crashed** before; **stable 190–470 MB** after.
- Output size matched the officially published quantized GGUF byte-for-byte in size: **79.21 GiB / 85,049,311,712 bytes**.
- The resulting file loads, generates correct text, and benchmarks normally (`llama-cli -st`, `llama-bench -ngl 0 -t 16 -p 32 -n 8`).
- Conversion wall time on this machine: ~25 min total for 1328 tensors (spinning rust aside, dominated by re-reading 79 GB of safetensors).

Would a contribution in this direction be welcome? I'm happy to clean it up (opt-in flag, e.g. `--two-pass`, plus tests) and send a PR.

## Environment

- llama.cpp build 10711 (commit 9723942ad)
- Windows 11, 32 GB RAM, RTX 5060 Ti 16 GB, 103 GB free disk
- Python 3.12, numpy / torch / gguf 0.19.0

items.title: [Feature] Integrate KVPress in order to try more KV cache optimization heuristics easily
items.author: vincentzed
items.body_excerpt:
# What is this?

In long context-serving instances, the KV cache can grow to a large size in `O(n)` complexity, and optimal compression can help us reach sub linear scaling of memory growth. KVPress library integrates many unique strategies to make it easier to try different heuristics for KV cache optimization in prefill.

# Background

KVPress provides a set of "presses" that compress the KV cache during the prefilling-phase. Each press is associated with a `compression_ratio` attribute that measures the compression of the cache. The easiest way to use a press is through our custom `KVPressTextGenerationPipeline`. It is automatically registered as a transformers pipeline with the name "kv-press-text-generation" when kvpress is imported and handles chat templates and tokenization for you:

Such a code example:

```python
from transformers import pipeline
from kvpress import ExpectedAttentionPress

device = "cuda:0"
model = "meta-llama/Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct"
model_kwargs = {"attn_implementation": "flash_attention_2"}
pipe = pipeline("kv-press-text-generation", model=model, device=device, model_kwargs=model_kwargs)

context = "A very long text you want to compress once and for all"
question = "\nA question about the compressed context"  # optional

press = ExpectedAttentionPress(compression_ratio=0.5)
answer = pipe(context, question=question, press=press)["answer"]
```

This compression is focused on the pre-fill phase, for example in prompt caching. 

# Design

The generic `BasePress` will use `compress` to return the compressed key and value tensor, with a lower sequence length dim. Some scores are based on heuristics to choose the KV pair with the lowest importance (there are 11 such presses so far). There are also other less straightforward methods of KV cache compression (I.e not the score based system above), which is part of the extensibility strategy we want to promote.

There is no quantization by default, but it can be enabled, with arbitrary precision. For now, Llama, Mistral, Phi, Qwen 2 and 3, and Gemma 3 are all tested.

It works with multiple GPUs, through the hugging face accelerate lib for the e2e inference.

[https://huggingface.co/docs/accelerate/en/index](https://huggingface.co/docs/accelerate/en/index)

In theory, it should be possible to use this in tandem with KV transfer backend. 

As a brief refresher, in tensor parallel, kvcache is sharded across a tension head, so each tpRank handles a subset, and in the disaggregated setup, the kvcache slice is transferred between prefill and decode.

See: python/sglang/srt/disaggregation/mooncake/conn.py

python/sglang/srt/layers/linear.py

In pipeline parallelism, the KV cache is distributed across layer. Each pipeline parallel stage handles specific layer range. And each has its distinct index from start to end layer, which is the logic to determine what layer each PP rank processes. Right now, we don't support pp on the decode side in PD moonncake backend.

Mooncake engine ref: python/sglang/srt/disaggregation/mooncake/conn.py

In data parallelism, each group has an independent KV cache replica. In this case, we can treat each KV cache separately and try to apply press on each of them independently. This would be a good place to start after the initial support.


https://github.com/NVIDIA/kvpress

https://github.com/sgl-project/sglang/issues/1347

# Success Criteria
One or more of the following will be possible. 
- [ ] You can run inference with KVPress on one node. 
- [ ] repeat the above step with any of the three parallelism strategies, maybe more than one 
- [ ] Make it work with PD and transfer(s) backend, but this is already covered by the point above.

**RFC: revive sparse KV-cache attention — wire Quest into the FlashAttention decode path**

Refreshed proposal for KVPress / sparse-attention work (refs #12607, #12933).

**Context.** The sparse-algorithm framework under `mem_cache/sparsity/` (`SparseCoordinator`, `QuestAlgorithm`, `FlashAttentionAdaptor`) is implemented but **not wired into serving** — `attention_begin/attention_end` have no callers, and `--enable-hisparse` only drives the separate DeepSeek/DSA host-offload path. **Proposal.** Start by **wiring the existing `QuestAlgorithm` into the non-MLA FlashAttention decode path** behind a default-off `--enable-sparse-attention` flag — turning the dormant framework into a tested, query-aware page-selection baseline (compute/bandwidth savings). Deliberately **no new algorithm** in this step (that was #12933's pitfall); SnapKV and others build on top.

**Status.** I have a working spike (validated on an RTX 4090, fa3, Qwen2.5-0.5B): it boots, runs end-to-end, output matches the dense baseline, and the decode selection path executes. It also surfaced and fixed two latent framework bugs (an int32/int64 `index_put` dtype error; a zero-selected-pages case zeroing `cache_seqlens`). items.title: Handling KV Cache Corruption During L2-to-L1 Promotion in HiCache
items.author: montagetao
items.body_excerpt:
**Background**

HiCache supports hierarchical KV cache management, allowing cached data to be transferred from L2 (host memory) to L1 (GPU memory) when a cache hit occurs.

However, what happens if the KV cache data stored in L2 is already corrupted when it is promoted back to L1?

As far as I understand the current implementation, there does not appear to be an explicit data integrity validation mechanism in this path to detect such corruption before the data is reused. If corrupted KV cache data is loaded into L1 and used for inference, it could potentially lead to incorrect model outputs or other unexpected behavior.

**Discussion Points**

I'd like to discuss how HiCache should handle this scenario:

Data integrity validation: Should we introduce checksums or hashes to detect corruption when transferring KV cache data from L2 to L1? What would be the performance overhead?

Corruption handling: If corruption is detected, should we discard the corrupted cache entry and recompute the KV cache from the original tokens, rather than reusing invalid data?

Error propagation and recovery: How should the system handle corrupted entries during cache promotion? Should it fall back to a cache miss and continue inference, or report an error in certain cases?

Validation granularity: Should integrity checks be performed per token, per page, or per cache entry? Given HiCache's page-based management, would page-level checks provide a reasonable balance between reliability and overhead?

Performance considerations: How can we introduce integrity protection without significantly affecting cache-hit latency and overall inference throughput?

items.title: [Bug] Client-supplied bootstrap address in Decode worker requests enables SSRF and blocks shared request processing
items.author: yyymk
items.body_excerpt:
### Checklist

- [x] I searched related issues but found no solution.
- [x] The bug persists in the latest version.
- [x] Issues without environment info and a minimal reproducible demo are hard to resolve and may receive no feedback.
- [x] If this is not a bug report but a general question, please start a discussion at https://github.com/sgl-project/sglang/discussions. Otherwise, it will be closed.
- [x] Please use English. Otherwise, it will be closed.

### Describe the bug

### Summary

A caller that can reach an SGLang Decode worker's HTTP API in a Prefill/Decode disaggregation deployment can supply `bootstrap_host`, `bootstrap_port`, and `bootstrap_room` in an inference request. The Decode worker uses the supplied address in a synchronous HTTP request without checking that it belongs to a configured Prefill worker. This allows a direct Decode caller to make the worker contact an attacker-selected HTTP endpoint. A slow endpoint also blocks shared Decode request processing and delays unrelated inference requests.

The issue was reproduced on the official SGLang v0.5.17 image. A source snapshot of current main at commit `74c032234201aa0ed64b7a58c738d9ea393e319c` still contained the same sink on 2026-08-14, but current main was inspected only and was not tested at runtime. The official Gateway overwrote the three client-supplied fields in our control tests, so the confirmed attack surface is direct access to the Decode worker API. Suggested severity is Medium.

### Details

In `CommonKVManager.try_ensure_parallel_info()`, the Decode side treats the per-request bootstrap address as the authority for an HTTP URL:

```python
def try_ensure_parallel_info(self, bootstrap_addr: str) -> bool:
    if bootstrap_addr in self.prefill_info_table:
        return True

    try:
        url = (
            f"http://{bootstrap_addr}/route?"
            f"prefill_dp_rank={-1}&prefill_cp_rank={-1}&"
            f"target_tp_rank={-1}&target_pp_rank={-1}"
        )
        response = requests.get(url, timeout=5)
        ...
```

Runtime-tested v0.5.17 source:

- https://github.com/sgl-project/sglang/blob/29481685462732237d80d86076d6563e1f658102/python/sglang/srt/disaggregation/common/conn.py

Source-inspected main snapshot:

- https://github.com/sgl-project/sglang/blob/74c032234201aa0ed64b7a58c738d9ea393e319c/python/sglang/srt/disaggregation/common/conn.py
- https://github.com/sgl-project/sglang/blob/74c032234201aa0ed64b7a58c738d9ea393e319c/sgl-model-gateway/src/routers/http/pd_router.rs

The official v0.5.17 test used one Prefill worker, one Decode worker, one Gateway, Mooncake TCP, Qwen3-0.6B, and loopback-only endpoints. A direct Decode request selected a local canary port. The canary received 15 requests with this path:

```text
/route?prefill_dp_rank=-1&prefill_cp_rank=-1&target_tp_rank=-1&target_pp_rank=-1
```

The direct request returned HTTP 500 after 14.057 seconds. The same stock-code run selected four separate canary ports and reached all four. Two further clean restarts each produced 15 canary hits and an HTTP 500 response after about 30.10 seconds when the canary delayed each response by two seconds.

We then repeated the latency comparison in three distinct Decode container lifecycles. These repeats used logging-only instrumentation; the measured request times and canary hits came from external clients and canary servers. In each lifecycle, one direct Decode request targeted a canary that delayed every response by two seconds. Three normal Gateway requests started about 50 ms later. Their mean latency was 20.357, 20.350, and 20.356 seconds. In matched zero-delay runs, the corresponding means were 0.245, 0.246, and 0.245 seconds. The overall means were 20.354 and 0.246 seconds, an 82.88-fold difference. All nine normal requests returned HTTP 200, so the confirmed effect is severe latency increase rather than request failure.

As a negative control, a request carrying the same attacker-selected bootstrap fields was sent through the official Gateway in each lifecycle. All three Gateway requests returned HTTP 200 and the attacker canary received zero requests. This matches `inject_bootstrap_into_value()`, which overwrites the client values with the selected Prefill worker's server-side values.

The Decode worker should not trust bootstrap routing data supplied by an inference client. It should derive the Prefill endpoint from authenticated server-side topology and bind it to the selected worker or request. If direct worker APIs must accept this metadata, they should authenticate the internal caller and validate the address against the configured Prefill set. The parallel-info fetch should also avoid synchronously blocking shared request processing.

### Reproduction

Run the following only in an isolated loopback SGLang v0.5.17 Prefill/Decode test deployment that you own. The script refuses non-loopback URLs and requires an explicit confirmation flag. With `--delay-s 0`, it demonstrates the server-side request. With `--delay-s 2` and `--gateway-url`, it also measures concurrent normal requests.

```python
#!/usr/bin/env python3
import argparse
import ipaddress
import json
import threading
import time
import urllib.error
import urllib.parse
import urllib.request
from http.server import BaseHTTPRequestHandler, ThreadingHTTPServer


def loopback_url(value):
    parsed = urllib.parse.urlparse(value)
    if parsed.scheme != "http" or not parsed.hostname or parsed.port is None:
        raise argparse.ArgumentTypeError("use http://127.0.0.1:PORT")
    try:
        address = ipaddress.ip_address(parsed.hostname)
    except ValueError as exc:
        raise argparse.ArgumentTypeError("use a literal loopback IP") from exc
    if not address.is_loopback:
        raise argparse.ArgumentTypeError("only loopback targets are accepted")
    return value.rstrip("/")


def post(url, body, timeout=45):
    started = time.monotonic()
    request = urllib.request.Request(
        url,
        data=json.dumps(body).enc

items.title: [Bug] Unauthenticated Mooncake STAGING_RSP chunk index causes Prefill scheduler OOM
items.author: yyymk
items.body_excerpt:
### Checklist

- [x] I searched related issues but found no solution.
- [x] The bug persists in the latest version.
- [x] Issues without environment info and a minimal reproducible demo are hard to resolve and may receive no feedback.
- [x] If this is not a bug report but a general question, please start a discussion at https://github.com/sgl-project/sglang/discussions. Otherwise, it will be closed.
- [x] Please use English. Otherwise, it will be closed.

### Describe the bug

### Summary

SGLang Prefill workers accept unauthenticated Mooncake PD control messages on their ZeroMQ rank socket. A network peer that can reach the socket first sends a normal-looking transfer message to create a fake room, then sends a `STAGING_RSP` message with an arbitrary `chunk_idx`. The Prefill side grows three Python lists to `chunk_idx + 1` entries with no bound, exhausting host memory. In a two-host test on SGLang 0.5.15.post1 this raised Prefill cgroup memory by 12.23 GiB, made overlapping inference requests 46.9 times slower on average, and the cgroup OOM killer terminated the Prefill scheduler. The dispatch and the unbounded growth are unchanged in v0.5.21, the latest release (source-checked; v0.5.21 was not runtime-tested). This is the opposite direction of CVE-2026-93838, which covers `STAGING_REQ` handled on the Decode side; fixing that path does not fix this one. Suggested severity is Moderate. The attacker must be able to reach the Prefill bootstrap and rank endpoints; a normal model API request cannot trigger this path.

### Details

The entry point is the Prefill receive thread started by `MooncakeKVManager.start_prefill_thread()` in `python/sglang/srt/disaggregation/mooncake/conn.py`. It trusts the first ZMQ frame as a message type or room ID. A normal-looking eight-frame message with an arbitrary room and session creates `self.transfer_infos[room][session]`. No real Decode worker or prior application request is required.

- [v0.5.15 conn.py, the runtime-tested version](https://github.com/sgl-project/sglang/blob/v0.5.15/python/sglang/srt/disaggregation/mooncake/conn.py#L1447-L1529)
- [v0.5.21 conn.py, the latest release](https://github.com/sgl-project/sglang/blob/v0.5.21/python/sglang/srt/disaggregation/mooncake/conn.py)

The same thread dispatches any message whose first frame is `STAGING_RSP` to `handle_staging_rsp()` in `python/sglang/srt/disaggregation/common/staging_handler.py`. The dispatch is not conditional on `SGLANG_DISAGG_STAGING_BUFFER`, so the path works with staging disabled. `handle_staging_rsp()` parses the sender-controlled chunk index, looks up the attacker-created room and session, creates `StagingTransferInfo`, and calls `set_chunk()`.

- [v0.5.15 staging_handler.py, the runtime-tested version](https://github.com/sgl-project/sglang/blob/v0.5.15/python/sglang/srt/disaggregation/common/staging_handler.py#L421-L464)
- [v0.5.21 staging_handler.py, the latest release](https://github.com/sgl-project/sglang/blob/v0.5.21/python/sglang/srt/disaggregation/common/staging_handler.py)

`StagingTransferInfo.set_chunk()` uses the received index as a host-memory growth target:

```python
def set_chunk(self, idx: int, offset: int, rnd: int, end: int):
    while len(self.offsets) <= idx:
        self.offsets.append(-1)
        self.rounds.append(0)
        self.ends.append(-1)
    self.offsets[idx] = offset
    self.rounds[idx] = rnd
    self.ends[idx] = end
```

There is no peer authentication, room ownership check, session binding, maximum chunk index, per-peer quota, or global quota before this allocation. The Prefill bootstrap `/route` endpoint returns the dynamic rank IP and port without authentication. A reachable peer can therefore impersonate a Decode-side sender and repeat the allocation under fresh room and session IDs.

The runtime reproduction used stock 0.5.15.post1 files that exactly match the official v0.5.15 tag:

```text
9106dfc8deb91662bdbac850f41612104a597b7f6a5cd15c8eb7ca17a20c8a0d  sglang/srt/disaggregation/mooncake/conn.py
886c87979abb015b63b0274e7f03ff6367767a665068f5bc08f0cb8fdcece9f5  sglang/srt/disaggregation/common/staging_handler.py
```

The same unchecked dispatch and list-growth logic was also present in `main` at commit `ae848116662ece923501131ce773a4602223237e`, inspected on 2026-08-01. The v0.5.21 tag was source-checked on 2026-10-18 and the code paths are unchanged: the Prefill receive thread still dispatches first-frame `STAGING_RSP` to `handle_staging_rsp()` before any other check, room creation is still unconditional, and `set_chunk()` still grows the three lists in the same `while` loop with no bound. The two PoC message formats below parse the same way in v0.5.21.

### Reproduction

Run this only in an isolated test deployment. Put only the Prefill process in a memory-limited cgroup. The validated setup used Linux, Python 3.12.13, SGLang 0.5.15.post1, mooncake-transfer-engine 0.3.11.post1, PyTorch 2.11.0, pyzmq 27.1.0, Qwen3-8B, two NVIDIA A100 80 GB GPUs, and one Prefill plus one Decode worker on the victim host. The attacker was a second host on the same network.

In the first terminal, start Prefill with its HTTP listener exposed to the test network and with staging explicitly disabled. The exact model path can be changed to a local Qwen3-8B path.

```

systemd-run --user --scope \

  -- python -m sglang.launch_server \
    --model-path Qwen/Qwen3-8B \
    --host 0.0.0.0 \
    --port 32400 \
    --tp-size 1 \
    --mem-fraction-static 0.50 \
    --disaggregation-mode prefill \
    --disaggregation-transfer-backend mooncake \
    --disaggregation-bootstrap-port 32498 \
    --engine-info-bootstrap-port 32489 \
    --served-model-name Qwen3-8B \
    --disable-cuda-graph
```

In a second terminal, start Decode outside that cgroup:

items.title: [Feature] Reduce redundant tokenizer initialization during startup
items.author: SouthWest7
items.body_excerpt:
### Motivation

Startup loads the same text tokenizer in both `Scheduler` and `TpModelWorker` within one process. `_fix_v5_tokenizer_components` also rebuilds the full vocabulary just to inspect the pre-tokenizer and decoder.

Reusing the scheduler's tokenizer and loading only those two components can make startup a little faster, including server restarts. A local Qwen3-32B-FP8 check reduced the component-loading step from about 240 ms to 18 ms.

comments.author: Kare0638

Hi @ProExpertProg,

  I’m working on FlashAttnMLA. Since all MLA backends share MLACommonImpl.forward(), removing the KV-cache update there now would break other MLA backends that haven’t
  migrated yet.

  Would you prefer one of these concrete options?

  Option 1 (two-phase, safest now):

  - In MLACommonImpl: add do_kv_cache_update() (using concat_and_cache_mla)
  - Keep the existing KV update inside MLACommonImpl.forward() for now
  - Do not flip behavior until MLA caller-side changes land
  - Later: add caller-side update, remove in-forward update, set forward_includes_kv_cache_update=False

  Option 2 (gate inside forward):

  - Add a conditional gate in MLACommonImpl.forward():
      - If forward_includes_kv_cache_update=True → keep current in-forward update
      - If False → skip in-forward update
  - Then FlashAttnMLA can set forward_includes_kv_cache_update=False once the MLA caller is updated to call do_kv_cache_update().

  Also, if MLA caller-side changes are needed (e.g., MLAAttention.forward / unified_mla_attention), who will handle those?

items.title: [Bug][Responses API] Zero-delta streaming items skip added/in_progress lifecycle events
items.author: mimran-khan
items.body_excerpt:
### Your current environment

Testing against `main`, CPU-only.

### Describe the bug

There's a known bug in `streaming_events.py` where items that complete with zero deltas never get their `response.output_item.added` or `response.output_item.done` events emitted. The code at line 614 already calls it out as a bug:

```python
if not state.sent_output_item_added and not state.is_first_function_call_delta:
    # Suppress done events for items had no delta and thus had no
    # added/in-progress lifecycle events. This is a bug.
    # TODO: Ensure added/in-progress events are emitted for zero-delta items.
    return []
```

There's also an xfail test for it at `test_serving_responses.py:644` that defines what the correct behavior should look like.

This comes up when a Harmony item resolves in the engine before any delta gets sent to the client. The item just vanishes from the SSE stream, which messes up any client tracking output items by lifecycle events.

### Expected behavior

Zero-delta items should still go through the full lifecycle: `added` then `done`. The xfail test covers text, function calls, code interpreter, and MCP tool item types.

Happy to take this on.

items.title: [Bug]: echo=true kills the stream with a ValidationError when the last message content is a list (multimodal content format) — non-streaming succeeds
items.author: abhay-codes07
items.body_excerpt:
### Your current environment

<details>
<summary>Environment</summary>

Pure-Python logic bug in the chat completions serving layer, reproducible on current `main` with a unit-level snippet — no GPU needed.

</details>

### 🐛 Describe the bug

With `"echo": true`, the streaming and non-streaming chat completion paths diverge when the last conversation message's `content` is a **list of text parts** — which is exactly what the chat template content format `"openai"` (used for multimodal models) produces.

The non-streaming generator flattens the list before echoing:

```python
if isinstance(last_msg_content, list):
    last_msg_content = "\n".join(msg["text"] for msg in last_msg_content)
```

The streaming generator has no such handling and passes the list straight into `DeltaMessage(content=last_msg_content)` — but `DeltaMessage.content` is `str | None`, so pydantic raises a `ValidationError`. The exception is swallowed by the stream's generic `except Exception` handler, so the client receives an **in-stream error chunk and a dead stream**, while the identical request with `"stream": false` succeeds and echoes the flattened text.

The streaming code even annotates the variable as `last_msg_content: str | list[dict[str, str]]`, documenting that the list case can occur, and then feeds it into the str-only field.

Reproducible by driving `chat_completion_stream_generator` directly (the pattern used in `tests/entrypoints/openai/chat_completion/test_serving_chat.py`) with `echo=true`, `add_generation_prompt=false`, and a conversation whose last message content is `[{"type": "text", "text": "..."}, ...]`: the stream yields `{"error": {...ValidationError...}}` instead of the echoed content.

Fix (PR incoming): apply the same list flattening in the streaming echo path so both paths behave identically.

items.title: [Bug]: Transcription streaming uses Chat Completions SSE format instead of OpenAI transcript events
items.author: wskr00
items.body_excerpt:
### Your current environment

//


### 🐛 Describe the bug

`POST /v1/audio/transcriptions` with `stream=true` returns Server-Sent Events in a Chat Completions-like format:

```text
data: {"id":"transcribe-...","object":"transcription.chunk","created":...,"model":"openai/whisper-large-v3-turbo","choices":[{"delta":{"content":" My"}}]}
```

This is not compatible with OpenAI's Transcriptions API streaming contract. OpenAI emits transcript events such as:

```text
data: {"type":"transcript.text.delta","delta":"My"}

data: {"type":"transcript.text.done","text":"My gosh, ...","usage":{...}}

data: [DONE]
```

Because of the incompatible event shape, OpenAI SDK clients cannot deserialize vLLM transcription streams as transcription events. For example, the OpenAI Java SDK treats each `transcription.chunk` event as an unknown `TranscriptionStreamEvent` variant.

The current implementation also emits a `finish_reason` chunk for every internally split audio chunk. A compatible implementation should emit text deltas while processing and exactly one `transcript.text.done` event after the complete transcription is assembled.

OpenAI references:

- [Transcription API reference](https://developers.openai.com/api/reference/python/resources/audio/subresources/transcriptions/methods/create#(resource)%20audio.transcriptions%20%3E%20(model)%20transcription_text_delta_event%20%3E%20(schema))
- [Translations API reference](https://developers.openai.com/api/reference/python/resources/audio/subresources/translations/methods/create)

## Minimal reproduction

Start vLLM with a transcription-capable model, then run:

```bash
curl -N http://localhost:8000/v1/audio/transcriptions \
  -F "file=@audio.wav" \
  -F "stream=true"
```

## Actual result

```text
data: {"id":"transcribe-...","object":"transcription.chunk","created":...,"model":"openai/whisper-large-v3-turbo","choices":[{"delta":{"content":" My"}}]}

data: {"id":"transcribe-...","object":"transcription.chunk","created":...,"model":"openai/whisper-large-v3-turbo","choices":[{"delta":{"content":""},"finish_reason":"stop","stop_reason":null}]}

data: [DONE]
```

## Expected result

```text
data: {"type":"transcript.text.delta","delta":" My"}

data: {"type":"transcript.text.delta","delta":" gosh"}

data: {"type":"transcript.text.done","text":" My gosh, ...","usage":{"type":"tokens","input_tokens":50,"output_tokens":50,"total_tokens":100}}

data: [DONE]
```

## Scope

This issue concerns `/v1/audio/transcriptions` only.

`/v1/audio/translations` should not be changed as part of this fix: OpenAI does not document streaming support for that endpoint, while the Transcriptions endpoint has a defined SSE event contract.

### Before submitting a new issue...

- [x] Make sure you already searched for relevant issues, and asked the chatbot living at the bottom right corner of the [documentation page](https://docs.vllm.ai/en/latest/), which can answer lots of frequently asked questions.

items.title: [Bug]: Responses API streaming aborts mid-stream (nameless ResponseFunctionToolCallItem) with Qwen3.8 + qwen3_coder + DFlash speculative decoding
items.author: ruiwarn
items.body_excerpt:
### Current environment

- vLLM `0.26.1rc1.dev1104` (main branch, 2026-08-22 dev build). Also verified that no released version up to and including v0.28.0 (2026-08-26) contains a fix for this bug.
- Model: Qwen3.8-27B (FP8)
- Speculative decoding: DFlash drafter enabled
- `--tool-call-parser qwen3_coder`
- `--reasoning-parser qwen3`
- Client: `/v1/responses` with `stream: true` (via LiteLLM)

### 🐞 Describe the bug

In agentic (tool-heavy) workloads, the Responses API SSE stream aborts mid-stream with no terminal `response.*` event, leaving the client with an unclassifiable truncated stream. The failure is intermittent but recurrent.

### Error message

```
pydantic_core._pydantic_core.ValidationError: 1 validation error for ResponseFunctionToolCallItem
name
  Input should be a valid string [type=string_type, input_value=None, input_type=NoneType]
...
RuntimeError: Caught handled exception, but response already started.
```

### Root cause analysis

The crash occurs when a single engine step spans the end of a tool call and the start of the following reasoning/content segment — speculative decoding makes such multi-boundary steps common.

`split_delta()` decomposes a compound `DeltaMessage` in the fixed order reasoning → content → tool_calls. When the tool-call part of the compound delta is the *argument tail* of an already-open tool call (its first `DeltaToolCall` carries no function name — e.g. the flush emitted by the parser engine at `</tool_call>`), replaying it *after* reasoning/content means the state machine has already transitioned away and closed the call. The tail then forces `SimpleStreamingEventProcessor.open()` to construct `ResponseFunctionToolCallItem(name=None)`, which fails pydantic validation. Because the SSE response has already started, the exception aborts the stream without any terminal event.

### Reproducing the problem

Serve the model with the configuration above, then send an agentic, tool-heavy prompt to `/v1/responses` with `stream: true`. The crash is intermittent (depends on where step boundaries fall relative to tool-call boundaries) but recurs reliably in tool-heavy workloads with speculative decoding enabled.

### Impact and workaround

We cannot use the `/v1/responses` streaming path for this deployment. As a workaround we set `use_chat_completions: true` in LiteLLM to route traffic through `/v1/chat/completions`, which loses the Responses API path for this deployment. There is no release containing a fix, so we are stuck on a dev build with no supported upgrade path.

items.title: [Bug] pause_generation(mode="keep", clear_cache=True) raises when a streaming-input session is parked between turns
items.author: shivasathishs-rp
items.body_excerpt:
## What breaks

`pause_generation(mode="keep", clear_cache=True)` raises `RuntimeError` and leaves the engine in `PauseState.PAUSED_ALL` whenever a resumable streaming-input session is parked between turns.

That call is verbatim the recipe in `docs/training/async_rl.md:18`:

```python
await engine.pause_generation(mode="keep", clear_cache=True)
```

It is also the only one of the four mode/clear_cache combinations that is both cache-sound and trajectory-preserving, and it is the only one that fails.

| mode | clear_cache | result |
|---|---|---|
| keep | True | **RuntimeError** |
| keep | False | ok, KV computed under the old weights survives the update |
| abort | True | ok, trajectory destroyed |
| abort | False | ok, trajectory destroyed |

Over HTTP this is `POST /pause?mode=keep`, where `clear_cache` defaults to `True`. The exception is caught by the generic handler at `vllm/entrypoints/rl/online/api_router.py:70` and returned as HTTP 500 at `api_router.py:74`.

## Reproducer

Pure CPU. No GPU, no weights, no model. Drop next to `tests/v1/core/test_scheduler.py::test_scheduler_reset_prefix_cache`.

The parking helper is lifted from the suite's existing `test_pause_new_ignores_streaming_session_waiting_for_input` (`tests/v1/core/test_scheduler.py:2710`), so this is the suite's own notion of a parked session rather than a hand-built state.

```python
def _park_streaming_session(scheduler):
    """Stop a resumable streaming request so it parks between turns."""
    stop_token = 7
    (session,) = create_requests(
        num_requests=1, num_tokens=4, stop_token_ids=[stop_token], req_ids=["s"]
    )
    session.resumable = True
    scheduler.add_request(session)
    output = scheduler.schedule()
    scheduler.update_from_output(
        output,
        ModelRunnerOutput(
            req_ids=["s"], req_id_to_index={"s": 0}, sampled_token_ids=[[stop_token]]
        ),
    )
    return session


def test_reset_prefix_cache_with_parked_streaming_session():
    scheduler = create_scheduler(enable_prefix_caching=True)
    session = _park_streaming_session(scheduler)

    assert session.status == RequestStatus.WAITING_FOR_STREAMING_REQ
    assert session in scheduler.kv_holding_waiting
    assert not scheduler.running
    # The parked session still holds its KV blocks.
    assert scheduler.kv_cache_manager.get_block_ids("s")[0]

    with pytest.raises(RuntimeError, match="Failed to reset KV cache"):
        scheduler.reset_prefix_cache(reset_running_requests=True)
```

That is the smallest failing call. One parked session is enough; one block held is enough.

Going through `EngineCore` reproduces the documented call and shows the second half of the problem, which is the state the engine is left in:

```python
def test_keep_pause_clear_cache_with_parked_streaming_session():
    scheduler = create_scheduler(enable_prefix_caching=True)
    _park_streaming_session(scheduler)

    core = object.__new__(EngineCore)
    core.scheduler = scheduler
    core.model_executor = Mock(is_sleeping=False)
    core.mm_receiver_cache = None
    core.batch_queue = None

    with pytest.raises(RuntimeError, match="Failed to reset KV cache"):
        core.pause_scheduler(mode="keep", clear_cache=True)

    # The engine is left paused: the pause state is set before the cache reset.
    assert core.is_scheduler_paused()
    assert scheduler.pause_state == PauseState.PAUSED_ALL
```

### Traceback

Captured before the `pytest.raises` wrapper was added.

```
tests/v1/core/test_scheduler.py: in test_keep_pause_clear_cache_with_parked_streaming_session
    core.pause_scheduler(mode="keep", clear_cache=True)
vllm/v1/engine/core.py:932: in pause_scheduler
    self._finish_pause(clear_cache)
vllm/v1/engine/core.py:904: in _finish_pause
    self._reset_caches()
vllm/v1/engine/core.py:891: in _reset_caches
    if not self.reset_prefix_cache(
vllm/v1/engine/core.py:859: in reset_prefix_cache
    return self.scheduler.reset_prefix_cache(
vllm/v1/core/sched/scheduler.py:2869: RuntimeError
E   RuntimeError: Failed to reset KV cache even when all the running requests are
    preempted and moved to the waiting queue. This is likely due to the presence of
    running requests waiting for remote KV transfer, which is not supported yet.

------------------------------ Captured log call -------------------------------
WARNING  vllm.v1.core.block_pool:block_pool.py:839 Failed to reset prefix cache because some blocks (1) are not freed yet
```

## Code path

Six links, each read at the commit below.

**1. A resumable request is not finished, so it is never freed.** `vllm/v1/core/sched/scheduler.py:2464`, `_handle_stopped_request` returns `False` for a resumable request after setting `WAITING_FOR_STREAMING_REQ` and calling `_enqueue_waiting_request`. The caller at `scheduler.py:2227` calls `_free_request` only on `True`.

**2. The request leaves `self.running` and lands in `kv_holding_waiting`.** Removal at `scheduler.py:2294`. `_enqueue_waiting_request` at `scheduler.py:2456` routes to `kv_holding_waiting` when `_holds_kv_blocks(request)` is true.

**3. `_holds_kv_blocks` is true for this request.** `scheduler.py:2444`. A session with trajectory tokens has `num_computed_tokens > 0`. Its own comment names the case: "While always the case when status is `WAITING_FOR_REMOTE_KVS` or `WAITING_FOR_STREAMING_REQ`".

**4. `reset_prefix_cache(reset_running_requests=True)` drains only `self.running`.** `scheduler.py:2839`, drain loop at `scheduler.py:2857-2859`. The string `kv_holding_waiting` does not appear anywhere in that function, so a parked session is never drained and its blocks are never released.

**5. `block_pool.reset_prefix_cache()` returns `False` because a block is still in use.** `vllm/v1/core/block_pool.py:827`, the used-block check at `block_pool.py:838`, the warning at `block_pool.py:839`. The repro log shows `blocks (1) are not freed yet`.

**6. The scheduler raises.** `if` at `scheduler.py:2868`, `raise` at `scheduler.py:2869

items.title: [Bug]: Hybrid GDN models (Qwen3.5) with n-gram speculative decoding: greedy outputs go wrong when drafts are partly accepted; the GDN state misses the last accepted token's update
items.author: DiaaAj
items.body_excerpt:
## Summary
On a Qwen3.5 text model (`Qwen3_5ForCausalLM`: Gated DeltaNet in 3 of every 4 layers), vLLM 0.31.0 with
`speculative_config={"method": "ngram", "num_speculative_tokens": 4, "prompt_lookup_max": 4,
"prompt_lookup_min": 2}` produces wrong greedy (temperature 0) outputs for some requests. Speculative
decoding must not change greedy outputs, and without it the same engine and workload are exact (12 other
configurations: three attention backends, prefix caching on and off, chunked prefill, eager, preemption,
bf16 SSM cache, both decode kernels, FP8 KV). SGLang 0.5.22 with NGRAM is exact on the same probe.

| vLLM 0.31.0, RTX 3090, 192 requests × 256 tokens | wrong requests |
|---|---|
| n-gram, k = 4, prefix caching on (default) | 8 |
| the same, `VLLM_GDN_DECODE_KERNEL=triton` (another 192 prompts) | 12 |
| the same, `enable_prefix_caching=False` (another 192 prompts) | 20 |
| no speculative decoding (12 configurations) | 0 |

It is deterministic (the same 967 wrong tokens in the same 8 requests on two hosts and on a rerun) and does
not depend on batching or scheduling:

| variant (same 192 prompts) | wrong requests |
|---|---|
| default above | 8 |
| `async_scheduling=False` | 8 (identical) |
| `enforce_eager=True` | 8 (identical) |
| `max_num_seqs=1` (one request at a time) | 8 (identical) |
| `num_speculative_tokens` 1 / 2 | 1 / 7 |
| `method="ngram_gpu"` | 5 |
| prompts without decoy fragments: every draft is accepted (32,712 of 32,712 draft tokens) | 0 |

So it needs drafts that are only partly accepted, i.e. a step where the state has to be taken at an
intermediate position.

## What goes wrong
The checkpoint is a probec probe twin: real Qwen3.5-0.8B shapes, synthetic weights whose correct outputs
are known exactly and are insensitive to reduction order, so a deviation is an engine error, not numerics.
Its GDN layers use the recurrent state as a table with one slot per class; every decoded token writes its
class's slot, and later steps read slots. So the output reveals which writes the state contains.

For every failing request, replaying the oracle shows the state was **missing the write of a token that had
been accepted earlier**, most often the token accepted in the step just before the first wrong output (6 of
8 requests); no failure is explained by a rejected draft's write being kept. Several requests are wrong for a
single token and then continue correctly, as a single missing write in the probe produces.

## Related
- #53912: MTP + prefix caching corrupts output on hybrid models; its rate tracks prefix-cache hits. This one
  uses n-gram drafts and also fails with prefix caching off (20 of 192), so it may be a separate path.
- #61738: wide verification (≥ 7 speculative tokens) on hybrid GDN models; here k = 1 already fails.

## Repro
```
git clone https://github.com/DiaaAj/probec && cd probec
pip install -e .            # into an environment with vllm 0.31.0
probec compile --like Qwen/Qwen3.5-0.8B -o h08
probec run h08 --engine vllm --matrix hybrid --only FLASH_ATTN/ngram_spec_decoys --out results.jsonl
probec report results.jsonl
```
The same failure one request at a time: `--matrix hybridspec --only FLASH_ATTN/ngram_spec_decoys_seqs1`. The
report lists each failing request with its first wrong step; the prompts are deterministic (seed 12).

## Environment
vLLM 0.31.0 (`vastai/vllm:v0.31.0-cuda-13.0` image: torch 2.13.0+cu130, transformers 5.17.0), RTX 3090 (SM86),
driver 595.91; two hosts.

items.title: [Bug]: HF3FSKVConnector ignores hf3fs_metadata_server_url (both metadata clients use localhost:18000)
items.author: sivabreddy
items.body_excerpt:
`HF3FSKVConnector` reads `hf3fs_metadata_server_url` from `kv_connector_extra_config` into `self._metadata_server_url`, but creates both metadata clients with `Hf3fsMetadataClient()` (no argument):

- `vllm/distributed/kv_transfer/kv_connector/v1/hf3fs/hf3fs_connector.py` line 511 (scheduler side) and line 598 (worker side) on `main` (`38127f62`); the same in v0.31.0 and v0.32.0.
- The client default is `http://localhost:18000` (`hf3fs_metadata_server.py`, `Hf3fsGlobalMetadataClient.__init__`).

So the configured URL is never used. With the metadata server in its own pod/service (shared by several vLLM instances), each TP worker fails at start-up in `initialize` with `[Errno 111] Connection refused` to `localhost:18000`, then `RuntimeError: Failed to connect to metadata server`, and the engine does not start.

**Environment:** vLLM 0.31.0 (`vllm/vllm-openai:v0.31.0`), Llama-3.1-70B-Instruct, TP4, two instances on two hosts, shared 3FS mount, `hf3fs_metadata_server.py` as a separate service.

**Fix** (2 lines):

```diff
-            self._metadata_client = Hf3fsMetadataClient()
+            self._metadata_client = Hf3fsMetadataClient(self._metadata_server_url)
```

in both places. With this change, all 4 ranks of both instances registered on the shared server, and instance B's first request for a prompt that instance A had computed (28,105 tokens) took 1.07–1.11 s (3 trials) against 2.37–2.39 s to compute it; 28,096 tokens came from the connector; the output was the same as on A.

I can open a PR with this change and a unit test (`Hf3fsMetadataClient` mocked, assert it is called with the configured URL).

items.title: [RFC] Evaluating io_uring DMA-BUF support for NVMe in LMCache
items.author: mcgrof
items.body_excerpt:
# RFC: evaluating io_uring DMA-BUF support for NVMe in LMCache

Linux DMA-BUF support for NVMe I/O through io_uring has been under public
review since at least [Pavel Begunkov's June 27, 2025 RFC](https://lists.infradead.org/pipermail/linux-nvme/2025-June/057145.html)
— roughly 16 months as of October 2026. A later
[upstream revision, posted September 28, 2026](https://lists.openwall.net/linux-kernel/2026/09/28/1685),
provides DMA-BUF-backed registered reads and writes for raw NVMe block
devices.

We extend that upstream effort in the experimental
[dmabuf-size-ceiling-v7.3-rc3 kernel branch](https://git.kernel.org/pub/scm/linux/kernel/git/mcgrof/linux.git/log/?h=dmabuf-size-ceiling-v7.3-rc3),
pinned at `856b6583ab2f4581e81670845eadb69de7a68b30`. The branch adds iomap,
ext4 and XFS direct-I/O enablement, larger-request handling, and selftests
and diagnostics for qualifying exporters and GPU/NVMe paths. Our testing
also evaluates larger I/O against controller Maximum Data Transfer Size
(MDTS), mapping-segment and queue limits; a large io_uring request does
not imply a single NVMe command.

The larger-I/O work is motivated by KV-cache geometry. Even one token can
carry substantial key and value state across the model's layers and KV
heads; offloading multi-token chunks produces correspondingly large
reads and writes. The [KV-cache I/O projections](https://kvcache.io/io-projections.html)
show how model layout and chunk size determine these transfer sizes.
The same motivation applies to [hybrids with linear attention](https://kvcache.io/hybrid-checkpoints.html):
offload needs attention KV and complete recurrent-state checkpoints,
including convolution history where present, at matching boundaries.
These checkpoints add large storage objects; this RFC's measured P/D
profile remains full attention.

This RFC evaluates that developing Linux interface for LMCache KV offload
and restore, including multiprocess (MP) mode. The main application work
is io_uring DMA-BUF support in LMCache, using raw-block and filesystem
storage paths. This is early ecosystem testing, not general hardware or
production qualification.

Storage-mediated prefill/decode (P/D) disaggregation is a natural
continuation of that storage support. NIXL already supports disaggregation,
so we first extend it with an io_uring DMA-BUF storage backend and evaluate
that path through a separate vLLM connector. We then ask whether LMCache
can support the storage-mediated handoff directly. The LMCache proof of
concept uses the same Linux I/O interface and makes NIXL optional.

The [Linux interface, platform constraints and reproduction guide](https://knlp.io/io-uring-dmabuf.html)
covers current vendor implementations, filesystem and larger-I/O
extensions, GPU/NVMe qualification, exporter workarounds and the pinned
knlp defconfig.

## Source and proposed review order

[Full 50-commit LMCache stack](https://github.com/mcgrof/LMCache/tree/2026-10-15-io-uring-dmabuf-full)
on upstream dev `e64b43ef9621bc1557e67bcbfc359a25fbb740b5`.
The branches are cumulative; compare each part with the preceding part:

| Part | New commits | Responsibility |
| --- | ---: | --- |
| [pr0](https://github.com/mcgrof/LMCache/compare/e64b43ef9621bc1557e67bcbfc359a25fbb740b5...aba876c5198470b7f624022b138b73c4e08bd2f9) | 15 | Transfer, ownership, recovery and admission prerequisites |
| [pr1](https://github.com/mcgrof/LMCache/compare/aba876c5198470b7f624022b138b73c4e08bd2f9...847c01e8b9b523c58077795e8d192a8d3695262f) | 3 | DMA-BUF registration and host/GPU staging |
| [pr2](https://github.com/mcgrof/LMCache/compare/847c01e8b9b523c58077795e8d192a8d3695262f...687f4360b82b7d597c3b7543b759886708afb7fb) | 6 | In-process storage publication, claim/ACK, connector and example |
| [pr3](https://github.com/mcgrof/LMCache/compare/687f4360b82b7d597c3b7543b759886708afb7fb...9a89c42019d430fae5ac7406ef681439e1cfabd6) | 1 | Optional experimental Vulkan/RM exporter |
| [pr4](https://github.com/mcgrof/LMCache/compare/9a89c42019d430fae5ac7406ef681439e1cfabd6...7a89acc7093221d1e009b2ff470d50533cbc82ea) | 1 | Initialized filesystem-target admission |

items.title: [Feature] Parallelize module loading to speed up server launch and refit for Diffusion models
items.author: zhaochenyang20
items.body_excerpt:
### Checklist

- [x] If this is not a feature request but a general question, please start a discussion at https://github.com/sgl-project/sglang/discussions. Otherwise, it will be closed.
- [x] Please use English. Otherwise, it will be closed.

### Motivation

Based on the detailed breakdown in issue #19087, the current launch process for SGLang Diffusion (using Qwen-Image as an example) is heavily bottlenecked by module loading, which currently happens sequentially.

As shown in the profiling results, `load_modules` takes approximately 63.20s out of the total 77.09s launch time (~82%).

- `text_encoder`: 32.96s (52% of loading time)
- `transformer`: 29.76s (47% of loading time)
- `vae/tokenizer/scheduler`: < 1s combined.

Since these modules (Text Encoder, Transformer, VAE) are independent during the instantiation and weight-loading phase, the current sequential execution is suboptimal. We should implement a parallel loading strategy for `load_modules`. By using multi-threading (e.g., `concurrent.futures.ThreadPoolExecutor` or other parallel weights load strategies in SGLang LLM already) to trigger the initialization and weight transfer of the text encoder and transformer simultaneously, we may theoretically reduce the module loading time from ~63s to ~33s (the max of the two major components).

Benefits:

1. Faster Cold Start: Significantly reduces the time for `launch_server`.
2. Optimized Refit/Wake-up: As discussed in #19090, if we support offloading and waking up, parallelizing the weight reload from CPU/Disk to GPU will make the "wake-up" latency much lower.

Implementation Consideration:

1. Ensure thread safety for CUDA context operations during `model.to(device)`.
2. Monitor Peak CPU memory usage when loading multiple state dicts into RAM simultaneously before moving them to GPU.


---------


Apart from this, it should also be helpful to validate whether we are loading the weights with Pageable memory.


https://github.com/sgl-project/sglang/issues/19087#issuecomment-3937649804

Spend 32s in loading `text_encoder` looks strange, since if we are using Pinned memory, the load speed could be much higher.

items.title: [Bug] [diffusion] OpenAI API hardening and runtime utils/pipeline bugs
items.author: OnePunchMonk
items.body_excerpt:
### Checklist

- [x] I searched related issues but found no solution.
- [x] The bug persists in the latest version.
- [x] Issues without environment info and a minimal reproducible demo are hard to resolve and may receive no feedback.
- [x] Please use English. Otherwise, it will be closed.

### Describe the bug

Bugs in the diffusion HTTP API (1-7) and in `multimodal_gen/runtime/utils` and `runtime/pipelines` (8-33). Findings that were checked but not fixed are tracked in OnePunchMonk/sglang#6.

### Fix plan (3 parts)

The fixes are split into three PRs that touch disjoint files and can merge in any order. None of them closes this issue on its own; it stays open until all three are merged.

- [ ] Part 1, HTTP API (items 1-7): #43585
- [ ] Part 2, runtime utils (items 8-24): #44887
- [ ] Part 3, pipelines and model helpers (items 25-33): #44888

**Part 1: HTTP API (#43585)**
1. An invalid `output_quality` returns 500 instead of 400.
2. `response_format="url"` without cloud storage or `output_path` runs the whole generation before returning 400; unsupported `response_format` values are not rejected up front.
3. A failed cloud upload returns a misleading 400 "requires cloud storage" and the generated file is lost.
4. URL image inputs are read fully into memory with no size cap.
5. `upscaling_model_path` / `frame_interpolation_model_path` accept any URL from a network client and the server fetches it.
6. The upscaler, RIFE and resolved-path caches grow without bound with client-chosen paths.
7. `frame_interpolation_scale` and `upscaling_scale` are not range-checked.

**Part 2: runtime utils (#44887)**
8. `load_video` never deletes the video it downloaded, so `/tmp` fills up, and the download has no timeout.
9. Line-wrapped base64 images are cut at the first line.
10. An unreachable Hub is treated as "repo has no model_index.json", so the cache fallback never runs.
11. The same condition sends `maybe_download_model_index` down the single-model path with a misleading "-Diffusers" error.
12. A local cache dir of `ltx-2.3-distilled` matches the `ltx-2.3` overlay by substring.
13. An overlay repo resolved by Hub id downloads only its manifest, so `model_index.json` is missing on a fresh cache.
14. `scheduler` anywhere in a component's path makes every component read `scheduler_config.json`.
15. Normalizing a ModelOpt `config.json` writes through the HF cache symlink and changes the shared blob.
16. The ModelScope LoRA path raises a `TypeError` when no weights are found.
17. A comment claims CI validation failures after download are retried; they are not.
18. `temporary_module_dtype` restores the whole module to the first parameter's dtype, undoing mixed precision.
19. All `RequestMetrics` instances compare equal.
20. `log_request_summary` ignores its `tag` argument.
21. `get_git_commit_hash` runs `git rev-parse` in the current directory instead of the sglang install dir.
22. The "log on every rank at DEBUG" rule reads the log level before `configure_logger` runs.
23. Enabling the NVTX hooks between a module's pre- and post-hook pops a range that was never pushed.
24. `get_bool_env_var` warns once per bad value instead of once per variable.

**Part 3: pipelines and model helpers (#44888)**
25. Plucker rays are built in bf16 when poses are bf16, so pixel columns above 256 share a ray (LingBot-World too).
26. The default texture and bake buffers use `(width, height)` where `(height, width)` is needed, breaking non-square textures.
27. `ImageProcessorV2.load_image` raises `UnboundLocalError` for an ndarray or tensor.
28. `DiffusersPipeline` output layout: NumPy videos are permuted twice, PIL lists are read as a batch, and several images are stacked as video frames.
29. `DiffusersPipeline.add_stage` takes its arguments in the reverse order of the base class.
30. SANA-Video always encodes the negative prompt at 300 tokens instead of `max_sequence_length`.
31. ErnieImage treats a `[null, null]` `pe` entry as a real prompt-enhancement model.
32. HunyuanImage3 ignores `--revision` when downloading weights.
33. Hunyuan3D picks an arbitrary checkpoint when several match the fallback glob.

### Reproduction

Most items have a unit test that fails on the unpatched code; each PR lists the few that do not. Tests and fixes: #43585, #44887, #44888

### Environment

sglang main with the diffusion extras, CPU-only Linux.

items.title: [Bug] Unauthenticated Mooncake Decode registrations can exhaust Prefill memory and cause inference denial of service
items.author: yyymk
items.body_excerpt:
### Checklist

- [x] I searched related issues but found no solution.
- [x] The bug persists in the latest version.
- [x] Issues without environment info and a minimal reproducible demo are hard to resolve and may receive no feedback.
- [x] If this is not a bug report but a general question, please start a discussion at https://github.com/sgl-project/sglang/discussions. Otherwise, it will be closed.
- [x] Please use English. Otherwise, it will be closed.

### Describe the bug

### Summary

SGLang 0.5.15.post1 accepts registration-shaped ZMQ messages from any peer that can reach a Prefill rank socket when the Mooncake PD backend is enabled. The sender is not authenticated or matched to a configured Decode worker. The receive path also has no per-message or table-wide resource limit. In a two-host test, an adjacent host queried the unauthenticated bootstrap route, sent unique fake sessions, exhausted a 16 GiB Prefill-only cgroup, caused the Prefill scheduler to be OOM-killed, and made routed completions unavailable until restart. The tested cross-host setup explicitly bound Prefill to `0.0.0.0`. We suggest Moderate severity with CVSS v3.1 `6.5 (AV:A/AC:L/PR:N/UI:N/S:U/C:N/I:N/A:H)`.

### Details

`CommonKVManager.__init__()` creates a ZMQ `PULL` socket and stores its dynamic rank port. The Prefill bootstrap HTTP `/route` endpoint returns the rank IP and port. Neither step requires a protocol credential.

In `MooncakeKVManager.start_prefill_thread()`, the inner `bootstrap_thread()` receives each multipart message. A message with `room == "None"` is parsed as a Decode registration and stored under the sender-provided session ID:

```
waiting_req_bytes = self.server_socket.recv_multipart()
room = waiting_req_bytes[0].decode("ascii")
mooncake_session_id = waiting_req_bytes[3].decode("ascii")
if room == "None":
    self.decode_kv_args_table[mooncake_session_id] = (
        KVArgsRegisterInfo.from_zmq(waiting_req_bytes)
    )
    continue
```



`KVArgsRegisterInfo.from_zmq()` passes frame 6 to `unpack_int_lists()`. The first integer in that frame controls the number of nested buffers. A 400,004-byte nested-buffer frame can declare 100,000 empty child buffers. The parser materializes 100,000 Python lists before any peer check or size check. A unique session ID keeps each parsed object in `decode_kv_args_table`. This path has no sender authentication, Decode identity binding, nested-buffer limit, table size limit, or expiry for a fake registration.

The retention behavior was checked with a diagnostic observer only. Fifty messages contained 20,003,050 bytes of application-frame data. Prefill PSS increased by about 365 MB. All 50 entries and sampled 100,000-list objects remained present for about 600 seconds and after `gc.collect()`. Restarting Prefill cleared the state.

The request effect was first checked on five fresh stock 1P1D stacks with no diagnostic hook. A 30-request baseline had a 0.7711-second median. Each attack run sent 20 unique 100,000-buffer registrations. Every run had one real completion take 3.2168 to 3.9460 seconds, or 4.17 to 5.12 times the baseline median. Three no-attack controls and three 1,024-buffer controls had per-run maxima below 0.820 seconds.

The final availability test used victim `192.168.55.134` and adjacent host `192.168.55.88`. Prefill was the only component placed in a cgroup with `memory.max=17179869184` and `memory.swap.max=0`. Five requests immediately before the attack returned HTTP 200 with a 0.2334-second median. The adjacent host received HTTP 200 from the bootstrap `/route` endpoint without credentials and connected directly to the returned ZMQ rank port. Victim-side socket records showed the ZMQ peer as `192.168.55.88:58898 -> 192.168.55.134:44437`.

The client submitted 12,620 unique registrations containing 5,048,782,440 bytes of application-frame payload before the receiver failed and the client reached its send timeout. Prefill cgroup usage rose from about 3.72 GB to 16.69 GB in the last sample before the kill. All 12 post-attack memory samples were non-decreasing. The final cgroup snapshot recorded `memory.peak=17180061696`, `max=42`, `oom=1`, and `oom_kill=1`. The Prefill scheduler was absent after the kill while the launcher and detokenizer remained. Prefill `/health` timed out. Eleven monitored routed completions during the attack timed out, and five additional routed completions after the OOM and before restart also timed out. Router `/health` still returned HTTP 200, and the Router and Decode processes remained alive. After a clean stack restart, 5/5 completions succeeded.


### Reproduction

This was tested on Linux with SGLang 0.5.15.post1, sglang-router 0.3.2, mooncake-transfer-engine 0.3.11.post1, Python 3.12.13, pyzmq 27.1.0, PyTorch 2.11.0+cu130, Qwen3-8B, and two NVIDIA A100 80 GB GPUs. Use an isolated test network. Keep Prefill inside a memory-limited cgroup. The commands below use the ports from the two-host test.

On the victim, start Prefill in a separate terminal. Set `MODEL` to the local model path if needed:

```
MODEL=Qwen/Qwen3-8B
systemd-run --user --scope \
  --unit=sglang-c4-prefill \
  -p MemoryMax=16G \
  -p MemorySwapMax=0 \
  --setenv=CUDA_VISIBLE_DEVICES=0 \
  --setenv=SGLANG_DISAGG_STAGING_BUFFER=0 \
  python -m sglang.launch_server \
    --model-path "$MODEL" \
    --host 0.0.0.0 \
    --port 32400 \
    --tp-size 1 \
    --mem-fraction-static 0.50 \
    --disaggregation-mode prefill \
    --disaggregation-transfer-backend mooncake \
    --disaggregation-bootstrap-port 32498 \
    --engine-info-bootstrap-port 32489 \
    --served-model-name Qwen3-8B \
    --disable-cuda-graph
```



Start Decode and the PD router in two more victim terminals:

```
MODEL=Qwen/Qwen3-8B
CUDA_VISIBLE_DEVICES=1 python -m sglang.launch_server \
  --model-path "$MODEL" \
  --host 127.0.0.1 \
  --port 32401 \
  --tp-size 1 \
  --mem-fraction-static 0.50 \
