### Changes proposed # [RFC]: [Store] Add object storage as a first-class replica tier This proposal introduces object storage as a first-class replica tier, reusing the [existing OSS adapter](https://kvcache-ai.github.io/Mooncake/design/store/oss-backend.html). The new types, configuration options, and protocol extensions below are proposed changes. ## 1. Goals and scope The current object storage integration follows the FileStorage / LOCAL_DISK path: the MEMORY owner performs uploads, and reads also depend on that owner. This proposal introduces an `OBJECT_STORAGE` replica alongside MEMORY, LOCAL_DISK, DFS, and NOF_SSD: - The Master manages object locations, replica states, and lifecycle; Clients access shared object storage directly using descriptors. - The Master configures one of three write modes: synchronous writes, asynchronous replication after a memory write, or direct offload on memory eviction. - Object replicas support deletion and background reclamation. - Once an object replica is committed, other Clients can read it even after the original writer/owner goes offline. The initial implementation reuses the OSS adapter while keeping the interface provider-neutral. Each Mooncake object maps to one backend object. Object aggregation, cascading MEMORY → SSD → object storage, a unified redesign of all external storage tiers, and general idempotency enhancements to the shared Start/End/Revoke protocol are out of scope. ## 2. Architecture ```mermaid flowchart TB subgraph MP["Master process"] M["Object directory, write mode, lease / pin"] M --> D["Existing MEMORY / LOCAL_DISK / DFS / NOF_SSD"] M --> O["New OBJECT_STORAGE
object_key + object_size"] M --> G["Pending deletions / retries
Existing background maintenance"] G -->|"DELETE after protection ends"| GA["ObjectStorageAdapter
Master-side instance"] end C["Requesting Client / SDK"] <-->|"PutStart / PutEnd / Query"| M C -->|"Synchronous writes / direct reads"| B["ObjectStorageBackend"] W["MEMORY owner
Offload executor"] -. "Fetch tasks / report completion" .-> M W -->|"Background upload from MEMORY"| B B --> A["ObjectStorageAdapter
Client-side GetBatch / PutBatch"] A --> S["Shared object storage"] GA --> S classDef added fill:#fff0d6,stroke:#d97706,stroke-width:2px; class O,B,G added; ``` - Backends and adapters are in-process modules, with separate instances in each participating process. The Master does not carry object GET/PUT data traffic, but uses its own adapter for background DELETE operations. - Deletion and retries reuse the Master's existing background maintenance mechanism, without requiring a dedicated GC thread or service. Only known pending deletions are processed; the entire bucket is not scanned. - Both background modes reuse the owner's offload queue, heartbeat, and source-replica protection, extending them with an object-storage target and completion reporting. Reads no longer depend on the owner after the object replica is committed. - As with DFS, the Master manages replicas while Clients access shared storage directly. Objects are addressed by key, without file-offset allocation or inheritance from the DFS allocator interface. ## 3. Metadata and configuration ### 3.1 Replica descriptor ```cpp struct ObjectStorageDescriptor { std::string object_key; uint64_t object_size; }; // Added to ReplicateConfig size_t os_replica_num{0}; ``` `ObjectStorageDescriptor` is added to the existing `Replica::Descriptor::descriptor_variant`. Replica `id` and `status` remain in the shared outer descriptor rather than being duplicated in the object descriptor. Enabling object replicas requires support in the Master and all participating Clients. The initial implementation does not promise mixed-version operation with older releases. - `os_replica_num` initially supports 0 or 1, defaulting to 0. A value of 1 requests one object replica according to the Master's policy. It is neither the object service's internal replication factor nor an indication that the replica is already complete. - The initial write requires at least one MEMORY replica. After the object replica is committed, MEMORY replicas may be evicted under the normal protection rules. - `object_key` is a backend object name allocated by the Master, separate from the application's key. The adapter handles prefixes and encoding. - Upsert, Put after Remove, and reallocation after abandoning an old task use new object names, so late uploads or old deletion tasks cannot affect new data. Ordinary retries of the same task reuse its `object_key`. This does not introduce a user-facing multi-version KV API. - Existing shared object-checksum metadata is reused; provider ETags are not treated as a generic content checksum. Using a separate object name isolates successive values of the same application key. For example, if `Put(K)` follows `Remove(K)` before the old background DELETE finishes, using K for both backend objects would let the delayed DELETE remove the new data. The Master maps the application key to an `object_key`, so old tasks operate only on the old object. The same isolation applies to Upsert and late uploads. ### 3.2 Cluster-wide backend configuration Initially, each cluster uses a single object storage backend. The Master publishes non-secret configuration to Clients: provider, endpoint, bucket/namespace, and prefix. Clients fetch and cache it during initialization. The Master uses the same storage target for reclamation; descriptors do not duplicate this configuration. An object's full location is **the cluster-wide endpoint / bucket / prefix plus `object_key`**. Client-side and Master-side adapters use credentials configured in their respective processes, reusing the existing OSS environment variables without introducing a credential service: ```text MOONCAKE_OSS_ACCESS_KEY_ID MOONCAKE_OSS_ACCESS_KEY_SECRET MOONCAKE_OSS_SECURITY_TOK

items.title: [RFC]: Restore reliable nightly CI and TestPyPI publishing
items.author: stmatengss
items.body_excerpt:
### Changes proposed

## Motivation and scope

Nightly should provide a timely, interpretable health signal for `main`, and validated nightly wheels should be publishable without repeatedly exhausting TestPyPI storage. Recent runs have instead mixed source regressions, unavailable hardware, hosted-runner failures, and publishing failures into an incomplete aggregate result.

This RFC proposes a staged recovery of the existing nightly workflow. It is a focused follow-up to the broader build/CI/release roadmap in #3556. The first implementation is #4750; storage administration and longer-term publication policy require separate decisions.

## Problems observed

| Area | Evidence | Conclusion and remaining uncertainty |
| --- | --- | --- |
| ROCm hardware scheduling | Nightly requires a runner with `self-hosted`, `Linux`, `X64`, `amd`, `rocm`, `gfx950`, and `mooncake-pd`. During investigation, the repository runner inventory contained only an ARM64 Ascend runner. The hardware job in [this nightly run](https://github.com/kvcache-ai/Mooncake/actions/runs/39048302137) remained unassigned; the run was later cancelled by a newer request in the `nightly-main` concurrency group. | Unconditional scheduling can prevent nightly from completing when no matching MI350X runner is available. A skipped hardware test must be reported as missing coverage. |
| Native test compilation | `scenario.cpp` still called `BatchProbeKey` with two arguments after the API required a `GrantLeasePolicy` argument. | Already fixed on `main` by #4729. The recovery PR does not duplicate that fix. Subsequent publication skips caused by failed prerequisites are not upload failures. |
| Docker runner loss | Several Docker jobs reported that the hosted runner lost communication with GitHub. Complete logs were unavailable for those failed jobs. | Resource pressure is a plausible cause, but the available evidence does not establish OOM or disk exhaustion. Bound build concurrency and collect diagnostics before attributing the failure. |
| TestPyPI publication | [An upload failed with HTTP 400](https://github.com/kvcache-ai/Mooncake/actions/runs/38596132610/job/116368595261) after transferring the first approximately 95 MB wheel. All 26 files had passed `twine check`. The server response body was absent from the log. | Public storage totals strongly suggest a capacity problem. Some other wheels also exceed the default per-file limit. The actual project limits and the original HTTP 400 reason still require confirmation. |

### TestPyPI storage evidence

Public JSON metadata was inspected during this investigation on October 19, 2026 (Asia/Shanghai). The sums below count the sizes of all listed files; private project settings were not accessible.

| Project | Listed files | Listed file bytes | Approximate size |
| --- | ---: | ---: | ---: |
| [`mooncake-transfer-engine`](https://test.pypi.org/pypi/mooncake-transfer-engine/json) | 131 | 10,667,841,775 | 9.94 GiB |
| [`mooncake-transfer-engine-cuda13`](https://test.pypi.org/pypi/mooncake-transfer-engine-cuda13/json) | 120 | 10,206,105,359 | 9.51 GiB |
| [`mooncake-transfer-engine-non-cuda`](https://test.pypi.org/pypi/mooncake-transfer-engine-non-cuda/json) | — | 4,499,499,434 | 4.19 GiB |

Warehouse defaults are 100 MiB per file and 10 GiB per project; project-specific limits may differ. Under the default project limit, the main package has only about 66 MiB available, less than the approximately 95 MB upload that failed. The collected wheel set also contains files around 119–121 MB, above the default per-file limit. These are two distinct limits and both need checking. See [storage-limit documentation](https://docs.pypi.org/project-management/storage-limits/) and [Warehouse defaults](https://github.com/pypi/warehouse/blob/main/warehouse/constants.py).

The latest visible main-package development release had only three files, so a successful upload of one file is not sufficient evidence that a nightly release is complete.

## Proposed changes

### 1. Restore bounded, explicit nightly behavior

Implemented in #4750:

- Select ROCm hardware coverage once per run. Enable it with the `NIGHTLY_ROCM_INTEGRATION=true` repository variable or the `run_rocm_integration` manual input. Otherwise emit a warning and job summary explaining the missing coverage. ROCm wheel builds and smoke tests remain required.
- Accept only the hardware job's intentional `skipped` result when it was disabled. When enabled, failure, cancellation, or skipping must fail the nightly gate. Preserve strict checks for all other required jobs and the existing explicit `skip_publish` mode.
- Run Docker builds through the configured Buildx builder, limit BuildKit concurrency to one operation, and default `BUILD_JOBS`/`MAX_JOBS` to two. Build the complete Dockerfile with a cache-only output, avoiding a second image-store export. Add memory/disk diagnostics and a 180-minute job timeout.
- Check that TestPyPI credentials are present before attempting uploads. Use noninteractive Twine with verbose responses so future failures include the actionable server error.
- Add regression tests that execute the workflow shell blocks and verify skip decisions, required-job failures, credential handling, and Docker exit-status propagation.

The tradeoff is explicit: a run may complete without MI350X hardware coverage while the runner is unavailable. It must not advertise that coverage as passing. Lower Docker concurrency may increase build time; the timeout and hosted measurements will show whether the default is practical.

### 2. Recover TestPyPI publishing with project-owner actions

1. Sign in to the **TestPyPI** account that owns these projects and open [project management](https://test.pypi.org/manage/projects/). Check each project's storage usage and configured limits.
2. Review old development releases and delete an agreed subset to reclaim space. A proposed starting policy is to retain the latest seven development releases for each p

items.title: [Bug]: [Store] batch_get_into into GPU memory crashes (SIGSEGV) when the local hot cache is enabled
items.author: Jackmeson1
items.body_excerpt:
## Bug Report

On main [`0e626c5`](https://github.com/kvcache-ai/Mooncake/tree/0e626c572ba3ceee30cef4692bb981487bf65913), `batch_get_into` and `batch_get_into_multi_buffers` crash the reading process with SIGSEGV when the destination is CUDA memory and the local hot cache is enabled (`MC_STORE_LOCAL_HOT_CACHE_SIZE`). With the default admission threshold the second read of a key crashes; with `MC_STORE_LOCAL_HOT_ADMISSION_THRESHOLD=1` the first one does. The same reads into pinned host memory, `get_into` into CUDA memory, and the batch read into CUDA memory without the hot cache all succeed.

```
#0 __memcpy_avx512_unaligned
#1 mooncake::LocalHotCacheHandler::SubmitPutTask(std::string const&, mooncake::Slice const&)
#2 mooncake::Client::ProcessSlicesAsync(...)
#3 mooncake::Client::BatchGet(...)
#4 mooncake::RealClient::batch_get_into_internal(...)
#6 mooncake::RealClient::batch_get_into(...)
```

The path, at `0e626c5`:
- `batch_get_into` hands the caller's buffers, device pointers included, to [`Client::BatchGet`](https://github.com/kvcache-ai/Mooncake/blob/0e626c572ba3ceee30cef4692bb981487bf65913/mooncake-store/src/real_client.cpp#L6509); the multi-buffer path does the same ([real_client.cpp:8137](https://github.com/kvcache-ai/Mooncake/blob/0e626c572ba3ceee30cef4692bb981487bf65913/mooncake-store/src/real_client.cpp#L8137-L8139)).
- After the transfer, `BatchGet` calls `ProcessSlicesAsync` on those slices ([client_service.cpp:1899](https://github.com/kvcache-ai/Mooncake/blob/0e626c572ba3ceee30cef4692bb981487bf65913/mooncake-store/src/client_service.cpp#L1899), and [:1646](https://github.com/kvcache-ai/Mooncake/blob/0e626c572ba3ceee30cef4692bb981487bf65913/mooncake-store/src/client_service.cpp#L1646) in `BatchGetWhenPreferSameNode`), which submits every slice of a remote replica to the hot cache ([client_service.cpp:5613-5634](https://github.com/kvcache-ai/Mooncake/blob/0e626c572ba3ceee30cef4692bb981487bf65913/mooncake-store/src/client_service.cpp#L5613-L5634)).
- `SubmitPutTask` copies the slice with [`std::memcpy(block->addr, slice.ptr, slice.size)`](https://github.com/kvcache-ai/Mooncake/blob/0e626c572ba3ceee30cef4692bb981487bf65913/mooncake-store/src/local_hot_cache.cpp#L542), a host copy from a device pointer.
- The single-key path avoids this because it stages GPU destinations through host memory whenever `IsHotCacheEnabled()` ([real_client.cpp:4701-4704](https://github.com/kvcache-ai/Mooncake/blob/0e626c572ba3ceee30cef4692bb981487bf65913/mooncake-store/src/real_client.cpp#L4701-L4704)). The batch paths have no such staging.

Draft #4619 replaces that `memcpy` with `RuntimeAccelerators().CopyToHost` (tested with a mocked accelerator), which looks like it would also fix this crash, although its description does not mention it. I'm filing the crash separately so it is tracked with a reproduction on a real GPU, whichever change lands.

## Environment

- Mooncake main `0e626c5`, built with `-DUSE_CUDA=ON` (HTTP and etcd metadata, unit tests), CUDA 13
- NVIDIA RTX PRO 6000 Blackwell (96 GB), Ubuntu, Python 3.13, torch 2.11.0+cu130
- One `mooncake_master`, TCP transport, `P2PHANDSHAKE`

## Steps to reproduce

```bash
mooncake_master --default_kv_lease_ttl=500 &
sleep 2                                # let the master start listening on 50051
python repro.py writer > writer.log &  # client without the hot cache puts a 64 KiB key, then waits
until grep -q "put ok" writer.log; do sleep 0.2; done
MC_STORE_LOCAL_HOT_CACHE_SIZE=$((64 << 20)) MC_STORE_LOCAL_HOT_BLOCK_SIZE=$((1 << 20)) python repro.py reader
```

Condensed from the script behind the results below (same calls and settings):

```python
# repro.py
import os, sys, time
import torch
from mooncake.store import MooncakeDistributedStore

KEY, SIZE, MASTER = "hot_cache_gpu_key", 64 * 1024, "127.0.0.1:50051"
data = bytes((i * 7 + 3) % 251 for i in range(SIZE))
s = MooncakeDistributedStore()

if sys.argv[1] == "writer":
    assert s.setup("localhost:17901", "P2PHANDSHAKE", 256 << 20, 64 << 20, "tcp", "", MASTER) == 0
    assert s.put(KEY, data) == 0
    print("put ok", flush=True)
    time.sleep(600)
else:
    assert s.setup("localhost:17902", "P2PHANDSHAKE", 16 << 20, 64 << 20, "tcp", "", MASTER) == 0
    for attempt in range(3):
        dst = torch.zeros(SIZE, dtype=torch.uint8, device="cuda")
        assert s.register_buffer(dst.data_ptr(), SIZE) == 0
        n = s.batch_get_into([KEY], [dst.data_ptr()], [SIZE])[0]
        torch.cuda.synchronize()
        print(attempt, n, bytes(dst.cpu().numpy()) == data, flush=True)
        time.sleep(0.5)  # as in the recorded runs; the crash does not depend on it
        s.unregister_buffer(dst.data_ptr())
```

Output: attempt 0 reads the 65536 bytes correctly; the next `batch_get_into` call then dies with `Segmentation fault` (exit 139) inside the hot-cache admission copy, before the call returns. The copy runs synchronously in `SubmitPutTask`, before the fill task is queued.

One recorded run per mode (the first four rows use `MC_STORE_LOCAL_HOT_ADMISSION_THRESHOLD=1`; the batch CUDA case crashed again under gdb, which gave the backtrace above; with the default threshold, the batch CUDA case crashed on the second read as described):

| destination | API | hot cache | result |
|---|---|---|---|
| pinned host | `batch_get_into` | on | 3 reads OK |
| CUDA | `batch_get_into` | off | 3 reads OK |
| CUDA | `get_into` | on | 3 reads OK |
| CUDA | `batch_get_into` | on | SIGSEGV |
| pinned host | `batch_get_into_multi_buffers` | on | 3 reads OK |
| CUDA | `batch_get_into_multi_buffers` | on | SIGSEGV |

## Expected behavior

A batch read into GPU memory with the hot cache enabled either fills the cache with a device-aware copy, as `get_into` effectively does, or skips admission for device slices; it should not crash the process.

This report was prepared with AI assistance (Claude Code); the reproduction was run on a real GPU against `0e626c5`.

items.title: Loop-carry detection skips `prev = cur` when both start as the same value, silently keeping the pre-loop value instead of carrying it
items.author: Hughshine
items.body_excerpt:
### Describe the bug


**TL;DR.** `CodeGenerator._find_carries` decides which variables of a `for` or `while` loop become `iter_args` by comparing IR values after one dry run of the body, instead of asking whether a value can differ between iterations. If `prev` and `cur` are the same IR value before the loop and the loop runs `prev = cur`, `prev` looks unchanged and is not carried, so it keeps its pre-loop value in every iteration and after the loop. Regression from #7200, first in 3.5.0 (3.4.0 is right). Possible fix: also carry every name that is assigned in the loop (as 3.4.0 did), or only those that share their initial IR value with another name.

**Why one dry run misses it.** `_find_carries` ([L485-L524](https://github.com/triton-lang/triton/blob/6fe3348e6e907584e07e593ab19a35caee95c37a/python/triton/compiler/code_generator.py#L485-L524), the comparison is [L513](https://github.com/triton-lang/triton/blob/6fe3348e6e907584e07e593ab19a35caee95c37a/python/triton/compiler/code_generator.py#L513)) runs the body once with every name bound to its pre-loop value. When `prev = cur` runs there, `cur` is still at its pre-loop value, so `prev` is bound to the value it already had. In the real body `cur` is a block argument, so `prev = cur` is a different value in every iteration. Seeing that takes a second pass that already knows `cur` is carried.

The smallest example. `prev` is `cur`'s value at the start of each iteration; `SAME=False` is the control, where `prev` is equal to `cur` but a different IR value:

```python
import torch
import triton
import triton.language as tl


@triton.jit
def kernel(out_ptr, n, SAME: tl.constexpr):
    cur = 0
    if SAME:
        prev = cur          # prev and cur are the same IR value
    else:
        prev = cur + 0      # control: equal to cur, but a different IR value
    for i in range(n):
        prev = cur          # prev is cur's value at the start of the iteration
        cur = cur + 1
    tl.store(out_ptr, prev)      # expected n - 1
    tl.store(out_ptr + 1, cur)   # expected n


n = 5
for same in (True, False):
    out = torch.zeros(2, dtype=torch.int32, device="cuda")
    k = kernel[(1, )](out, n, same)
    print(f"SAME={same!s:5} prev, cur = {out.tolist()}, expected {[n - 1, n]}")
    print("   ", [l.strip() for l in k.asm["ttir"].splitlines() if "scf.for" in l][0].split(" : ")[0])
```
```
SAME=True  prev, cur = [0, 5], expected [4, 5]
    %cur = scf.for %i = %c0_i32 to %n step %c1_i32 iter_args(%cur_0 = %c0_i32) -> (i32)
SAME=False prev, cur = [4, 5], expected [4, 5]
    %prev:2 = scf.for %i = %c0_i32 to %n step %c1_i32 iter_args(%cur = %c0_i32, %prev_0 = %c0_i32) -> (i32, i32)
```
With `SAME=True` only `cur` is an `iter_arg`. 3.4.0 has two `iter_args` in both cases and returns `[4, 5]`. Without an `iter_arg`, `prev` is still bound to its pre-loop value when the body starts, and `enter_sub_region` restores that binding when the loop ends ([L146](https://github.com/triton-lang/triton/blob/6fe3348e6e907584e07e593ab19a35caee95c37a/python/triton/compiler/code_generator.py#L146)).

**Why since 3.5.0.** Up to 3.4.0 every name that is assigned in the loop and live before it was carried ([visit_For](https://github.com/triton-lang/triton/blob/d4432f6b89ef554007a53ef90f2499d90792d7e7/python/triton/compiler/code_generator.py#L1114-L1115), [visit_While](https://github.com/triton-lang/triton/blob/d4432f6b89ef554007a53ef90f2499d90792d7e7/python/triton/compiler/code_generator.py#L1153-L1154)). #7200 (2025-06-23, "Improve detection of loop carries", for builtins that modify their arguments) replaced that with the comparison of IR values; v3.5.0 is the first tag that contains it. The existing tests for shared initial values (`test_loop_carry_shared_initial_value` and its while and tuple variants in test_frontend.py, #11369) update the aliased variables independently (`a = a + 1`, `b = b + 2`), so none has a copy between them.

**Possible fix.** Two variants, both tested as source patches on main @6fe3348e6.

Carry every name that is assigned in the loop, as 3.4.0 did, and keep the comparison:
```diff
--- a/python/triton/compiler/code_generator.py
+++ b/python/triton/compiler/code_generator.py
@@ -493,6 +493,9 @@ class CodeGenerator(ast.NodeVisitor):
         self.scf_stack.pop()
         block.erase()
 
+        # A name that is assigned in the loop may have copied another one, which an unchanged handle doesn't show.
+        assigned = {n.id for n in ast.walk(node) if isinstance(n, ast.Name) and isinstance(n.ctx, ast.Store)}
+
         # If a variable (name) has changed value within the loop, then it's
         # a loop-carried variable. (The new and old value must be of the
         # same type)
@@ -510,7 +513,7 @@ class CodeGenerator(ast.NodeVisitor):
 
                 live_handles = flatten_values_to_ir([live_val])
                 loop_handles = flatten_values_to_ir([loop_val])
-                if live_handles != loop_handles:
+                if name in assigned or live_handles != loop_handles:
                     names.append(name)
                     init_tys.append(live_val.type)
                     init_handles.extend(live_handles)
```
The comparison was added by #7200 for builtins that modify their arguments in place. #8832 (2025-11-25) removed that case ("now that we ban mutations") together with its tests, attribute and item assignment raise, and aggregates cannot be assigned to after construction, so a name whose IR value changes is a name that is assigned. In test_frontend.py and the Gluon frontend tests, 57 of the 181 (name, loop) pairs that `_find_carries` looked at had a changed IR value, and all 57 are assigned in the loop. The set of assigned names comes from the AST, so it does not depend on what the dry run did; that also covers a branch that only the lowering takes (see below). It over-carries assigned names whose value does not change (`x = x`); they become `iter_args` and the canonicalizer in `make_ttir` removes them (the TTIR of t

items.title: Pipelining drops `volatile=True` and `cache_modifier=".cv"` on loads
items.author: shuyilinn
items.body_excerpt:
### Describe the bug

In a pipelined loop, a load with `volatile=True` or `cache_modifier=".cv"` is turned into a `cp.async` copy, which drops the volatile / `.cv` semantics. The load is also issued `num_stages - 1` iterations early. With `num_stages=1` the PTX has `ld.volatile.global` / `ld.global.cv` as expected.

```python
import re
import torch
import triton
import triton.language as tl


@triton.jit
def kernel(X, Y, NUM_STAGES: tl.constexpr, VOLATILE: tl.constexpr, CACHE: tl.constexpr):
    offs = tl.arange(0, 128)
    acc = tl.zeros([128], tl.float32)
    for i in tl.range(0, 8, num_stages=NUM_STAGES):
        acc += tl.load(X + i * 128 + offs, volatile=VOLATILE, cache_modifier=CACHE)
    tl.store(Y + offs, acc)


X, Y = torch.empty(1024, device="cuda"), torch.empty(128, device="cuda")
for volatile, cache, expected in ((True, "", "ld.volatile.global"), (False, ".cv", "ld.global.cv")):
    for num_stages in (1, 3):
        ptx = kernel.warmup(X, Y, num_stages, volatile, cache, grid=(1, )).asm["ptx"]
        print(f"volatile={volatile} cache_modifier={cache!r} num_stages={num_stages}: "
              f"{expected} x{len(re.findall(re.escape(expected), ptx))}, cp.async x{len(re.findall(r'cp\.async\.c[ag]', ptx))}")
```

```
volatile=True cache_modifier='' num_stages=1: ld.volatile.global x8, cp.async x0
volatile=True cache_modifier='' num_stages=3: ld.volatile.global x0, cp.async x10
volatile=False cache_modifier='.cv' num_stages=1: ld.global.cv x8, cp.async x0
volatile=False cache_modifier='.cv' num_stages=3: ld.global.cv x0, cp.async x10
```

`AssignLatencies` does not exclude volatile loads or `.cv` loads from pipelining. `LowerLoops` passes `isVolatile` to `AsyncCopyGlobalToLocalOp`, but its NVIDIA lowering never reads it and maps the cache modifier to `cp.async.ca` / `.cg`. A volatile load polling a flag written by another CTA would then read a stale value, prefetched iterations earlier. I only have PTX-level evidence; I did not observe a stale read in a spin test on this GPU.

### Environment details

items.title: Upgrade to Transformers v5
items.author: hmellor
items.body_excerpt:
## What is this issue?

This issue serves as a living tracker for the current issues preventing us from upgrading vLLM to Transformers v5.

We will use sub-issues to track individual failures and PRs should be made against these sub-issues.

The solutions to these issues may need to be applied to either:

- Transformers in the form of:
  - Adding missing backward compatibility (usually for custom code models)
  - General bug fixes/improvements to new features of v5
- vLLM in the form of:
  - Forward compatibility with how something is now done in v5
  - Edge case handling for issues that v4 ignored (such as config validation)

Sometimes, the issue is simply with the model checkpoint itself, for example if it:

- Contains a malformed `config.json` that cannot be used to instantiate the newly input validated `PreTrainedConfig` class
- Custom code* uses deprecated/removed APIs

In these situations, the best solution will likely be to skip these tests in vLLM and open a PR to Transformers to contribute this model. This will be faster and more sustainable than waiting for the model vendor to fix their custom model code, sometimes they nevert do.

Contributing the new model should be done using the new [Modular Transformers](https://huggingface.co/docs/transformers/main/en/modular_transformers) so that the implementation is easy to maintain and will remain maintained by the Transformers team.

_*particularly in the parts of the model implementation that vLLM tries to directly reuse, such as config/tokenizer/multimodal processor_

items.title: [Performance] Measure Transformers backend startup time vs native
items.author: hmellor
items.body_excerpt:
This comes from an old comment and was never backed by measurements, so the first
task is to establish whether the effect is real at all. It may not be.

Runtime throughput was brought in line with native implementations in #47187, but
nobody has measured startup time either before or since.

### Step 1: is there a difference?

Time engine init for a model that has both implementations, e.g.:

    vllm serve Qwen/Qwen3-0.6B --model-impl transformers
    vllm serve Qwen/Qwen3-0.6B --model-impl vllm

Compare time-to-ready across a few runs and a couple of model sizes. Warm vs cold
HF cache matters, so control for it.

If there is no meaningful difference, say so and close this issue. That is a
perfectly good outcome and still worth having measured.

### Step 2: only if a delta shows up

The backend does some work at load time that native implementations do not, so
these are plausible starting points rather than known causes:

- `fuser.py` — `get_fuser` traces each module class with `fx` to match it against
  the available fusers. Cached per class, but tracing is not free.
- `base.py` — `recursive_replace` walks the module tree applying fusers per instance.
- Config resolution and `auto_map` handling for remote-code models.

A profile of init (py-spy or cProfile) will be more informative than guessing from
this list.

### Done when

Either the startup delta is quantified and explained, or it is shown that there
isn't a meaningful one and this is closed.

items.title: Starting a localization (l10n) effort for LMCache
items.author: quaid
items.body_excerpt:
I'd like to propose we start building a localization community around LMCache, beginning with blog posts and expanding to documentation and other parts of the website over time.

tl;dr – 
- localizing content and software is valuable to all of us;
- we can automate the toil of translation but we need human editors who can review the translations and make sure they are properly localized;
- localization means words and phrases are fixed so the final product makes more sense to a native reader;
- we can use RHLF to improve this process and reduce toil over time.

## What is the problem

We already receive blog posts written natively in Mandarin and English. This is a good thing.

But we also need to localize this content without putting a burden on people. Fortunately this content has completed a technical review before being translated, so the focus can be on fixing idioms and grammar for better understanding by the widest audience.

## Why this matters

Ultimately this is about attracting more users to LMCache, some of whom will become intentional contributors over time.

Twenty-five years ago, localization (l10n) projects were one of the main ways Linux distributions and communities like the Fedora Project made headway into new parts of the world. It usually wasn't a corporate initiative. It was people who were enthusiastic about bringing free and open source software to their fellow country members, and who put in the effort to translate strings and make the software make sense locally. That work produced translations AND collaborations. It grew contributors, built regional communities, and carried the free software and open source ethos into places it hadn't reached before.

LMCache has users and watchers all over the world, and there are almost certainly people already adjacent to this project who could help bring information and education about the software to their local communities.

## What I'm proposing

We form loosely as `l10n-sig` out of anyone who wants to be an editor and approver for one or more languages. Languages get added when someone steps forward to take one. Rather than announcing a target list and hoping it fills in, we start with whoever volunteers.

I'm volunteering to be an editor and reviewer for anything translated to English, and I'd love more help with that role. I'm confident we can get Mandarin covered right away. But what else and how?

Japanese and Korean are the obvious early candidates given where our users are, but the principle is that a language becomes active when a person is willing to own it.

It only takes one person to get things started and be the gravity to bring another language.

As I said above, this isn't only English needing localizing. I currently have an original blog post written in Mandarin that I want to bring into English through this same process. I'd like to stop doing one at a time reviews by asking around in Slack to see who might need a break from creating features or fixing bugs. I'd rather offer the opportunity to people who aren't or can't create features or fix bugs.

Therefore, posts written originally in any language are welcome, and translation should flow in whatever direction it needs to.

## This is not a request for volunteer translation labor

LLM translation is pretty good now, and we should lean on it for the first pass. What we need is a human review step, and there are two kinds of people who can do that well.

The first is someone capable in both the source and target language, who can read the machine translation and confirm the meaning carried over and the tone is right. Not necessarily final-polish copy editing — a human or AI copy edit can always be applied later — just confirmation that it makes sense and reads naturally.

The second, and possibly just as valuable, is someone technical who knows their own language well and doesn't necessarily read the source language at all. Because the models are good enough now, a domain expert can look at a translated technical passage and say "ah, I see what this was trying to say" and correct the terminology so it's actually right in their language. Technical accuracy matters as much as idiomatic flow, and that person is well placed to catch it.

So the ask is much closer to "read this and tell us if it sounds right" than "translate three thousand words."

## How the workflow might look

Initially all of this can be manual, while we work out which models produce the best tone for technical writing in each language and we develop any necessary skills.

Longer term this could be automated — a GitHub Action that sends a published post to a translation model, then loads the result into WordPress as a draft where a translation editor reviews and approves it. It could also live partly outside the repo, with approval happening after the fact rather than as a gate. The goal is to distribute this work rather than make it dependent on a paid staffer, and to remove the need to ask permission before contributing.

If anyone already knows of a toolchain or process for this, please say so. I'd much rather adopt something that works than stand up and maintain our own infrastructure.

## What I'm looking for

Ideas or helping hands for:

- Thoughts on the approach
- Pointers to existing tooling
- Anyone in

items.title: [Bug][MP] L1 eviction_ratio uses key count instead of allocated bytes
items.author: JasperChan929
items.body_excerpt:
## Describe the bug

MP L1 `eviction_ratio` and `--eviction-ratio` are documented as a fraction of **allocated memory**, but `L1EvictionController` forwards the ratio to a policy selecting a fraction of **key count**. Different object sizes can therefore reclaim substantially less or more memory than configured.

Pinned baseline: current `dev` **f24bfe9840599f796c844ac7bdfb6be791be8122**. This reproduces through an independently launched, unmodified official MP server and the supported CPU engine-driven PREPARE/COMMIT protocol, without a GPU or model weights.

Sources:
- [Configuration contract](https://github.com/LMCache/LMCache/blob/f24bfe9840599f796c844ac7bdfb6be791be8122/lmcache/v1/distributed/config.py#L484)
- [CLI documentation](https://github.com/LMCache/LMCache/blob/f24bfe9840599f796c844ac7bdfb6be791be8122/docs/source/mp/configuration.rst#L568)
- [L1 controller](https://github.com/LMCache/LMCache/blob/f24bfe9840599f796c844ac7bdfb6be791be8122/lmcache/v1/distributed/storage_controllers/eviction_controller.py#L160)
- [Count-based LRU target](https://github.com/LMCache/LMCache/blob/f24bfe9840599f796c844ac7bdfb6be791be8122/lmcache/v1/distributed/eviction_policy/lru.py#L128)

## Expected and observed behavior

L1 capacity: 80 KiB; watermark: 0.65; eviction ratio: 0.25; alignment: 4 KiB. All writes complete and no objects are read/write locked before the first eviction.

Both layouts contain 8 objects and allocate exactly 64 KiB. **Both targets are integral:** 25% of keys is 2 keys, and 25% of allocated bytes is 16 KiB. The byte target is achievable with whole objects.

| Layout in insertion order | Observed allocated-byte sequence | Triggered controller cycles |
|---|---|---|
| Seven 4 KiB objects, then one 36 KiB object | 64 -> 56 -> 52 -> 48 KiB | 3 |
| Eight 8 KiB objects (control) | 64 -> 48 KiB | 1 |

The mixed first cycle releases 8 KiB (12.5%), rather than the documented 16 KiB (25%). It takes two additional ordinary one-second controller intervals to reach 48 KiB. A byte-target prototype reaches the same final allocation in one cycle, leaving the uniform control unchanged. This prototype is a causal check, not a production patch.

A separate admission probe submits four 8 KiB chunks just after the first reclamation. Baseline then has 24 KiB free: the real all-or-nothing batch allocator cannot reserve 32 KiB, and actual allocated bytes/object count remain unchanged. The prototype has 32 KiB free and admits all four chunks. Three independent services per variant reproduced **0/3 versus 3/3 full admissions**.

This is a controlled capacity consequence, not a production incidence estimate, model-serving failure, or TTFT/throughput benchmark. Admission is determined from actual allocator bytes and object count. The current inline store boolean can be True for an empty reservation; it is not used as proof of admission or reported as a separate issue here.

## Environment and setup

Linux x86_64 (WSL2 kernel 6.18.33.1), Python 3.12.13, Torch 2.14.0, numpy 2.2.6, documented **NO_GPU_EXT=1 native CPU build**. GPU visibility and usage telemetry are disabled. A C++ compiler is required. The source-only NO_NATIVE_EXT mode is insufficient for the native allocator.

```bash
git clone --branch dev https://github.com/LMCache/LMCache.git
cd LMCache
git checkout f24bfe9840599f796c844ac7bdfb6be791be8122
uv venv --python 3.12 .venv
uv pip install --python .venv/bin/python \
  'torch==2.14.0' ninja packaging 'setuptools>=77,<81' setuptools_scm \
  'grpcio==1.78.0' 'grpcio-tools==1.78.0' wheel
NO_GPU_EXT=1 MAX_JOBS=2 uv pip install --python .venv/bin/python -e . --no-build-isolation
uv pip check --python .venv/bin/python
```

Save the complete script below as `repro_l1_byte_budget_mp.py` in the checkout root, then run:

```bash
CUDA_VISIBLE_DEVICES='' .venv/bin/python repro_l1_byte_budget_mp.py \
  --repo . --layout mixed --output /tmp/l1-byte-budget-mixed
CUDA_VISIBLE_DEVICES='' .venv/bin/python repro_l1_byte_budget_mp.py \
  --repo . --layout uniform --output /tmp/l1-byte-budget-uniform
CUDA_VISIBLE_DEVICES='' .venv/bin/python repro_l1_byte_budget_mp.py \
  --repo . --layout mixed --probe --output /tmp/l1-byte-budget-admission
```

Each invocation starts/stops its own official `lmcache.v1.multiprocess.http_server`, binding only loopback ephemeral ports. It writes the exact CLI/environment and source hash to `launch.json`, original service output to `server.log`, and public `/status` observations to `result.json`.

Expected baseline console summaries:

```text
mixed:   initial_target_bytes=16384, used_byte_timeline=[65536,57344,53248,49152], triggered_controller_cycles=3
uniform: initial_target_bytes=16384, used_byte_timeline=[65536,49152], triggered_controller_cycles=1
probe:   initial_target_bytes=16384, used_byte_timeline=[65536,57344], probe_admitted_bytes=0
```

The script registers different synthetic model names with valid single-group CPU KV layouts in one L1 pool. It uses the supported typed inline CPU codec. There is no manager injection, fake allocator, scheduler hook, private-state access, or actual model inference. The probe measurement is rejected if it spans a second controller cycle; the controller is never paused.

"""Exercise byte-oriented L1 eviction through the supported CPU MP protocol."""

from __future__ import annotations

import argparse

items.title: bug(sampling): top_k_arr/min_p_arr are validated against input rows but indexed by output row, reading out of bounds when indices is longer than probs
items.author: kahyunnam
items.body_excerpt:
### Summary

`top_k_sampling_from_probs` and `min_p_sampling_from_probs` validate their per-request parameter tensor against the **input** batch but index it by the **output** row. When `indices` is longer than `probs.size(0)`, every output row at or past `probs.size(0)` reads past the end of the parameter tensor and silently samples with a garbage `top_k` / `min_p`.

- `check_tensor_param(maybe_top_k_arr, probs)` — [`csrc/sampling.cu:216`](https://github.com/flashinfer-ai/flashinfer/blob/main/csrc/sampling.cu#L216) — requires `top_k_arr.size(0) == probs.size(0)`, via [`csrc/sampling_utils.h:34`](https://github.com/flashinfer-ai/flashinfer/blob/main/csrc/sampling_utils.h#L34). Same for `min_p` at [`csrc/sampling.cu:262`](https://github.com/flashinfer-ai/flashinfer/blob/main/csrc/sampling.cu#L262).
- The kernels read [`top_k_arr[bx]`](https://github.com/flashinfer-ai/flashinfer/blob/main/include/flashinfer/sampling.cuh#L872) and [`min_p_arr[bx]`](https://github.com/flashinfer-ai/flashinfer/blob/main/include/flashinfer/sampling.cuh#L1129), where `bx` is `blockIdx.x`, i.e. the output row.

The sibling kernels get this right and index by the input row: [`top_p_arr[row_idx]`](https://github.com/flashinfer-ai/flashinfer/blob/main/include/flashinfer/sampling.cuh#L1006) in `TopPSamplingFromProbKernel`, and [`top_k_arr[row_idx]` / `top_p_arr[row_idx]`](https://github.com/flashinfer-ai/flashinfer/blob/main/include/flashinfer/sampling.cuh#L1228-L1229) in `TopKTopPSamplingFromProbKernel`. So only the two `[bx]` sites are wrong.

### Reproduction

On a B200 (SM100), 4 input rows, 16 output rows via `indices = arange(16) % 4`, vocab 512. The parameter tensor is a length-4 view carved out of a 4096-element buffer whose tail holds a conspicuous value, so an out-of-bounds read returns that tail instead of faulting:

| Call | Parameter tensor | Output rows violating the parameter |
|---|---|---|
| `top_k_sampling_from_probs` | length-4 `top_k`, all `1`, buffer tail `500` | **12 / 16** — exactly rows 4–15 |
| `min_p_sampling_from_probs` | length-4 `min_p`, all `1.0`, buffer tail `0.0` | **12 / 16** — exactly rows 4–15 |
| `top_p_sampling_from_probs` (control) | length-4 `top_p`, all `1e-6`, buffer tail `1.0` | **0 / 16** |

With `top_k = 1` every output row must return `argmax(probs[indices[i]])`; rows 4–15 do not. The `top_p` control isolates the cause to the `bx` / `row_idx` choice rather than anything about the harness.

Note that `compute-sanitizer --tool memcheck` does **not** flag this: the read stays inside the PyTorch caching-allocator segment, so a memcheck-clean run is not evidence of safety here.

<details>
<summary>Repro script</summary>

```python
import torch
from flashinfer import sampling

torch.manual_seed(0)
IN, OUT, V = 4, 16, 512
probs = torch.softmax(torch.randn(IN, V, device="cuda"), dim=-1)
indices = torch.arange(OUT, device="cuda", dtype=torch.int32) % IN

# Length-IN views carved out of a larger buffer whose tail holds a conspicuous value.
k_buf = torch.full((4096,), 500, dtype=torch.int32, device="cuda")
k_buf[:IN] = 1
top_k = k_buf[:IN]

p_buf = torch.zeros(4096, dtype=torch.float32, device="cuda")
p_buf[:IN] = 1.0
min_p = p_buf[:IN]

tp_buf = torch.full((4096,), 1.0, dtype=torch.float32, device="cuda")
tp_buf[:IN] = 1e-6
top_p = tp_buf[:IN]

argmax = probs.argmax(dim=-1)


def violations(out):
    return [(i, int(out[i])) for i in range(OUT) if int(out[i]) != int(argmax[indices[i]])]


out_k = sampling.top_k_sampling_from_probs(probs, top_k, indices=indices, deterministic=True)
print("top_k=1  violations:", len(violations(out_k)), "/", OUT, violations(out_k)[:6])

out_p = sampling.min_p_sampling_from_probs(probs, min_p, indices=indices, deterministic=True)
print("min_p=1  violations:", len(violations(out_p)), "/", OUT, violations(out_p)[:6])

# Control: top_p indexes by input row, so it must be unaffected.
out_tp = sampling.top_p_sampling_from_probs(probs, top_p, indices=indices, deterministic=True)
print("top_p    violations:", len(violations(out_tp)), "/", OUT)
```

```
top_k=1  violations: 12 / 16 [(4, 189), (5, 226), (6, 216), (7, 345), (8, 459), (9, 92)]
min_p=1  violations: 12 / 16 [(4, 320), (5, 147), (6, 350), (7, 300), (8, 42), (9, 113)]
top_p    violations: 0 / 16
```

</details>

### Fix

Two options, and the choice is a contract decision rather than a mechanical one:

1. Index by the input row — change `top_k_arr[bx]` to `top_k_arr[row_idx]` and `min_p_arr[bx]` to `min_p_arr[row_idx]`, matching the existing validation and the two sibling kernels.
2. Keep output-row indexing and fix the validation to use the output batch instead of `probs`, which is what `top_k`/`min_p` being *per-request* arguably implies.

Option 2 matches what the docstrings suggest (`indices` maps outputs to distributions, so a per-request parameter is naturally per-output) and is the convention #5745 uses for `seed`/`offset`, which validates against `output.size(0)`. Option 1 is the smaller change and keeps all four kernels consistent with each other. Either way the four kernels should agree, and a test with `len(indices) > probs.size(0)` plus a tensor-valued parameter would have caught this.

### Environment

NVIDIA B200 (SM100, CC 10.0), CUDA 13.0, torch 2.14.0+cu130, Python 3.10, `main` @ `1cad38165`. Nothing about this is architecture-specific.

comments.author: AckerMan5659
comments.body:
I investigated #5878 against current main and found two separate results.

1. The original out-of-bounds case no longer reproduces on current main: the sampling kernels already use `row_idx`. I added a local regression test covering `top_k`, `min_p`, and `top_p` with 4 input rows, 16 output rows, and `indices = arange(16) % 4`; it passes 3/3. Would a test-only PR be welcome, or is this issue considered already fixed?

2. Separately, on an SM89 host (RTX 4080 SUPER), stock main's top-k sampling kernel fails before output comparison with `too many resources requested for launch`; `min_p` and `top_p` pass with the same inputs. A scoped change that uses 512 threads only for top-k on SM8x, while keeping 1024 threads on SM90+, makes all three pass. Would you prefer separate PRs for the regression test and the SM8x dispatch fix, or a combined change?

I have not submitted either PR yet. I will not include the local torch-2.6 compatibility shim or the broader all-kernels 512-thread experiment. Please let me know the preferred scope.

comments.author: AckerMan5659
comments.body:
Follow-up: I opened the two separate PRs so the scopes can be reviewed independently:

items.title: llama : integer type consistency in `llama.h`
items.author: MarcusDunn
items.body_excerpt:
# Feature Description

llama.h should prefer to use `sized` (always) + `signed` (mostly) integers.

# Motivation

The integer types in `llama.h` right now are.

| Count | Type            |
|---------|------------------|
| 33      | `int`              |
| 10      | `int32_t`       |
| 24      | `uint32_t`     |
| 2        | `int64_t`       |
| 2        | `uint64_t`    | 

In #4540 there was a discussion around preferences for integer types on new methods. 

Avoiding `int` makes cross platform code simpler at essentially no cost.
Signed makes arithmetic simpler at the cost of some bits if you need something large.

# Possible Implementation

1. Change all `int`'s to `int32_t`
2. As code changes try to prefer signed integers.

We could also do some higher-impact things, but I'd take the lower-impact slower changes over a large find-and-replace.

items.title: [Bug] Classic RDMA client (real_client.cpp): crash and silent write failures on peer-membership change
items.author: sivabreddy
items.body_excerpt:
## Summary

Two distinct, reproducible problems in the "classic" RDMA client
(`real_client.cpp`), both triggered by a change in who's in the client pool
(a pod joining or leaving, by any method):

1. **A crash.** The client segfaults, taking down the entire host process, not
   just the Mooncake connection.
2. **A silent write failure.** A `Put` can fail with `TRANSFER_FAIL` with no
   error surfaced to the caller — the data is never actually written to the
   shared store, but nothing above the Transfer Engine layer is told this
   happened.

Both are reproducible on the latest PyPI release at time of testing
(`mooncake-transfer-engine==0.3.13.post1`, 2026-08-31). We believe both may
share a root cause with the already-fixed #3595 (a stale/self-referential
peer reference surviving a membership change), but in the older/classic
transport, which does not appear to carry that fix.

## Environment

- **Mooncake version**: `mooncake-transfer-engine` 0.3.13.post1 (PyPI,
  installed via `uv pip install mooncake-transfer-engine`, no source
  modifications)
- **Integration**: vLLM v0.17.1 + LMCache `v0.4.1-gdfc914cba`
  (`LMCacheConnectorV1`), using Mooncake Store as LMCache's remote backend
  (`remote_url: mooncakestore://...`) — not the vLLM-native
  `MooncakeStoreConnector`
- **Deployment**: Kubernetes, 2-3 vLLM pods across 2 physical nodes, Mooncake
  master + metadata server as separate lightweight pods in the same
  namespace
- **Transport**: RDMA (RoCEv2), Mellanox mlx5 devices, `GID index 3`
- **OS / platform**: Linux containers (RHEL/UBI-based vLLM image)

`mooncake-config.yaml` used throughout (templated; `local_hostname` set to
each pod's own IP at container start):
```yaml
chunk_size: 256
remote_url: "mooncakestore://<master-host>:50051/"
remote_serde: "naive"
local_cpu: True
max_local_cpu_size: 100
extra_config:
  local_hostname: "<pod IP, from $POD_IP>"
  metadata_server: "http://<metadata-host>:8080/metadata"
  master_server_address: "<master-host>:50051"
  protocol: "rdma"
  device_name: "mlx5_0,mlx5_1,mlx5_2,mlx5_3,mlx5_6,mlx5_7,mlx5_8,mlx5_9"
  global_segment_size: 17179869184
  local_buffer_size: 8589934592
  transfer_timeout: 1
```
Of the 8 listed devices, only `mlx5_0` has a real network attachment in our
environment; the other 7 fail to open at startup with a clear, non-fatal
warning and are excluded from the data path. This is expected and not itself
the bug — it becomes relevant in one test below.

---

## Issue 1: segfault on peer-membership change

### What we did (1): confirm the mechanism works normally

Deployed 2 vLLM+Mooncake pods (Pod A, Pod B) on separate nodes. Pod A stored a
prefix. Pod B requested the same prefix.

### What we found (1)

A genuine cross-pod RDMA retrieve, confirmed from LMCache's own log line on
Pod B (`Inference Engine computed tokens: 0` — Pod B never computed this
itself — followed by a real `Retrieved N tokens` line). No errors. This is
the expected, working behavior.

### What we did (2): change pool membership, then send a real request

Changed which pods were in the pool, by each of these methods independently:
- Force-deleted one pod (`kubectl delete pod --grace-period=0 --force`) and
  let Kubernetes replace it.
- Gracefully deleted one pod (`kubectl delete pod`, default grace period,
  clean SIGTERM) and let Kubernetes replace it.
- Simply added a brand-new pod to the same pool, with no deletion at all.

After each change, sent a real inference request that would cause a Mooncake
`Get` or `Put` — to **either** the new/replacement pod **or** an existing
pod that was never itself replaced.

### What we found (2)

**Whichever pod's turn it was to perform that next real operation segfaulted
— every time, regardless of which of the three membership-change methods was
used, and regardless of whether it was the new pod or an untouched existing
pod.** This reproduced independently on 4 separate occasions. Exactly one
crash occurred per membership-change event. The affected process self-healed
after one container restart (10-15 seconds) and was stable again until the
next membership change elsewhere in the pool.

Crash log, one example (a replacement pod's first retrieve attempt):
```
(APIServer pid=1) INFO:     Application startup complete.
E1008 17:59:52.045347   870 real_client.cpp:2287] Client is not initialized
E1008 17:59:52.045735   870 real_client.cpp:2287] Client is not initialized
E1008 17:59:52.045954   870 real_client.cpp:2287] Client is not initialized
(EngineCore_DP0 pid=483) LMCache INFO: Reqid: ..., Total tokens 907, Inference Engine computed tokens: 0, LMCache hit tokens: 768, need to load: 768
E1008 17:59:52.051139  1057 real_client.cpp:3154] Client is not initialized
!!!!!!! Segfault encountered !!!!!!!
  File ".../runtime/sys_linux_amd64.s", line 330, in runtime.sigfwd
(APIServer pid=1) ERROR [core_client.py:691] Engine core proc EngineCore_DP0 died unexpectedly, shutting down client.
vllm.v1.engine.exceptions.EngineDeadError: EngineCore encountered an issue.
```

A second example (a replacement pod's own client failing to initialize at
all, before any successful operation) shows the retry-then-crash shape more
fully:
```
W1008 10:00:39.777729   167 real_client.cpp:858] Failed to create client on port 13476, retry 1/20
W1008 10:00:39.987325   167 real_client.cpp:858] Failed to create client on port 14180, retry 2/20
... (18 more retries, a different ephemeral port each time) ...
W1008 10:00:45.268965   167 real_client.cpp:858] Failed to create client on port 12411, retry 20/20
!!!!!!! Segfault encountered !!!!!!!
vllm.v1.engine.exceptions.EngineDeadError: EngineCore encountered an issue.
```

### What we did (3): test a candidate fix (MC_USE_TENT)

Found `MC_USE_TENT` as a string inside the installed `mooncake/engine.so` via
`strings`, hypothesizing it would opt into the newer TENT RDMA transport,
which already has a fix (#3598/#3603) for a structurally similar crash
(#3595: SIGSEGV in `RailMonitor::updateBestMapping()` af

comments.body:
## Follow-up: retested with a corrected RDMA device list and checked TENT directly from source

Posting an update since we found something that changes the picture from the original report above.

### 1. Is TENT available as a way around this? No — confirmed from source, not guessed

We'd read about TENT (the newer failure-handling transport) and wondered if it was reachable from
the published package. Cloned `kvcache-ai/Mooncake` fresh and checked directly:

- `mooncake-common/common.cmake`: `option(USE_TENT "option for building Mooncake TENT" OFF)` —
  **TENT is a CMake build-time flag, default OFF**, not a runtime environment variable.
- This confirms why our earlier `MC_USE_TENT=1` attempt (mentioned in the original report) had no
  effect — there is no such runtime flag in this transport. The published
  `mooncake-transfer-engine` PyPI wheel is a standard build (`USE_TENT` not set), so TENT is not
  present in it regardless of environment variables.

### 2. Our original device-list mismatch, corrected — the crash got worse, not better

The original report used a `device_name` list of 8 devices, of which only 1 (`mlx5_0`) actually
had a routable RoCEv2 identity on our cluster — we wondered if this mismatch itself was a
contributing factor. Re-checked fresh: still true, no change, confirmed via `ibv_devinfo` and a
scan of `/sys/class/infiniband/*/ports/1/gids/*` on both nodes.

Redeployed with `device_name` corrected to `"mlx5_0"` only (the one real device). Result:

**All three client pods failed to establish a working Mooncake RDMA client at startup — 20/20
connection retries exhausted on every pod, 0/3 successful:**

```
W1013 11:51:04.798380  1450 real_client.cpp:858] Failed to create client on port 12628, retry 1/20
...
W1013 11:52:28.016795  1450 real_client.cpp:858] Failed to create client on port 13693, retry 20/20
E1013 11:52:28.116932  1450 real_client.cpp:865] Failed to create client after 20 retries
E1013 11:52:28.118700  1450 real_client.cpp:3379] Client is not initialized
```

**A separate issue found here:** the Mooncake master's own metrics showed `Clients: 0` for the
entire test, even though every pod logged `MooncakeConnector initialized successfully` on the
LMCache side. LMCache's `MooncakestoreConnector` appears to report success regardless of whether
the underlying C++ client actually has a working connection — there's no visible warning anywhere
that the connector is non-functional. (We realize this specific piece may belong on the LMCache
side rather than here, flagging for completeness since it compounds the diagnosis difficulty.)

**The crash itself still reproduced, and more readily than before — not gated behind a
membership-change event anymore, but firing on literally the first real cache operation:**

```
LMCache INFO: Reqid: ..., LMCache hit tokens: 256, need to load: 256
E1013 12:09:16.147480  1949 real_client.cpp:2287] Client is not initialized
E1013 12:09:16.701977  2350 real_client.cpp:3154] Client is not initialized
!!!!!!! Segfault encountered !!!!!!!
```

Confirmed independently on 2 of the 3 pods (identical file/line numbers, identical trigger: a
lookup reporting a partial local hit that needs to load the remainder from the remote tier). One
pod was also force-deleted and replaced to confirm the original membership-change trigger
specifically — same result, crashes immediately on the replacement pod's first real request.
Total: 5 independent crash observations across 3 pods, 100% reproduction rate, 0 successful real
cache operations observed anywhere in this retest.

### 3. What this changes about our read of the original report

- Correcting the device-list mismatch does **not** fix the crash — if anything, it removes the
  one device that was letting any connection succeed at all in our original 8-device config,
  without touching whatever is fragile in `real_client.cpp`'s client-creation/reconnection path.
- We could not re-isolate the silent-write-failure bug from the original repo

comments.body:
**Update after a re-test: the failed writes came from our RDMA configuration; the crash is the null-client path that #4633 fixes.**

On 2026-10-17 we re-tested with the same versions: vLLM 0.17.1, LMCache 0.4.1 (`LMCacheConnectorV1`, `mooncakestore://`), Mooncake 0.3.13.post1 and Llama-3.1-8B TP1. We used the same LMCache YAML and the HTTP metadata server, with 3 pods on 2 nodes. Several RDMA pods on each node share one RoCE device. Differences from the original run: an Ubuntu CUDA image with pip, and LMCache 0.4.1 built from source.

**1. What was wrong on our side**
- **A fixed GID index.** We set `MC_GID_INDEX=3`. A cluster policy also injected `NCCL_IB_GID_INDEX=3`, which Mooncake uses when `MC_GID_INDEX` is not set (`mooncake-transfer-engine/src/config.cpp` L144-145). When pods share one RDMA device, each pod also sees the GID entries of the other pods. So a fixed index points to at most one pod's own GID, or to another pod's GID. Without a fixed index, `findBestGidIndex` ranks GIDs that have a readable sysfs netdev first, and each pod selected its own IPv4 GID (indexes 11–27).
- **RDMA devices without a network in `device_name`.** We listed 8 devices, and only one has a network.

**2. Re-test with automatic GID selection**

| | 8-device list | connected device only |
|---|---|---|
| Requests during and after 3 membership changes (force delete, delete, new pod) | 51 of 51 answered | 51 of 51 answered |
| Segfaults / engine restarts / `Failed to create client` retries | 0 / 0 / 0 | 0 / 0 / 0 |
| `Put ... TRANSFER_FAIL` log lines (4 pods) | 320 (master rate metrics: no completed `PutEnd`) | 0 |
| Cross-pod loads | none | yes (2,560 of 2,560 tokens) |

Store-only test (Python client, 4 clients, 2 per node, 16 keys of 4 MB each, P2PHANDSHAKE, connected device only): with `MC_GID_INDEX=3`, 16 of 16 puts failed on every client and 0 of 64 keys were readable; with automatic selection, 64 of 64 keys were readable.

**3. The crash: #4633 matches our logs**
In our crash logs the process first fails to create the client (`Failed to create client ... retry 20/20`) or logs `Client is not initialized`; in one log the last Mooncake line before the segfault is `real_client.cpp:3154] Client is not initialized` (`batch_get_buffer_internal`, 0.3.13.post1). In 0.3.13.post1, `RealClient::batch_get_buffer` (L3366-3373) passes an always-true success predicate to `execute_timed_operation`, so the observer calls `client_->ObserveTransferOperation(...)` with a null `client_`. The same pattern is in the other 7 batch wrappers (L4024, 4086, 4377, 4656, 5435, 6053, 6097) and is still on `main`. This is exactly what #4633 fixes (thanks @pjdurden). So the chain in our case was: fixed GID index → client creation fails → LMCache keeps calling the batch API (it does not check the `setup()` result) → null `client_` in the metrics observer → segfault. With automatic GID selection the client is created and the crash path is not reached, which is why the re-test had 0 crashes. We did not re-run the crash setup with #4633 applied.

**4. What we suggest**
- Merge #4633 (or an equivalent null check). It turns the crash into per-key errors.
- Docs: `docs/source/design/transfer-engine/index.md` L473 says the default of `MC_GID_INDEX` is 3. In the code the default is -1 = automatic selection (`mooncake-transfer-engine/include/config.h` L46). Proposed text: "`MC_GID_INDEX` (or `NCCL_IB_GID_INDEX` when `MC_GID_INDEX` is not set): GID index per device. Default: automatic selection, which prefers a GID that has a network device. Do not set a fixed index when several containers share one RDMA device: the GID table holds entries for the interfaces of all containers on the node." We can send this as a PR.
- For users: when several pods share one RDMA device, do not set `MC_GID_INDEX` / `NCCL_IB_GID_INDEX`, and list only RDMA devices that have a network in `device_name`.

items.title: [RFC]: Mooncake Store KV Cache Reshard
items.author: LLLL114
items.body_excerpt:
### Changes proposed


This proposal adds KV cache reuse to Mooncake Store without tying cached data to the topology that wrote it. One complete KV page is identified by one logical key. Writers retain their own sharding and physical layouts. Readers use the source layout manifest stored in the Store, together with their current target layout, to plan the required byte ranges. This allows inference instances with different tensor parallelism (TP), pipeline parallelism (PP), and physical layouts to share cached KV data.

The intended audience is maintainers of Mooncake Store, the Reshard SDK, and inference frameworks. The main changes are Store reshard planning in Python and framework integration. The underlying object capabilities depend on [[multipart RFC #4366](https://github.com/kvcache-ai/Mooncake/issues/4366)](https://github.com/kvcache-ai/Mooncake/issues/4366). Implementation begins with a minimal multipart demo that provides the capabilities required here, followed by Store reshard. The internal multipart design is covered by its separate RFC and is not repeated here.

## Motivation and goals

When a KV page is stored as separate rank-local shards and its data keys encode TP or PP ranks, the cached KV for a token sequence becomes tied to the topology that wrote it. An instance with a different topology must locate multiple source keys, identify the source layout, and reconstruct its target shards. Once the writer exits, readers must also be able to operate without its runtime addresses or participation in communication.

The proposal separates logical content identity, the source layout in the Store, and target runtime memory:

- **Logical content identity** determines whether data represents the same reusable KV content. It excludes TP and PP ranks and physical layout.

- **The source layout manifest** describes the layers, KV heads, and byte layout covered by each Part in the Store.

- **The target memory binding** describes the reading rank's registered buffers, page locations, and strides. It is valid only for the current runtime.

The goals are to support reads across TP, PP, and physical layouts; preserve HiCache's existence filtering, prefetch, cancellation, hit accounting, and fallback behavior; and allow reads after the source inference instance exits. The initial implementation does not require writers to anticipate future reader topologies or convert all KV data to a single physical layout.

## Scope and dependencies

[[Multipart RFC #4366](https://github.com/kvcache-ai/Mooncake/issues/4366)](https://github.com/kvcache-ai/Mooncake/issues/4366) only needs the object capabilities used by this proposal: independent writes to designated Parts, existence and metadata queries for complete objects, an immutable reference to application metadata, and batched byte-range reads from Parts.
This proposal includes:

1. A model semantic domain, page keys, and shared source layout manifests.

2. Logical planning and byte-range generation driven by the target rank's requirements.

3. Local caching of source manifests and read templates that contain no live addresses.

4. Initial SGLang HiCache integration and functional validation.

The initial scope excludes dtype conversion, page-size reshaping, KV conversion between models, automatic layout rewriting, selecting among multiple stored layouts for the same page, and full multipart persistence, migration, and high-availability extensions. Receiver-side auto staging, #4117, #4502, page-unified layouts, and new CUDA transfer kernels are separate optimization topics, not prerequisites for this proposal.

The existing runtime-to-runtime (R2R) reshard implementation and snapshot contracts remain unchanged. The Store path uses a separate memory binding and does not relax R2R identity constraints to enable reuse of stored KV data.

## Responsibilities
Layer | Responsibilities
-- | --
Inference framework | Provide actual layer and head ownership, host-pool layouts, and registered memory; coordinate TP and PP ranks; manage the prefetch lifecycle; and transfer data from host memory to the GPU.
Mooncake Python Reshard | Manage source manifests, intersect source coverage with target requirements, generate and reuse byte-range templates, and validate target addresses and read results.
Mooncake Store and Transfer Engine | Provide multipart objects, metadata, valid replica information, and general byte-transfer capabilities.

**Logical planning runs in the Python SDK inside the reader process, not in the Store Master.** The Master does not need to understand model layers, attention heads, TP, PP, or SGLang page slots. The framework does not need to implement its own algorithm for intersecting KV layer and head ranges.

```mermaid
flowchart LR
    K[Logical page key] --> O[Store object metadata]
    O --> M[Source manifest reference]
    M --> C[Reader manifest cache]
    C --> P[Python planning and range templates]
    T[Target placement and memory binding] --> P
    P --> R[Store range reads]
    R --> H[HiCache host pool]
    H --> G[Existing framework H2D path]
```
## Logical keys and source manifests

### Object keys

A data key identifies the logical content of a complete page, rather than a rank-local shard. The SGLang prototype reuses the framework's token-prefix hash and adds the model semantic domain and a protocol suffix:

```text
page_key = <backend/model prefix>_<token prefix hash>_<model_domain>
```

`model_domain` includes the namespace, model identity and revision, semantic configuration that affects KV content, and descriptors such as dtype, page size, the global layer set, total KV-head count, and K/V head dimensions. TP, PP, rank identities, and physical axis order are excluded.

This gives the same page key to the same model semantics and token prefix across different topologies. A shared model name alone is not sufficient for KV reuse: revisions and settings such as RoPE that affect the content must be isolated by the semantic doma

comments.body:
Thanks for writing this up — the split between logical content identity, the stored source layout, and the target runtime binding is the part that makes this tractable, and keeping logical planning in the reader process (rather than the Master) is the right boundary.

I would like to contribute a first slice rather than take over the whole RFC: the logical planning half, as a new pure-Python subpackage next to the existing R2R planner — model semantic domain + logical page keys, content-addressed source layout manifests (with derived byte geometry), target-driven byte-range generation, and the read-template cache. Draft PR: #4741.

It deliberately does not touch the Store write protocol (that stays with multipart #4366) or the SGLang HiCache integration, so it can be reviewed on its own. It currently covers PLHD/LPHD/HPLD with the full 3x3 conversion matrix verified element-by-element, uneven PP layer subsets, head-sharded sources, and requirements whose head interval spans Part boundaries.

Two things I would like the RFC author's opinion on, since they change the shape of the plan:

1. Part byte geometry: I derive part length / K-V offsets / strides from the manifest layout + logical descriptor (K region first, then V) rather than storing them. If the prototype stores an explicit geometry, I would rather match it than invent a second representation.
2. Manifest lifetime: the RFC leaves reclaiming unreferenced manifests to productionization. For the first slice I treat manifests as immutable and content-addressed (readers verify the digest on decode), which is compatible with any later reclamation policy — but if you expect manifests to be mutated in place (e.g. re-published under the same key), digest verification would need to become advisory.

items.title: GSP: grammar-conditioned sparse LM-head projection - replication and SGLang integration feedback wanted
items.author: StealthEyeLLC
items.body_excerpt:
I am sharing an open research artifact that may be relevant to SGLang's structured-generation path.

GSP (Grammar-Conditioned Sparse Projection) consumes a packed grammar legality mask before/during the target-model LM-head projection instead of computing the full vocabulary projection and masking afterward.

The current artifact includes:
- packed-mask row-sparse Triton projection for latency-oriented decoding
- batched block-GEMM that skips grammar-inactive vocabulary tiles
- density-aware dense fallback for permissive/mixed states
- support/top-1 correctness checks
- raw paired end-to-end Qwen3.5-2B results

On the reference RTX 5060 Laptop GPU, 30 paired AB/BA trials gave median end-to-end ratios of 1.0756x (enum JSON), 1.0642x (tool-call JSON), and 1.0842x (nested-array JSON). The free-string control is not claimed as a reliable mean speedup.

This is not claiming first invention of batch-1 grammar-aware LM-head filtering; the contribution boundary is the packed-mask batched execution, heterogeneous routing, and controlled target-model evaluation.

I would especially value:
- SGLang integration feedback
- datacenter GPU replication
- heterogeneous-batch measurements
- negative results / dense-winning crossover cases

Release, verified preprint, source, raw evidence:
https://github.com/StealthEyeLLC/grammar-sparse-projection/releases/tag/v0.1.1

items.title: Questions on Triton basic concepts
items.author: peastman
items.body_excerpt:
I'm just getting started with Triton.  I can't find any documentation on some very basic concepts.  If you can point me to something I missed I'd be grateful.  If not, perhaps someone could answer these questions?

What types of values can be passed to a kernel?  PyTorch tensors obviously, as well as ints, floats, and bools.  Anything else?

The grid is defined by a lambda that takes a single argument called `meta`.  What is `meta`?

How do I access a single element of a tensor?  Say `a` and `b` are tensors and `i` is an int.  I want to write `c = a[i]*b` to multiply `b` by an element of `a`.  That produces an error.  What's the correct way of doing it?

What is the difference between a `tensor_descriptor` and a `TensorDescriptor`?  What is each used for and how do I use them?

What is the exact significance of annotating an argument with `tl.constexpr`?  Does it mean the kernel will get recompiled every time a new value of that argument is encountered?  What can be done with a constexpr value that can't be done with other ones?

How about `tl.const`?  Is it just for error checking, to avoid accidentally modifying something that shouldn't be modified, or does it have other effects?

Thanks for your help!

items.title: [RFC] Asymmetric P/D deployment for DeepSeek-V4.1 Flash
items.author: gz944367214
items.body_excerpt:
## Summary This RFC proposes an asymmetric Prefill/Decode deployment for DeepSeek-V4.1 Flash. For a prompt of length `N` and replay window `W = 128`: - The **Prefill worker** processes only the prefix `[0, N-W)` and produces its KV cache. - The **Decode worker** receives that prefix KV and processes the final prompt window `[N-W, N)` as a bounded prefill/replay. - Decode then samples the first output token and continues normal speculative decoding with per-request `q_len = 1 + num_spec_tokens`. The key property is that Decode does not need separate encoder and decoder workloads. Every layer sees the same token count in a given step: ```text first Decode step: L0-L39 process W prompt tokens later Decode steps: L0-L39 process 1 + num_spec_tokens tokens per request ``` ```text P: prompt tokens [0, N-W) -> prefix KV | v D: prompt tokens [N-W, N) -> first output token D: generated tokens -> normal decode / speculative verify ``` The Prefill worker only needs the causal encoder and the decoder's first KV-producing projection path. The Decode worker keeps the full model. The main goal is to remove almost half of the model weights from each Prefill replica. A secondary goal is to avoid running a separate, low-density late-decoder workload on Prefill. Decode remains architecturally simple: its first step is a bounded prefill through the full model, followed by normal decode steps through the same full model. ## Motivation DeepSeek-V4.1 Flash has 40 transformer layers, a sliding-window size of 128, and shared compressed-KV source layers at 2, 8, 14, and 20. With the current decoder bounded-replay optimization, Prefill still loads the full model: ```text L0-L20: process the full uncached prompt L21-L39: process only the final 128 tokens ``` This saves arithmetic in the late layers, but it has two limitations: 1. Prefill still stores all late decoder weights, even though those layers process only a short window. 2. Prefill usually has few concurrent requests, so the late-layer MoE kernels see only a small number of tokens. The proposed design moves the entire final prompt window to Decode instead of changing the token set in the middle of the model. All Decode layers therefore process the same rows in every step. ## Proposed Design ### Model placement and token split ```mermaid flowchart LR I[Prompt: N tokens] I -->| Compute N-W| P I -->| Compute final W tokens| D subgraph P[Prefill worker: partial model] PE[Encoder L0-L19] PK[L20 KV / Indexer
projection path] PE --> PK end subgraph D[Decode worker: full model] BR[First step: bounded prefill
L0-L39, q_len = W] FT[Sample first token] ND[Later steps: normal decode
L0-L39, q_len = 1 + num_spec_tokens] BR --> FT --> ND end P -->| Transfer N-W KV | D ``` For prompts shorter than the window, P performs no model forward and D processes the complete prompt. For the current checkpoint, the conceptual ownership is: | Worker | Resident model components | Work | | --- | --- | --- | | Prefill | Embedding, causal encoder L0-L19, minimal L20 KV/Indexer projection modules | Prefix `[0, N-W)` | | Decode | Full L0-L39 model and LM head | Final prompt window, first token, and subsequent decode | ### Request flow ```mermaid sequenceDiagram participant P as Prefill worker participant D as Decode worker P->>P: Run prefix tokens [Prefix, N-W) P->>P: Produce prefix KV P->>D: Send KV D->>D: First step: run final W tokens through L0-L39 D->>D: Sample the first output token D->>D: Later steps: Normal decode ``` Moving first-token generation to Decode is an intentional part of the proposal. To minimize changes to the P-node scheduler, the P-node can compute the entire prompt (N tokens) instead of (N−W) tokens, since W is generally much smaller than N and the resulting redundant computation is negligible. ### Uniform full-model execution on Decode Decode has two step shapes, but no encoder/decoder layer split: ```text new request, first step: q_len = W_i, where W_i <= 128 active layers = L0-L39 later speculative decode steps: q_len = 1 + num_spec_tokens active layers = L0-L39 ``` If bounded-prefill requests and ongoing decode requests are scheduled in the same iteration, their sequence lengths are still different, so piecewise CUDA graphs may be useful. This is only a request-level scheduling issue: within either request type, all model layers execute the same number of rows. ## Why This May Help ### 1. Smaller Prefill Instance P no longer needs the complete decoder stack or LM head. It retains only the encoder and the minimal projection modules needed to create the shared prefix KV. This is expected to remove close to half of the model weights from each Prefill replica. An important deployment target is fitting one production Prefill replica on a single B300 GPU. ### 2. Avoid a separate low-density decoder tail on P The bounded replay contains at most 128 tokens per new request. Running it on P produces a small decoder-layer MoE batch because Prefill batchsize is usually low. On D, bounded prefill is a normal full-model step over up to 128 tokens per new request. It can be batched across newly admitted requests and, where useful, scheduled alongside the larger Decode workload. The arithmetic is not eliminated, but P no longer runs a separate late-layer tail with low token density. ### 3. Cleaner and uniform execution semantics P only processes a prefix ending at `N-W`. Chunked Prefill, Prefix cache and context parallelism apply normally to that prefix. D receives ordinary token IDs for the final window and executes an ordinary bounded prefill. This avoids changing `q_len` between encoder and decoder layers. The same logical prompt should produce the same split regardless of the Prefill chunk size. ## Cost and Trade-offs T
