items.title: [Bug] [XPU] DSpark drafts all rejected under full decode graph with TP=2: TP ranks diverge on draft graph replay
items.author: arathi-hlab
items.body_excerpt:
### Checklist

- [x] I searched related issues but found no solution.
- [x] The bug persists in the latest version.
- [x] Environment info and a reproducible test are included below.

### Describe the bug

On Intel XPU, DSpark speculative decoding with `--cuda-graph-backend-decode full` and `--tp 2` rejects almost every draft: accept length is ~1.0, vs ~3.3 without the decode graph. Output stays correct, because the target verify runs eagerly and corrects every token, but speculative decoding gives no speedup.

Found in the Intel kernel-main nightly, 2-GPU job (https://github.com/sgl-project/sglang/actions/runs/39063278229). It was hidden behind a CUDA-only assert that crashed `setUpClass`, which is fixed in #45033. That PR also disables `test/registered/e2e/xpu/test_dspark_intel_xpu.py` in the XPU nightly registry until this issue is fixed.

**Expected:** Accept length close to eager mode: `TestBasicSanityDSparkXpuIntelXpu` (no decode graph) averages ~3.25, and Triton without a graph ~3.33.

**Actual:** `AssertionError: avg_spec_accept_length=1.000 did not exceed threshold 2.0`. 288 of 291 decode logs show `accept len: 1.00`. Accuracy tests in the same class pass, because the target verify runs eagerly and corrects every token.

#### Investigation

| Experiment | Avg accept length |
|---|---|
| No decode graph, intel_xpu / triton | 3.25 / 3.33 |
| Full graph, intel_xpu (CI config) | 1.00 |
| Full graph, triton backend | 1.00 |
| Full graph + `SGLANG_SPEC_TP_SYNC=all,-dspark-draft` (no in-graph draft broadcast) | 1.00 |
| Full graph + `SGLANG_DSPARK_USE_GREEDY_DRAFT=1` (argmax draft) | 1.10 |
| Full graph + `SGLANG_DSPARK_FOLDED_PROPOSAL=0` (sampler outside graph) | 1.52 |
| Full graph + `UR_L0_V2_FORCE_DISABLE_COPY_OFFLOAD=1` | 1.00 |

Debug dumps:
- **Inputs are correct.** For the same step, the draft graph's attention metadata matches eager exactly: `cache_seqlens=[13]`, `cu_seqlens_q=[0,7]`, `cu_seqlens_k=[0,13]`, page 1, write slots 134..140. Target hidden states are injected into the draft KV eagerly in both modes (`commit_hidden`; the CUDA-only verify epilogue isn't used on XPU).
- **Outputs are wrong from the first step.** With the same bonus token, positions, and seq_len, eager drafts `[13, 576, 3283, 374, ...]` and graph drafts `[1103, 49614, 748, ...]`. After that, the graph's last 6 draft tokens are the same at every step.
- **TP ranks diverge only in graph mode.** I ran the same draft batch eagerly, then through the graph, and compared `hidden_states`. Eager: both ranks have identical per-row norms (107.7, 110.9, 112.9, ...). Graph: rank 0 gives (113.5, 113.4, 114.3, ...) and rank 1 gives (113.3, 110.9, 111.2, ...). After a TP all-reduce the ranks must match, so the reduction doesn't take effect in the replayed XPU graph.

#### Suspected cause

On XPU, `GroupCoordinator.all_reduce` routes to `inplace_all_reduce`, which calls `torch.distributed.all_reduce` on the XCCL device group. Inside `torch.xpu.XPUGraph` capture, the collective is likely executed at capture time but not recorded (oneCCL works on its own queue), so replays skip it and each rank carries its partial sum.

Not yet confirmed for non-speculative models: XPU CI never runs a decode graph with TP>1 (all decode logs in the 2-GPU job show `cuda graph: False`, since XPU defaults decode graphs off). An attempt with Llama-3.1-8B TP=2 + full graph stalled in graph capture (scheduler watchdog) while another experiment shared GPU 1, so it needs a clean rerun.

#### Suggested next steps

1. Rerun Llama-3.1-8B TP=2 with `--cuda-graph-backend-decode full` on idle GPUs and check gsm8k. If it also degrades, the bug is general to XPU decode graphs with TP>1.
2. Short term: have `handle_xpu_backends` (`python/sglang/srt/arg_groups/platform_hook.py`) disable the decode graph when tp_size > 1, with a warning.
3. Long term: a graph-capturable all-reduce on XPU (sglang custom all-reduce, or XCCL/oneCCL recording into SYCL graphs). Then re-enable `test_dspark_intel_xpu.py`.

The debug patches (draft-token dump, attention-metadata dump, eager-vs-graph hidden-state compare) and the full logs from the Intel CI runner are available on request.

### Reproduction

1. Apply PR #45033, or at least its `dspark_draft_sampler.py` change. Without it, setUpClass crashes first.
2. Re-enable the file locally, then run:
   `python3 test/registered/e2e/xpu/test_dspark_intel_xpu.py TestBasicSanityDSparkXpuIntelXpuDecodeGraph.test_fwd_occupancy`
   That class is `TestBasicSanityDSparkXpuIntelXpu` plus `--cuda-graph-backend-decode full`.

### Environment

- Runner: aicf-jf-cicd-06, 8x Arc Pro B60 (BMG), kernel 6.17.0-35-generic (xe), GuC fw 70.45.2
- Image: `intel/sglang-dev:latest-kernel-main` (a890b33dced6): sglang 0.5.23.dev300+g8dee3f6bd, sgl-kernel-xpu 0.4.0, torch 2.14.0+xpu
- Model: Qwen/Qwen3-14B target + deepseek-ai/dspark_qwen3_14b_block7 draft, bf16, `--tp 2 --base-gpu-id 1`
- Attention: `intel_xpu` for target and draft (Triton behaves the same)

items.title: [Bug] Unbounded compiled-grammar cache in BaseGrammarBackend leaks host memory with per-request JSON schemas
items.author: GinDoliee
items.body_excerpt:
### Checklist
- [x] 1. I have searched related issues but cannot get the expected help.
- [x] 2. The bug has not been fixed in the latest version (the cache code is unchanged on `main` as of 2026-10-19).
- [x] 3. Environment info and a minimal reproducible script are included below.
- [x] 4. This is a bug report, not a question.
- [x] 5. Written in English.

## Describe the bug

`BaseGrammarBackend.cache` (`python/sglang/srt/constrained/base_grammar_backend.py`) is a plain `dict` with no size limit, and the xgrammar backend creates `GrammarCompiler(tokenizer_info=tokenizer_info)` with xgrammar's default unbounded internal cache. Every request whose `response_format.json_schema` (or regex / EBNF) has not been seen before adds one compiled grammar to both caches, and nothing ever evicts it while the server is up. Only `/flush_cache` clears it, and `/flush_cache` is refused unless the scheduler is completely idle.

When clients send a slightly different schema per request (very common with LLM-agent frameworks that embed per-call enums, defaults, descriptions or examples in the schema), scheduler RSS grows linearly until host RAM and swap are exhausted.

## What we observed (production, 2026-10-13)

- Qwen3.6-35B-A3B-FP8, SGLang 0.5.10.post1, `--tp-size 1 --dp-size 4`, 4× H100 NVL, 128 GB host RAM + 61 GB swap.
- One client sent ~8,000 structured-output requests/day with ~1,250 distinct schemas (same prompt family, per-call enum/const values inside the schema).
- Each DP rank's scheduler process grew from 3.5 GB to 35 GB over 11 days; total 4 ranks ≈ 140 GB (RAM + swap full), server became unresponsive, 25-minute outage until manual restart.
- Memory never returned while idle. Growth happened only while structured-output requests were processed.

Measured cost per *new* schema (vocab 151k, xgrammar 0.1.32): **+250–380 MB RSS per scheduler process**. Re-sending the *same* schema 4× costs ~+6 MB total. A 60 KB schema costs several GB.

## Reproduction

Start any model with default args (xgrammar backend). Then:

```python
import json, requests, uuid
URL = "http://127.0.0.1:30000/v1/chat/completions"
for i in range(20):
    schema = {"type": "object",
              "properties": {f"field_{j}": {"type": "string", "enum": [f"{uuid.uuid4()}" for _ in range(5)]} for j in range(30)},
              "required": [f"field_{j}" for j in range(30)]}
    body = {"model": "default", "max_tokens": 64,
            "messages": [{"role": "user", "content": "Return an object."}],
            "response_format": {"type": "json_schema", "json_schema": {"name": f"s{i}", "schema": schema}}}
    requests.post(URL, json=body, timeout=120)
```

Watch `VmRSS` of the `sglang::scheduler` process between requests: it grows by hundreds of MB per iteration and does not come back. Sending the same schema 20× does not grow it.

## Expected behavior

The compiled-grammar cache should be bounded (LRU by entry count and/or bytes), and the bound should be configurable. A request that is never repeated should not permanently consume host memory.

## Proposed fix (I can open PRs)

1. Make `BaseGrammarBackend.cache` an LRU (`OrderedDict`, evict oldest on insert) with a configurable max entry count. In-flight requests already hold their own `copy()` of the grammar object, so eviction is safe.
2. Pass `cache_limit_bytes` to xgrammar's `GrammarCompiler` (xgrammar ≥ 0.1.21 supports it) with a sane default (e.g. 1 GiB).
3. Optionally skip caching grammars whose key string exceeds a size threshold (very large schemas are almost never reused and dominate memory).

We have been running (1)+(2)+(3) in production since 2026-10-14: 17.5 h uptime now plateaus at 12–21 GB total across 4 ranks instead of growing without bound, throughput unchanged (333 vs 334 tok/s single stream).

## Environment

- SGLang 0.5.10.post1 (problem code is unchanged on current `main`: `self.cache: Dict[...] = {}`, `GrammarCompiler(tokenizer_info=tokenizer_info)`)
- xgrammar 0.1.32, torch 2.x, CUDA 12.x, 4× NVIDIA H100 NVL, Ubuntu 20.04
- Grammar backend: xgrammar (default)

items.title: Vague CompilationError
items.author: fpgaminer
items.body_excerpt:
Working on a kernel I got a CompilationError when trying to launch it, and while the CompilationError message points to the "problem" it doesn't specify what the problem is.  I eventually figured out that it doesn't like when you call `load` with `other` set but `mask` set to None.  I don't mind that restriction, but it would be nice if the CompilationError message said something to that effect.  I didn't see any specifics in the error message.  Perhaps it's buried in the traceback, but the trackback gets truncated in Jupyter notebooks because it's so exceedingly long.

Triton version 2.0.0.dev20221202

The kernel:

```
@triton.jit
def _clip_embed_fused(
	A,         # *Pointer* to first input vector (257xN).
	Out,       # *Pointer* to output vector (257xN).
	Position,  # *Pointer* position vector (257xN).
	Weight,    # *Pointer* weight vector (N).
	Bias,      # *Pointer* bias vector (N).
	eps: tl.constexpr,
):
	# position of elements processed by this program
	row = tl.program_id(0)
	Out += row * 1024
	A += row * 1024
	Position += row * 1024

	# loads
	cols = tl.arange(0, 1024)
	mask = cols < 1024
	a = tl.load(A + cols, other=0.).to(tl.float32)
	weight = tl.load(Weight + cols)
	bias = tl.load(Bias + cols)
	position = tl.load(Position + cols, other=0.).to(tl.float32)

	# position embedding
	a += position

	# compute mean
	mean = tl.sum(a, axis=0) / 1024

	# compute variance
	var = tl.sum((a - mean) * (a - mean), axis=0) / 1024
	rstd = 1 / tl.sqrt(var + eps)

items.title: [Bug]: Cross-request context contamination via shared-prefix KV reuse in PD disaggregation with automatic prefix caching — clean with `--no-enable-prefix-caching`
items.author: Siquan-Li
items.body_excerpt:
## Summary

With automatic prefix caching enabled (the default) in a NIXL prefill/decode disaggregated deployment serving DeepSeek-V4.1-Flash, responses intermittently contain **content from other requests** — cross-request context contamination ("crosstalk"). We have a scriptable reproducer on `/v1/chat/completions` (details below): with a long **identical shared prefix** across requests, 46/48 *sequential* requests returned another request's canary code; at concurrency 128 it was 122/128. Disabling prefix caching on the prefill node **and** all decode nodes (`--no-enable-prefix-caching`) eliminated the contamination.

## Deployment topology (at reproduction time)

```
Clients (multi-turn agent sessions; every request starts with the same large system prompt)
        |
        v
vllm-router 0.1.15  --policy round_robin --kv-connector nixl   (port 30000)
        |
   +----+------------------+
   v                       v
Prefill node              2x Decode nodes
1x node, 8x H100, TP=8    1x node each, 8x H100, TP=8
kv_producer  :8001        kv_consumer  :8002
        \____ NIXL KV transfer ____/
```

(Since 2026-10-12 we run 2P1D; all reproduction data below was collected on the 1P2D topology above.)

## Environment

- vLLM 0.31.0, built from main @ `db9527a46` (2026-10-02), local build tagged `+cu129`; torch 2.13.0+cu129, transformers 5.17.0, nixl 1.4.1
- Driver 550.54.15, nodes of 8× H100 80GB (sm90)
- Model: DeepSeek-V4.1-Flash (1M context), `FLASHMLA_SPARSE_DSV41` attention backend, block size 64
- Speculative decoding: `{"method":"dspark","num_speculative_tokens":5,"draft_sample_method":"probabilistic","rejection_sample_method":"block","enable_adaptive_verification":true}`
- `--max-num-batched-tokens 4096 --max-num-seqs 32 --gpu-memory-utilization 0.92`
- Note: PR #57662 (fix for #57661) was **not merged** at the time of writing, so this build cannot contain it.

## Symptom

Every request shares a long common prefix — in the wild this was Claude Code on the Anthropic-compatible `/v1/messages` endpoint, whose fixed large system prompt is identical across all sessions. With automatic prefix caching on, users in **different, unrelated sessions** intermittently received responses containing content from *another* session (the model "remembered" details, file names, or instructions belonging to someone else's conversation). Affected requests completed with HTTP 200; no errors or warnings in server logs.

## Reproducer (scriptable, `/v1/chat/completions`)

Design: N requests, each consisting of a **long identical shared prefix** plus a per-request distinct tail that embeds a unique canary code. After all responses complete, each output is scanned for canary codes belonging to *other* requests ("foreign" hits).

Results with automatic prefix caching **enabled** (default):

| Scenario | Requests | Outputs containing a foreign canary code |
|---|---|---|
| Sequential (C=1) | 48 | **46/48** |
| Concurrent (C=128) | 128 | **122/128** |

Key observations:

- Concurrency is **not** required — sequential single-stream requests contaminate at ~96%. Sharing a long identical prefix is the trigger.
- Canaries that varied the prefix, or shared only long *suffixes*, did **not** reproduce; earlier negative canary results were a design gap, not evidence against the bug.
- With `--no-enable-prefix-caching` on P **and** both D nodes: 0 foreign hits, and the Claude Code symptom disappeared entirely (verified by the same users plus a 16-way concurrent keepalive, ~3,000 rounds over 17 h).

The canary script is available on request.

## What we have *not* isolated

- We disabled prefix caching on all three nodes at once, so we cannot attribute the reuse to the prefill-side cache, the decode-side cache, or the P↔D KV-transfer interplay (e.g. a consumer trusting producer block IDs for freed/reused blocks, or refcount/eviction asymmetry between P and D).
- No root-cause analysis on the vLLM side yet; happy to invest in narrowing this down with maintainer guidance.

## Hypothesis (unverified)

Under PD disaggregation, prefix-cache blocks belonging to a completed request are re-served to a later request that hashes to the same shared prefix, but the physical KV content behind those blocks has been freed/reassigned — so the later request decodes against another request's KV. The serial (C=1) repro suggests the race is between request completion/reuse bookkeeping rather than simultaneous scheduling.

## Why this is not #57661

#57661 (and fix PR #57662 — still unmerged) describes NIXL transfer regions deduplicated by `base_addr` alone, truncating the compressor `state_cache` transfer for hybrid-attention layers, producing **garbled/empty output**. Our failure mode is different:

1. Symptom: our outputs are coherent but contain **another request's content**; we never observed garbling or empty content/reasoning fields.
2. Toggle sensitivity: our contamination disappears completely with `--no-enable-prefix-caching`; the region-geometry bug in #57661 is independent of the prefix-caching toggle.
3. Mechanism: truncated/misaligned compressor state cannot inject well-formed content from a different request.

We plan to validate our repro against #57662's branch as well, to rule out any interaction; both issues affect the same model + NIXL PD combination with silent HTTP-200 failures.

## Related issues

- #57661 — NIXL P/D silent output corruption (hybrid-attention region dedup), fix PR #57662 (unmerged at writing)
- #56009 — request/response cross-talk symptom, no root cause identified
- #52627 — silent output corruption in 1P1D NIXL PD, different connector combination
- #47930 — DSpark draft acceptance collapse with automatic prefix caching (another prefix-caching × disaggregation interaction)

## Offer

We keep a H100 1P2D/2P1D testbed with this exact model and can: share the canary script, run targeted repro attempts on candidate patches (including #57662), or provide `collect_env.py` output on request.

items.title: [Bug]: Intermittent XGrammar request termination with V2 DFlash probabilistic drafting and block rejection
items.author: tomasruizt
items.body_excerpt:
[Machine-written]

### Environment

Upstream main at `a7b7bc1fbe1f5c4e47c53b0f02a3ecfbcd8054b9`, Model Runner V2, one H100 80GB per server, TP=1, PP=1. Python 3.12.12, PyTorch 2.13.0+cu130, xgrammar 0.2.8, transformers 5.19.0, flashinfer-python 0.7.0.post1, NVIDIA driver 580.126.09. Source checkout with precompiled extensions.

### Observed failure

A valid structured JSON request was terminated during generation with Qwen3-4B, DFlash probabilistic drafting, block rejection sampling and async scheduling. The schema has category/priority enums and free-text advice. Sampling was temperature=1, top-k=50, top-p=0.9, max_tokens=512, with an explicit per-request seed and thinking disabled.

Three 61-request runs at concurrency 1 and two 540-request runs at concurrency 16 completed. During the third concurrency-16 run, the server logged:

```text
[backend_xgrammar.py:201] Failed to advance FSM for request chatcmpl-b2055da1fad0f46b-a7547c73 for tokens 0. Please file an issue.
[scheduler.py:2199] Unexpected: grammar rejected tokens [756, 414, 0] for request chatcmpl-b2055da1fad0f46b-a7547c73. Terminating request.
[serving.py:203] Request chatcmpl-b2055da1fad0f46b failed with an internal error during generation
```

The streaming client received `{"message":"Internal server error","type":"InternalServerError","param":null,"code":500}`. This was an error in the SSE stream, not an observed initial HTTP 500 response. Tokens `[756, 414, 0]` decode to `",\n`, five spaces, and `!`.

**This report does not claim an engine crash.** The benchmark runner raised on the failed request and then explicitly sent SIGTERM to its server. We did not check server health between that original failure and the runner's shutdown.

### Reproduction status

The original run on October 12, 2026 **did fail**. Its measured batches were:

| Original run | Requests planned | Observed failures | Outcome |
|---|---:|---:|---|
| Concurrency 1, repeats 1–3 | 183 (3 × 61) | 0 | All three completed |
| Concurrency 16, repeats 1–2 | 1,080 (2 × 540) | 0 | Both completed |
| Concurrency 16, repeat 3 | 540 | 1 | Aborted at the first observed failure |

Warmup and pilot requests are excluded from this table. The failed batch did not complete, and its completed-request count was not retained. **We cannot infer a failure rate of 1/540.** The confirmed observation is one failed request during that third concurrency-16 batch, logged at `16:52:32` in the server log.

I have not obtained a reliable minimal reproducer. The table below covers only the **subsequent clean reduction attempts**, not the original failing run. Those attempts completed 26,742 requests without reproducing the error:

| Attempt | Requests | Failed |
|---|---:|---:|
| Original schema, concurrency 16, initial rerun | 1,620 | 0 |
| Original schema, new seeds, concurrency 16 and 64 | 10,800 | 0 |
| Two-choice and single-field schemas, concurrency 1, 16 and 64 | 6,144 | 0 |
| Original schema, warmup/pilot stages and workload order, including concurrency 64 | 8,178 | 0 |

The reduction runner kept the server alive after requests and checked `/health` after every batch. All those health checks returned 200. These passing attempts do not establish recovery after the original failure, nor prove the bug is fixed.

The commands and self-contained client below reproduce the workload conditions, **not a guaranteed failure**. Prefix caching is disabled and the same server is reused across repeats. The exact failing request's index/seed was not retained by the original fail-fast runner.

```bash

export OMP_NUM_THREADS=1
CUDA_VISIBLE_DEVICES=0 vllm serve Qwen/Qwen3-4B \
  --served-model-name benchmark --host 127.0.0.1 --port 19213 \
  --max-model-len 2048 --max-num-seqs 64 --gpu-memory-utilization 0.85 \
  --no-enable-prefix-caching --disable-uvicorn-access-log --async-scheduling \
  --structured-outputs-config '{"backend":"xgrammar"}' \
  --speculative-config '{"method":"dflash","model":"z-lab/Qwen3-4B-DFlash-b16","num_speculative_tokens":15,"draft_sample_method":"probabilistic","rejection_sample_method":"block"}'
```

### Request-side workload

Save the client below as `repro.py`, then run it in a second terminal while the server above is running:

```bash
python -m pip install aiohttp
BASE_URL=http://127.0.0.1:19213 python -u repro.py

The client includes the full prompt, JSON schema and per-request sampling seeds. It reports request failures and server health without shutting down the server.

items.title: [RFC]: Explicit row layouts for routed-expert capture
items.author: Liamup777
items.body_excerpt:
## Motivation

Routed-expert capture (R3, `enable_return_routed_experts`) records the logical expert IDs selected for each token on the current DP rank. The router computes `topk_ids` and invokes `capture_fn` before EPLB maps logical IDs to physical experts. The current `RoutedExpertsCapturer.capture(layer_id, topk_ids)` then infers which rows belong to this DP rank from the tensor's row count and `dp_metadata`.

That inference works for the layouts currently encoded in the capturer, but an out-of-tree MoE backend can split, gather, and pad `hidden_states` and `router_logits` **before routing**. The resulting `topk_ids` inherits that physical row layout. Row count alone does not describe the ownership, ordering, or padding of those rows. In particular, different TP ranks can see different row counts in the same forward, so inferring whether to enter a collective from each rank's local shape is unsafe.

vLLM-Ascend currently [replaces the entire capturer method](https://github.com/vllm-project/vllm-ascend/blob/main/vllm_ascend/patch/worker/patch_routed_experts_capture.py) to handle its communication layouts. This duplicates upstream capture logic and couples it to Ascend communication modes. A previous [padded all-gather fix, #43737](https://github.com/vllm-project/vllm/pull/43737), addressed one layout by adding another shape branch; the broader issue is that the component which knows the row arrangement cannot communicate it to the capturer.

### Concrete Ascend layouts

These are **routing-input layouts before expert dispatch**, not the later EP all-to-all exchange of token activations:

1. **All2All with uneven TP shards.** For five local token rows `[A,B,C,D,E]` and TP=2, Ascend's prepare stage can split the routing inputs into `[A,B,C]` on TP0 and `[D,E]` on TP1. The router therefore produces 3 and 2 rows of `topk_ids`. With DP metadata, the upstream SP branch recognizes only `ceil(5/2)=3`: TP0 may enter the capture all-gather while TP1 does not match that branch. Without DP metadata, the current early return treats each shard as a complete local capture. The desired recorded order is `[A,B,C,D,E]`.

2. **MC2/SP with padding inside each TP shard.** For the same five rows, a fixed per-rank physical capacity of four can produce `[A,B,C,pad]` and `[D,E,pad,pad]`. After gathering, the valid rows are at `[0:3]` and `[4:6]`; taking the first five rows would include a padding row and omit `E`. An unpadded local row count and a padded physical shard size are both needed.

3. **Padded DP all-gather.** If DP0 has five rows and DP1 has seven, padding each to seven before DP all-gather yields `[DP0's 5,pad,pad,DP1's 7]`, or 14 rows. The unpadded total is 12. DP1's rows start at physical offset 7, not logical offset 5. This is the case motivating #43737.

These examples show why adding more `n == ...` cases to the generic capturer is brittle: the producer of the physical layout already knows the exact split sizes and valid row ranges, while the capturer does not.

## Proposed Change

Allow the capture call to accept an **optional, backend-provided row layout**. One possible minimal contract is:

```python
@dataclass(frozen=True)
class RoutedExpertsCaptureLayout:
    # Ordered (start, length) spans after an optional gather.
    source_ranges: tuple[tuple[int, int], ...]
    gather_group: dist.ProcessGroup | None = None
    shard_sizes: tuple[int, ...] = ()

def capture(
    self,
    layer_id: int,
    topk_ids: torch.Tensor,
    *,
    layout: RoutedExpertsCaptureLayout | None = None,
) -> None: ...
```

A backend that transforms routing inputs would construct this description in its MoE preparation stage and pass it through expert selection to the existing router capture callback. The capturer would optionally gather `topk_ids`, select the ordered valid ranges, validate bounds and shard sizes, then write the current DP rank's rows into its existing device buffer. In the examples above, All2All uses `shard_sizes=(3,2), source_ranges=((0,5),)`; padded MC2 uses `(4,4), ((0,3),(4,2))`; padded DP all-gather needs no capture-time gather and selects the current DP block directly.

When `layout=None`, existing backends retain the current inference path. The callback remains after logical expert selection and before EPLB mapping. No model-specific structure or public R3 output format changes are proposed. Layout construction and any capture-only collective happen only when routed-expert capture is enabled.

This is a proposed **minimal row-restoration contract**, not a claim that gather-plus-ranges describes every possible backend layout. The implementation PR can be scoped to the capturer/router seam and unit tests; vLLM-Ascend would supply layouts and remove its method replacement separately.

### Design questions

- Is an optional row layout on the capture call the right extension point, or would maintainers prefer a backend-provided normalization callback?
- Is an optional gather followed by ordered contiguous ranges an appropriate minimal representation? Should the name emphasize that it is a capture plan rather than a general MoE token layout?
- What validation should the core capturer enforce for equal/unequal shards, collective participation, and graph replay stability?

## Validation plan and current status

A local prototype covers the three layouts with unit tests, including mocked collectives and invalid-range checks. These establish the interface behavior, not NPU/HCCL correctness. Before a ready implementation PR, we plan to compare captured per-token, per-layer logical IDs with a routing reference on real NPU workers across TP=1/2, uneven DP=2 batches, All2All, MC2, and AllGather paths, including padding. We will also validate the intended eager/graph execution modes, repeated steps, and symmetric collective participation. Those real multi-DP and graph results are **not claimed by this RFC**.

## Feedback period

At least one week for design feedback before treating the proposed API as se

items.title: What is the first practical limit of persistent KV across Agent steps?
items.author: RyanX0198
items.body_excerpt:
Hi maintainers — I’m Rui from Psync.labs. Recent sampling and decode-interface work led me to a question about long-running local Agent workloads.

Persistent KV could reduce repeated prefill, but only if cache identity, layout, eviction and framework boundaries stay correct as models, adapters and stages change. Which condition is most likely to invalidate the idea in practice: layout incompatibility, model or tokenizer changes, fragmentation, eviction quality loss, scheduler interference, or missing cross-framework contracts?

One counterexample or minimum test would be especially useful. @yzh119

— Rui, Psync.labs

comments.author: eprogressing
comments.body:
For an agent that changes adapters or rewrites its prompt between steps, I would check **cache identity/correctness before fragmentation or scheduling**. That is a conditional priority, not a measured ranking of workloads.

A concrete counterexample is switching from adapter A to adapter B while retaining A's KV. If B changes the value projection (or earlier hidden states), identical token IDs and identical tensor shapes do not make those cached values valid for B. Similarly, editing earlier tool results breaks reuse past the unchanged token prefix in an ordinary causal transformer. Rendering the same conversation differently can also change that prefix.

I would start with this small integration test:

1. Under A, prefill a short token prefix P, then process suffix S using the cached prefix. Compare the next-token logits with a fresh A forward pass on P+S, within an appropriate numerical tolerance.
2. Use a distinct, nonzero B adapter that affects `v_proj`. Repeat with a fresh B prefill as the reference. Your cache manager should reject A's cache; forcibly reusing it is the negative control, which can expose a discrepancy.
3. Edit one early token in P and verify that cache lookup stops at the unchanged prefix. Check logits, rather than just generated text: argmax can hide a difference.

This is consistent with [vLLM's prefix-cache design](https://docs.vllm.ai/en/latest/design/prefix_caching/), which keys blocks using the parent hash, block tokens and extra hashes such as LoRA IDs. Adapter IDs also need versioning/invalidation if their weights can change in place.

After that, check the storage contract separately: [FlashInfer's KV layout documentation](https://docs.flashinfer.ai/tutorials/kv_layout.html) specifies NHD/HND layouts and page metadata. Matching semantics alone does not make a buffer portable between frameworks.

Prepared with Codex assistance from the linked documentation. The integration test above was initially a proposal; the execution update below now supplies an actual mechanism test. Is your agent retaining one model/adapter with append-only history, or switching adapters and rewriting history?


---
**GPU experiment update (2026-10-11):** I ran the actual Transformers/PEFT forward path on an A100-SXM4-40GB, plus CPU controls: Torch 2.14.1+cu130, Transformers 5.19.0, PEFT 0.21.2. This is a random three-layer Llama (hidden 64, four attention heads/two KV heads), with rank-four v_proj LoRA; it does not exercise FlashInfer's attention kernel or a production agent cache manager.

Across seeds 0/1/2, CPU/CUDA and float32/float64, all 72 comparison expectations held. Correct same-adapter reuse, an adapter-name change with exactly zero update, and reuse limited to the two tokens preceding a prefix edit agreed with fresh forwarding (maximum absolute logit error <=1.49e-7; predeclared tolerances float32 1e-5 / float64 1e-10). Forcibly reusing A's KV with nonzero B produced max-absolute differences 0.2205–0.2727; retaining the old full prefix after the edit produced 0.1082–0.2622. Each stale-cache case changed argmax in only 4/12 trials, so comparing all logits matters. Each path used a newly created cache with asserted sequence lengths.

This supports the specific correctness counterexample, not a universal ranking against fragmentation/scheduling. It does not measure answer quality, throughput, cross-framework layout compatibility, or automatic rejection by a cache manager. [Reproduction scripts, full inputs/logits, versions and results](https://gist.github.com/eprogressing/84db3e068aabbe449f8629a3f362a6e5). Prepared with Codex assistance; these runs were actually executed.

## Purpose It's used to share the performance data on Intel GPU with **SYCL backend**. The performance data is only used as reference, since we don't double check the data. It **can not** be used as any commercial purpose. ## Rule 1. Encourage to test with default setting (environment variables). If you want to update the data with special building or running setting, please create a new table. 2. Create/update the tables directly following the format. 3. Insert new record, instead of update it for same keys; Sort the records by col1, col2, col3. 4. Add your comments in the latest for more discussion. 5. Don't add table to compare with other hardware, framework or backend. 6. Please run 1+ times and update with the stable data. ## Tips and tricks 1. Multiple GPUs - Xe driver gives a huge boost over i915. - Combined with IOMMU and Xe, `--split-mode tensor` gives decent number on prefill - 2 x Arc A770 can give usable speeds, at least with benchmark 512+128 regimes. Refer to: https://github.com/ggml-org/llama.cpp/discussions/23313#discussioncomment-18057036 2. FP32 vs FP16 (building) - FP16 made the biggest impact on the performance of PP than FP32, but a little decrease of TG. - FP32 has better accuracy, and TG performance in more LLMs. User can choose them according to the test result. Quick build scripts: ``` ./examples/sycl/build.sh fp32 (default) ./examples/sycl/build.sh fp16 examples\sycl\win-build-sycl.bat fp32 (default) examples\sycl\win-build-sycl.bat fp16 ``` 3. AOT (not recommend to common user) - Build with AOT helping squeeze a few more percent. It can speed up the first startup time by skipping JIT. - It will take more time (n times) and make the binary file increase size to 2-3 times. - It will bring some trouble if you are not familiar with programming. ## Performance data on Intel GPU ### Default setting Build: ``` #fp32 ./examples/sycl/build.sh #fp16 set -DGGML_SYCL_F16=ON in ./examples/sycl/build.sh ./examples/sycl/build.sh ``` Run: ``` # choose the used GPUs in the test. export ONEAPI_DEVICE_SELECTOR="level_zero:0" source /opt/intel/oneapi/setvars.sh ./build/bin/llama-bench -fa 0,1 -m ../models/llama-2-7b.Q4_0.gguf ``` Data: |LLM|GPU|Host|OS|Fp32

items.title: CUDA inference on Qwen3.8-27B Q6_K causes RTX 5090 display loss and NVIDIA GSP/full-chip reset on Linux
items.author: rgalichon
items.body_excerpt:
## Description

Running Qwen3.8-27B Q6_K through llama.cpp on an RTX 5090 can cause the entire graphical display to go black after several normal inference requests. Recovery requires a reboot. The failure reproduces through Codex and previously also through DeepSeek Harness, both using the same local llama.cpp server.

This is not a normal server-only crash: the NVIDIA graphical stack loses the GPU and the desktop becomes unusable.

## Delayed-onset history

Before the first black-screen failure, the same Qwen3.8-27B Q6_K model and llama.cpp backend ran successfully for approximately 2–3 days and tens of hours of inference. The user executed a sequence of substantial coding and verification tasks sequentially, one at a time, with some tasks taking approximately 20 minutes and others taking more than an hour. All preceding tasks completed without a display failure.

The first failure occurred during the final acceptance phase. That phase required the agent to inspect the complete project context, including the product specification, built HTML, source, tests, and acceptance requirements. The phase document itself is only a short acceptance contract; the relevant workload difference was the larger accumulated prompt/context and request sequence, not the size of the markdown file.

After the first display failure, similar black-screen failures recurred after only several subsequent Codex requests, including while running the older kernel 7.0.0-29. This suggests a delayed or workload-triggered CUDA/GPU failure that became reproducible, rather than an immediate model-load incompatibility.

## Cross-runtime reproduction

As a differential test, the user switched Codex from the local llama.cpp endpoint to Ollama's official `qwen3.8:27b-q4_K_M` model tag. This changed the quantization from Q6_K to Q4_K_M, changed the runtime from the local llama.cpp server to Ollama, and removed the original llama.cpp MTP server configuration from the test. The Q4 model was present locally and exposed by Ollama's OpenAI-compatible endpoint.

After using Codex with the Ollama Q4 model, the displays again went black and a reboot was required. This reproduces the critical symptom across both runtimes and quantizations. It does not prove that Ollama itself caused the failure, because both runtimes still depend on the NVIDIA CUDA/GPU stack.

After reboot, Ollama's daemon was running but reported no usable VRAM and fell back to CPU compute; no Ollama model was loaded during the post-reboot inspection. This is consistent with the GPU remaining unavailable after the reset, but the preceding Ollama runner log was not captured.

## Reproduction environment

- OS: Ubuntu 24.04
- Kernel during latest reproduction: 7.0.0-29-generic
- NVIDIA GPU: GeForce RTX 5090, 32607 MiB VRAM
- NVIDIA driver: 610.43.02 open kernel module
- CUDA toolkit used to build llama.cpp: 13.2.86
- llama.cpp commit: 50f068fff
- llama.cpp version: 0.3.0-dev, build 10679
- Model: Qwen3.8-27B-Q6_K GGUF
- GGUF architecture metadata: qwen35
- Model native context metadata: 262144
- Multimodal projector: mmproj-BF16.gguf

## llama-server configuration

```text
-c 196608
-ngl 999
--flash-attn on
--cache-type-k q4_0
--cache-type-v q4_0
--parallel 1
--image-min-tokens 1024
--reasoning on
--reasoning-effort xhigh
--reasoning-format deepseek
--reasoning-preserve
--spec-type draft-mtp
--spec-draft-n-max 2
--spec-draft-type-k q4_0
--spec-draft-type-v q4_0
--host 127.0.0.1
--port 8080
```

Only one llama-server process and one inference slot were active. No second model copy was observed.

## Steps observed

1. Boot Ubuntu with kernel `7.0.0-29-generic`.
2. Start the above llama-server configuration.
3. Use Codex against the local OpenAI-compatible endpoint.
4. Submit approximately 3–4 ordinary coding questions.
5. The server successfully processed multiple requests, including requests with prompts of approximately 8,600, 5,400, 1,400, 1,200, and 900 tokens, and generated normally at approximately 85–117 tokens/second.
6. The display then went black. A reboot was required to recover the graphical session.

## Relevant server behavior before failure

The server logged normal completed requests, including:

```text
n_ctx_slot = 196608
n_slots = 1
is_child = 0
MTP draft acceptance values between approximately 0.50 and 0.90
```

The process then exited:

```text
Main process exited, code=dumped, status=6/ABRT
Failed with result 'core-dump'
```

## Relevant NVIDIA/kernel evidence

Immediately around the failure, the kernel logged repeated NVIDIA GSP RPC failures and full-chip-reset assertions:

```text
NVRM: GPU0 rpcRmApiFree_GSP: GspRmFree failed ... status=0x0000000f
NVRM: GPU0 nvAssertFailedNoLog: Assertion failed: (status == NV_OK) || (status == NV_ERR_GPU_IN_FULLCHIP_RESET)
NVRM: GPU0 _issueRpcAndWait: rpcSendMessage failed with status=0x0000000f
NVRM: GPU0 kgmmuInvalidateTlb_GM107: TLB invalidation failed waiting for prior invalidate (status=0x0000000f)
NVRM: GPU0 _deviceTeardown: Disable of Cuda limit activation failed
```

The graphical session was lost at the same time. Earlier reproductions also logged CUDA failures such as:

```text
CUDA error: unspecified launch failure
CUDA error: the launch timed out and was terminated
CUDA error: an internal operation failed
```

with failures in `ggml_cuda_op_l2_norm`, `cublasSgemm_v2`, `cudaStreamSynchronize`, and `cudaLaunchKernelEx`, followed by NVIDIA display-driver recovery attempts and browser/desktop GPU context loss.

## Comparison information

- The failure occurred previously on kernel `7.0.0-30-generic` as well.
- A short request succeeded once on kernel `7.0.0-29`, but several normal Codex requests later reproduced the black-screen failure on that same kernel.
- Therefore the kernel rollback did not resolve the issue.
- The older llama.cpp build was `0.1.2-dev`, build 10489, commit `169e4a7ff`.
- The current build is a clean upstream build at `50f068fff`; the failure still occurs.
- The NVIDIA driver was pre

items.title: Eval bug: HIP/ROCm on Windows gfx1201 (R9700), batched target scoring changes logits/top-1; Vulkan control is stable
items.author: bluesch2023-web
items.body_excerpt:
llama.cpp b10909
commit a2878d30df0130dde503a7d9ba30d3d21bd71b9f
Windows 11 build 26200
ROCm 10
AMD clang 23.0.0

### Operating systems

Windows

### GGML backends

HIP

### Hardware

AMD Ryzen 9 5900X + AMD Radeon AI PRO R9700 (gfx1201)

### Models

Gemma4 31B

### Problem description & steps to reproduce

I am seeing a reproducible HIP/ROCm correctness issue on Windows with an AMD Radeon AI PRO R9700 (gfx1201).

Using the same Gemma 4 31B model, the same token prefix, the same absolute token positions and seq_id=0, changing only the target scoring shape changes the HIP logits enough to flip the greedy top-1 token.

Environment:

Windows 11 build 26200

AMD Radeon AI PRO R9700 / gfx1201

Driver 32.0.31041.1004

ROCm 10

llama.cpp b10909

Commit a2878d30df0130dde503a7d9ba30d3d21bd71b9f

Model: gemma-4-31B-it-qat-UD-Q4_K_XL.gguf

ctx=2048

batch=512

ubatch=128

threads=6

F16 KV

Flash Attention ON

61 GPU layers

Steps to reproduce:

1. Load the model using the HIP backend.

2. Use a fixed sequence consisting of 29 prompt tokens followed by 26 teacher-forced suffix tokens.

3. Clear KV state before each scoring request.

4. Score the same 27 prediction positions using:

   * single-token scoring
   * three-token batched scoring
   * repeated single-token scoring

5. Request logits for all scored positions. This produces 81 requested output rows in total.

6. Compare the target logits for the same prefix, absolute position and seq_id.

Expected result:

Changing only the scoring batch shape should not change the greedy target token.

Actual HIP result:

The first greedy top-1 reversal occurs at completion index 22, predicting absolute position 51.

Single-token scoring selects token 237646.

Three-token batched scoring selects token 237075.

A second top-1 reversal occurs at index 24.

The repeated single-token run is stable.

Control:

I repeated the same scoring test using Vulkan on the same machine and same llama.cpp b10909 version.

Vulkan passes: all 81 rows are valid, all 27 top-1 predictions remain the same across the tested scoring shapes, and selected full float32 logits rows are byte-identical.

This reproduction does not use MTP or a draft model. The discrepancy occurs in target evaluation itself.

This looks similar in symptom to #28211, but I am not claiming the same root cause. My GPU is a discrete gfx1201 device and hipGetDeviceProperties reports integrated=false.


### First Bad Commit

_No response_

### Relevant log output

There is no crash or HIP runtime error. The scoring process exits normally; the failure is a silent numerical/correctness difference.

Representative captured result:

HIP backend:

completion index: 22

consumed position: 50

predicted absolute position: 51

### Feature Description

llama.cpp has been an integral part of my dissertation. I want to cite to it appropriately. Perhaps consider adding your preferred bibtex citation to the readme.

Adding a preferred citation makes it easier for researchers to properly attribute llama.cpp in their work. Using a common format like bibtex makes copying/pasting easier for citation management.

@software{gerganov_llamacpp_2026,

	author = {Gerganov, Georgi},

}

items.title: DSpark drafters on an 11 GB RTX 2080 Ti: Gemma 4 26B-A4B +76 % code / +24 % prose, and where DSpark loses
items.author: homeofe
items.body_excerpt:
Since DSpark landed (#25173), community drafters have appeared for several models. We measured three of them on consumer hardware with the whole quality and speed setup we use for our own local gateway, including the case where DSpark is slower than what the model already has.

**Hardware:** RTX 2080 Ti 11 GB (Turing, sm_75, PCIe 3.0 x16), Threadripper 3960X (24 cores), 4-channel DDR4-3200, 125 GiB, Linux.

**How we measured:** `llama-server`, 8 prompts (4 code tasks, 4 English prose), 256 tokens, temperature 0, one slot (`-np 1`). Confirmation runs: 3 interleaved rounds, 12 requests per category, median. A request counts only if other processes used under one core before and during it (the box is shared); contaminated passes were rerun. Quality: our hard panel (code with hidden tests, tool scenarios, German, long context, formats) and an agent-tools panel (multi-step tool use), card sampling, 3 seeds.

### Gemma 4 26B-A4B UD-Q4_K_M with williamliao's DSpark drafter

Drafter: `williamliao/dspark_gemma4_26b-a4b-it-GGUF`, Q8_0 (1.3 GB). It loads as is: DFlash backbone with Markov head, block 7 with bonus anchor, its own 32000-token head with a `d2t` map.

```
llama-server -m gemma-4-26B-A4B-it-UD-Q4_K_M.gguf --jinja -c 32768 -np 1 \
  --spec-type draft-dspark -md gemma4_26b-a4b-DSpark-Q8_0.gguf -ngld 99 \
  --spec-draft-n-max 3 --spec-draft-p-min 0 --spec-draft-n-ubatch 32
```

| Setting | Code tok/s | English tok/s | Acceptance code / English |
|---|---:|---:|---:|
| no drafter | 56.1 | 56.3 | |
| DSpark n-max 3 (3 rounds) | **98.7 (+76 %)** | **69.7 (+24 %)** | 84.5 / 54.3 % |
| DSpark n-max 6 (1 round) | 104.0 (+83 %) | 56.6 (+0.4 %) | 67.5 / 33.5 % |
| DSpark n-max 3 on the official b11719 release (1 round) | 99.7 | 69.9 | 85.3 / 52.0 % |

- Panels with DSpark n-max 3: hard 42 of 42 (no drafter: 42 of 42), agent-tools 35 of 36 (no drafter: 35 of 36, the same single miss).
- VRAM 9.9 GB with the drafter, so it fits an 11 GB card with 32K context.
- Greedy texts with the drafter differ from the no-drafter texts on 5 of 8 prompts, always at near-ties; the drafter verifies 4 tokens per step, which changes the batch shape of the target. The panels did not move.

### Ling-3.0-flash IQ4_XS with inclusionAI's DSpark drafter

Drafter: `inclusionAI/Ling-3.0-flash-dspark` (safetensors), converted to GGUF Q8_0 with the stock `convert_hf_to_gguf.py` (no `--dspark` switch; that one is for DeepSeek-V4). Ling does not fit the card, so both rows use the same GPU expert cache from our fork (routed experts in RAM, hot experts in VRAM); only the drafter changes.

| Drafter | Code tok/s | English tok/s | Acceptance code / English |
|---|---:|---:|---:|
| built-in MTP, n-max 3 | 50.9 | 47.5 | 68 / 53 % |
| DSpark n-max 3, p-min 0 (3 rounds) | **66.5 (+31 %)** | **51.9 (+9 %)** | 96 / 58 % |
| DSpark n-max 7, p-min 0.7 (code only) | 78.3 (+54 %) | 47.4 (0 %) | 89 / 79 % |

Panels with DSpark n-max 3 (context 8192): hard 39 of 42 (all three misses are the long-context task, which does not fit 8192), agent-tools 36 of 36.

Why DSpark helps so much here: Ling's MTP head loses accuracy with each extra step (per position 0.84 / 0.61 / 0.47 on English), which is what DSpark's Markov head is meant to fix.

### Qwen3.6-35B-A3B UD-Q4_K_M with williamliao's DSpark drafter: slower on prose

Drafter: `williamliao/Qwen3.6-35B-A3B-DSPARK-GGUF`, Q8_0. Target with `--n-cpu-moe 32`. One round.

| Drafter | Code tok/s | English tok/s |
|---|---:|---:|
| built-in MTP, n-max 2 | 88.6 | 77.2 |
| DSpark n-max 3 | 99.8 (+12.7 %) | 73.5 (-4.8 %) |
| DSpark n-max 7 | 109.9 (+24 %) | 52.0 (-33 %) |

Qwen3.6's own MTP head is already good, so DSpark only pays off on code here. We keep MTP 2 for general use.

### What we take from it

1. Measure against what the model already has. Against no drafter (Gemma 26B) DSpark is a big win; against a strong MTP head (Qwen3.6) it is a trade between code and prose.
2. Block length 3 was the best general setting for all three; longer blocks win on code and lose on prose every time.
3. `--spec-draft-p-min` did not help us on prose with MTP either: acceptance rises, accepted length per step stays the same (details in #25198).
4. Run a quality panel when texts change, even with greedy decoding; here the panels stayed equal.

Raw numbers and scripts can be shared if useful. Thanks to williamliao and inclusionAI for publishing the drafters.

AI disclosure: the measurements were run by AI agents (Anthropic Claude, OpenAI Codex) under our direction on our hardware

items.title: server : reuse image features within a SystemOne request
items.author: mshr-h
items.body_excerpt:
When a `/v1/systemone` request contains several questions about the same image, the server can repeat vision encoding and projection for each question. This adds redundant work as the number of questions grows.

I propose computing the image features once and sharing them across questions within the request. The request would own these features and release them when processing finishes.

I tested a [prototype](https://github.com/mshr-h/llama.cpp/tree/systemone-request-image-features) covering both causal and non-causal paths with:

- d1-omni-600M: FP16 and Q8_0
- vllm-d3-edge, vllm-d3-nano, and d1-3B: Q8_0

Measurements used Jetson AGX Orin, CUDA Release, `parallel=1`, and context/batch/ubatch sizes of 4096. Each condition used the same 30 images at 448x448 over three rounds, excluding warmup and disabling previous-request caching.

For requests with 2, 4, and 8 questions, encode calls decreased from 2, 4, and 8 to 1. Across the 1,350 Before/After request pairs, answers and probabilities matched exactly.

For example, d1-omni-600M FP16 with four questions reduced median server time, including CUDA synchronization, from 246.5 ms to 159.3 ms (-35.37%). Single-question requests retained one encode call; D3-edge Q8_0 showed a 1.16% increase in median server time. Other models, hardware, and `parallel>1` remain untested.

Related work:

- #13366 : a helper for consuming precomputed image embeddings.
- #26994 : repeated image processing when the text suffix changes across requests.
- #30201 : checkpoints after media to address that issue.

AI assistance: Codex generated the implementation, tests, and benchmark scripts. All changes were reviewed by a human.

This issue tracks how the `MasterService` half of RFC #3670 lands in `main`. #4370 carries the whole migration as one PR (+7.3k/−6.6k), which is too large to review, so the work is split into 17 PRs. Each PR builds, passes the tests and is correct on its own, and the order below is the order they can merge in. The code for the whole series is already written. Each PR is cut from the finished end state, so reviewing it means reviewing that slice of a design that is already complete, not code still in progress. Review comments are welcome on any PR in the series, and on this issue for the overall plan. Anyone whose review suggestion is adopted is added as a co-author of the PR that takes it. ## Status Last updated 2026-10-16. In the dependency graph below, green is merged and yellow has an open PR. | Step | PR | State | |---|---|---| | 4. Tenant quota control plane | #4563 | Merged | | 1. Per-key `ObjectState` | #4562 | Merged | | 3. Dynamic replication controller | #4589 | Merged | | 2. Promotion candidate tracker | #4586 | Merged | | 5. Object route | #4585 | Merged | | 9. Accessor contract and write paths | #4717 | Open | | 6. Namespace layer | #4721 | Open | | everything else | — | Waiting on its dependencies | Phase 1 is complete and step 9 (#4717) is open; steps 10 to 14 wait on it. Step 5 is merged and step 6 (#4721) is open; steps 7 and 8 wait on it. ## Design ### Before: shard-level ownership ```mermaid flowchart TB MS["MasterService"] --> SH subgraph SH["1024 MetadataShards (hash of tenant and key, one lock each)"] TS["TenantState
one per shard and tenant"] TS --- MD["metadata map
ObjectMetadata + TenantQuotaLedger"] TS --- SM["7 per-key side maps
+ lease map"] end subgraph SIDE["Also inside MasterService"] GD["GroupDomain
all groups, one lock"] OL["ObjectOperationLock
4096 striped mutexes"] EV["BatchEvict · NoFBatchEvict
EvictTenantMemoryForQuota"] end SH -->|"census of every shard, every pass"| EV ``` - **Ownership.** A shard holds fragments of many tenants. Each `TenantState` in it keeps the object map plus seven separate per-key maps (processing keys, replication, offload and promotion tasks, promotion candidates, dynamic-replication pending records and cooldowns) and a map of dynamic-replication leases. Empty tenant states are erased by hand on about 55 paths. - **Locking.** One shard lock covers every object that hashes to it, so unrelated keys contend. Puts and upserts also take a striped `ObjectOperationLock`. Groups live in a separate single-lock `GroupDomain`. - **Background work.** Memory, NoF and tenant-quota eviction each run a census over all 1024 shards, and the expired-processing sweep walks every object. The eviction denominator depends on a per-shard `disk_object_count`. - **Quota.** Every path that changes replicas books or releases the tenant's charge through the ledger on the object, so correctness depends on each path doing it. - **Subsystems inline.** Dynamic replication, promotion retry, eviction and the quota control plane are all inside `master_service.cpp` (15.2k lines), reading and writing the shard maps directly. ### After: tenant-first namespaces with per-key locks ```mermaid flowchart TB MS["MasterService"] --> NT["NamespaceTable
tenant id → Namespace"] NT --> NS subgraph NS["Namespace (one per tenant)"] RT["ObjectRoute
1024 stripes"] --> KS["KeySlot (one per key)

PromotionCandidateTracker"] QP["TenantQuotaPolicy
(a NamespacePolicy)"] EV["eviction::Evictor"] end KS <-.->|"ObjectState via *Locked"| TASK HOOK -->|"settle charge"| QP EI -->|"cursor, lowest rank first"| EV ``` - **`route::ObjectRoute`** owns one tenant's keys. Every key has a `KeySlot`: its lock, the object record when one is published, and the per-key `ObjectState` that replaces the side maps (the task in flight of each kind, the promotion candidate, the dynamic-replication pending record and cooldown). The lock belongs to the key, not to a publication, so a writer can lock a key that has no object yet and replace an object without a window in which the key is absent. - **Generations.** Each publication gets a `Generation`. Code that lets go of a key and comes back later (a scan that acts afterwards, a durable callback) holds an `ObjectRef{key, generation}` and acts only while that same publication is still there. - **Lock rules.** A stripe lock is held only to find, create or collect a slot, or across a cursor that only tries slot locks. items.title: [RFC]: Rethinking the Master Global State Lock: Lifecycle Isolation and Finer-Grained Synchronization
items.author: Icedcoco
items.body_excerpt:
### Changes proposed

> **Status: discussion draft.** No implementation has been approved. This document is intentionally written to be challenged on GitHub.
>
> The purpose of this RFC is to review the remaining role of `snapshot_mutex_`, now named `master_state_mutex_`, after [PR #4406][pr4406] removed the legacy Master snapshot path. Please treat every proposed decomposition as a hypothesis: reviewers are encouraged to identify incorrect assumptions, missing call paths, unsafe interleavings, and simpler designs. The goal of this discussion is to improve the model before implementation begins.
>
> Audit baseline: local commit `db969643a00cb91f059acbccce34760ca0dabf23`. The main implementation files referenced here match the merged PR #4406 commit `342c8aeece6b4eefb76c6b8b31ccfac8dde07aa3`; source links therefore point to that merge commit. Function names and line numbers refer to this baseline and may move later.

## 1. Proposal and review goals

PR #4406 removed the legacy Master snapshot path, retained the OpLog-backed snapshot, and renamed `snapshot_mutex_` to `master_state_mutex_`. The old snapshot requirement for a global Master freeze is gone, but many guard sites remain. Some of those sites now protect unrelated lifecycle or metadata interactions that accumulated around the original barrier.

The direction proposed here is to give recovery, memory-segment remount, and LOCAL_DISK registration lifecycle explicit protocols; then gradually remove the global shared lock from ordinary RPCs and background scans; and finally decide whether the `master_state_mutex_` member can be removed entirely.

Here, “finer grained” means reducing the conflict domain. Unmounting one client's disk or remounting one segment should not automatically block every object operation in the Master. It does not primarily mean reducing the memory occupied by a mutex object or shortening one critical section in isolation.

The current preliminary assessment is deliberately open to correction:

- There is no evidence yet that one global `std::shared_mutex` must remain permanently.
- Removing all guard statements in one sweep would be unsafe with the current object-lifetime and publication model.
- The hardest issue is `ReMountSegment()` retaining metadata pointers after releasing shard locks. The next hardest issues are internal concurrency during restore and ordering between LOCAL_DISK deregistration and replica admission.
- A few narrow guard sites may be independently removable, but most metadata paths need the remount, readiness, and lifecycle questions resolved first.

The first questions for reviewers are:

1. Does production or embedded mode require restoring an already-serving Master, or can restore be startup-only?
2. What visibility and atomicity boundary does a multi-segment remount actually promise?
3. Can the same client UUID be registered again while an older LOCAL_DISK registration is being swept, or must registrations be generation-scoped?

Answers to these questions determine whether the eventual design is a small protocol split or a substantially broader state-publication change. Please also point out if this RFC overstates the protection provided by the current global lock, or if it misses callers that bypass it.

## 2. Background

### 2.1 From a snapshot freeze lock to a general state barrier

The old `snapshot_mutex_` was introduced with Master metadata persistence and recovery. The basic arrangement was shared locking for ordinary state access and exclusive locking for snapshot-like operations that needed to pause protocol participants. The historical entry point is described in [the Master persistence and recovery commit][history-persistence].

Over time, other workflows began relying on the same barrier:

- HA recovery and post-recovery segment remount coordinate metadata and allocator reconstruction.
- Explicit LOCAL_DISK unmount needs to prevent a registration admitted under the old state from landing after the owner sweep, as described in [PR #3316][history-local-disk].
- Client liveness and asynchronous offboarding introduced client-level lifecycle guards, as described in [PR #2991][history-liveness], while some paths continued to use the global shared lock.
- The graceful-unmount scheduler once formed an ABBA deadlock with this lock, as fixed in [PR #2486][history-deadlock].

Therefore, keeping the lock after #4406 does not by itself mean that legacy snapshots were incompletely removed. It means that the original snapshot barrier accumulated responsibilities beyond snapshots. The next cleanup should separate those responsibilities instead of assuming they have one common lifetime.

### 2.2 Relationship to the retained OpLog snapshot

The current batch OpLog snapshot captures state from the `HotStandbyService` metadata store. It checks cursor consistency at an applied durable-prefix boundary, pauses the standby replication loop, copies metadata in chunks, and releases the capture. That protocol has its own synchronization and lifetime rules and does not acquire the Master's global state lock; see [the standby capture path][source-oplog-capture]. It answers how an applied log state becomes a coherent snapshot. This RFC addresses how the recovered state is accessed at runtime after it has been installed in Master.

This RFC does not propose changing the OpLog snapshot format, replay order, durable prefix, or leadership fencing. Those persistence guarantees remain owned by the OpLog protocol.

The separation under discussion is **runtime synchronization for Master in-memory state**. The existence of an OpLog snapshot does not imply that the Master-wide lock is required. Conversely, removing the legacy snapshot path does not prove that every historical guard site is now unnecessary.

## 3. Current state: what the lock actually protects

### 3.1 Guard sites and existing local synchronization

At the audit baseline, `master_service.cpp` directly constructs a guard for `master_state_mutex_` a

items.title: [Bug]: Potential incorrect metadata removal for shared-address multi-protocol registrations
items.author: xp2001-coder
items.body_excerpt:
### Bug Report

## Description

I noticed a potential metadata consistency issue in the classic Mooncake Transfer Engine while investigating multi-protocol registration with the **MACA backend on MetaX GPUs**.

Under `ENABLE_MULTI_PROTOCOL`, multiple transport-specific `BufferDesc` entries may refer to the same memory address. However, `TransferMetadata::removeLocalMemoryBuffer()` currently identifies the descriptor to remove **only by its address, without considering the transport protocol**.

When multiple protocol descriptors share the same address, this may remove the wrong descriptor and potentially leave stale metadata for a transport that has already been unregistered.

### Environment

The preliminary reproduction was performed with the following configuration:

- **Mooncake commit:** `a9983dcd600270fcc5c0cc6df92906b1e1785f8c`
- **Transfer Engine:** Classic
- **Build options:** `USE_MACA=ON`, `ENABLE_MULTI_PROTOCOL=ON`
- **Hardware:** 2 × MetaX C600-A GPUs (single node)
- **MACA version:** 3.9.0.29
- **Driver version:** 3.9.6
- **OS:** Ubuntu 24.04

The observed metadata behavior was reproduced using synthetic buffer descriptors. A full hardware-backed same-address multi-protocol unregister scenario has not yet been validated.

### Relevant Code

The current removal logic in `TransferMetadata::removeLocalMemoryBuffer()` essentially performs:

```cpp
if (iter->addr == (uint64_t)addr) {
    new_segment_desc->buffers.erase(iter);
    break;
}
```

The removal interface does not accept a protocol identifier, so it cannot distinguish between descriptors belonging to different transports at the same address.

Additionally, `TransferEngineImpl` tracks local memory regions using an address-based index, while the multi-protocol unregister path invokes transport-specific unregister operations.

This raises a potential mismatch between **per-transport registration ownership** and **address-based metadata cleanup**.

### Preliminary Reproduction

A synthetic metadata test was constructed with two `BufferDesc` entries sharing the same address, ordered as `[tcp, maca]`.

The intended operation was to remove the MACA registration. However, the underlying metadata removal interface receives only the address, without any protocol information.

**Observed behavior:**

```text
Initial descriptors:   [tcp, maca]
Intended removal:      maca
Actual descriptors:    [maca]
Expected descriptors:  [tcp]
```

Because the removal logic selects the first descriptor matching the address, it removes the TCP descriptor while retaining the MACA descriptor.

This demonstrates that **address-only removal is insufficient to distinguish protocol-specific descriptors** in the constructed multi-protocol scenario.

The reproduction isolates metadata removal behavior; it does not establish that the complete hardware-backed unregister path necessarily exhibits the same outcome.

### Related Issues and Prior Work

I reviewed several related multi-protocol registration and unregister fixes:

- **#2724 / #2725:** Addressed incorrect transport-specific descriptor selection when the same GPU memory was registered under both HIP and RDMA. This demonstrates a real shared-address multi-protocol scenario, but the fix focuses on **transfer-time descriptor lookup**, rather than metadata removal during unregister.

- **#4240 / #4243:** Address partial unregister failures and recovery of per-transport registration state. PR #4243 introduces tracking of transport-specific registration and unregister progress, which is closely related to the ownership semantics discussed here. However, it does not explicitly establish protocol-aware `BufferDesc` removal as part of the reported fix.

- **#2962:** Improved best-effort unregister behavior by attempting unregister operations across transports even when an individual transport reports an error.

The concern reported here is specifically about **which protocol-specific metadata descriptor is removed when multiple descriptors share the same address**, rather than transfer-time selection or recovery from partial unregister failures.

It would also be useful to clarify whether the ongoing ownership-tracking work in #4243 is expected to address this metadata consistency concern.

### Questions for Maintainers

1. Is registering and publishing multiple transport-specific descriptors for the same memory address range an intended and supported use case across the available backends?
2. Should metadata removal identify the target descriptor using **(address, transport protocol)** rather than address alone?
3. Should `TransferEngineImpl` retain per-transport registration ownership in coordination with the metadata layer?
4. How should partial registration rollback and protocol-specific unregister operations maintain consistency with shared metadata, particularly in light of the ongoing work in #4243?

### Validation Scope

This finding is based on source inspection and a synthetic metadata reproduction performed while investigating MACA multi-protocol behavior.

End-to-end validation of the same-address MACA + RDMA registration/unregistration flow on real hardware has not yet been completed. Therefore, the impact on actual multi-protocol deployments remains to be confirmed.

I would like to clarify the intended registration ownership and metadata cleanup semantics before proposing changes to the Transfer Engine implementation.

- [x] Ensure you searched for relevant issues and read the [documentation]

items.title: [RFC]: [Store] HA: graceful leader shutdown on SIGTERM/SIGINT (release the lease before exit)
items.author: tensorcopy
items.body_excerpt:
### Changes proposed

### Summary

In HA mode, SIGTERM ends the master process with no cleanup. When that master is the leader, its etcd lease stays alive until it expires, and only then can a standby acquire leadership and begin its warmup. A planned restart (pod delete, rollout) therefore costs as much as a crash.

This RFC proposes that the HA master handle SIGTERM and SIGINT. It stops taking new work, waits for admitted admin handlers before the release and drains the healthy OpLog writer's ready queue (retaining today's failure behavior), revokes the leadership lease exactly once, and exits within a fixed deadline. A planned leader restart then costs about one warmup instead of lease expiry plus warmup. There are no data-plane changes, no new persistent state and no wire changes. The work is split into two PRs of about 520 and 440 lines (Section 9).

All code references are to `main` at `3aa0f716`. Related: #3808 (HA roadmap), #4559, #4666, #4706.

#4601, merged after `3aa0f716`, runs RPC handlers on a worker pool that the serving exit drains after the server future returns and before step 2 of 2.3; the ordered exit keeps that drain. It shifts later line numbers in `master_service_supervisor.cpp` and `master.cpp`.

### 1. Current behavior

- `main()` installs SIGINT/SIGTERM handlers only in the non-HA branch (`mooncake-store/src/master.cpp:1653-1658`). The HA branch builds a `MasterServiceSupervisor` and returns `supervisor.Start()` (`master.cpp:1612-1618`). In `mooncake-store/src` these are the only SIGINT/SIGTERM handlers on the master's path, so in HA mode SIGTERM takes its default action and ends the process without running destructors. The etcd backend's Go `c-shared` library does not install a SIGTERM handler either: Go installs handlers for asynchronous signals in that mode only when `signal.Notify` is called, and the wrapper does not call it.
- The supervisor loop (`mooncake-store/src/ha/leadership/master_service_supervisor.cpp:330`) has no stop condition. It leaves only through `return -1`: on a fatal backend error, or when the RPC listener fails to start (`:667-680`).
- The etcd coordinator grants the lease with `DEFAULT_MASTER_VIEW_LEASE_TTL_SEC` (5 s, `mooncake-store/include/types.h:101`) and creates the `master_view` key under that lease (`mooncake-store/src/ha/leadership/backends/etcd/etcd_leader_coordinator.cpp:216-228`), so a revoke deletes the key. For an acquired leadership session, normal cleanup revokes through `ReleaseLeadership` (`etcd_leader_coordinator.cpp:567-613`) or the destructor (`:155`, `:653-704`). SIGTERM's default termination does not run those cleanup paths.
- A new leader keeps renewing for one full lease TTL in warmup before it serves (`WarmupLeadership`, `master_service_supervisor.cpp:189-217`; the deadline is set at `:191`).
- A standby waits on an etcd watch of the `master_view` key (`etcd_leader_coordinator.cpp:436-531`), in 1 s slices (`master_service_supervisor.cpp:31`, `:392-393`, `:409-410`). It sees a delete at once (within one 1 s slice if the old leader was still warming up).

With lease TTL `T`, the two cases compare like this:

| | Leader killed (today) | Leader releases the lease (proposed) |
| -- | -- | -- |
| Successor can acquire | when the old lease expires, up to `T` after the kill | when the old leader revokes, at the end of its cleanup |
| Then | producer-view claim and catch-up/promotion, warmup `T`, then restore and serving startup | producer-view claim and catch-up/promotion, warmup `T`, then restore and serving startup |

The saving is up to `T` per planned leader restart. It grows with the TTL, which #4706 makes configurable up to 60 s.

### 2. Proposed behavior

#### 2.1 Signal intake

- `main()` installs SIGINT and SIGTERM handlers in the HA branch, before `supervisor.Start()`, so no lease can be acquired without them. If installation fails, the master refuses to start.
- The handler does one lock-free atomic exchange on a sticky "shutdown requested" flag (asserted lock-free at compile time). It does not log, lock or call a backend.
- The handlers are installed with `sigaction` and `SA_ONSTACK`. The etcd and k8s HA backends are Go `c-shared` libraries in the master process (`mooncake-common/etcd/CMakeLists.txt:3`, `CMakeLists.txt:83`), and Go requires `SA_ONSTACK` on any handler that non-Go code installs ([os/signal docs](https://pkg.go.dev/os/signal#hdr-Non_Go_programs_that_call_Go_code)). The `std::signal` calls in the non-HA branch (`master.cpp:1657-1658`) are not a model for this.
- A second signal calls `_exit(128 + signo)` (130 for SIGINT, 143 for SIGTERM), the convention the Transfer Engine watcher already follows (`graceful_shutdown.cpp:151`). This is the escape hatch for a shutdown that does not finish.
- The supervisor receives the request as a predicate (`std::function<bool()>`) that defaults to the process flag, so tests can inject their own.

The Transfer Engine already has a SIGTERM/SIGINT watcher that uses a self-pipe (`mooncake-transfer-engine/src/graceful_shutdown.cpp:146-167`, `:181-211`). The master's HA path does not construct a `TransferEngine` (in `mooncake-store/src`, only `client_service.cpp` does), and `mooncake_master` does not link `transfer_engine` (`mooncake-store/src/CMakeLists.txt:712-725`), so that watcher is not active here. Its design is a reference for open question 4.

#### 2.2 Supervisor: a shutdown request is handled like a lease loss, then the loop exits

The loop already has a release path for every phase after acquisition, because each failure calls `ReleaseLeadership` (`HandleLeadershipPhaseError`, `master_service_supervisor.cpp:179-187`, and the `LogLeadershipReleaseWarning` call sites). The change makes each phase notice the request and then leaves the loop instead of retrying.

| Phase | Today | With a shutdown request |
| -- | -- | -- |
| Outer loop and coordinator creation (`:330-338`) | retries every 1 s on error | checked at the top of each outer iteration; exits with no

items.title: [Bug][Store] Tenant-watermark eviction removes objects without an OpLog record and releases quota before durability
items.author: apex-mochen
items.body_excerpt:
### Summary

With `enable_ha` + `enable_oplog` + `enable_multi_tenants`, the eviction thread's tenant pass (`EvictTenantsOverWatermark` → `EvictTenantMemoryForQuota`, on by default at `tenant_eviction_high_watermark_ratio = 0.90`) removes memory replicas, releases the tenant's committed quota and erases the metadata **without appending any OpLog entry**.

`BatchEvict` handles the same removal differently: `persist_evict_oplog_or_skip` marks the replicas `REMOVED`, appends `REMOVE` / `PUT_END` with a durable finalize, and frees the replicas and quota only in `FinalizeRemovedReplicasAfterDurable` ("HA strong-consistency: persist the post-eviction state before the helper mutates metadata"). The tenant pass has no equivalent step.

Checked on main `20fc0bc` and again on `129c961`.

### Reproduction (deterministic)

Regression test in `master_service_evict_scenario_test.cpp` (in the linked PR):
- HA config, `tenant-a` quota = 1 KiB, one completed, lease-expired 1 KiB object `cold`;
- no explicit eviction: wait 2 s so the tenant pass runs;
- `cold` no longer exists, but OpLog batch 3 never appears (`ETCD_KEY_NOT_EXIST`).

On unfixed main the test fails 5/5, both on `20fc0bc` and on `129c961`.

### Where it already shows up

- `MasterServiceEvictScenarioTest.OpLogDurabilityGatesTenantQuotaReclamation` fails intermittently: nightly run 37339233838, triaged in #4485; a PR run on 2026-09-15 is also mentioned in #4136.
- The failure always produces the same three messages:
  - `before-durable succeeded`
  - batch 3 `ETCD_KEY_NOT_EXIST`
  - `after-durable TENANT_QUOTA_EXCEEDED`
- With 32 CPU-burning processes (on `20fc0bc`), 33 of 50 repeats fail with exactly these messages; idle, 50/50 pass. No failing iteration contains `[EVICT-RESULT]`, so the explicit `EvictMemory` found nothing to evict, because the tenant pass had already removed `cold`.
- #4155 isolated two HA tests from the same interaction ("Background eviction can remove that object and release its quota before the tested operation, bypassing the blocked OpLog transaction"). It treated this as a test issue and left production unchanged.

### Possible consequence (not reproduced end to end)

A standby replays only the OpLog, so it would keep the evicted key with its old memory descriptor. If the primary later reuses that address, the standby could hold two live-looking descriptors for one range. That is the "overlapping memory descriptors" condition from #3760, where the maintainer note says overlap "is not expected during normal operation" and the source of the stale descriptor was still open. #3760's cluster ran with `-enable_multi_tenants=true`. I don't know whether a tenant quota was configured there, so I can't say this path caused it; it is one path that can produce the overlap.

### Proposed fix

Route the tenant pass through the same persist-before-mutate step as `BatchEvict` (shared helper), and leave quota release, metadata erase and the KV-removed publish to the durable finalize when the OpLog is on. I have this fix plus the regression test ready and will open a PR shortly.
