items.title: [Feature] kv-shard: Pass Q instead of KV for short prefills with long cached prefixes
items.author: Shunkangz
items.body_excerpt:
### Checklist

- [x] If this is not a feature request but a general question, please start a discussion at https://github.com/sgl-project/sglang/discussions. Otherwise, it will be closed.
- [x] Please use English. Otherwise, it will be closed.

### Motivation

## Background

With `--enable-kv-cache-sharding`, each CP rank stores \(1/N\) of every cached prefix. Today, extend batches are zigzag-split across all ranks, and every request’s prefix KV is all-gathered to every rank one layer ahead.

For agentic and multi-turn workloads, a short prefill often extends a long cached prefix, so prefix KV dominates communication. DCP avoids this for decode by passing Q instead of KV, but directly applying it to prefill would replicate new-token computation across ranks.

## Overall Design

Use **per-request placement**: each request has one home CP rank that computes all its new tokens. Choose the communication policy per request based on \(P/T\):

- Pass-KV for short prefixes: the home fetches only its requests’ prefix stripes via all-to-all.
- Pass-Q for long prefixes: all-gather Q, attend over each rank’s local prefix stripes, and return partial outputs and LSE to the home for merging with its causal new-token attention.

Overlap both pass-Q collectives with the home’s local attention and use copy-engine transfers for large messages. In the 8× B200 per-layer harness, exposed communication is 0.1–1.2% of layer time at 128K–256K prefixes; choosing pass-Q when \(P/T > 128\) is within 1.9% of the best measured split on average.

## PR Stack

The following PRs will be released soon.

### 1/5 — Enable FA4 for GQA KV Sharding and Fix Sharded KV Writes

- Enable FA4 for GQA KV sharding on Blackwell.
- Fix a silent wrong-logits bug where fused RoPE + KV writes bypass the sharded pool on short extends, affecting both FA3 and FA4.
- Validation: sharded and unsharded outputs are bit-exact at CP4.

### 2/5 — Add Symmetric-Memory Transports for Pass-Q Attention

- Add `PassQCommunicator` with variable-size Q all-gather, partial O + LSE all-to-all, and LSE merging.
- Support Triton SM-push and copy-engine transports using Torch symmetric memory.
- Add multi-GPU tests.

### 3/5 — Add Per-Request CP Placement for Prefill

- Assign whole requests to CP ranks when the batch can be balanced, using one FA call per rank.
- Fetch only each rank’s own requests’ prefix stripes via all-to-all instead of all-gathering every prefix.
- Validation: sharded and unsharded outputs are bit-exact at CP4 with B=4.
- Reduce latency versus zigzag placement by 8 ms unsharded and 5 ms sharded at 32K/64K.

### 4/5 — Pass Q Instead of KV for Long-Prefix Requests

- Add `--kv-shard-pass-q-ratio` for per-request P/T policy selection.
- Add pass-Q-aware placement, including B < N, and pool stripe tables.
- Implement Q all-gather, local prefix-stripe attention, partial O + LSE all-to-all, and merging.
- Start with a serial schedule.

### 5/5 — Overlap Pass-Q Communication with Local Attention

- Run communication on a side stream.
- Split the home rank’s local attention across both collectives to **overlap** communication and computation.
- Select the transport by message size.
- Run end-to-end A/B validation at CP8.

### Related resources

_No response_

items.title: Use atomic_cas inside a loop
items.author: giorgio-arena
items.body_excerpt:
Hi, I'm experimenting with a simple kernel that reduces a rank-3 tensor on its last dimension. The kernel uses atomics to sum across one tensor row (I know it's not efficient, this is just a simple reproducer). I'm using two versions of the atomics, the first using atomic_add, and the second using the lock-like mechanism with atomic_cas and atomic_xchg.

```
@triton.jit
def _sum_kernel(X, Locks, O, width: tl.constexpr, use_atomic_add: tl.constexpr):
  in_off = tl.program_id(0) * width
  out_off = tl.program_id(0)

  for w in range(0, width):
    x = tl.load(X + in_off + w)
    if use_atomic_add:
      tl.atomic_add(O + out_off, x)
    else:
      while tl.atomic_cas(Locks + out_off, 0, 1) == 1:
        pass
      tl.store(O + out_off, tl.load(O + out_off) + x)
      tl.atomic_xchg(Locks + out_off, 0)


def _sum_fn(a, use_atomic_add):
  b, h, w = a.shape
  locks = torch.zeros([b, h], dtype=torch.int32, device='cuda')
  out = torch.zeros([b, h], dtype=a.dtype, device='cuda')
  _sum_kernel[(b * h,)](a, locks, out, width=w, use_atomic_add=use_atomic_add)
  return out

if __name__ == "__main__":
  x = torch.empty((8, 64, 128), dtype=torch.float32, device="cuda").normal_()
  ref = torch.sum(x, axis=-1)
  rtol = 1e-03

  print(torch.allclose(ref, _sum_fn(x, True), rtol=rtol))
  print(torch.allclose(ref, _sum_fn(x, False), rtol=rtol))
```

Unfortunately for the second version I get
```

  File "/usr/local/home/giorgio/triton/python/triton/compiler.py", line 741, in visit_For
    assert for_op_region.size() == 1, "We use SCF, so the loop body should only have one block"
AssertionError: We use SCF, so the loop body should only have one block
```

Any help would be appreciated, thanks.

items.title: [RFC][Plugin] Add MLIR Dialect Whitelist for Preserving TypeIDs and Generic Plugin Module Extension
items.author: hongziqi
items.body_excerpt:
## Abstract

The upstream Triton plugin system only supports table-driven registration of Passes, Dialects, and OpInfo. **It cannot let a plugin inject a custom IR Builder subclass.** At the same time, `libtriton.so` built with `--as-needed` drops TypeIDs of dialects such as Linalg and Tensor.
Triton-Ascend ships as the out-of-tree plugin `libtriton_ascend.so` and shares one MLIRContext / PassManager with the host. In that setup, Pass execution breaks and IR construction fails.

This proposal has two parts:

1. Bump the plugin ABI to v3. Add a host-side module extension callback, `HostExtendCallback`, and a top-level Python API, `ir.extend_module_with`. Build nanobind as its own shared library.
2. Add a dialect whitelist so the listed dialect TypeIDs stay in `libtriton.so` at link time.

After the change, an out-of-tree plugin can attach a custom IR Builder, extend the Python IR with a submodule, and reuse the host MLIR context and Pass pipeline.

## 1. Background

Triton-Ascend uses the **out-of-tree plugin** `libtriton_ascend.so`. It shares the upstream Triton MLIRContext and PassManager, reuses the existing Dialects, Passes, and OpInfo, and does not fork the main repository.

Two gaps show up when this is wired up: a custom IR Builder cannot be injected, and MLIR dialect TypeIDs are missing between the host and the plugin.

### 1.1 GAP-P2: Missing Linalg/Tensor TypeIDs

Upstream `libtriton.so` is built with `--as-needed` by default. If a symbol in a static library is not referenced directly by a host translation unit, the linker drops that archive member. TypeIDs for Linalg, Tensor, and the Complex and Bufferization dialects that Ascend lowering depends on are stripped. When the plugin and the host share one MLIRContext, the required MLIR symbols are missing and Pass execution fails.

### 1.2 GAP-P1: The current plugin mechanism cannot support a custom IR Builder subclass

What the existing plugin extension APIs can and cannot do:

| API | Capability | Typical use | Limit for Ascend |
| :-- | :-- | :-- | :-- |
| `passes.plugin.extend_with` | Register Passes and expose `add_*` callbacks | Add an MLIR Pass | Sufficient for Passes |
| `ir.extend_dialects_with` | Register a new Dialect | Add a standalone dialect | Sufficient for Dialect registration |
| `ir.builder.extend_with` (OpInfo table) | Attach op factories on the upstream `ir.builder`. C++ ABI is `void (*)(TritonOpBuilder&, vector<Value>&)`. Host Python wraps it as `create_*(list[Value]) → Value` | Add a simple Op whose arguments are a fixed list of Values | **Not sufficient** |

`ir.builder.extend_with` only supports flat op factory functions. **It does not support a Builder subclass, kwargs, or affine expressions.**
Ascend's `AscendNPUIROpBuilder` subclasses `TritonOpBuilder`, and the IR construction lives in `ascend_ir.cc`. The OpInfo table can only append `create_*` factories. **It cannot replace the Builder type, and it cannot add a Python IR submodule.**

The missing piece is a **host IR module extension hook (HostExtend)** so a plugin can initialize its own IR module inside the host process.

## 2. Design

Each gap maps to an upstream change and a plugin-side hookup:

| Gap | Upstream change | Ascend plugin hookup |
| :-- | :-- | :-- |
| **Linalg / Tensor TypeIDs are not visible** | Add a dialect TypeID whitelist, `python/src/plugin_ext_dialects.whitelist`. CMake reads it and generates `plugin_ext_dialects.gen.cc`, which takes a strong reference with `TypeID::get`. On GNU ld, `--whole-archive` pulls the corresponding dialect static libraries into `libtriton.so`. The initial list is Linalg, Tensor, Complex, and Bufferization. | The plugin reuses the whitelisted dialect TypeIDs exported by the host. TypeIDs of plugin-defined dialects stay inside the plugin `.so`. |
| **`ir.builder` factories are not expressive enough** | Add `HostExtensionArgs` and `HostExtendCallback`. Append an `extend` field at the end of `PluginInfo`, read only when `apiVersion >= 3`. Add the top-level Python API `ir.extend_module_with`. When `TRITON_EXT_ENABLED=1`, build nanobind as a separate `libnanobind.so`. | The plugin sets `PluginInfo.extend = ascendExtendHost`. The callback registers a nanobind submodule and exposes `ir._ascend` and `AscendNPUIROpBuilder`. The plugin is built with `NB_SHARED` and links the host `libnanobind.so`. |

Benefits:

- **IR**: An out-of-tree plugin can inject a Builder subclass, with kwargs, affine expressions, and custom op wrappers, instead of being limited to the fixed OpInfo signature `create_*(list[Value])`.
- **ABI**: The v3 `extend` field is appended at the end of `PluginInfo`. The host reads it only when `apiVersion >= 3`, so existing v2 plugins still load. The `OpInfo` layout is unchanged.
- **whitelisted MLIR symbols**: Each whitelisted dialect TypeID exists once in the host `.so`. Type identity is consistent inside one MLIRContext.
- **Python bindings**: The host and the plugin share `libnanobind.so`. IR objects can cross the `.so` boundary, and Python can use the plugin submodule `ir._ascend` directly.

## 3. Implementation

### 3.1 Support MLIR whitelist: Keeping Linalg/Tensor and related symbols

The whitelist `python/src/plugin_ext_dialects.whitelist` names the MLIR dialects whose TypeIDs must be exported. Each line has three columns: CMake target, header, and C++ type.

```text
# format: cmake_target|include_header|TypeExpr
MLIRLinalgDialect|mlir/Dialect/Linalg/IR/Linalg.h|mlir::linalg::LinalgDialect
MLIRTensorDialect|mlir/Dialect/Tensor/IR/Tensor.h|mlir::tensor::TensorDialect
MLIRComplexDialect|mlir/Dialect/Complex/IR/Complex.h|mlir::complex::ComplexDialect
MLIRBufferizationDialect|mlir/Dialect/Bufferization/IR/Bufferization.h|mlir::bufferization::BufferizationDialect
```

`CMakeLists.txt` reads the whitelist and does two things:

1. Collect the CMake targets into `TRITON_PLUGIN_EXT_DIALECT_LIBS` and, on GNU ld, link them into `libtriton.so` with `--whole-archive`.
2. Generate `plugin_ext_dialects.gen.cc`

items.title: Pushing MTP to the limit with --spec-draft-p-min (15% faster)
items.author: sanmai
items.body_excerpt: The guides for draft model MTP often call for a single knob: n-max or number of tokens to draft for speculative decoding. ``` --spec-type draft-mtp --spec-draft-n-max 2 ``` If we increase just the n-max, eventually the generation speed starts to fade. But there's also an important knob to increase the minimum speculative decoding probability. It stop the drafting head earlier, once it starts getting unsure: ``` --spec-draft-p-min 0.8 ``` In other words, with this knob the drafting head does _less work_ when it isn't sure; say, on novel work when a draft head is essentially guessing, this limit stops the head from generating too many tokens. ## How can we use it? But there's a flip side: if an output is fully encoded in the context, the drafting head can output a lot of tokens with a very high probability. So if we increase the p-min from the default 0.0 to say 0.8, and bump the n-max to a higher number, say 16, we could get the best of both worlds: a sensible speedup on novel workloads without waste, and a major speedup for common code generation and refactoring tasks that usually include significant unchanged chunks of the existing code. I tried the exact combo on a pair of dense models on a synthetic yet realistic agentic coding benchmark: refactor a function and emit the result. ``` --spec-type draft-mtp --spec-draft-n-max 8 --spec-draft-p-min 0.8 ``` And it did not disappoint: | config | gemma-4-31B | Qwen3.6-27B | |---|---:|---:| | no speculation | 47 | 50 | | `n_max=1` | 78 | 77 | | `n_max=4` | 112 | 112 | | `n_max=8, p_min=0.8` | **163** | **178** | I also tried this combo with a code recital benchmark (cite a function from a large file): | config | gemma-4-31B | Qwen3.6-27B | |---|---:|---:| | no speculation | 47 | 50 | | `n_max=1` | 80 | 83 | | `n_max=4` | 118 | 140 | | `n_max=8, p_min=0.8` | **218** | **225** | Feel free to try this for yourself. Hardware used: 5090 power limited to 400W.

### Feature Description

Add support for the following model to llama.cpp:

Xing4.0-29B-A4B

### Motivation


The Xing4.0-29B-A4B model is a domestically developed LLM from China Telecom AI Technology Co., Ltd. (TeleAI), originally named "telechat," or "xingchen4" and is scheduled to be open-sourced soon. 
The model is designed for lightweight inference on PC hardware, and llama.cpp is particularly friendly to consumer-grade GPUs on the edge side. In my actual usage, the Xing4.0-29B-A4B model provides a great experience.

So far, I have completed the following work:

Registered the xingchen4 model architecture in the llama.cpp framework with parameter alignment.
Implemented conversion and quantization of the model's safetensors weights to GGUF format.
Added CPU backend inference support.
Added GPU backend inference support, along with specific GGML operator implementations.
Wrote and tested operator test cases.
Conducted llama-perplexity and llama-bench evaluations.

### Possible Implementation

Given that the 29b parameter count is relatively large for PC hardware and consumer-grade GPUs, pure CPU inference has limited practical value. 
Therefore, I aim to also support GPU inference improvements. 
I plan to enhance the model architecture registration module, weight conversion and quantization tools, the CPU backend, and the GPU backend (including GGML operators).

items.title: iSWA: seq_pos_max answers from the sliding cache, so a batch without positions lands at 0 after a partial seq_rm and leaks base-cache cells
items.author: juliusbangert
items.body_excerpt:
### Name and Version

b11010 (vendored in llama.rn 0.13.0-rc.4); first seen on b10256. llama-kv-cache-iswa.cpp seq_pos_max and the derivation in llama-batch.cpp are unchanged between them.

### Operating systems

Mac

### Which llama.cpp modules do you know to be affected?

libllama (core library)

### Command line

```shell

```

### Problem description & steps to reproduce

This is the llama.cpp end of a problem I tracked down in a downstream wrapper (llama.rn, issue linked below). I think the wrapper is doing something llama.cpp tells it not to (`llama_batch_get_one` after a partial `seq_rm`), so I'm mainly asking whether `seq_pos_max` for iSWA is returning what you intend, because the consequence is a silent KV leak rather than an error.

### What happens

`llama-kv-cache-iswa.cpp`:

```cpp
llama_pos llama_kv_cache_iswa::seq_pos_min(llama_seq_id seq_id) const {
    // the base cache is a superset of the SWA cache, so we can just check the SWA cache
    return kv_swa->seq_pos_min(seq_id);
}

llama_pos llama_kv_cache_iswa::seq_pos_max(llama_seq_id seq_id) const {
    return kv_swa->seq_pos_max(seq_id);
}
```

The superset argument holds for `seq_pos_min` in the normal flow, but after `seq_rm(seq, p0, -1)` with `p0` below the sliding window the two caches disagree: the base cache still holds positions 0…p0−1, the sliding cache holds nothing for that sequence (its cells for those positions were purged as the sequence grew), and `seq_pos_max` returns −1 while the base cache's answer would be p0−1.

A caller that then decodes a batch without positions gets, in `llama_batch_allocr::init`:

```cpp
p0[s] = memory->seq_pos_max(s) + 1;   // = 0
```

so the new tokens are written at positions 0, 1, 2, … on top of the base cache's existing cells 0…p0−1. No error: the consecutive-positions check is skipped when `seq_pos_max` is −1. Each such turn adds `min(n_new, p0)` duplicate base cells that sit below anything a later `seq_rm(seq, n_past, -1)` reaches. They accumulate until `find_slot` fails ("failed to find a memory slot"), which then persists until a full clear. The turn is also computed at the wrong positions.

Measured on Gemma 4 E2B (12 sliding + 3 global KV layers, `n_swa` 512, sliding cache 1,024 cells, base 6,144): with `saveSession`'s file size as the cell count (it writes every non-empty cell), a sequence of deep-divergence turns went +277 → +699 → +1,099 → +1,542 → +1,954 → +2,808 → +3,559 cells above the live sequence, then both caches full, then the failure.

### Why I'm raising it here rather than only downstream

`llama.h` already says of `llama_batch_get_one`: "this is a helper function to facilitate transition to the new batch API — avoid using it", and llama-server never relies on derived positions (it always uses `common_batch_add` with explicit positions and has its own `pos_min` guard against reusing a prefix past the window, `server-context.cpp`, referencing #13194). So the wrapper is at fault for using the helper, and I've fixed it there with explicit positions plus a port of the server's guard.

But two things seem worth a look on this side:

1. **`seq_pos_max` for iSWA.** If the base cache is the superset, `kv_base->seq_pos_max(seq_id)` is the true maximum of the sequence and would give the derived-positions path the right answer (p0) in this situation. Is answering from the sliding cache deliberate — e.g. so `seq_pos_max` agrees with `seq_pos_min` about what the sliding layers can actually attend to?
2. **No error on the collision.** `llama_batch_allocr::init` validates consecutive positions only when `seq_pos_max ≥ 0`. When the derived start is 0 but the base cache already holds cells at those positions, a check against `kv_base` (or against any cache in the iSWA pair) would turn a silent leak into a decode error, which is much easier to find. The `probeStateCache`-style TODO in the wrapper existed for months without anyone connecting it to this.

### Version

b11010 (vendored in llama.rn 0.13.0-rc.4); first seen on b10256. `llama-kv-cache-iswa.cpp` `seq_pos_max` and the derivation in `llama-batch.cpp` are unchanged between them.

### Minimal reproduction

Any iSWA model, default `swa_full = false`, one sequence, plain `llama_decode` with `llama_batch_get_one`:

1. Decode ~1,500 tokens (prompt or prompt + generation).
2. `llama_memory_seq_rm(mem, 0, 400, -1)`.
3. `llama_memory_seq_pos_max(mem, 0)` → −1 (expected 399 from the base cache's point of view).
4. Decode 500 more tokens with `llama_batch_get_one` → no error; `llama_state_save_file` grows by ~400 base cells more than the token count explains.
5. Repeat 2–4 with fresh tokens until `find_slot` fails.

Downstream issue with the wrapper-side fix and before/after numbers: mybigday/llama.rn#396.

### First Bad Commit

_No response_

### Relevant log output

<details>
<summary>Logs</summary>
<!-- Copy-pasted short logs go into the "console" area here -->

```console
decode: failed to find a memory slot for batch of size 402
decode: failed to find a memory slot for batch of size 512
```
</details>

items.title: gfx1103 inference becomes twice slower after a minute or two!?
items.author: l29ah
items.body_excerpt:
Decode performance goes off the cliff after some indeterminate time. This happens especially quickly with qwen4exp, going from ~11t/s to ~5.5.
AMD Ryzen 5 7640U w/ Radeon 760M on Framework 13 laptop here. Running the Vulkan backend at 0.6.0 and git master.

GGML_VK_PERF_LOGGER=1 demonstrated that at the cliff timing reports begin to have ~2x more expensive CPY, GATED_DELTA_NET, GET_ROWS and MUL_* calls, during the cliffs the fast ~90ms reports (that are present since the beginning of the inference) are interspersed with slow ~170ms reports (that start appearing and then begin being overwhelmingly common at the cliff).

It feels like thermal throttling, as seems like it runs at full speed for longer after the laptop idled for a bit, but the reported SoC power is unchanged (limited to 30W by cooling) when the cliff happens, and playing with ryzenadj(1) didn't get me anywhere (could there be some additional unseen throttling that only impacts RAM or something?). I've also exhausted my troubleshooting options with [claude fable's assistance](https://claude.ai/share/9a9130a0-00df-4ac0-8d4e-d5d276ca1e11).

## Motivation

Contributes to #3244.

The existing multi-node example expands `$SLURM_NODEID` in the batch shell, before `srun` creates its per-task environments. Both launches can therefore receive the same node rank. The existing readiness loop also checks only whether a TCP port is open.

This PR covers basic multi-node serving, single-node serving, and offline batch inference. #29991 has a separate scope around PD disaggregation and Apptainer.

## Changes

- Evaluate `$SLURM_PROCID` inside each `srun` task and use Slurm `%n` patterns for per-node logs.
- Use configurable HTTP and distributed-init ports, a bounded `/health` check, and early process-exit detection.
- Add a single-node serving job with cleanup and an SSH forwarding hint.
- Add an offline job that writes a real Python file with a `__main__` guard, as required by the Engine multiprocessing setup.
- Document the log-directory prerequisite and cluster-specific scheduler, network, port, and model-cache settings.

## Validation

- `bash -n` on all three batch scripts.
- `mint validate`.
- `mint broken-links`.
- Parsed and mock-executed the offline Python example, including Engine context cleanup.
- Checked task-side rank expansion with `SLURM_PROCID=0` and `SLURM_PROCID=1`.
- Cross-checked the Engine `spawn` setup, context-manager support, `/health` behavior, and referenced server arguments against the PR base revision.

I did not run these examples end to end on a Slurm GPU cluster. The `#SBATCH` resource values, partition name, network interfaces, and port availability remain site-specific.

items.title: Why does num_warps affect numerical precision?
items.author: yaozhenghangma
items.body_excerpt:
I'm testing a Flash Attention kernel, and I've placed the test code at the end. In short, when performing an attention operation using q, k, and v matrices with `num_batchs = 8`, `seq_len = 128`, `num_heads = 128`, and `head_dim = 128`, I observed that setting `num_warps = 4` and `num_warps = 8` produce different output results. The maximum difference between the output matrices is `0.00048828125`, and this difference remains consistent across repeated runs. Moreover, when keeping all other parameters the same and setting `seq_len` to 32 or smaller, the discrepancy disappears. 

I'm using an Nvidia T4 GPU, with CUDA version 12.4 and Triton version 3.1.0.

```python
import math
import torch
import triton
import triton.language as tl


@triton.jit
def flash_attention_kernel(
    q_ptr, k_ptr, v_ptr, o_ptr,
    start_loc, seq_len,
    q_stride_batch_seq, q_stride_head, q_stride_dim,
    k_stride_batch_seq, k_stride_head, k_stride_dim,
    v_stride_batch_seq, v_stride_head, v_stride_dim,
    o_stride_batch_seq, o_stride_head, o_stride_dim,
    num_head,
    kv_group_size,
    d_scale,
    BLOCK_SIZE_M: tl.constexpr,
    BLOCK_SIZE_N: tl.constexpr,
    BLOCK_SIZE_D: tl.constexpr
):
    # q k v: [batchs*seq, heads, dim]
    q_block_id = tl.program_id(0) # m id
    batch_and_head_id = tl.program_id(1)
    batch_id = batch_and_head_id // num_head
    head_id = batch_and_head_id % num_head
    kv_head_id = head_id // kv_group_size

    batch_start = tl.load(start_loc + batch_id)
    batch_seq_len = tl.load(seq_len + batch_id)

    m_ranges = tl.arange(0, BLOCK_SIZE_M)
    n_ranges = tl.arange(0, BLOCK_SIZE_N)
    m_start = q_block_id * BLOCK_SIZE_M
    m_offsets = m_ranges + m_start
    embed_offsets = tl.arange(0, BLOCK_SIZE_D)

    q_offsets = (
        (batch_start + m_offsets[:,None]) * q_stride_batch_seq
        + head_id * q_stride_head
        + embed_offsets[None,:] * q_stride_dim
    )

    k_offsets = (
        (batch_start + n_ranges[:,None]) * k_stride_batch_seq
        + kv_head_id * k_stride_head
        + embed_offsets[None,:] * k_stride_dim
    )

    v_offsets = (
        (batch_start + n_ranges[:,None]) * v_stride_batch_seq
        + kv_head_id * v_stride_head
        + embed_offsets[None,:] * v_stride_dim
    )

    o_offsets = (
        (batch_start + m_offsets[:,None]) * o_stride_batch_seq
        + head_id * o_stride_head
        + embed_offsets[None,:] * o_stride_dim
    )

    q_mask = m_offsets[:,None]  < batch_seq_len
    q = tl.load(q_ptr + q_offsets, mask=q_mask, other=0.0)

    acc = tl.zeros((BLOCK_SIZE_M, BLOCK_SIZE_D), dtype=tl.float32)
    m_i = tl.zeros((BLOCK_SIZE_M,), dtype=tl.float32) - float("inf")
    l_i = tl.zeros((BLOCK_SIZE_M,), dtype=tl.float32)

    m_mask = tl.where(m_start < batch_seq_len, 1, 0) # loop for m > seq_len is ignored
    n_size = tl.minimum(m_start + BLOCK_SIZE_M, batch_seq_len) # inter block casual mask

    for n_idx in range(0, n_size * m_mask, BLOCK_SIZE_N):
        k_mask = n_idx + n_ranges[:,None] < n_size
        k = tl.load(k_ptr + k_offsets + n_idx * k_stride_batch_seq, mask=k_mask, other=0.0)
        v = tl.load(v_ptr + v_offsets + n_idx * v_stride_batch_seq, mask=k_mask, other=0.0)

        qk = tl.zeros((BLOCK_SIZE_M, BLOCK_SIZE_N), dtype=tl.float32)
        qk += tl.dot(q, tl.trans(k))

        # intra block casual mask
        q_off = m_offsets
        k_off = n_idx + n_ranges
        mask = q_off[:,None] >= k_off[None,:]
        qk = tl.where(mask, qk * d_scale, -float("inf"))

        pad_mask = n_idx + n_ranges < n_size
        qk = tl.where(pad_mask[None,:], qk, -float("inf"))

        m_j = tl.max(qk, axis=1)
        m_new = tl.maximum(m_i, m_j)
        alpha = tl.exp2(m_i - m_new)

        P_j = tl.exp2(qk - m_new[:,None])
        l_j = tl.sum(P_j, axis=1)
        l_i = l_i * alpha + l_j

        o_scale = alpha
        acc = acc * o_scale[:, None]
        P_j = P_j.to(v_ptr.dtype.element_ty)
        acc += tl.dot(P_j, v)

        m_i = m_new

    acc = acc / l_i[:, None]

    tl.store(o_ptr + o_offsets, acc, mask=q_mask)


def flash_attention(q: torch.Tensor, k, v, start_loc, seq_len, num_warps):
    _, num_head, d_size = q.shape
    _, num_kv_head, _ = k.shape
    kv_group_size = num_head // num_kv_head
    num_batch = seq_len.shape[0]
    max_seq_len = int(torch.max(seq_len).item())
    d_scale = 1.0 / math.sqrt(d_size) * 1.4426950408889634

    grid = lambda meta: (
        triton.cdiv(max_seq_len, meta["BLOCK_SIZE_M"]),
        num_batch * num_head,
        1
    )
    num_stages = 1

    o = torch.empty_like(q, dtype=q.dtype, device=q.device)
    flash_attention_kernel[grid](
        q, k, v, o,
        start_loc, seq_len,
        *q.stride(), *k.stride(), *v.stride(), *o.stride(),
        num_head=num_head,
        kv_group_size=kv_group_size,
        d_scale=d_scale,
        BLOCK_SIZE_M=64,
        BLOCK_SIZE_N=64,
        BLOCK_SIZE_D=d_size,
        num_warps=num_warps,
        num_stages=num_stages,
    )

    return o


class TestFlashAttention:
    def test_flash_attention(self):
        num_batchs = 8
        seq_len = 32
        num_heads = 128
        head_dim = 128
        dtype = torch.float16
        device = 'cuda'
        tensor_shape = (num_batchs, num_heads, seq_len, head_dim)

        q = torch.rand(tensor_shape, dtype=dtype, device=device)
        k = torch.rand(tensor_shape, dtype=dtype, device=device)
        v = torch.rand(tensor_shape, dtype=dtype, device=device)

        qt = q.permute(0,2,1,3).contiguous().view(-1, num_heads, head_dim)
        kt = k.permute(0,2,1,3).contiguous().view(-1, num_heads, head_dim)
        vt = v.permute(0,2,1,3).contiguous().view(-1, num_heads, head_dim)
        start_loc = torch.arange(0, num_batchs*seq_len, seq_len, device=device)
        seq_len_list = torch.full((num_batchs,), seq_len, device=d

items.title: Constexprs that compare equal but differ in type or sign (1 and 1.0, 0.0 and -0.0) reuse each other's binary
items.author: shuyilinn
items.body_excerpt:
### Describe the bug

When a kernel is launched with a constexpr that compares equal to the value of an earlier launch but has a different type or sign (`1` and `1.0`, or `0.0` and `-0.0`), the second launch reuses the binary compiled for the first one. The result depends on which value was launched first.

```python
import torch
import triton
import triton.language as tl


@triton.jit
def kernel(X, out, C: tl.constexpr):
    tl.store(out, tl.load(X) * C)


x = torch.tensor([2**30 + 1], dtype=torch.int32, device="cuda")
for order in [(1, 1.0), (1.0, 1)]:
    kernel.device_caches.clear()
    results = []
    for c in order:
        out = torch.zeros(1, dtype=torch.int32, device="cuda")
        kernel[(1, )](x, out, c)
        results.append(out.item())
    print(order, results)
```

```
(1, 1.0) [1073741825, 1073741825]
(1.0, 1) [1073741824, 1073741824]
```

Expected: `x * 1` is `1073741825` and `x * 1.0` (computed in fp32) is `1073741824`, regardless of launch order. In the same way, launching with `C=0.0` and then `C=-0.0` stores `0.0` for the second launch.

The on-disk cache is not affected: the string key built from the specialization differs (`1` vs `1.0`, `0.0` vs `-0.0`). The problem is the in-memory lookup in `compute_cache_key` (`python/triton/runtime/jit.py`):

```python
key = (tuple(specialization), str(options))
cache_key = kernel_key_cache.get(key, None)
```

The specialization contains `("constexpr", value)`, and tuple equality treats `1 == 1.0 == True` and `0.0 == -0.0` (with equal hashes) as the same key, so the string key of the first launch is returned. This cache was added in #7768.

### Environment details

Triton: main @ 41846bc965
GPU: NVIDIA RTX 4090 (sm_89), driver 570 / CUDA 12.8

items.title: `tl.reduce` over a tuple with `axis=None` pairs values with the wrong indices
items.author: shuyilinn
items.body_excerpt:
### Describe the bug

`tl.reduce` over a tuple with `axis=None` can pair values with the wrong indices. An argmax written as `tl.reduce((x, idx), None, combine)` returns the right maximum but the wrong index. The same reduction with `axis=0` on the same 1-D input is correct.

```python
import torch
import triton
import triton.language as tl


@triton.jit
def combine(v1, i1, v2, i2):
    gt = (v1 > v2) | ((v1 == v2) & (i1 < i2))
    return tl.where(gt, v1, v2), tl.where(gt, i1, i2)


@triton.jit
def argmax(X, O, N: tl.constexpr, AXIS_NONE: tl.constexpr):
    off = tl.arange(0, N)
    x = tl.load(X + off)
    if AXIS_NONE:
        v, i = tl.reduce((x, off), None, combine)
    else:
        v, i = tl.reduce((x, off), 0, combine)
    tl.store(O, i)
    tl.store(O + 1, v)


N = 1024
torch.manual_seed(0)
x = torch.randperm(N, device="cuda", dtype=torch.int32)
for axis_none in (False, True):
    o = torch.zeros(2, dtype=torch.int32, device="cuda")
    argmax[(1, )](x, o, N, axis_none, num_warps=4)
    print(f"axis={'None' if axis_none else 0}: max={o[1].item()} index={o[0].item()} (expected index {x.argmax().item()})")
```

```
axis=0: max=1023 index=535 (expected index 535)
axis=None: max=1023 index=901 (expected index 535)
```

For `axis=None`, `reduction` in `python/triton/language/semantic.py` flattens each operand separately with `reshape(..., can_reorder=True)`. The two reshapes are free to reorder their elements independently, and here the loaded `x` and the `arange` end up in different orders, so the combine function sees `x[p]` together with `idx[q]`, `q != p`.

This is the same failure as #12099; its fix (#12124) covers the reshape the compiler inserts, not this frontend path. Reshaping the operands with `can_reorder=False`, or reshaping them together, would keep the pairing.

### Environment details

Triton: main @ 41846bc965
GPU: NVIDIA RTX 4090 (sm_89), driver 570 / CUDA 12.8

items.title: fp64 downcast with `fp_downcast_rounding="rtz"` fails with "Unsupported rounding mode for conversion"
items.author: shuyilinn
items.body_excerpt:
### Describe the bug

Casting fp64 to fp32, fp16 or bf16 with `fp_downcast_rounding="rtz"` fails to compile with `LLVM ERROR: Unsupported rounding mode for conversion.` The frontend accepts it, and the `cast` docstring documents `fp_downcast_rounding` for any float downcast. The interpreter computes the right result.

```python
import torch
import triton
import triton.language as tl


@triton.jit
def cast_rtz(X, Y):
    offs = tl.arange(0, 16)
    tl.store(Y + offs, tl.load(X + offs).to(Y.dtype.element_ty, fp_downcast_rounding="rtz"))


x = torch.full((16, ), 1 + 2**-30, dtype=torch.float64, device="cuda")
y = torch.zeros(16, dtype=torch.float32, device="cuda")
cast_rtz[(1, )](x, y)
print(y[0].item())
```

```
Unsupported conversion from f64 to f16 with rounding mode rtz
LLVM ERROR: Unsupported rounding mode for conversion.
...
RuntimeError: PassManager::run failed
```

Expected `1.0`. fp16 and bf16 destinations fail the same way; the message names f16 for the fp32 destination as well.

For a non-default rounding mode, `cast` in `python/triton/language/semantic.py` emits `tt.fp_to_fp` with that mode, but `FpToFpOpConversion` (`third_party/nvidia/lib/TritonNVIDIAGPUToLLVM/ElementwiseOpToLLVM.cpp`) has no conversion with an f64 source. With the default RTNE the frontend emits `arith.truncf` instead, which works. For fp32, PTX has `cvt.rz.f32.f64`.

### Environment details

Triton: main @ 41846bc965
GPU: NVIDIA RTX 4090 (sm_89), driver 570 / CUDA 12.8

items.title: Docs: MP mode needs GPU memory headroom (first request OOM at --gpu-memory-utilization 0.90 with GLM-5.3, TP8)
items.author: sivabreddy
items.body_excerpt:
With vLLM 0.31.0 + `LMCacheMPConnector` (LMCache v0.5.6, Mooncake Store L2), GLM-5.3 (NVFP4 checkpoint), TP8 on 80 GB H100, `--kv-cache-dtype fp8 --block-size 64 --max-model-len 65536 --gpu-memory-utilization 0.90`, the first request failed on all 8 GPUs:

- `CUDACachingAllocator`: "trying to allocate 2147483648 bytes (free: 1439236096)", that is 2.00 GiB requested with 1.34 GiB free.
- It surfaced as `RuntimeError: torch_call_dispatcher("aten::new_empty" ...)` in FlashMLA `sparse_decode_fwd`, not as a clear out-of-memory error.

With `--gpu-memory-utilization 0.85` it worked (vLLM then reported 6.5 GiB of KV cache memory instead of 10.46 GiB). The same model and flags with vLLM's built-in `MooncakeStoreConnector` (no LMCache) worked at 0.90.

We think the `lmcache server` process uses GPU memory (CUDA contexts / streams on each GPU) after vLLM has sized its KV cache, but we did not measure it.

The GLM-5.3 recipe (`docs/source/recipes/glm5_3.rst`) uses the vLLM default (0.9). A note there and in the MP docs (for example: "leave headroom for the LMCache server process; lower `--gpu-memory-utilization` if the first request fails with a CUDA out-of-memory error") would save time. If you know how much memory the server process needs per GPU, that number would help even more.

items.title: sm120_mxfp4_mxfp8_bf16_cake: DeepSeek-V4.1-Flash geometry (E384/H5120/I2304) spills one register (STACK 16 B) and _build_workspace refuses every transport table
items.author: xqoasis
items.body_excerpt:
### Before submitting

- [x] I have searched existing issues and did not find a solution or an existing report.

### Environment

```text
(the full `python -m flashinfer.collect_env` output is in the first comment below; the values here were read from the same container during the measurements.)

flashinfer : 0.7.2+cake.399b6c1, __git_commit__ 399b6c1d (source checkout on PYTHONPATH, JIT only, no AOT cubins; the image's installed wheel 0.7.1+cake.2c1c052 is shadowed)
torch      : 2.13.0a0+9186a08b2c.nv26.07 (CUDA 13.3 build); torch.cuda.nccl.version() = (2, 30, 7); ProcessGroupNCCL exposes _comm_ptr / get_runtime_nccl_version
NCCL       : 2.30.7 system install, NCCL_HOME=/opt/deepep/nccl-system (nccl.h NCCL_VERSION_CODE 23007, nccl_device.h, libnccl.so.2.30.7)
CUDA       : nvcc Build cuda_13.3.r13.3/compiler.38244171_0; driver libcuda 580.173.02 (host driver; the container's compat libcuda 610 breaks P2P and was not used)
Python     : 3.12; apache-tvm-ffi 0.1.11
GPUs       : 8x sm_120 (compute capability 12.0, 72 GB, 110 SMs), PCIe Gen5, two switches x 4 GPUs, 2x 400G RDMA NICs per switch; Linux x86_64 container
Env        : FLASHINFER_CUDA_ARCH_LIST=12.0a FLASHINFER_DISABLE_VERSION_CHECK=1 NCCL_GIN_TYPE=3 NCCL_WIN_ENABLE=1 NCCL_CUMEM_ENABLE=1 NCCL_P2P_LEVEL=SYS NCCL_NET_DISABLE_INTRA=1
```

### Bug description

## Setup
- flashinfer 399b6c1d (#6346 merge point), source tree on PYTHONPATH, NCCL 2.30.7 found via `NCCL_HOME`, CUDA 13.3, torch 2.13.
- 8x sm_120 GPUs (72 GB, 110 SMs, CC 12.0), one host, two PCIe Gen5 switches with 4 GPUs each, no NVLink; EP8 over an NCCL process group, GIN available (RDMA NICs behind each switch).
- Geometry: DeepSeek-V4.1-Flash routed experts E=384, H=5120, I=2304, top-k 6, `swiglu_limit=10`, `max_tokens_per_rank=2048`, noshared variant.

## What happens
`validate_init` passes (EP8 <= `REGISTER_BUDGET_VERIFIED_MAX_RANKS`, so nothing is compiled there), but the first `warmup()` / forward raises in `_build_workspace`:
- `transport_table="all_gin"` -> `RuntimeError: sm120_mxfp4_mxfp8_bf16_cake: m128_nocopier uses local memory`
- any table with LSA cells (`all_lsa`, `lsa_where_reachable`, explicit tuple) -> `... m64_copier uses local memory`

`cuobjdump --dump-resource-usage` on the JIT cubins: the refused instances report STACK 16 B (one 8-byte slot above `LOCAL_BYTES_LIMIT = 8`), LOCAL 0, REG 168/166.

| instance | REG | STACK | LOCAL |
|---|---|---|---|
| m128_copier (MOE_LSA_COPIERS 1 / 3 / 7) | 168 | 8 | 0 |
| m64_copier | 166 | 16 | 0 |
| m128_nocopier | 168 | 16 | 0 |
| m64_nocopier | 166 | 8 | 0 |

So at this geometry the device build spills one register and the backend refuses to load the workspace for every transport table, i.e. the kernel cannot be used for DeepSeek-V4.1-Flash on sm_120 as shipped.

## What I expected
The README's qualified "DeepSeek-V4-Flash" point is E256/H4096/I2048; the released DeepSeek-V4.1-Flash routed geometry is E384/H5120/I2304 (48 experts per rank at EP8). I expected either a spill-free build for it or `validate_init` rejecting it up front.

With `LOCAL_BYTES_LIMIT` raised to 16 for measurement (host constant only, device code and cubins unchanged) every table runs and is correct: output matches the pure-torch kernel-boundary oracle of `tests/moe_ep/test_moe_ep_sm120_w4a8_cake_mega.py` (rel L2 1.6e-4 .. 3.2e-4 over 512 rows/rank, three routings incl. one 2.5x hot rank), `protocol_error` stays 0, CUDA-graph replay is bit-identical to eager.

Ask: cover this geometry in the register-budget grid (or ship a build that does not spill at it), or document the local-memory limit as advisory. The layer-time comparison against the unfused PCIe path and the feature asks that follow from it are filed separately as #6757; this issue is only the spill and the refused workspace.

### Minimal reproduction

```python
# torchrun --standalone --nproc_per_node=8 repro.py
# 8x sm_120 GPUs on one PCIe host; NCCL 2.30.7 found via NCCL_HOME (nccl.h, nccl_device.h, libnccl.so.2)
import os
import torch
import torch.distributed as dist
from flashinfer.moe_ep.backends.mega.kernel.sm120.mxfp4_mxfp8_bf16_cake.cake_synthetic import (
    Geometry, make_layer, random_inputs, random_weights)

local = int(os.environ["LOCAL_RANK"])
torch.cuda.set_device(local)
dist.init_process_group("nccl", device_id=torch.cuda.current_device())
rank, world = dist.get_rank(), dist.get_world_size()

# DeepSeek-V4.1-Flash routed experts (not the E256/H4096/I2048 "v4flash" point of the test matrix)
g = Geometry(hidden=5120, intermediate=2304, experts=384, top_k=6)
table = os.environ.get("TABLE", "all_gin")  # all_gin -> m128_nocopier spills; all_lsa / any LSA table -> m64_copier spills
layer = make_layer(rank, world, random_weights(rank, world, g, shared=False), g,
                   max_tokens_per_rank=2048, shared=False, transport_table=table, swiglu_limit=10)
layer.warmup(random_inputs(2048, g, seed=rank))
# RuntimeError: sm120_mxfp4_mxfp8_bf16_cake: m128_nocopier uses local memory   (cake_backend._build_workspace)
dist.destroy_process_group()
```

### Error messages / logs

```text
flashinfer.jit: Compiling Cake SM120 MegaMoE m128_nocopier for -DMOE_RANKS=8 -DMOE_EXPERTS=384 -DMOE_TOPK=6 -DMOE_MAX_ROWS=2048 -DMOE_HIDDEN=5120 -DMOE_INTERMEDIATE=2304 -DMOE_SHARED_EXPERT=0 -DMOE_SWIGLU_LIMIT=10 -DMOE_CODEC_OVF_BLOCKS=16 -DMOE_LSA_COPIERS=1
flashinfer.jit: Compiling Cake SM120 MegaMoE m64_nocopier for -DMOE_RANKS=8 -DMOE_EXPERTS=384 -DMOE_TOPK=6 -DMOE_MAX_ROWS=2048 -DMOE_HIDDEN=5120 -DMOE_INTERMEDIATE=2304 -DMOE_SHARED_EXPERT=0 -DMOE_SWIGLU_LIMIT=10 -DMOE_CODEC_OVF_BLOCKS=16 -DMOE_LSA_COPIERS=1
flashinfer.jit: Building JIT module cake_sm120_megamoe_nocopier_faf93d71e7c04e2bd350; this can take several minutes on first use.
Traceback (most recent call last):
  File ".../flashinfer/moe_ep/modes/mega_layer.py", line 377, in warmup
    fleet_params, _backend_workspace = self._resolve_workspace(workspace)
  File ".../flashinfer/moe_ep/modes/mega_layer.py", line 188, in _ensure_work

items.title: [Question] How to force certain computations to occur in float16?
items.author: vedantroy
items.body_excerpt:
I have the following kernel:
```python3
@triton.jit
def unmasked_blend_kernel(
    img1_ptr, img2_ptr, ratio: float, total_items: int, BLOCK_SIZE: tl.constexpr
):
    block_idx = tl.program_id(0)
    offset = block_idx * BLOCK_SIZE
    item_element_idxs = tl.arange(0, BLOCK_SIZE)
    img1_item_ptrs = img1_ptr + offset + item_element_idxs
    img2_item_ptrs = img2_ptr + offset + item_element_idxs

    if offset + BLOCK_SIZE > total_items:
        mask = item_element_idxs < total_items % BLOCK_SIZE
        img1 = tl.load(img1_item_ptrs, mask=mask, other=0)
        img2 = tl.load(img2_item_ptrs, mask=mask, other=0)
        out = ratio * img1 + (1.0 - ratio) * img2
        tl.store(img1_item_ptrs, out, mask=mask)
    else:
        img1 = tl.load(img1_item_ptrs)
        img2 = tl.load(img2_item_ptrs)
        out = ratio * img1 + (1.0 - ratio) * img2
        tl.store(img1_item_ptrs, out)
```

Given that this kernel is blending 2 uint8  tensors, I figured it would make sense to do the computation ` out = ratio * img1 + (1.0 - ratio) * img2`  since I don't need high precision.

However, I can't figure out how to force the Triton compiler to do the computations in FP16.
I tried doing:

```python3
        img1 = tl.load(img1_item_ptrs, mask=mask, other=0).to(tl.float16)
        img2 = tl.load(img2_item_ptrs, mask=mask, other=0).to(tl.float16)
```
but from looking at the generated PTX, it just seems like the float16s are just converted to float32s before the multiplication 
occurs.

Is there a way I can force the Triton  compiler  to make the multiplications float16? (Or is this impossible for a good reason;  i.e maybe this is not what I actually want)?

items.title: [WS] getPartitionOutputs assertion in NVWSHoistTmemStore with warp_specialize=True on a pointer-load persistent matmul
items.author: builtin-pb
items.body_excerpt:
### Describe the bug

**Summary.** Compiling for Blackwell (`cuda:100` or `cuda:103`) stops with an internal assertion in `getPartitionOutputs`, during `NVWSHoistTmemStore`, when the outer tile loop uses `tl.range(..., warp_specialize=True)`, the inner K loop uses plain pointer loads and `tl.dot`, and C is written with a plain `tl.store`. We are not asking for this loop to be specialized, only for no assertion. Adding to HoistTmemStore's loop collection the `hasPartition(loop)` check that `NVWSInsertAref` uses may be sufficient; see Suggested fix.

#### Reproduce

The script is compile-only and needs no GPU; the kernel is never launched (it assumes full tiles and 16-byte-aligned, contiguous fp16 A and B and fp32 C).

```python
"""Compile-only reproducer (no GPU needed).

Requesting automatic warp specialization on a persistent tile loop whose body is
an ordinary pointer-load matmul makes Triton hit an internal assertion:
    getPartitionOutputs: Assertion `op->hasAttr(kPartitionOutputsAttrName)' failed.

    python ws_assert_min.py              # warp_specialize=True: assertion
    python ws_assert_min.py --ws 0       # same kernel without it: compiles

--inner 0 drops the inner K loop (one tl.dot per tile); --dot 0 replaces tl.dot
with row/column sums; --cdesc 1 stores C through a TMA tensor descriptor
(as Triton's own persistent warp-specialization test does); --arch picks the target (100 = B200, 103 = B300, 90 = H100);
--warps and --stages set num_warps (default 4) and num_stages (default 3).
"""
import argparse
import inspect

import triton
import triton.language as tl
from triton.backends.compiler import GPUTarget
from triton.compiler import ASTSource


@triton.jit
def ws_min(A, B, C, num_tiles, k_iters,
           BM: tl.constexpr, BN: tl.constexpr, BK: tl.constexpr,
           WS: tl.constexpr, INNER: tl.constexpr, DOT: tl.constexpr, CDESC: tl.constexpr):
    rm = tl.arange(0, BM)
    rn = tl.arange(0, BN)
    rk = tl.arange(0, BK)
    K = k_iters * BK
    if CDESC:
        c_desc = tl.make_tensor_descriptor(C, shape=[num_tiles * BM, BN], strides=[BN, 1], block_shape=[BM, BN])
    for tile in tl.range(tl.program_id(0), num_tiles, tl.num_programs(0), warp_specialize=WS):
        rows = tile * BM + rm
        acc = tl.zeros((BM, BN), tl.float32)
        if INNER:
            for k in range(k_iters):
                a = tl.load(A + rows[:, None] * K + (k * BK + rk)[None, :])
                b = tl.load(B + (k * BK + rk)[:, None] * BN + rn[None, :])
                if DOT:
                    acc = tl.dot(a, b, acc)
                else:
                    acc += tl.sum(a.to(tl.float32), 1)[:, None] + tl.sum(b.to(tl.float32), 0)[None, :]
        else:
            a = tl.load(A + rows[:, None] * K + rk[None, :])
            b = tl.load(B + rk[:, None] * BN + rn[None, :])
            if DOT:
                acc = tl.dot(a, b, acc)
            else:
                acc += tl.sum(a.to(tl.float32), 1)[:, None] + tl.sum(b.to(tl.float32), 0)[None, :]
        if CDESC:
            c_desc.store([tile * BM, 0], acc)
        else:
            tl.store(C + rows[:, None] * BN + rn[None, :], acc)


def main():
    p = argparse.ArgumentParser()
    p.add_argument("--ws", type=int, default=1)
    p.add_argument("--inner", type=int, default=1)
    p.add_argument("--dot", type=int, default=1)
    p.add_argument("--cdesc", type=int, default=0)
    p.add_argument("--arch", type=int, default=100)
    p.add_argument("--warps", type=int, default=4)
    p.add_argument("--stages", type=int, default=3)
    args = p.parse_args()

    constants = dict(BM=128, BN=64, BK=64, WS=bool(args.ws), INNER=bool(args.inner), DOT=bool(args.dot), CDESC=bool(args.cdesc))
    runtime = dict(A="*fp16", B="*fp16", C="*fp32", num_tiles="i32", k_iters="i32")
    names = list(ws_min.arg_names)
    signature = {n: runtime.get(n, "constexpr") for n in names}
    attrs = {(names.index(n),): [["tt.divisibility", 16]] for n in ("A", "B", "C")}
    key = "constexprs" if "constexprs" in inspect.signature(ASTSource).parameters else "constants"
    src = ASTSource(ws_min, signature=signature, attrs=attrs, **{key: constants})
    print(f"triton {triton.__version__}, target cuda:{args.arch}, warps {args.warps}, stages {args.stages}, {constants}", flush=True)
    compiled = triton.compile(src, target=GPUTarget("cuda", args.arch, 32),
                              options=dict(num_warps=args.warps, num_stages=args.stages))
    ttgir = compiled.asm["ttgir"]
    print("COMPILED; ttg.warp_specialize ops in TTGIR:", ttgir.count("ttg.warp_specialize("), flush=True)


if __name__ == "__main__":
    main()
```

`python ws_assert_min.py` stops with:

```
Partitioning.cpp:24: ... mlir::triton::gpu::getPartitionOutputs(mlir::Operation*): Assertion `op->hasAttr(kPartitionOutputsAttrName)' failed.
... Pipeline failed while executing [`TritonGPUAutomaticWarpSpecialization` on 'builtin.module' operation, `NVWSHoistTmemStore` on 'builtin.module' operation]
RuntimeError: PassManager::run failed
```

This reproduces on Triton 3.8.0 (PyPI wheel; there the assertion is at `Partition.cpp:354`) and on main (`0d4e0a0c`). The controls:

| Command (`--arch 100` or `--arch 103`) | 3.8.0 and main |
|---|---|
| `python ws_assert_min.py` (also with `--stages 1` or `--warps 8`) | assertion |
| `--ws 0` | compiles |
| `--cdesc 1` (C stored through a tensor descriptor) | compiles and emits one `ttg.warp_specialize` |
| `--inner 0` or `--dot 0` | compiles, without specialization |

We ask only for no assertion: `warp_specialize` is documented as an attempt, and loops it cannot partition are otherwise left alone, as with the controls above. Triton's own `test_warp_specialize_tma_matmul_persistent` has the same structure with pointer loads for A and B and expects `ttg.warp_specialize`; it differs only in storing C through a descriptor.

#### Cause

From reading the source at `0d4e0a0c` (we did not trace the passes):
- Partition scheduling writes `ttg.partition` and `ttg.partit

items.title: [Bug]:  v0.25.0 picks FlashInfer mnnvl allreduce when multicast bind fails, then crashes with illegal memory access (2x H100)
items.author: dreamer-89
items.body_excerpt:
### Describe the bug
On some nodes, CUDA multicast bind fails at runtime. vLLM 0.25.0 still selects `mnnvl` for the fused allreduce + RMSNorm. The engine then dies in the first warmup pass. I hit it on two different nodes with the same image. 

### Your current environment
- 2x H100 80GB HBM3, single node, container. NV18 between the GPUs. Fabric State Completed, Status Success.
- Driver 595.71.05 (open kernel module), CUDA 13.2.
- vLLM 0.25.0, PyTorch 2.11.0+cu130, flashinfer-python 0.6.13, NCCL 2.28.9.


### Steps to reproduce
1. Check the node with this PyTorch-only probe (no vLLM or FlashInfer). On the bad nodes it prints `0x0` on both ranks:
```python
# torchrun --nproc_per_node=2 probe.py
import os, torch, torch.distributed as dist
import torch.distributed._symmetric_memory as symm_mem
torch.cuda.set_device(int(os.environ["LOCAL_RANK"]))
dist.init_process_group("nccl")
t = symm_mem.empty(1 << 20, dtype=torch.float32, device="cuda")
h = symm_mem.rendezvous(t, group=dist.group.WORLD.group_name)
print(os.environ["RANK"], hex(h.multicast_ptr))  # prints 0x0 on the bad nodes
```
2. On the same node, run this with the default `VLLM_FLASHINFER_ALLREDUCE_BACKEND` (TP=2):
```python
from vllm import LLM

if __name__ == "__main__":
    LLM(model="Qwen/Qwen2.5-32B-Instruct", tensor_parallel_size=2, dtype="bfloat16",
        max_num_seqs=128, max_model_len=7128, gpu_memory_utilization=0.9,
        enable_prefix_caching=False)
```
3. About 2 minutes in, the engine fails during CUDA graph warmup with the logs below.

### Logs
```
[W CUDASymmetricMemory.cu:595] Warning: CUDA driver error: the operation cannot be performed in the present state (function init_multicast_for_block)
[W CUDASymmetricMemory.cu:612] Gracefully skipping multicast initialization.
NCCL INFO Failed to bind NVLink SHARP (NVLS) Multicast memory of size 2097152 : CUDA error 401 'the operation cannot be performed in the present state'. Proceeding without NVLS support.
INFO [flashinfer_all_reduce.py:119] Auto-selected flashinfer allreduce backend: mnnvl
INFO [flashinfer_all_reduce.py:168] Initialized FlashInfer Allreduce norm fusion workspace with backend=mnnvl
...
vllm/v1/worker/gpu/cudagraph_utils.py:333 forward_fn(CUDAGraphMode.NONE)
RuntimeError: ... trtllm_mnnvl_allreduce_fusion failed with error code an illegal memory access was encountered
```

In a second run on another node, the same fault surfaced one op later as a plain `torch.AcceleratorError: CUDA error: an illegal memory access was encountered`, in the same warmup pass.

### Why I think it crashes
1. PyTorch returns a handle with `multicast_ptr == 0` when the bind fails. NCCL hits the same error and falls back cleanly.
2. FlashInfer 0.6.13 stores that pointer without a check (`trtllm_mnnvl_ar.py`, `self.mc_ptr = self.handle.multicast_ptr`), and the kernel writes through it.
3. vLLM falls back to `trtllm` only when workspace creation raises. Here creation succeeded, so there was no fallback.

vLLM already checks `multicast_ptr == 0` for its own `SymmMemCommunicator` (`symm_mem.py`), just not for this workspace.

### Workaround
`VLLM_FLASHINFER_ALLREDUCE_BACKEND=trtllm`. The engine starts and serves normally on the same node.

### Possibly fixed by
- #49043 (in v0.27.0): rejects invalid MNNVL workspaces.
- #56891 (main): changes backend selection.



### 🐛 Describe the bug

Provided in description above

### Before submitting a new issue...

- [x] Make sure you already searched for relevant issues, and asked the chatbot living at the bottom right corner of the [documentation page](https://docs.vllm.ai/en/latest/), which can answer lots of frequently asked questions.

items.title: [RFC] FlashInfer Release-Quality Action Plan
items.author: YangXu1990uiuc
items.body_excerpt:
# FlashInfer Release-Quality Action Plan

*Owner: Yang Xu · written for community review — feedback welcome.*

> **Status update 2026-09-06.** Both harnesses are merged and gate CI by default; the MoE fuzzer has
> since caught two more real bugs; Stream 0 landed a per-unit timeout runner. Sampling and Attention
> are still unstarted (contributors wanted — see §3); Norm/RoPE is being picked up by @0z5a. Changes
> from the June text are marked *(updated)*. Running tally of harness-found bugs added at the end of §3.

## TL;DR

Recent release-quality gaps cluster in low-precision and MoE, and reached users mainly because the
test signal was too weak to gate on and architecture coverage was thin. The plan: port one proven
test kit — 7 invariant oracles + an authoritative reference + adversarial inputs — op by op, run it
on a trustworthy, gating CI signal, and back it with complementary tiers (perf, compute-sanitizer,
framework-integration). Two harnesses (MoE, scaled GEMM) are already built and each found real bugs
soon after landing; the rest are net-new. Then re-audit what still escapes and repeat the loop.

## Why this doc exists

Downstream serving frameworks and users have flagged gaps in FlashInfer's recent release quality,
and the pattern is visible directly in our own issue tracker — e.g. attention quality regressions
(#1645), BF16 MoE stability (#3364), hangs (#3329), and MoE perf (#3521).

This plan lays out, grounded in that history: **what's broken, why it escapes today's tests, what
we're building to catch it before release, and — issue by issue — how much of the historical bug
stream each piece addresses.** The catch-rate figures are forward-looking estimates — from reviewing
past issues one at a time and judging what each harness will catch once fully built out, across
backends/dtypes/architectures — not a measurement of today's coverage, and are given as ranges.

## Precedent — a proven playbook, not a bet

The design here is borrowed from cuDNN, where it already worked. After cuDNN shipped
`test_mhas_v2` — a single consolidated attention fuzzer (one strong harness, an authoritative
reference, adversarial inputs), the direct model for the design below — attention-related bug
reports dropped substantially and the time from kernel-completion to end-to-end convergence
shortened (far fewer silent-correctness round-trips). We are porting that working system to
FlashInfer, op by op. The sharpest techniques carry over directly:

- **sparse + exact-grid inputs** so structural bugs aren't averaged away (a low-precision analog of
  the sparse-integer trick);
- **an authoritative reference recipe** as the single source of truth;
- **output-buffer poison** for the uninitialized / padding-leak class;
- **per-backend determinism (CRC) + a device-state probe** after each config;
- **compute-sanitizer racecheck + SASS forensics** for Heisenbugs (§4).

The point: this is a portable system, not a one-off. It is now validated on **two** ops (MoE and
scaled GEMM, §3) — and in both cases it found real bugs shortly after landing.

## 1. Diagnosis — why bugs reach users today

From a census of 2026-H1 issues (~131 bug issues, 161 merged fix-PRs):

1. **The dominant clusters are low-precision and MoE.** MoE alone ≈ 31% of bug issues; the
   low-precision FP4/FP8/MXFP8 GEMM+MoE cluster ≈ 36%; attention/KV is another large slice.
2. **~60% of fixes land in the Python dispatch / validation / marshaling layer, not deep in the
   kernel** — i.e. most bugs are integration and contract bugs, not exotic math.
3. **The test signal was too weak to gate on.** Some classes — notably hangs and timeouts — could
   pass without surfacing, and the suites that did run were too gentle to fail on real bugs (point
   4). Together these let bugs reach users even on paths CI nominally exercised. Strengthening the
   signal so a real bug reliably turns the build red is the highest-leverage fix and is in progress.
4. **Existing low-precision tests are gentle:** fixed shape grids, loose `cosine > 0.97`, a single
   autotune mode, no edge inputs / output-poison / determinism / device-state checks.

The takeaway that shapes everything below: **the same ~7 failure classes recur across every op**
(§2). So we don't need 7 unrelated test efforts — we need **one invariant "kit"** (no-crash,
reference-numeric, determinism, output-poison, autotune sweep + real-path, device-state probe)
applied per op, where the only per-op work is the **authoritative reference** and the **input
model**. That kit is now proven on two ops; it generalizes.

## 2. The recurring bug classes (and the oracle that catches each)

| # | Bug class | Representative examples (any op) | Oracle that catches it |
|---|---|---|---|
| C1 | Numerical wrong-output / accuracy | MoE #3197, #2822; GEMM #3103; fp8 #2431; sampling #2320 | numeric vs authoritative reference + sparse exact-grid inputs |
| C2 | NaN / Inf where ref is finite | #2595 (cutlass fp8), #1646 (cutlass MoE), sampling #2402 | reference-aware no-NaN |
| C3 | Crash / IMA / device-assert | MoE #3427, #2776; GEMM #2516, #3085 | no-crash + device-state probe (+ compute-sanitizer, §4) |
| C4 | Uninitialized / padding-leak into real output | mm_fp4 #2861 | output-buffer poison |
| C5 | Determinism / intermittent | sampling #3470, #2284; intermittent MoE NaN | per-backend CRC determinism + N-run stress (§4) |
| C6 | Autotune: tactic / profiling / cache | MoE #3168, #3197; bmm_fp8 #3085 | tactic sweep + autotune-ON real path + cache-coherence |
| C7 | Arch coverage / dispatch / marshaling | MoE #3466 (missing SM103 cubin), #3359; mm_fp4 #2577 | arch axis in matrix + build-manifest oracle |

These seven are the engine. Each op below is just *which classes dominate + what the reference is.*

## 3. Per-op map — status, dominant classes, and projected catch

Denominator throughout = **bug issues only** (feature requests / RFEs excluded entirely).

| Op | Harness status | Dominant classes | Representative issues | Pr

items.title: Feature Request: do not hide the build or version number anymore
items.author: FlorinAndrei
items.body_excerpt:
### Prerequisites

- [x] I am running the latest code. Mention the version if possible as well.
- [x] I carefully followed the [README.md](https://github.com/ggml-org/llama.cpp/blob/master/README.md).
- [x] I searched using keywords relevant to my issue to make sure that I am creating a new issue that is not already open (or closed).
- [x] I reviewed the [Discussions](https://github.com/ggml-org/llama.cpp/discussions), and have a new and useful enhancement to share.

### Feature Description

Yes, the --version option is a thing. But everything else hides the version, or build number.

Docker image? It's `ghcr.io/ggml-org/llama.cpp:server-cuda13`, impossible to tell.

Docker logs? llama-server starts, and not a single peep about the version, or build number.

llama-ui? If the version is exposed anywhere, it must be very well hidden. I could not find it.

This is probably not intentional, but to the user it kind of does look like llama.cpp tries very hard to hide the version/build numbers. This is not helpful.

### Motivation

I never know what version of llama-server I'm running. I always have to bend over backwards to figure it out, especially when running the UI.

If I don't know the version, I do not know which features are supported.

### Possible Implementation

llama-ui should display the version number and the release string somewhere. Not hidden.

llama-server should print the same in the logs, when it starts.

items.title: [RFC] Review MC_USE_TENT=1 gaps for classic TE callers
items.author: staryxchen
items.body_excerpt:
## How this list was produced

Started as a static pass over:

- the C++ shim (`mooncake-transfer-engine/src/transfer_engine.cpp`, `use_tent_` branches)
- the Python wrapper (`mooncake-integration/transfer_engine/transfer_engine_py.cpp`)
- inference-engine call sites that use `mooncake.engine.TransferEngine`

Local runtime (2026-09-10, installed TENT wheel, 1P1D PD) then confirmed
some items and left others unverified. Status below is as of **2026-09-17**
(`origin/main` `c4d632888b`). Please still reproduce on your tree before
treating a remaining item as confirmed.

## Why the compatibility layer

We are wiring inference engines to TENT's **native** APIs, but that work is
not finished. Until it is, we use the classic TE compatibility layer
(`MC_USE_TENT=1`) to validate TENT **runtime** stability against existing
callers (PD disaggregation and others). This RFC tracks gaps in that layer.
It is not the native-API migration itself.

## Summary

`MC_USE_TENT=1` (and `MC_USE_TEV1=1`) is meant to run existing
`mooncake::TransferEngine` / `mooncake.engine.TransferEngine` code on the TENT
runtime. Register + sync submit/poll are wired up enough for PD KV transfer.

PD happy path **works** under `MC_USE_TENT=1` (local 1P1D Qwen3-4B
`/generate` 200). This RFC is not a claim that PD is broken today.

Most of the original P0/P1/P2 shim holes now have merged PRs. What is still
open is protocol pinning for `efa`/`ascend`, Python sync/poll semantics, and
`installTransport()` returning `nullptr` for classic C/Go/EFA callers.

If you find a **new** compatibility-layer issue, please report it on this
issue. We will add it to the work-item list.

## Non-goals

- Landing inference-engine (or Mooncake Store) native-API migration in this RFC
  (that work is separate and in progress, e.g. #4070).
- Teaching applications to `installTransport` under TENT. Making the shim
  honor the classic `Transport*` contract so existing callers do not treat a
  successful TENT init as failure **is** in scope (`P1-install-transport`).
- Changing TENT runtime scheduling / failover policy.

## Work items

Priority is "if the reading holds, impact is high" — not "already on fire".

| ID | Problem | Difficulty | PR | Status |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| P0-send_probe | Python `send_probe` SIGSEGV (`getMetadata()` is null) | M | #4081, follow-up #4115 | **done** |
| P0-stale-handle | Transfer failure may keep a dead peer's cached handle (`CheckSegmentStatus` was always OK) | M | #4109 | **partial** |
| P0-device-filter | `initialize(device=...)` still opened all HCAs | M | #4028 | **done** |
| P0-force-tcp | `MC_FORCE_TCP=1` / `protocol=tcp` may still select RDMA | M | #4027, follow-up #4113 | **done** |
| P0-efa-ascend | `protocol=efa\|ascend` may no-op or look successful without that transport | H | — | **open** |
| P1-sync-status | Python `transferSync` retry / `CANCELED` handling may not match TENT failover | S–M | — | **open** |
| P1-error-codes | Shim returned TENT `Status::Code` (non-negative); classic callers expect `ERR_*` | M | #4139 | **done** |
| P1-request-options | `priority` / `remote_accessible` were dropped at the shim | M | #4114 | **done** |
| P2-first-buffer | `getFirstBufferAddress` also called `getMetadata()` (same null deref as `send_probe`) | S | #4138 | **done** |
| P1-install-transport | TENT `installTransport()` returns `nullptr`; classic C/Go/EFA callers treat that as install failure | M | — | **open** |

### Residuals on landed items

These do not reopen the row, but they are not "the original hole is gone with no leftover":

- **P0-send_probe.** Python no longer dereferences `getMetadata()`. #4081 closed the segment after probing, which invalidated a handle already stored in Python `handle_map_`; #4115 stopped closing it. C++ `getMetadata()` is still `nullptr` under TENT — any remaining `getMetadata()->sendProbe` caller will still crash.
- **P0-stale-handle.** `CheckSegmentStatus` now probes via `probePeerAliveByID`. Python only calls it when **`submitTransfer` fails**. Peer death that shows up as `getTransferStatus` `FAILED` / `TIMEOUT` still leaves `handle_map_` intact. That leftover belongs with **P1-sync-status**. The unit test covers an never-opened handle, not a still-mapped handle whose RPC probe fails.
- **P0-force-tcp.** #4113 makes `forceTcp()` disable HP TCP so a config with both enabled does not fail init.
- **P1-error-codes.** Integer-returning APIs go through `tentToClassicError()`. `submitTransfer` still wraps TENT failures as `Status::Context(...)`. No in-tree test that failed on main and passed after (#4139 checklist).
- **P1-request-options.** Shim forwards `remote_accessible` → TENT perms and `TransferRequest::priority` on submit. Python `transferSync` does not set `priority` (default MEDIUM). No in-tree red/green test (#4114 checklist).

### Still open

- **P0-efa-ascend.** `init(..., protocol)` is now forwarded, but the TENT branch only special-cases `"tcp"`. `"efa"` / `"ascend"` do not pin those transports. On `USE_EFA` / `USE_CXI` Python builds, `initialize` still calls `installTransport()` after init; under TENT that returns `nullptr` and `initialize` returns `-1`. #4122 is classic TE Ascend Direct selection, not this shim item.
- **P1-sync-status.** `transferSync` still retries `numContexts()+1` times; under TENT `numContexts()` is hardcoded `1`. The poll loop handles `COMPLETED` / `FAILED` / `TIMEOUT` only — not `CANCELED` — and does not evict the cached handle on poll failure.
- **P1-install-transport.** Added from @chlins (2026-09-14). The TENT branch logs `"installTransport not used by TENT"` and returns `nullptr`. Classic contract: `nullptr` means install failed. Store already skips this via `isUsingTent()` (#2596). C / Go (`transfer_engine_c.h`) and EFA/CXI Python do not. Proposed fix A (TENT returns a non-null sentinel; in-tree callers only null-check) is preferred over gating every caller (B) or fixing only the C shim (C). Waiting on TENT owners (@alogfans) before a PR. R

items.title: [Bug]: trtllm-gen FMHA JIT requires /usr/local/cuda/bin/nvcc (ignores CUDA_HOME / PATH) even with NVRTC, failing MLA generation and executor warmup when the toolkit lives elsewhere
items.author: lucifer1004
items.body_excerpt:
### System Info

- TensorRT-LLM main @ e88d19ca3b, PyTorch backend, `TrtllmAttention`
- Any container or host where the CUDA toolkit is not at `/usr/local/cuda`, for example conda/pixi environments. `CUDA_HOME` is set, and `nvcc` is on `PATH`.
- Seen on SM107. The code path (trtllm-gen FMHA NVRTC JIT) is not architecture-specific.

### Who can help?

Same module as #20507 (`fmha/lib/<arch>/libTrtLlmGen.a`, the prebuilt trtllm-gen archive). Related: #12612 (trtllm-gen FMHA JIT), #14851 (JIT warmup).

### Reproduction

Any configuration where a trtllm-gen FMHA kernel takes the NVRTC path, for example MLA generation. The unit test is enough:

```bash
# In a TensorRT-LLM container built from main, as root: move the toolkit away from /usr/local/cuda
mv /usr/local/cuda /usr/local/cuda-real
export CUDA_HOME=/usr/local/cuda-real
export PATH=$CUDA_HOME/bin:$PATH
export LD_LIBRARY_PATH=${LD_LIBRARY_PATH//\/usr\/local\/cuda/$CUDA_HOME}
which nvcc && nvcc --version | tail -1          # nvcc is found
cd tests/unittest && pytest -q _torch/attention/test_attention_mla.py
```

Result: 28 failed, 68 passed. Each failure is:

```
[E] [GenCtx.cpp:68]: Cannot parse NVCC version from /usr/local/cuda/bin/nvcc. Output:
sh: 1: /usr/local/cuda/bin/nvcc: not found
[E] [FmhaInterface.cpp:426]: Error parsing configs: Cannot parse NVCC version from /usr/local/cuda/bin/nvcc. Output:
...
RuntimeError: Error parsing configs: Cannot parse NVCC version from /usr/local/cuda/bin/nvcc.
```

The printed kernel config has `"usesNvRtc": true`.

In serving, the same error comes from the trtllm-gen FMHA JIT warmup (`Running TRTLLM-Gen FMHA JIT warmup`). The first MLA generation warmup step fails on every rank, and executor creation fails with `Failed to initialize executor on rank 0: Error parsing configs: Cannot parse NVCC version from /usr/local/cuda/bin/nvcc`.

### Expected behavior

The JIT uses the toolkit the environment points to (`CUDA_HOME`, or `nvcc` on `PATH`). Better, it does not need `nvcc` at all when it compiles with NVRTC.

### Actual behavior

`libTrtLlmGen.a` (`GenCtx.cpp`) runs `/usr/local/cuda/bin/nvcc --version` and parses `release X.Y` from the output. That path is the default of the `GenCfg` `nvccPath` field, and TensorRT-LLM's generated config (`populateJsonConfig` in `fmha/fmhaKernels.h`) does not set it. The version query does not consult `CUDA_HOME`, `CUDA_PATH` or `PATH`: `GenCtx.cpp.o` in the archive does not call `getenv` and contains none of those names. This happens with `usesNvRtc: true`, so it applies even though the kernel is compiled by NVRTC.

I checked what the JIT actually needs from `nvcc`, on the same test file, with `CUDA_HOME` set and the toolkit outside `/usr/local/cuda` in all three runs:

| `/usr/local/cuda/bin/nvcc` | result |
|---|---|
| absent | 28 failed, 68 passed (140 × `nvcc: not found`) |
| symlink to the real `nvcc` | 96 passed |
| stub that answers only `--version` (via the real `nvcc`), logs every call, and fails on anything else | 96 passed; the stub was called once, with `--version` only |

So `nvcc` is needed only for the version query. All compilation goes through NVRTC.

### Additional notes

Suggested fix, in the trtllm-gen archive (`GenCtx`), in order of preference:

1. When `usesNvRtc` is set, take the version from NVRTC (`nvrtcVersion`, which the archive already references) and do not require `nvcc`.
2. Otherwise resolve `nvcc` in this order: an explicit `nvccPath`, then `$CUDA_HOME/bin/nvcc`, then `$CUDA_PATH/bin/nvcc`, then `nvcc` on `PATH`, and only then `/usr/local/cuda/bin/nvcc`. Report the path that was tried in the error.

Possible TensorRT-LLM-side stopgap until the archive is refreshed: emit `"nvccPath"` in `populateJsonConfig`, resolved as in item 2. I have not verified that the archive honors the field when it is set from the generated config; I only see the field name next to its default in the archive's string table.

Workaround for affected environments: provide `/usr/local/cuda/bin/nvcc`, for example a symlink to the real toolkit.

What is verified: the table above, on SM107 with a build of main at e88d19ca3b in a container whose toolkit is not under `/usr/local/cuda`. I have not run the "rename `/usr/local/cuda`" variant in an official image, but it recreates the same condition.

Cross-reference #20507: the serving warmup goes through `warmupOneKernel`, and the config printed with this error there has `"smVersion": "107a"`. That is the path #20507 describes, which hands `Sm107a` to the archive without the `Sm100f` rewrite that `run()` applies. The unit-test failures above go through `run()` and print `"smVersion": "100f"`.

items.title: [Feature]: Support NVIDIA Nemotron 3.5 ASR Streaming (nemotron-3.5-asr-streaming-0.6b)
items.author: robin-bially
items.body_excerpt:
### 🚀 The feature, motivation and pitch

NVIDIA recently released **Nemotron 3.5 ASR Streaming** ([nemotron-3.5-asr-streaming-0.6b](https://huggingface.co/nvidia/nemotron-3.5-asr-streaming-0.6b)), a 600M-parameter multilingual streaming ASR model under the OpenMDW-1.1 license.

Key features:
- **Native streaming architecture** with Cache-Aware FastConformer-RNNT, supporting configurable chunk sizes from 80ms to 1120ms
- **35 languages** (19 transcription-ready + 13 broad-coverage + 8 adaptation-ready), including German, English, French, Spanish, Japanese, Korean, etc.
- **Automatic language detection** via `target_lang=auto`
- **Punctuation & capitalization** built-in
- On a single H100: **240 concurrent streams at 80ms chunk**, ~17x more than Parakeet RNNT 1.1B

This would be a great addition to vLLM's supported ASR models, complementing the existing Voxtral Realtime and Qwen3-ASR support. The model is already available in HuggingFace Transformers (`AutoModelForRNNT`) and NVIDIA NeMo.

### Alternatives

Currently, the only open-source streaming ASR options in vLLM are:
- **Voxtral Realtime (4B)** — high VRAM due to persistent encoder KV-cache, limiting concurrent streams
- **Qwen3-ASR (0.6B/1.7B)** — segment-based (5s chunks), higher latency

Nemotron 3.5 would fill the gap for a lightweight, truly native streaming model with low latency and high throughput.

### Additional context

- HuggingFace: https://huggingface.co/nvidia/nemotron-3.5-asr-streaming-0.6b
- Architecture: FastConformer-CacheAware-RNNT with language-ID prompt conditioning
- Primary framework: NeMo, with Transformers support added
- Release date: June 4, 2026

### Before submitting a new issue...

- [x] Make sure you already searched for relevant issues, and asked the chatbot living at the bottom right corner of the documentation page, which can answer lots of frequently asked questions.

items.title: [Bug]: [SSD] Offload keys deferred to the ungrouped pool lose their tasks — NACKed at deferral, silently dropped next cycle, never written to SSD
items.author: ccgibson

comments.author: github-actions
comments.body:

A maintainer will triage this when possible. To help us respond faster, please include:

- Mooncake version or commit SHA
- Environment (OS, CUDA/driver, RDMA stack if relevant)
- Steps to reproduce and expected vs. actual behavior

Useful links: [Documentation](https://kvcache-ai.github.io/Mooncake/) · [Contributing guide](https://github.com/kvcache-ai/Mooncake/blob/main/CONTRIBUTING.md)

> This message was posted automatically by the issue bot.

comments.author: ccgibson
comments.body:
Requested details:

**Version / commit**
- Observed in production on `v0.3.12-pre1` (tag `8a836903`) with #2658 cherry-picked on top (the NACK sweep is what makes the loss silent — see the issue body for the pre-#2658 symptom, the 600s `Offloading task expired` storm).
- Code path verified byte-identical on `main` @ `fc04cb1` (the deferral branch in `GroupOffloadingKeysByBucket`, the NACK sweep at `file_storage.cpp:642`, and the task-filter drop at `file_storage.cpp:516`).

**Environment**
- Linux x86_64, 3-node shared pool, RDMA (RoCE v2, bonded 2×100G), eager offload (`enable_offload=1`, `offload_on_evict=0`), bucket storage backend (~236 MB effective bucket size ⇒ ~5 objects/bucket at ~47 MB objects), drain cycle ≈ 10 s via `OffloadObjectHeartbeat`. Not RDMA/CUDA-specific — the bug is pure task-lifecycle logic in the offload worker.

**Steps to reproduce**
1. `MOONCAKE_OFFLOAD_BUCKET_KEYS_LIMIT=10`, eager offload enabled.
2. PUT 35 objects, let one heartbeat drain them.
3. `GroupOffloadingKeysByBucket` emits 3 full buckets and defers the 5-key tail to `ungrouped_offloading_objects_` (the in-tree test `GroupOffloadingKeysByBucket_bucket_keys_limit` already asserts exactly this grouping). The end-of-`OffloadObjects` sweep NACKs those 5 (`data_size=-1`), erasing their `offloading_tasks` and releasing the source-replica refcount.
4. Next heartbeat: the pool prepends the 5 keys into a bucket, but `task_by_storage_key` (rebuilt from that drain only) has no entry for them → the filter at `file_storage.cpp:516` drops them silently.

**Expected:** all 35 objects reach the SSD tier.
**Actual:** 30 do; the 5 deferred keys are never written (no `LOCAL_DISK` replica on the master, `BatchLoad`/existence probes miss), and once memory-evicted they are gone. No log or counter records the drop — attribution required correlating master-side eviction telemetry with worker-side `VLOG(1)` grouping lines (in our production window: every other abandonment path counted 0, deferral counted ~209/hour, matching the loss rate).

**Heads-up: we are building fix (A) from the issue body on our fork and will validate it in production in parallel** — `AllocateOffloadingBuckets`/`GroupOffloadingKeysByBucket` gain an optional out-param reporting the deferred keys; `FileStorage` keeps a small carried-task map, merges it into the next cycle's `task_by_storage_key`, and the NACK sweep exempts deferred keys (deliberate skips still NACK). Side benefit: the source-replica refcount pin now survives the one-cycle deferral, so the memory replica is guaranteed readable when the key is re-emitted. It composes with #2967 (different region of `OffloadObjects`). Happy to open a PR here once it has soaked, if (A) is the direction maintainers prefer.

comments.author: ccgibson
comments.body:
PR opened: #3009 (option A — carry the task across the deferral).

Production soak since deploying this fix on our 3-node pool (on `v0.3.12-pre1` + #2658; the PR is the same change rebased onto `main` @ `fc04cb1`, clean cherry-pick):

- **3.7 hours, +92,350 pool exits vs +92,350 disk-tier evictions — exactly equal.** Gap growth zero; pre-fix it was ~12% of pool exits.
- NACK rate ~50/min → **~0.02/min** (the residual being genuine deliberate skips — already-on-disk / over-size-limit — which should NACK).
- `Offloading task expired` stayed at 0 throughout: the carried refcount pins do not recreate the pre-#2658 TTL leak.

All three affected test suites pass built from `main`'s own builder stage (`file_storage_test` 25, `offload_on_evict_test` 9, `storage_backend_test` 72).

One design note worth reviewer attention (details in the PR): previously carried keys must be *retained* while un-emitted, not rebuilt from the deferral report each cycle — an empty effective input leaves the pool untouched and reports nothing, so the seemingly simpler rebuild variant silently re-introduces the bug. Our first draft had it; the regression test caught it.
