items.title: [Roadmap]Fast Engine Recovery: Weight Cache Daemon
items.author: liusy58
items.body_excerpt:
# [Roadmap] Fast Engine Recovery: Weight Cache Daemon 
@liusy58 @QiuMike @alexnails 
Phase 1 landed in #27139 — a per-rank daemon holds post-quantized weights and serves them over CUDA IPC; weight load drops from ~306–327s to <1s on Qwen3-235B FP8 ([blog](https://www.lmsys.org/blog/2026-08-21-sglang-fast-recovery)). This issue tracks the next steps. Contributions and feedback are welcome.

Related: #27052 (Fast Recovery framework), #27310 (GPU Memory Service / VMM)

Goals: <10s cold restart and <1s warm standby switch; broaden model & quant coverage; make the cache outlive the daemon; make resident weights usable beyond the one GPU they sit on.

Where Phase 1 stands: TP + PP, single-node and multi-node launch (each node spawns its share of ranks and joins one dist group), zero-copy IPC per GPU, unquantized + block-wise FP8. Not yet: cross-node daemon coordination / failover, DP & EP shard keying, spec-decoding draft models, weight update / sleep-wake, cache surviving daemon death.

## Model & quantization coverage

- [ ] parity harness — disk-load vs daemon-load `state_dict` diff (names / shape / dtype / stride / byte hash) + short GSM8K gate; required evidence for every new allowlist entry
- [ ] carry post-processing metadata in the manifest (final shape/stride, layout tag, whitelisted module attrs) instead of reproducing `process_weights_after_loading` on a meta-init model — this is what blocks most quant methods today
- [ ] quant methods: per-tensor fp8 / w8a8 int8 / mxfp8 / nvfp4 / compressed-tensors / awq / gptq-marlin #32398 
- [ ] archs: MoE (DeepSeek V3/V4, Ling, Kimi K3) / hybrid linear attention / multimodal (vision tower + projector) / LoRA base weights https://github.com/sgl-project/sglang/pull/33684
- [ ] MTP & EAGLE draft models (per-rank draft daemon), removing the `--speculative-algorithm` rejection in `server_args.py` #32744
- [ ] generic post-map rebuild hook to replace the hardcoded `_rebuild_stale_views`; make tied storages, param→buffer flips and non-persistent buffers explicit in the manifest
- [ ] publish the support matrix in docs; unsupported combinations keep hard-erroring (no silent wrong numerics)

## Transport: CUDA VMM shareable handles (#27310 §4.2)



- [ ] `vmm_fd` backend (skeleton already in `weight_cache/transport.py`): `cuMemCreate` + FD handles over `SCM_RIGHTS`, VA reservation on import, `torch_ipc` stays the fallback, `--weight-cache-transport {auto,torch_ipc,vmm_fd}` #33279
- [ ] `mooncake` backend https://github.com/sgl-project/sglang/pull/36293


## Weight update without reload

- [ ] epoch handoff on stable VAs: readers unmap → writer commits → readers remap at the same VAs, so captured CUDA graphs stay valid
- [ ] daemon as the weight delivery agent for trainer pushes (NCCL/RDMA); un-gate the `update_weights_*` rejections in `weight_updater.py`
- [ ] colocated RL: engine itself takes the writer role, same protocol, no daemon in the loop

## Multi-instance & cross-GPU sharing

- [ ] key the cache by physical GPU UUID + config fingerprint (plus optional `--weight-cache-namespace`) under a configurable runtime dir. Today the socket is `/tmp/sglang_weight_cache_rank{global_rank}.sock`, so 2× tp=4 on one 8-GPU node collide and rank 0 of the second instance attaches to the GPU 0 daemon
- [ ] discovery: replace static socket paths with a lightweight registry (file-based dir, optionally etcd) so an engine rank selects a daemon by `CacheConfig` match rather than by process rank, and locates daemons across nodes without a manual `--weight-cache-socket`
- [ ] `--weight-cache-peer-copy` — when no daemon holds the shard on the local GPU, `cudaMemcpyPeerAsync` it from a peer-GPU daemon (NVLink-domain check, chunked on a low-priority stream, bandwidth cap so a serving neighbour is not disturbed). 1× memory per instance, sub-second over NVLink vs ~300s from disk
- [ ] preference order local zero-copy > peer copy > disk, reported per rank
- [ ] fleet fill: a daemon fills itself from a peer daemon instead of disk (P2P on-node, NCCL/RDMA cross-node), so a fleet cold start pays one disk read per shard group — the real bottleneck for 1T+ models on shared FS; align with the checkpoint-engine broadcast path
- [ ] out of scope for now: resharding across TP/EP topologies (tp=4 daemon → tp=8 engine)

## Multi-node, DP & EP

- [ ] primary–secondary daemon coordination for multi-node TP (e.g. TP=16 = 2 nodes × 8 GPUs): primary orchestrates daemon startup, cross-node NCCL process-group formation and readiness signalling; secondaries load their local shards in parallel and serve IPC handles to engines on their own node. Basic multi-node launch already works via `--nnodes/--node-rank/--dist-init-method`; what is missing is the cluster state machine
- [ ] cross-node daemon lifecycle: primary tracks which secondaries are alive, triggers coordinated restarts, signals engines on a dead secondary's node to fall back to disk; promote a secondary when the primary dies
- [ ] DP support: every DP rank on a GPU maps the same daemon's handles, so a model is read from disk and quantized exactly once per GPU regardless of DP degree (today each DP rank disk-loads independently). This is about supporting SGLang's DP deployment model, not cross-GPU sharing
- [ ] EP support: expert shards differ per EP rank, so cache and key them by `ep_rank`; handle partial expert loading when a rank owns a subset of experts
- [ ] `CacheConfig`: add `ep_rank`, `dp_rank` and `node_rank` for correct shard identification under EP and multi-node (`dp_size`/`ep_size` are already there)

## Ops & reliability

- [ ] `daemon status` command + Prometheus metrics (resident bytes, attached clients, load time, hit / mismatch / fallback), and an engine endpoint reporting how each rank got its weights
- [ ] runtime dir with owner-only permissions + `SO_PEERCRED` check before handing out handles (no world-writable `/tmp` sockets)
- [ ] `protocol_version` in the handshake with a documented skew policy (the env stamp alrea

items.title: [NVIDIA] ProxyFenceInsertion: no fence between tcgen05 async-proxy reads and later generic writes to a reused buffer
items.author: builtin-pb
items.body_excerpt:
### Describe the bug

**Summary.** `ProxyFenceInsertion` (`lib/Dialect/TritonNvidiaGPU/Transforms/ProxyFenceInsertion.cpp`) inserts `fence.proxy.async` when a generic shared-memory access is followed by an async-proxy access to an overlapping buffer, but checks async accesses only against earlier generic ones, so it never fences an async-proxy access followed by a generic access. That direction needs no fence for `cp.async.bulk` and `wgmma`, but PTX states no such implicit fence for `tcgen05`, so the pass does not fence when the allocator reuses a `tcgen05` operand buffer for generic accesses, as in the Gluon tutorial `06-tcgen05.py` (latent; see Scope). Either the pass should also fence here, or NVIDIA should confirm that `tcgen05` completion carries the implicit fence; see Options.

#### Evidence

In the tutorial, `blocked_matmul_kernel` allocates `c_smem` after the K loop, and the allocator places it at offset 0, over `a_smem`. In the PTX (sm_100a, Triton 3.8, c01b677), both are at `%r5 = global_smem`:
- the A-tile TMA load writes `[%r5]`;
- the epilogue's `st.shared` writes `[%r5 + %r132]`;
- the TMA store reads `[%r5]`.

The MMAs read A through the async proxy. Each K iteration ends with `mbarrier.try_wait.parity` on the MMA barrier (line 192 in the peeled first iteration, 224 in the loop). The epilogue then runs `tcgen05.ld` (323) and writes `c_smem` with four `st.shared::cta.v4.b32` (422–443), with no `fence.proxy.async` in between. The only fence in the kernel (447) is the tutorial's own `fence_async_shared()` before the TMA store. The overlap is made by the allocator, so the user cannot see it and has no reason to fence there.

The PTX is Triton 3.8's output for the tutorial, as published in a public corpus (gpu-verifier/sentryward, `corpus/tritongluon-06-tcgen05-blocked-matmul.ptx`). On main (2122e24), `ProxyFenceInsertion` still has the same structure ("Async-proxy accesses are retained only while they can still conflict with generic accesses preceding the current function").

PTX ISA 9.4:
- `cp.async.bulk` and `wgmma`: their completion "is followed by an implicit generic-async proxy fence" (§9.7.10.28.2 and §9.7.17.4). ConSan relies on the same reading (#10668: "for all relevant accesses ptx spec claims that after such wait no fence is required").
- `tcgen05` is the exception. §9.7.18.6.5 says the shared-memory accesses of `tcgen05.mma` and `tcgen05.cp` "are performed asynchronously and via the asynchronous proxy" and that "Accessing the same memory location across multiple proxies needs a cross-proxy fence". The `tcgen05` chapter states no implicit fence at their completion (`tcgen05.commit` and an mbarrier wait).

#### Options

Expected, one of:
- the pass also fences when bytes last accessed through the async proxy by a `tcgen05` op (`tcgen05.mma`, `tcgen05.cp`) are next accessed by generic ops, with the fence after the completion wait and before the generic access;
- or NVIDIA confirms that `tcgen05` completion carries the same implicit generic-async proxy fence as `wgmma` and bulk copies, in which case only the PTX text is missing it.

#### Scope

- Affected: any kernel in which the allocator reuses a `tcgen05` operand buffer for generic accesses with no fence in between, such as this tutorial.
- Latent: it is a read followed by an overwrite, very likely ordered on current hardware, and we have not seen a failure. We found it by checking the PTX against the ISA.
- Related: #12340 fixes the other direction at the Tensor Memory base-address slot, which `tcgen05.alloc` writes at offset 0 and a TMA load then overwrites.

#### Why there is no PR

Which option is right depends on how NVIDIA defines `tcgen05` completion, which we can't settle from the ISA text. If you'd like the pass change, tell us and we'll write it with a lit test.

### Environment details

Triton main 2122e24 (source reading; we have compiled and run nothing). PTX for sm_100a from Triton 3.8 (c01b677), from the corpus named above.

items.title: [RFC] Autotuner v2: FlashInfer-managed persistent cache and deployment-matched measurement
items.author: YangXu1990uiuc
items.body_excerpt:
**Status (2026-10-18)**: The managed-cache foundation (#3861), distributed mixed-hit fix (#6185), and vLLM integration (vllm-project/vllm#55671) are **merged**. The merged vLLM integration enables managed v2 only for eligible **single-rank** deployments; multi-rank retains the legacy path and measurement remains `auto`. Distributed managed tuning has new single-node B200 prototype evidence, including partial-cache recovery and a locally validated, not-yet-submitted cached-selection agreement follow-up. See [the October 18 progress update](https://github.com/flashinfer-ai/flashinfer/issues/3920#issuecomment-6248335250) for results and limits. SGLang has merged default-candidate coverage (sgl-project/sglang#43927), while managed persistence remains follow-up work. The design and graduation plan live in `docs/design_docs/autotuner_v2.md`; this RFC remains the roadmap and discussion thread.

## Summary

FlashInfer should own the persistence and compatibility rules for its autotuning results. Frameworks such as vLLM and SGLang should decide *when* to warm up and how to coordinate distributed workers — but they should not construct FlashInfer cache keys, interpret its JSON schema, or manage cache files, as they do today.

The proposal has four parts:

1. **A managed persistent cache** (`autotune_v2()`): environment-hashed directories, one atomic entry per tuned operation, invalid entries are misses (never errors), old generations left on disk.
2. **A measurement policy** (`MeasurementPolicy`): tune the way you deploy — eager vs CUDA-graph execution as the primary axis, cold-L2 as a secondary one.
3. **A runner contract**: rules that make "serving executes the tactic the tuner chose" structurally guaranteed rather than convention-enforced.
4. **An accuracy harness**: tuner quality ("picks the fastest tactic") becomes a measured claim (regret vs. an oracle), not an assumption.

Autotune data is a disposable performance optimization. Cross-version cache migration is a non-goal: after an upgrade, paying the tuning cost once for the new environment is acceptable. This follows the compiler-cache patterns of Triton and `torch.compile`/Inductor: key artifacts by program + compiler + environment, publish atomically, treat unusable entries as work to rebuild, own the local cache, and expose only an opaque export/import boundary.

## Evidence 1: how frameworks actually use v1

The following is the **July 2026 survey**, retained as design motivation rather than a description of current framework behavior. Both frameworks used one-shot startup warmup around a whole-model dummy forward, before CUDA Graph capture, with serving outside any context. Current migration status is in roadmap item 6; vLLM now retains per-rank legacy persistence for multi-rank deployments.

- **vLLM**: rank 0 runs `autotune(tune_mode=True, cache=<path>)`, broadcasts the raw JSON file bytes, every rank atomically rewrites the file and calls `load_configs(path)`. The cache path is a vLLM-computed `sha256(compile-factors)` directory — vLLM had to reinvent cache hashing, atomic writes, and an enable knob.
- **SGLang**: every rank tunes simultaneously (the dummy forward contains collectives, so rank-0-only tuning deadlocks DeepEP), with **one JSON file per rank**, its own model/quant/parallelism hash, its own disable env.
- **Features with zero external use**: `tune_mode=False` in serving, `tuning_buckets`, `round_up`, direct `save_configs`, `FLASHINFER_AUTOTUNER_LOAD_FROM_FILE` (the last has been silently broken since #3367 with zero reports — confirming zero users). `skip_ops` has latent demand (vllm-project/vllm#46238 wants per-op exclusion; SGLang disables autotune entirely for some models because one op crashes).
- **Exhibit A for key completeness**: vllm-project/vllm#43119 — the v1 file cache missed `use_8x4_sf_layout` in its key, invalid tactics were replayed, and vLLM **disabled the persistent cache for all multi-rank deployments** (at the time of that survey, even after the FlashInfer-side fix in #3367). A single key-completeness bug cost the feature its default.

Implications used throughout: reuse must not require an active context; the hashing/broadcast/knob code both frameworks built is exactly the policy FlashInfer should own; concurrent all-ranks tuning must be safe; key completeness needs a contract, not vigilance.

## Evidence 2: what field issues say

An audit of open autotuner-related issues clusters them into buckets; this RFC addresses the first four:

| bucket | issues | how this RFC addresses it |
|---|---|---|
| cross-rank tactic divergence | #3186, #3537 | shared store/reload, #3187 timing coordination, and #6185 mixed-hit coordination; cached-selection agreement and broader group correctness remain follow-up work |
| tuned tactic slower than default | #3537, #3622, #3409 | accuracy harness diagnoses; planned regression guard (default path always races as a candidate) |
| stale/invalid tactic at execute time | #3566 (mitigated by #3437), vllm#43119 | runner contract rules 1/4/5; environment-fingerprint invalidation |
| measurement ≠ deployment | #3648, #3719 | `MeasurementPolicy(execution_mode=...)` |
| probe-tensor crashes | #3558, #3569, #3085 | `skip_ops` quarantine is the mitigation; root fixes are separate work |
| kernel/candidate coverage (SM120 etc.) | #2992, #3119, #2577 | out of scope (kernel-side); harness quantifies the cost |

Notably, none of the open issues complains about v1's persistence file itself — the field pain is consistency, selection quality, and validity. That is why measurement policy and the runner contract are first-class parts of this proposal rather than afterthoughts.

## Limitations of the v1 cache (brief)

The caller owns too much FlashInfer-specific policy (filename choice = cache identity); environment mismatch is awkward (whole file rejected, refuses to save back); a monolithic JSON is a poor concurrent-update unit (read/merge/write races; one corrupt file kills every entry);

items.title: RPC: DeepSeek V4 output degenerates to a repeated token with two RPC workers after a long prompt, and the slot stays corrupted
items.author: bobsummerwill
items.body_excerpt:
### Name and Version

`llama-server` built from 42c787e8c (2026-10-07) on all three hosts, `-DGGML_RPC=ON`.

### Operating systems

Linux (main host, one RPC worker), macOS (one RPC worker)

### Which llama.cpp modules do you know to be affected?

llama-server, RPC backend (`ggml-rpc-server`)

### Problem description & steps to reproduce

With DeepSeek-V4-Flash-0731 (unsloth `UD-IQ4_XS` GGUF, `deepseek4` arch) split across the main host
and **two** RPC workers, a long prompt (~18k tokens) returns the same token over and over
(`DDDDDDDD…`, token id 38). The slot that processed it then stays broken: every later request
served from that slot, short ones included, returns the same repeated token, and requests with a
grammar (tools, `response_format`) fail with `Unexpected empty grammar stack after accepting piece:
D (38)`. Requests served by the other slot are fine. The same build, model, flags and requests
give correct output with no RPC, or with either RPC worker alone.

**Setup** (1 GbE LAN, ~0.3–0.6 ms between hosts)

| host | role | hardware | build |
|---|---|---|---|
| A | `llama-server` | 2× RTX 3090 (sm_86, driver 595.84), Ryzen 9 9950X3D, 62 GB, Ubuntu 24.04, kernel 7.0 | CUDA 12.6, `-DGGML_CUDA=ON -DGGML_CUDA_NCCL=ON -DCMAKE_CUDA_ARCHITECTURES=86` |
| B | `ggml-rpc-server -H <ip> -p 50052 -d CUDA0 -c` | RTX 5070 12 GB (sm_120, driver 580.178.04), Ubuntu 24.04 | CUDA 12.8, `-DCMAKE_CUDA_ARCHITECTURES=120` |
| C | `ggml-rpc-server -H <ip> -p 50052 -d MTL0 -c` | Mac mini M4 Pro 64 GB, macOS 27.0.1 | Metal (default) |

**Server command (host A)**

```
llama-server -m DeepSeek-V4-Flash-0731-UD-IQ4_XS-00001-of-00004.gguf \
  --rpc <B>:50052,<C>:50052 --fit on --fit-target 1024 --ctx-size 65536 --parallel 2 \
  --batch-size 2048 --ubatch-size 512 --flash-attn on --jinja --reasoning-format deepseek \
  --reasoning off --temp 0.7 --top-p 0.95
```

**Reproducer:** `dsv4_rpc_repro.py` in [this gist](https://gist.github.com/bobsummerwill/8010490af0fb6d55875a51389e6f5ae3) (Python standard library only). It sends, at
temperature 0 with thinking disabled: a warm-up and three short prompts; a ~18k-token prompt built
from `llama.cpp/src/*.cpp`; two concurrent 300-token requests; twelve OpenAI-style tool-calling
requests (`--short`: one); and three times a short "reply with exactly SHADOWFAX-EXACT-7" probe.

```
python3 dsv4_rpc_repro.py --url http://127.0.0.1:8080 --llama-src /path/to/llama.cpp [--short]
```

**Results** (fresh server for each row; full client logs in the [gist](https://gist.github.com/bobsummerwill/8010490af0fb6d55875a51389e6f5ae3))

| RPC workers | sequence | degenerate replies |
|---|---|---|
| B + C | full | **`prefill_16k`, `concurrent_2`, `tool:error_recovery`, `exact_1..3`** |
| B + C | short | **`prefill_16k`, `concurrent_2`, `exact_1..3`** |
| none (host A only) | full | none |

Earlier runs of the same sequence through our benchmark harness: corrupted with B + C (2 of 2
runs), clean with B only, C only, and none (1 run each). With B + C but without the long prompt
first, the tool-call and probe requests were all correct (2 runs).

**Observations**
- The first bad reply is the long prompt itself. Afterwards, every request served by that slot
  degenerates, even after its cache is cut back to 1 token (`cached_tokens: 1`) or reused (18
  tokens). The other slot keeps answering correctly (`concurrent_1`, most tool calls).
- Throughput looks normal (no crash, no RPC error in the server log at default verbosity).
- Either worker alone is fine, so this does not look like a CUDA-on-sm_120 or Metal kernel
  problem by itself, but like state that goes wrong only with two RPC workers. Possibly related
  to #28047 (split scheduler shipping views to the wrong RPC worker with >= 2 workers, also
  reproduced with deepseek4), which crashed rather than corrupting output; this build includes
  its fix.
- Not tried yet: other models, a single host with two `ggml-rpc-server` processes, or which part
  of the prompt length triggers it.

### First Bad Commit

Unknown (only 42c787e8c tested).

### Relevant log output

```
DEGENERATE prefill_16k              prompt=18455 cached=0  276.1s  :: 'DDDDDDDDDDDDDDDDDDDD…'
ok         concurrent_1             prompt=20 cached=0   37.2s  :: '**TCP Congestion Control: Variant 1 (Tahoe)**…'
DEGENERATE concurrent_2             prompt=20 cached=0   37.2s  :: 'DDDDDDDDDDDDDDDDDDDD…'
DEGENERATE tool:error_recovery      prompt=907 cached=1  138.4s  :: 'DDDDDDDDDDDDDDDDDDDD…'
DEGENERATE exact_1                  prompt=22 cached=1    4.0s  :: 'DDDDDDDDDDDDDDDDDDDD…'

server: got exception: Unexpected empty grammar stack after accepting piece: D (38)
```

items.title: Should LMCacheMPConnector honor kv_transfer_config.kv_role — or is MP mode intentionally always-kv_both?
items.author: kezboard233
items.body_excerpt:
## Context

We run a production-shaped POC on 8×V100 (two vLLM TP4 instances of Qwen3.8-27B-FP8 sharing one LMCache MP server with a CPU L1 tier) and filed #5143 with a runtime-verified repro: an engine launched with `kv_role="kv_consumer"` still stores every request's KV into the shared L1 — a single 32K-token cold request produced `168 × "Stored 784"` lines (= full prefix × 4 TP ranks), and the only engine that received any request in that window was the `kv_consumer` one.

We later found #4665 (closed by its author without maintainer response) reporting the same mechanism from the CacheBlend angle: the single-process connector honors `kv_role` / `skip_save`, the MP connector honors neither. As of today's `dev`, `lmcache_mp_connector.py` still contains no occurrence of `kv_role` / `kv_consumer` / `kv_producer` / `force_skip_save`.

## The design question

Before we contribute a patch, we want to check intent: **is MP mode intentionally "every connected engine writes"?** Two readings:

1. **Contract gap** — vLLM makes `kv_role` mandatory, documents it as "Whether this vLLM instance produces, consumes KV cache, or both", and exposes `is_kv_producer` / `is_kv_consumer` for connectors to branch on; LMCache's own single-process adapter honors it (`force_skip_save` in `vllm_v1_adapter.py`). Under this reading we'd gladly contribute a small PR that skips store-metadata generation when `is_kv_consumer` (mirroring the single-process gate), so warm-then-read-only fleets and PD-style topologies become possible on the MP path.

2. **Intentional always-kv_both** — the MP tier is a shared scratch space where every connected engine contributes. Under this reading we'd instead ask for the intent to be documented, plus ideally a one-line warning at connector init when `kv_role != "kv_both"`, so users aren't misled (we only noticed via instrumented counter evidence ourselves).

Happy to do either — a steer from maintainers decides which.

(Impact context: no correctness issue — stored content is identical — but a consumer-role engine burns D2H bandwidth and shared-L1 capacity; a 32K prefix on our model is ≈8.6 GB across 4 ranks.)

items.title: [Bug]: trtllm-gen FMHA CudaArchDecl.h numbers Sm107a as 4, but the prebuilt libTrtLlmGen archives use 4 for 105a and 5 for 107a
items.author: lucifer1004
items.body_excerpt:
### System Info

- TensorRT-LLM main @ e88d19ca3b
- Affects SM107 builds (the trtllm-gen FMHA target is compiled with `TLLM_RUBIN_FEATURES`, see `cpp/tensorrt_llm/kernels/trtllmGenKernels/fmha/CMakeLists.txt`). The reproduction below is CPU-only and uses the checked-in prebuilt archives, on both x86_64 and aarch64.

### Who can help?

Related: #18518 and #19038 (enable `TLLM_RUBIN_FEATURES` for the FMHA target and refresh the archives), #18758 (maps SM107 to `Sm100f` for NVRTC), #20054 (latest archive update).

### Reproduction

`cpp/tensorrt_llm/kernels/trtllmGenKernels/fmha/trtllmGen_fmha_export/trtllm/gen/CudaArchDecl.h` declares:

```cpp
enum class CudaArch {
  Sm90a = 0,  // 0
  Sm100a,     // 1
  Sm100f,     // 2
  Sm103a,     // 3
#ifdef TLLM_RUBIN_FEATURES
  Sm107a,     // 4
#endif
};
```

The prebuilt `fmha/lib/<arch>/libTrtLlmGen.a` and `libTrtLlmGenFmhaLib.a` were compiled with an enum that also has `105a`. Value 4 is `105a` there, and `107a` is 5:

- `strings libTrtLlmGen.a` contains `90a 100a 100f 103a 105a 107a`.
- In the archive's `trtllm::gen::cudaArchToString`, the jump table covers 0..5.
- In the archive's `trtllm::gen::getMaxNumTmemCols`, values 1..3 return 512, 5 returns 576, and anything else goes to the "unsupported" error path.

Minimal CPU-only reproduction, from the repository root:

```cpp
// repro.cpp
#include "CudaArchDecl.h"
#include <cstdio>
#include <exception>
namespace trtllm { namespace gen { int getMaxNumTmemCols(CudaArch); } }
using trtllm::gen::CudaArch;
int main() {
  std::printf("header: Sm103a=%d Sm107a=%d\n", int(CudaArch::Sm103a), int(CudaArch::Sm107a));
  for (int v : {1, 2, 3, 5})
    std::printf("libTrtLlmGen getMaxNumTmemCols(%d) = %d\n", v, trtllm::gen::getMaxNumTmemCols(CudaArch(v)));
  try {
    std::printf("getMaxNumTmemCols(CudaArch::Sm107a) = %d\n", trtllm::gen::getMaxNumTmemCols(CudaArch::Sm107a));
  } catch (std::exception const& e) {
    std::printf("getMaxNumTmemCols(CudaArch::Sm107a) threw: %s\n", e.what());
  }
}
```

```bash
D=cpp/tensorrt_llm/kernels/trtllmGenKernels/fmha
g++ -std=c++17 -DTLLM_RUBIN_FEATURES -I$D/trtllmGen_fmha_export/trtllm/gen repro.cpp \
    $D/lib/$(uname -m)-linux-gnu/libTrtLlmGen.a -o repro && ./repro
```

Output (identical on x86_64 and aarch64):

```
header: Sm103a=3 Sm107a=4
libTrtLlmGen getMaxNumTmemCols(1) = 512
libTrtLlmGen getMaxNumTmemCols(2) = 512
libTrtLlmGen getMaxNumTmemCols(3) = 512
libTrtLlmGen getMaxNumTmemCols(5) = 576
getMaxNumTmemCols(CudaArch::Sm107a) threw: Unsupported CUDA arch: 105a
[E] [TmemTile.cpp:46]: Unsupported CUDA arch: 105a
```

So `CudaArch::Sm107a`, as compiled into TensorRT-LLM, is `105a` to the archive.

### Expected behavior

`CudaArch` values passed across the boundary to the prebuilt archives mean the same architecture on both sides.

### Actual behavior

On SM107, `TllmGenFmhaKernel` sets `options.mCudaArch = intToCudaArch(107) = Sm107a` (4) in `checkIfKernelExist`, `warmupOneKernel` and `run` (`fmha/fmhaKernels.h`). It then hands those `FmhaOptions` to archive code that reads `mCudaArch`:

- `fmha::FmhaAutoTuner::selectKernel()` (through `selectKernelAutotuned`), on every path;
- `fmha::FmhaInterface::generateAndCompileKernel()`, on the NVRTC path.

`run()` rewrites `mCudaArch` to `Sm100f` before NVRTC compilation for non-spcompress kernels (added in #18518). `warmupOneKernel()` does not. So the JIT warmup path, and every autotuner call, gives the archive `105a` instead of `107a`. Any SM107-specific branches in the archive are therefore not taken, and the archive's TMEM limit lookup for that value is the error path shown above.

### Additional notes

Suggested fix: make the header match the archives. The smallest change is:

```cpp
#ifdef TLLM_RUBIN_FEATURES
  // SM107. 4 is Sm105a in the prebuilt trtllm-gen archives.
  Sm107a = 5,
#endif
```

A more robust alternative is to export the archive's value (or the enum header itself) together with the archives, and add a CPU-only check. Something like the reproduction above, run as a unit test, would catch the next drift when the archives are refreshed.

The other `CudaArchDecl.h` copies (`batchedGemm/trtllm/gen/`, `batchedGemm/trtllmGen_bmm_export/trtllm/gen/`) also number `Sm107a` as 4. As far as I can tell, they do not pass the value into a prebuilt archive.

What is verified: the reproduction above, on x86_64 and aarch64 against the archives at e88d19ca3b, and the code paths listed under "Actual behavior". Our SM107 builds carry `Sm107a = 5`. I have not run an SM107 build with the unpatched value end to end, so I cannot say exactly which kernel selections change with 4.

I have the one-line fix and can open a PR.

items.title: [Bug]: Expired etcd worker lease is reported as refreshed and blocks re-registration
items.author: codebreaker77
items.body_excerpt:
### Summary and impact

After an etcd-backed worker registration lease expires, `Etcd3ClusterStorage.expire()` returns `True` even though the key remains absent. The worker's heartbeat consequently advances its local registration-expiry timestamp and keeps running without restoring registration. An explicit re-registration through the same storage object also fails because its cached lease is already dead.

This is a recovery/availability problem: a live worker can remain missing from service discovery after a temporary worker stall or lease loss. I reproduced the registration/heartbeat behavior against a real local etcd server; I have not measured model-serving traffic or GPU effects.

### System info and validation boundary

- Upstream `main` commit: `3163e66b2c5b8e5de2995f87dafb06ef62148446`.
- Client host: Windows, Python 3.10.11; server: Linux Docker, `quay.io/coreos/etcd:v3.5.21`.
- `etcd-sdk-python==0.0.7` (the repository pin), `grpcio==1.84.0`, `protobuf==6.33.6` (within repository constraints).
- CPU-only component run. The full unchanged upstream `cluster_storage.py` and `disagg_auto_scaling.py` modules were loaded with `importlib`; package namespaces bypassed TensorRT/native bootstrap. The config dataclasses and role enum were taken unchanged from the same source to avoid their unrelated native dependency chain. I/O used the real pinned etcd SDK and a real etcd process; no fake lease responses or modified production methods.
- The normal full-package import/GPU stack was not exercised locally. The snippet below uses normal production imports for reproduction in a matching TensorRT-LLM environment.

### Minimal reproduction

Start a dedicated etcd 3.5 server listening on `127.0.0.1:2379`, then run:

```python
import asyncio
import uuid
import grpc
from tensorrt_llm.serve.cluster_storage import Etcd3ClusterStorage

async def main():
    endpoint = "etcd://127.0.0.1:2379"  # dedicated local etcd
    storage = Etcd3ClusterStorage(endpoint, "repro")
    fresh = Etcd3ClusterStorage(endpoint, "repro")
    key = "/trtllm-lease-repro/" + uuid.uuid4().hex
    try:
        assert await storage.set(key, "alive", ttl=2)
        assert await storage.expire(key, ttl=2)
        assert await storage.get(key) == "alive"  # live-lease control
        deadline = asyncio.get_running_loop().time() + 15
        while await storage.get(key) is not None:
            assert asyncio.get_running_loop().time() < deadline
            await asyncio.sleep(0.1)

        print("refresh expired:", await storage.expire(key, ttl=2))
        print("key after refresh:", await storage.get(key))
        for attempt in range(3):
            try:
                print("retry:", await storage.set(
                    key, "recovered", overwrite_if_exists=True, ttl=2))
            except grpc.RpcError as error:
                print("retry error:", error.code(), error.details())
        print("fresh object:", await fresh.set(
            key, "recovered", overwrite_if_exists=True, ttl=2))
        print("fresh value:", await fresh.get(key))
    finally:
        await fresh.delete(key)
        storage.client.close()
        fresh.client.close()

asyncio.run(main())
```

### Actual behavior

All three independent component runs produced:

```text
refresh expired: True
key after refresh: None
retry error: StatusCode.NOT_FOUND etcdserver: requested lease not found
retry error: StatusCode.NOT_FOUND etcdserver: requested lease not found
retry error: StatusCode.NOT_FOUND etcdserver: requested lease not found
fresh object: True
fresh value: recovered
```

The raw SDK keepalive response for the expired lease has `TTL=0`. The original storage object retains the same lease ID across all failed retries; the fresh object creates a different lease and succeeds.

I also exercised the unchanged `DisaggClusterWorker` background heartbeat with `heartbeat_interval_sec=1`, `inactive_timeout_sec=2`. After a four-second simulated worker-event-loop stall, real etcd removed the registration. Across three completed heartbeat refreshes after resumption, the heartbeat task stayed running and the worker moved its claimed expiry into the future, while the key remained absent each time. Thus the issue is observable through the real worker logic, not only a standalone storage API call.

### Expected behavior

An expired/missing lease must not be reported as a successful TTL refresh. Recovery should invalidate the dead cached lease and obtain a usable lease before registration is restored. A healthy resumed worker should either regain a visible registration or expose an explicit recovery failure, rather than continue apparently successful heartbeats for an absent key.

### Relevant paths / possible direction

- [`Etcd3ClusterStorage.expire`](https://github.com/NVIDIA/TensorRT-LLM/blob/3163e66b2c5b8e5de2995f87dafb06ef62148446/tensorrt_llm/serve/cluster_storage.py#L663) consumes the keepalive response but returns `True` without inspecting its TTL/result.
- [`_get_lease`](https://github.com/NVIDIA/TensorRT-LLM/blob/3163e66b2c5b8e5de2995f87dafb06ef62148446/tensorrt_llm/serve/cluster_storage.py#L616) retains leases by key; registration retries reuse the expired lease.
- [`DisaggClusterWorker._refresh_registration`](https://github.com/NVIDIA/TensorRT-LLM/blob/3163e66b2c5b8e5de2995f87dafb06ef62148446/tensorrt_llm/serve/disagg_auto_scaling.py#L389) trusts the successful refresh and stamps a new local expiry. `_heartbeat` re-registers only when refresh returns false.

A focused fix could validate the keepalive response and invalidate/recreate cached leases on expiry or lease-not-found, with real-etcd and CPU regression coverage. The intended recovery policy should be confirmed before implementation.

I searched issues and PRs for `etcd lease`, `lease not found`, `etcd heartbeat`, and `cached lease`. I found the original etcd implementation (#8210) and unrelated/annotation work, but no matching recovery report or fix.

items.title: [Performance]: CuTe DSL MLA split-KV plan kernel takes ~75 us per decode step at small batch
items.author: lucifer1004
items.body_excerpt:
### Proposal to improve performance

The CuTe DSL MLA decode computes a per-request split-KV plan once per step (`launch_mla_split_kv_plan` in `attention/backends/fmha/cute_dsl_mla.py`, launched by the first MLA layer of the step). `_mla_split_kv_plan_kernel` is a single program with `BLOCK = 1024` lanes that loops over the 32 candidate piece counts, each iteration doing two block-wide reductions over 1024 lanes, whatever the batch size. On Rubin single GPU (200-SM engineering sample) that launch takes about 75 us for a batch of 16 or fewer requests, and the decode step waits for it: for Kimi K3 decode at small batch it is about 0.07 ms per step.

Proposal: for batches up to 512 requests, evaluate all candidate piece counts at once as a (candidates x requests) tile with the request block sized to the batch (`next_power_of_2(num_requests)`, at least 16), pick the cheapest candidate (ties to fewer pieces, as now), and keep the loop kernel for larger batches. The plan is unchanged. Measured on the same GPU: 2.3 us for 16 or fewer requests, 7.9 us for 64.

Separately, the loop kernel always evaluates 32 candidates while the host mirror `plan_mla_split_kv` stops at `max_split`, so for `max_split < 32` the two can disagree (101 of 200 random batches with `max_split` in {1, 4, 8, 16}). No caller passes `max_split` today, so this is latent; the PR restricts the kernel's candidates to `max_split` as well. PR to follow.

items.title: [Performance]: MLA DSpark drafter runs each layer's q and kv paths serially on one stream
items.author: lucifer1004
items.body_excerpt:
### Proposal to improve performance

In `MLADSparkForCausalLM.dflash_forward` (MLA DSpark drafter block decode), every drafter layer runs its q path (`q_a_proj` -> `q_a_layernorm` -> `q_b_proj` -> RoPE -> k absorption) and its kv path (`kv_a_proj_with_mqa` -> RMSNorm/RoPE -> block write into the context pool) one after another on one stream. The two paths are independent until attention, and at decode sizes each is a chain of small GEMMs and elementwise kernels that leaves most of the GPU idle. On top of that, the kv path writes its RMSNorm/RoPE output to a staging buffer that is then scattered into the pool.

Proposal: an opt-in switch that runs the kv path on an aux stream concurrently with the q path, joined before attention. On the CuTe DSL block-decode variant, the RMSNorm/RoPE kernel also stores the block latents straight into the pool, at the block fixup's pages / offsets. Same kernels and same arithmetic, so it is bit-exact.

Measured on Rubin, TP8 across 2 nodes (MNNVL), Kimi K3 with an MLA DSpark drafter, CUDA graphs, single request, decode step time, on top of #20548: -0.053 / -0.038 / -0.025 / -0.037 / -0.023 / -0.018 ms at 2K / 32K / 64K / 96K / 128K / 393K context (cross-job comparison). Accepted tokens per step unchanged. On a later stack, turning it off cost about +0.06 ms per step.

PR to follow (draft, stacked on the #20548 PR).

items.title: [Performance]: DFlash prefill context store blocks on a D2H read at every chunk, idling the GPU between chunks
items.author: lucifer1004
items.body_excerpt:
### Proposal to improve performance

With a DFlash drafter bound to the draft KV cache manager, `DFlashWorker._store_prefill_context` (`tensorrt_llm/_torch/speculative/dflash.py`) reads the context rows' draft page counts with `(self._ctx_block_counts[:num_contexts] * page_size).tolist()` at the end of every context forward. `_ctx_block_counts` is filled on the GPU earlier in the same forward, so this `.tolist()` waits for the whole forward's GPU work. The executor's host work between chunks (resource update, scheduling, input preparation) then cannot overlap the next chunk, and with chunked prefill the GPU idles at every chunk boundary.

Measured on Rubin, TP8 across 2 nodes (MNNVL), Kimi K3 with a DFlash-style drafter, 128K prompt with chunked prefill: about 11 ms of GPU idle at every chunk boundary, and the `.tolist()` itself blocks for up to about 190 ms (the rest of the forward).

Proposal: the page counts are a function of `draft_kv_cache_block_offsets`, which `attn_metadata.prepare()` fills before the forward is enqueued. Compute them in `DFlashSpecMetadata.prepare()` with the same formula on the same tensor, copy them non-blocking into pinned memory behind an event, and let `_store_prefill_context` use that snapshot (waiting only on the event, which completes when the forward starts). Fall back to the current read whenever the snapshot does not match the forward (different tensor, row count, manager or pool). Opt-in first via `TLLM_DFLASH_PREFILL_CTX_SNAPSHOT=1`. With it, 128K TTFT dropped by about 0.36 s in the setup above. PR to follow.

items.title: [Performance]: Kimi KDA verify runs the qkvg and [f_a | b] projections as two GEMMs on two streams
items.author: lucifer1004
items.body_excerpt:
### Proposal to improve performance

In the Kimi KDA mixer's MTP verify (`KimiKDALinearAttention._project_verify_inputs`, `tensorrt_llm/_torch/modules/kimi_kda/kimi_kda_mixer.py`), the BF16 full-rank-gate path runs two GEMMs on the same input: the fused `[q | k | v | g]` projection (`_qkvg_proj_weight`) and the fused `[f_a | b]` gate projection (`_bfa_proj_weight`, padded to 8 rows), forked onto two streams for up to 128 rows. At decode sizes (M = 8 x batch rows) both GEMMs are tiny, so two launches plus the stream fork / join cost more than one GEMM with 144 more output rows.

Measured on Rubin single GPU, Kimi K3 KDA layer shapes per rank, own weights per layer, CUDA graph, µs per layer for the verify projection GEMMs, batch 1 / 2 / 3 / 4 / 6 / 8 / 12 / 16 (M = 8 x batch):

| | 1 | 2 | 3 | 4 | 6 | 8 | 12 | 16 |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| qkvg and [f_a \| b] (two GEMMs) | 15.6 | 15.7 | 17.7 | 15.2 | 19.7 | 17.0 | 18.2 | 18.5 |
| one stacked GEMM | 12.9 | 13.2 | 15.8 | 13.5 | 13.0 | 13.1 | 14.1 | 13.7 |

Proposal: in `finalize_decode_weights`, stack the two fused weights into one `[q | k | v | g | f_a | b | pad]` buffer and repoint `_qkvg_proj_weight`, `_bfa_proj_weight` and the per-projection weights to row views of it (no extra memory; prefill and decode GEMMs unchanged). The verify projection then runs one GEMM and takes qkvg and `[f_a | b]` as column views of its output; the verify kernel already reads the sections as strided views. Opt-in first via `TLLM_KDA_FUSE_VERIFY_PROJECTION=1`. PR to follow.

Related: #20174 routes `_project_gate_inputs` through the low-M dispatcher. The two compose (the stacked GEMM can go through the dispatcher too: 10.3–11.5 µs per layer at batch 1–4 in the same setup).

items.title: [Performance]: CuTe DSL MLA decode split-KV reduction is load-latency bound at small batch
items.author: lucifer1004
items.body_excerpt:
### Proposal to improve performance

The split-KV reduction of the CuTe DSL MLA decode kernels (`reduction_kernel` in `cute_dsl_kernels/blackwell/attention/mla/mla_decode_fp16.py` and `mla_decode_fp8.py`) accumulates the per-split partials one split at a time: each iteration issues a global load of `gAccO[i, ...]` and immediately consumes it, so with tens of splits the loop is load-latency bound. The runner also always launches it with one D band per row (`reducer_d_tiles = 1`), so at small batch (few rows) only a handful of CTAs run it.

Measured on Rubin single GPU (200-SM engineering sample), CUDA graph, Kimi K3 shapes (target FP8 KV, 12 heads, q = 8; drafter BF16, 8 heads, q = 7; batch 1, page 32), reduction time per call with the production split plan, current → prefetching loop with 4 D bands per row:

| KV (splits) | 2K (16) | 32K (64) | 128K (94) | 393K (100) | 1M (100) |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| FP8 reduction µs | 5.10 → 4.00 | 10.79 → 4.95 | 14.63 → 6.43 | 15.73 → 6.91 | 8.47 → 2.88 |
| BF16 reduction µs | 4.83 → 3.73 | 10.73 → 4.98 | 14.95 → 5.95 | 15.45 → 6.77 | 15.30 → 6.66 |

Proposal: an optional prefetch in the reduction loop (load a group of 32 splits' partials into registers with a clamped split index, then accumulate them in split order with a mask, so every output element sees the same multiply-adds in the same order and the result is bitwise unchanged), and have the runner use 4 D bands per row while that grid fits a few SM waves. Opt-in first via `TLLM_CUTE_DSL_MLA_REDUCTION_PREFETCH=1`. End to end on Rubin, TP8 across 2 nodes (MNNVL), Kimi K3 with MTP decode, the decode step period dropped by 0.05 ms at 2K and 0.15–0.22 ms at 32K–393K context, with accepted tokens per step unchanged. PR to follow.
score_reasons: 匹配 KV 与存储、Kernel 与正确性

items.title: [MPS][Inductor] `expm1` and `log1p` compile to `exp(x)-1` and `log(1+x)`, losing precision for small x
items.author: jzluo
items.body_excerpt:
### 🐛 Describe the bug

This is the compiled counterpart of #198708.  On MPS, Inductor lowers `torch.expm1` to `exp(x) - 1` and `torch.log1p` to `log(1 + x)`, which loses precision for small `x`. #198771 addressed eager `expm1`. 
`F.softplus` decomposes to `log1p(exp(x))`, so it's also affected. Eager softplus was addressed in #197000. 

Repro (printing largest relative error against fp64 CPU reference):
```python
import torch
import torch.nn.functional as F

x = torch.tensor([1e-4, 1e-3], device="mps")
ops = {"expm1": torch.expm1, "log1p": torch.log1p, "softplus": lambda t: F.softplus(t.log())}
for name, op in ops.items():
    ref = op(x.cpu().double())
    for mode, fn in (("eager", op), ("compiled", torch.compile(op))):
        print(name, mode, f"{((fn(x).cpu().double() - ref) / ref).abs().max().item():.2e}")
```

On 2.14.0:
```
expm1 eager 1.16e-04
expm1 compiled 1.16e-04
log1p eager 1.24e-08
log1p compiled 1.66e-04
softplus eager 1.66e-04
softplus compiled 1.66e-04
```

On 2.16.0.dev20261018:
```
expm1 eager 4.65e-08
expm1 compiled 1.16e-04
log1p eager 1.24e-08
log1p compiled 1.66e-04
softplus eager 1.04e-07
softplus compiled 1.66e-04
```

Opus 5.5's suggested fix:

> `MetalOverrides` in `torch/_inductor/codegen/mps.py` defines neither op, so the generic versions in `codegen/common.py` are used instead. Lowering them the way the eager kernels compute them fixes it:
> - `log1p`: call `c10::metal::log1p`.
> - `expm1`: use the same piecewise expression as `expm1_functor`, `|x| < 0.1 ? c10::metal::expm1f(x) : exp(x) - 1`.
>

items.title: MPS backend hangs (uninterruptible sleep) after ~100-600s of sustained encoding on Apple Silicon
items.author: nicobrenner
items.body_excerpt:
## What happens

When running `SentenceTransformer.encode()` on the MPS device, the process silently freezes after about 100-600 seconds of cumulative GPU encoding. It enters uninterruptible sleep (U state at 0% CPU) and doesn't respond to SIGINT or SIGTERM, only `kill -9`.

This happens both across multiple encode() calls (cumulative time in one process) and during a single large encode() call if it needs more than ~100s of GPU time.

## Environment

- Apple M3 Max, 64 GB unified memory, 40-core GPU
- macOS 15.6.1 (Build 24G90)
- Python 3.12
- PyTorch 2.14.1
- SentenceTransformers (latest)
- Model: BAAI/bge-large-en-v1.5 (335M params)

```
$ python -c "import torch; print(torch.__version__); print(torch.backends.mps.is_available()); print(torch.backends.mps.is_built())"
2.14.1
True
True
```

## Repro

```python
from sentence_transformers import SentenceTransformer
import time

model = SentenceTransformer("BAAI/bge-large-en-v1.5", device="mps")

# enough text to sustain encoding for > 100s
texts = [f"This is sample text number {i} with some additional content to process." for i in range(50000)]

print("Starting encode...")
t0 = time.time()
# this will hang after ~100-600s of GPU encoding time
embeddings = model.encode(texts, batch_size=256, show_progress_bar=True)
print(f"Done in {time.time()-t0:.1f}s")
```

With `show_progress_bar=True` you can see it making progress before it freezes. No error, no exception, it just stops.

## What I see in ps

```
USER  PID  %CPU  STAT  TIME
nico  1234  0.0   U    3:43.68
```

The process is in U state (uninterruptible sleep, kernel-level wait) at 0% CPU. It accumulated ~3:43 of CPU time before hanging. Only `kill -9` works.

## What I've tried

1. **CPU instead of MPS** (`device="cpu"`): works reliably but ~10x slower
2. **Fresh subprocess per workload**: spawning a new Python process for each encoding batch resets the MPS state. Works for smaller workloads (<100s encoding each) but doesn't help if a single encode() call exceeds the threshold
3. Haven't tested `torch.mps.empty_cache()` between calls yet, might help if the root cause is memory pressure from MPSGraph caching

## Observations

- The hang correlates with cumulative GPU encoding time in the process, not with sample count
- Smaller datasets (1K-5K short texts) complete fine in fresh processes
- Larger datasets (50K texts) trigger the hang even in a fresh process during a single encode() call
- The threshold varies (100-600s), suggesting it depends on memory allocation patterns
- Memory usage grows steadily during normal operation before the hang (consistent with #154329)

## Possibly related

- #154329 (MPS memory leak, MPSGraph cache grows unboundedly). The unbounded memory growth could cause Metal command buffer submission to deadlock once memory pressure hits a threshold, which would explain the kernel-level uninterruptible sleep.

items.title: torch.distributions: Exponential/Cauchy cdf and icdf lose small tail probabilities
items.author: techi101
items.body_excerpt:
### 🐛 Describe the bug

Some distribution CDFs return 0 for very small probabilities. I compared them with a high-precision library and found rounding errors in the formulas.

#### AI-generated analysis (Claude Code)

> Small tail probabilities are rounded to zero (or lose most of their digits) by three cdf/icdf formulas in `torch.distributions`:
>
> | Code | Formula | Problem |
> |---|---|---|
> | `Exponential.cdf` | `1 - torch.exp(-rate * x)` | cancels for small `rate * x`; `-torch.expm1(-rate * x)` is exact |
> | `Cauchy.cdf` | `atan((x - loc) / scale) / pi + 0.5` | cancels in the lower tail; equal to `atan2(scale, loc - x) / pi` |
> | `Cauchy.icdf` | `tan(pi * (q - 0.5))` | `q - 0.5` drops the digits of small `q`; `icdf(0)` / `icdf(1)` are finite (see #186824) |
> | `TransformedDistribution._monotonize_cdf` | `sign * (value - 0.5) + 0.5` | applied whenever `sign` is a tensor, even when it is `+1`, so it rounds any small cdf value of e.g. `Weibull`, `Gumbel`, or a user `AffineTransform` with tensor parameters |
>
> ```python
> import torch
> from torch.distributions import Cauchy, Exponential, TransformedDistribution, Weibull
> from torch.distributions.transforms import AffineTransform
>
> torch.set_default_dtype(torch.float64)
> t = torch.tensor
> print(Exponential(t(1.0)).cdf(t(1e-20)))       # tensor(0.)  expected 1e-20
> print(Weibull(t(1.0), t(2.0)).cdf(t(1e-9)))    # tensor(0.)  expected 1e-18
> d = TransformedDistribution(Exponential(t(1.0)), AffineTransform(t(0.0), t(2.0)))
> print(d.cdf(t(1e-20)))                         # tensor(0.)  expected 5e-21
> print(Cauchy(t(0.0), t(1.0)).icdf(t(1e-15)))   # -3.1547e+14 expected -3.1831e+14 (0.9% error)
> print(Cauchy(t(0.0), t(1.0)).icdf(t(0.0)))     # -1.6331e+16 expected -inf
> ```
>
> Worst relative error against mpmath (50 digits) on a grid of tail values:
>
> | | float32 now | float32 fixed | float64 now | float64 fixed |
> |---|---|---|---|---|
> | `Exponential.cdf` | 1.0 | 6e-08 | 1.0 | 0 |
> | `Weibull.cdf` | 1.0 | 2e-07 | 1.0 | 2e-16 |
> | `Cauchy.cdf` (lower tail) | 1.0 | 9e-08 | 6e-03 | 2e-16 |
> | `Cauchy.icdf` | 1.7 | 7e-08 | 1.0 | 3e-16 |
>
> The fixes above are one-line changes each and keep the current values elsewhere. `Normal.cdf` has the same kind of problem but is already covered by #189234, and the Gumbel upper tail by #200013 / #200618.

I have a fix with a regression test ready on a branch: https://github.com/techi101/pytorch/tree/distributions-cdf-tail-precision. All of `test/distributions` passes locally (CPU). I will open the PR once this issue is marked actionable.

items.title: [RFC]: AIBrix Multi-Modality: Best-in-Class Omni-Modal Serving Platform
items.author: Jeffwan
items.body_excerpt:
### Summary

vLLM-Omni already provides the multi-stage serving framework with pluggable connectors, Cache-DiT acceleration, and OpenAI-compatible APIs. AIBrix provides Kubernetes-native inference infrastructure with gateway routing, autoscaling, PrisKV KV cache store, and StormService orchestration.

This proposal integrates them deeply — making AIBrix the best platform to run multi-modal models powered by vLLM-Omni.


### Motivation


Multi-modal AI is moving from research demos to production workloads. Applications now combine text chat, image generation, video generation, speech recognition (ASR), and text-to-speech (TTS) in a single user experience. Serving these workloads efficiently requires solving problems that neither standalone LLM inference nor single-model diffusion serving addresses:

- Heterogeneous pipeline stages — An omni pipeline chains ASR (1.7B params, lightweight) → LLM (235B params, compute-heavy prefill, memory-bound decode) → DiT (burst GPU for diffusion steps) → TTS (real-time audio streaming). Each stage has fundamentally different resource profiles.
- Inter-stage data transfer — KV caches, visual tokens, and audio embeddings must flow between stages with minimal latency. CPU-staged copies are a bottleneck.
- Independent scaling — Image generation traffic spikes don't correlate with text chat load. Scaling the entire pipeline uniformly wastes GPUs.
- GPU cost — A naive deployment dedicates one GPU per model. For a full omni pipeline (ASR + LLM + DiT + TTS), that's at least 4+ GPUs minimum, even when most models are idle most of the time.
- Cloud-native orchestration — Production deployments run on Kubernetes. Ray adds a second distributed runtime on top of K8s, increasing operational complexity.

items.title: Support otlp_traces_endpoint for trtllm
items.author: Jeffwan
items.body_excerpt:
### 🚀 Feature Description and Motivation

v1.2.0 and above.

```
  # disagg_config.yaml (proxy)
  otlp_config:
    otlp_traces_endpoint: "http://jaeger:4317"
```

the disagg proxy itself does NOT create spans.
```
Client (traceparent) → Proxy (no span) → CTX Worker (llm_request span) -> → GEN Worker (llm_request span)
```

The two worker spans share the same traceparent from the client, so they appear as siblings under the same trace in Jaeger/Zipkin, but there's no parent span from the proxy showing the orchestration (ctx→gen sequencing, routing decisions, etc.).


some limitations
- No proxy-level spans — routing decisions, ctx/gen orchestration timing not traced
- Worker spans are created at request completion, not request start — they're retroactive spans with corrected timestamps
- No automatic span propagation between proxy→worker HTTP calls — the OpenAIHttpClient doesn't inject traceparent headers into forwarded requests (it passes through the original client's headers if present)
- return_perf_metrics: true is required on workers for spans to have meaningful timing data

items.title: [Gluon] async_load accepts a pointer whose element type differs from the shared memory buffer
items.author: shuyilinn
items.body_excerpt:
### Describe the bug

Gluon's `async_copy.async_load` (and `async_copy_global_to_local` in general) does not check that the pointer element type matches the shared memory element type. Copying from an fp32 pointer into an fp16 buffer compiles and copies raw bytes, and the reverse faults with a misaligned address. `smem.store` rejects the same mismatch at compile time.

```python
import torch
from triton.experimental import gluon
from triton.experimental.gluon import language as gl
from triton.experimental.gluon.language.nvidia.ampere import async_copy


@gluon.jit
def kernel(inp, out, SMEM_DTYPE: gl.constexpr, N: gl.constexpr):
    L: gl.constexpr = gl.BlockedLayout([4], [32], [4], [0])
    offs = gl.arange(0, N, L)
    smem = gl.allocate_shared_memory(SMEM_DTYPE, [N], gl.SwizzledSharedLayout(1, 1, 1, [0]))
    async_copy.async_load(smem, inp + offs)
    async_copy.commit_group()
    async_copy.wait_group(0)
    gl.store(out + offs, smem.load(L))


N = 512
inp = torch.arange(N, device="cuda", dtype=torch.float32) + 0.5
out = torch.zeros(N, device="cuda", dtype=torch.float16)
kernel[(1, )](inp, out, gl.float16, N)  # fp32 pointer -> fp16 smem: compiles, wrong values
print(out[:8].tolist())

inp = torch.arange(N, device="cuda").to(torch.float16)
out = torch.zeros(N, device="cuda", dtype=torch.float32)
kernel[(1, )](inp, out, gl.float32, N)  # fp16 pointer -> fp32 smem
torch.cuda.synchronize()                # RuntimeError: CUDA error: misaligned address
```

```
[0.0, 1.75, 0.0, 1.9375, 0.0, 2.28125, 0.0, 2.34375]
RuntimeError: CUDA error: misaligned address
```

The first kernel should print `[0.5, 1.5, 2.5, ...]`; instead each 8-byte copy moves the raw bytes of two fp32 values into four fp16 slots.

Expected: a compile-time error for both, like `smem.store` gives for a value whose dtype does not match the buffer.

The frontend (`python/triton/experimental/gluon/language/nvidia/ampere/async_copy.py`, and the AMD `cdna4`/`cdna5` versions) only checks the shapes, and `AsyncCopyGlobalToLocalOp::verify` only checks that the destination is mutable. The lowering sizes each copy by the shared memory element type, so a mismatch reads with the wrong stride.

### Environment details

Triton: main @ 41846bc965
GPU: NVIDIA RTX 4090 (sm_89), driver 570 / CUDA 12.8

comments.author: he-yufeng
comments.body:
Opened #12341, picking up where the closed #12250 left off (same verifier + frontend-check shape, extended to both AMD copy directions).

The builtins now reject the mismatch at the frontend on every NVIDIA and AMD async-copy path, and AsyncCopyGlobalToLocalOp verifies it for non-Gluon producers. The regression test is red without the frontend check and green with it on this machine (no GPU here, so the byte-level runtime repro stays as documented in the issue).

items.title: [Bug]: Kimi K3 / MLA unit tests on SM107: two KDA files skip SM107, a cute_dsl_mla routing case contradicts the perf table, and an indexed-pool decode test compares two code paths bit-exactly
items.author: lucifer1004
items.body_excerpt:
### System Info

- TensorRT-LLM main @ e88d19ca3b, PyTorch backend
- GPU with compute capability 10.7 (SM107). Item 2 is a host-side routing test (it monkeypatches the SM version) and fails independently of the GPU.

### Who can help?

Related: #19960 (adds the `test_cute_dsl_mla` case below and extends Kimi K3 to SM107), #18599 (the `(96, 1)` entry in the FP8 perf table), #18938 (the KDA decode kernel and dispatch).

### Reproduction

Three test-only problems seen when running the Kimi K3 / MLA unit tests on SM107. They are grouped here to keep the noise down. None of them is a product bug as far as I can tell. Each item lists the fix I verified.

**1. Two KDA test files skip everything on SM107**

`tests/unittest/_torch/modules/kimi_kda/test_kda_cache_soundness.py:57` and `test_kda_prefill_state_parity.py:40` gate on

```python
torch.cuda.get_device_capability(0) in {(10, 0), (10, 3)}
```

with reason "Kimi K3 is supported only on Blackwell (SM100/SM103)". The runtime predicate `is_kda_optimized_supported()` (`_torch/modules/kimi_kda/_kda_kernels.py:66`) accepts `(100, 103, 107)`, and the neighbouring files (`test_kda_decode_op.py`, `test_kda_prefill_op.py`) already gate on it. So on SM107 these two files report 6 and 15 skips and cover nothing.

Fix: gate on `is_kda_optimized_supported()` like the other files. With `(10, 7)` added, `test_kda_cache_soundness.py` gives 5 passed and 1 skipped on SM107; the remaining skip is its own runtime condition, "could not obtain a recycled cu_seqlens tensor ID". `test_kda_prefill_state_parity.py` gives 15 passed.

Related stale comment: the `_has_supported_gpu()` comments in `test_kda_decode_op.py:33` and `test_kda_prefill_op.py:38` still say the predicate "accepts SM100/SM103 only; SM107 takes the FLA fallback".

**2. `test_cute_dsl_mla.py::test_mla_generation_routes_wide_head_fp8_verify_away_from_trtllm_gen[103-96-1-True-False-cute_dsl_mla]` fails independently of the GPU**

```
pytest tests/unittest/_torch/attention/test_cute_dsl_mla.py -k routes_wide_head
E       AssertionError: assert 'trtllm_gen' == 'cute_dsl_mla'
```

The case `(103, 96, 1, True, False, "cute_dsl_mla")` ("Single-token H=96 is unchanged (measured perf-table entry)") goes through the FP8 perf gate. `_PERF_MIN_BATCH_FP8[(96, 1)] = 8` (`attention/backends/fmha/cute_dsl_mla.py:419`), but `_select_mla_generation_fmha` always builds a decode batch of `batch_size = 4` (`test_cute_dsl_mla.py:148`). So the gate rejects CuTe DSL MLA and the selection falls through to the TRTLLM-Gen stub. The code behaves as the table says; the expectation is wrong for batch 4.

Fix: either expect `"trtllm_gen"` for that case (verified: the parametrization then gives 10/10 passed), or add a `batch_size` parameter to the helper and assert `"cute_dsl_mla"` at batch 8, which would test the table entry the comment refers to.

**3. `test_kda_decode_op.py::test_optimized_decode_updates_indexed_recurrent_state_pool_in_place` (all 3 ids) fails on SM107**

```
torch.testing.assert_close(indexed_output, local_output, rtol=0, atol=0)
E       Mismatched elements: 2154 / 21504 (10.0%)
E       Greatest absolute difference: 0.00048828125
```

The test compares two different code paths bit-exactly:

- The "local" reference calls `_run_production_decode(...)` without `ssm_state_indices`. `KimiKDALinearAttention.forward_decode` then routes to `forward_decode_fallback` (`ssm_state_indices is None`), which runs separate q/k/v/g projections.
- The indexed call passes `ssm_state_indices` and takes the optimized path with the fused `qkvg` projection.

On SM107 the two GEMM shapes round differently, by one bf16 ulp on 10% of the elements. That difference then also shows up in the fp32 recurrent state. Each path is deterministic: two local runs are bit-identical. Running the same core output through `_project_output` twice is bit-identical too.

Fix: compute the local reference on the same path with dense indices, so that the test checks only the pool addressing:

```python
dense_indices = torch.arange(batch_size, dtype=torch.int32, device="cuda")
local_output, local_cache = _run_production_decode(
    optimized,
    hidden_states,
    copy.deepcopy(initial_cache),
    slot_indices=dense_indices.long(),
    ssm_state_indices=dense_indices,
)
```

With this, the indexed output and the indexed recurrent state are bit-identical to the reference for `many-dense-pool`, `many-strided-pool` and `compact-dense-pool`. The test then gives 3 passed on SM107. I have not checked whether the two paths happen to agree bit-exactly on SM100/SM103.

### Expected behavior

These tests run and pass on SM107 (items 1 and 3), and item 2 passes on any GPU.

### Actual behavior

On SM107, item 1 skips everything and item 3 fails as shown above. Item 2 fails independently of the GPU.

### Additional notes

All three fixes are test-only. I can put them in one PR.

items.title: [Feature]: sm120 Cake MegaMoE for PCIe hosts: MXFP4-activation (W4A4) variant, int8/FP8 return codec, switch-level dedupe
items.author: xqoasis
items.body_excerpt:
### Before submitting

- [x] I have searched existing issues and this request has not been filed yet.

### Problem

On PCIe-only sm_120 hosts (8 GPUs behind two PCIe Gen5 switches, no NVLink; ~49-55 GB/s per direction on the x16 links and on the inter-switch fabric) `sm120_mxfp4_mxfp8_bf16_cake` is slower per MoE layer than an unfused DeepEP-style all-to-all + DeepGEMM grouped-GEMM path, because its wire format carries roughly twice the bytes:

- dispatch records carry FP8 activations: 5120 + 160 (+224 header) B per row at H=5120, where an MXFP4 dispatch carries 2560 + 160 B;
- expert results return through the lossless BF16 codec, ~7.8 KB per route, where an int8 combine (per-128 fp32 scale) carries 5.3 KB;
- records are deduplicated per destination rank only; on a two-switch host, one copy per destination switch with the partial sums reduced inside the switch before crossing sends 2.2x fewer cross-switch bytes at EP8.

Measured at the DeepSeek-V4.1-Flash routed geometry (E=384, H=5120, I=2304, top-k 6; EP8, 2048 tokens/rank, 6-layer CUDA graph, slowest rank, us/layer; the local-memory guard was raised to 16 B so the kernel loads at this geometry, see #6755):

| path | uniform | hot (one rank 2.5x) | recorded routing |
|---|---|---|---|
| unfused: all-to-all (one copy per destination switch, in-switch partial-sum reduction) + DeepGEMM grouped GEMM, **MXFP4 activations, int8 combine** | 3850 | 6243 | 4390 |
| same unfused path with **FP8 activations** (per-128 fp32 scales), int8 combine | 5623 | 9449 | 6447 |
| cake, `transport_table` = LSA inside each switch / GIN across (explicit table) | 4745-4936 (two runs) | 7478 | 5677 |
| cake `all_gin` / `all_lsa` | 6067 / 6050 | 7718 / 7615 | 7632 / 6247 |

Against the same-precision unfused path the fused kernel is 14-26% faster, so the overlap works; against the MXFP4-activation path it is 20-28% slower. Switching only the unfused path's activations from MXFP4 to FP8 moves its dispatch from 692 to 1328 us/layer (per-card egress 23.9 -> 46.4 MB/layer), so on these links bytes are time. Numerics for reference (rel L2 vs an fp32 reference with unquantized activations, 512 rows/rank): cake 4.7%, FP8-activation unfused path 4.8%, MXFP4-activation path 22%; cake vs the kernel-boundary oracle of `tests/moe_ep/test_moe_ep_sm120_w4a8_cake_mega.py` 1.6e-4 .. 3.2e-4.

### Requested outcome

A configuration of the sm120 Cake MegaMoE whose bytes on the wire match the unfused W4A4 path on PCIe hosts:

1. an MXFP4-activation variant (e2m1 + UE8M0 per-32 scales, `mma.sync kind::mxf4nvf4`): dispatch rows become 2560 + 160 B and both GEMMs run at the FP4 rate instead of the FP8 rate;
2. an int8 (per-128 fp32 scale) or FP8 return option in place of the lossless BF16 codec, selectable per deployment, with the combine summing the dequantized partials;
3. optionally, topology-aware dedupe in the transport table: one copy per destination LSA group (PCIe switch or host) with in-group fan-out on dispatch and in-group partial-sum reduction on return.

(1) + (2) alone remove the byte handicap, which is the whole 20-28% gap in the table above; what remains after that is the overlap efficiency of the protocol on PCIe (in these runs the kernel hides about a third of the communication time). The kernel's numerics already match the unfused FP8 path, so the request is about the transport format, not a new precision recipe.

### Target hardware

SM120 (RTX PRO 6000, RTX 50-series)

### Inference engine

vLLM

### Affected model or model family

DeepSeek-V4.1-Flash (MXFP4 routed experts: E=384, H=5120, I=2304, top-k 6, 1 shared expert)

### Workload and configuration

- Data type and quantization: MXFP4 expert weights (e2m1 + UE8M0 per-32) from the checkpoint; activations MXFP4 in our production path, FP8 (per-128 fp32 scale) in the same-precision control and FP8 (UE8M0 per-32) inside Cake; int8 combine (per-128 fp32 scale) on the unfused path, lossless BF16 codec in Cake
- Batch size or request concurrency: prefill, 2048 tokens per rank per step (also 384 and 1024 for the M64 schedule)
- Sequence lengths or token counts: 2048 tokens per rank per layer; routings: uniform, one rank 2.5x hot, and a recorded production routing
- Parallelism: DP8 / EP8 on one host (TP1, PP1); EP16/EP32 across hosts is the next step (GIN) and was not measured
- Relevant shapes: hidden 5120, intermediate 2304, 384 experts (48 per rank at EP8), top-k 6, swiglu_limit 10, max_tokens_per_rank 2048; 8x sm_120 72 GB GPUs, 110 SMs, two PCIe Gen5 switches x 4 GPUs, 2x 400G RDMA NICs per switch
- Environment: output of `python -m flashinfer.collect_env` is attached as a comment on #6755 (flashinfer 399b6c1d source tree, torch 2.13 + NCCL 2.30.7, CUDA 13.3)

### Current workaround

We run the unfused path: DeepEP-style all-to-all with MXFP4 activations on dispatch, DeepGEMM `m_grouped_fp8_fp4_gemm_nt_contiguous` (FP4 x FP4) for both GEMMs, int8 combine, one copy per destination PCIe switch with in-switch partial-sum reduction. Its limitation is that communication and expert GEMMs are serial (about 1.97 ms + 1.93 ms per layer at this shape); a fused kernel could hide most of the smaller term, which is exactly what Cake does, but only if it does not double the bytes first.

### Impact

Throughput, Latency

### Acceptance criteria

- At E=384 / H=5120 / I=2304 / top-k 6, EP8, 2048 tokens per rank on an 8-GPU PCIe sm_120 host, the fused layer is not slower than the unfused MXFP4-activation path (3850 us/layer uniform, 4390 us/layer on recorded routing in our runs) and keeps the overlap gain measured against the same-precision unfused path (>= 10%).
- Per-card dispatch bytes at that shape ~24 MB/layer (MXFP4 rows) instead of ~46 MB; return bytes per route <= 5.3 KB.
- Correctness: passes `tests/moe_ep/test_moe_ep_sm120_w4a8_cake_mega.py`-style oracle checks (rel L2 <= 2%) for the new activation/return formats, protocol_error stays 0, CUDA-graph replay bit-identical to eager, across EP4/8/16 and both row schedules.

items.title: Misc. bug: CUDA FA stream-k block count not a multiple of ntiles_dst on RTX 5090 (170 SMs) → long-context prefill 10–13% slower than RTX 4090 (+37–40% when fixed)
items.author: Nebiforever
items.body_excerpt:
### Name and Version

llama.cpp b11674 (59d5fad), CUDA 13.4.59, driver 595.91.07. The relevant code in `ggml/src/ggml-cuda/fattn-common.cuh` is unchanged on master (ff5a2337, 2026-10-19).

### Operating systems

Linux

### Which llama.cpp modules do you know to be affected?

llama-bench

### Command line

```shell
llama-bench -m Qwen3.5-9B-Q4_K_M.gguf -ngl 99 -fa on -ctk q8_0 -ctv q8_0 -b 2048 -ub 512 -p 512 -n 0 -d 0,4096,16384,32768,65536,131072 -r 5
```

### Problem description & steps to reproduce

On an RTX 5090, prefill with a long existing context (`-d 65536/131072`) is slower than on an RTX 4090 for Qwen3.5-9B and Qwen3.8-27B (head_dim 256, GQA 4 and 6), although the 5090 is ~20% faster at short context and in all token-generation runs. With FA off the 5090 is 1.6x faster than the 4090 at 128K, so the gap is in the FA path.

Cause (as far as we can tell): for these shapes the MMA kernel (ncols=64, nbatch_fa=32) runs 2 blocks/SM, so stream-k gets `max_blocks = 2*nsm`: 256 on the 4090 (128 SMs) but 340 on the 5090 (170 SMs). `ntiles_dst` is 128 (9B, pp512) or 256 (27B). 256 divides both, 340 divides neither; rounding 340 down loses more than the 5% threshold, so the raw 340 is kept and the general fixup path is used. Forcing the block count (debug env var in a local build) to a multiple of `ntiles_dst` removes the gap.

RTX 5090, prefill t/s at 128K (pp512 @ d131072, q8_0 KV):

| model | default (340) | 256 | 384 | 512 | 340 (forced) | RTX 4090 default |
|---|---:|---:|---:|---:|---:|---:|
| Qwen3.5-9B Q4_K_M (GQA 4, ntiles 128) | 3951 | 5378 | 5361 | 5384 | 3957 | 4412 |
| Qwen3.8-27B UD-Q4_K_M (GQA 6, ntiles 256) | 1224 | 1704 | – | 1700 | – | 1403 |
| Qwen3.6-35B-A3B UD-Q4_K_S (GQA 8, ntiles 128) | 4542 | 4499 | – | 4517 | 4540 | 3762 |

Proposed change: when rounding down exceeds the efficiency-loss threshold, round to the nearest multiple of `ntiles_dst` instead of keeping the raw count:

```diff
-            const int nblocks_stream_k = efficiency_loss_percent <= max_efficiency_loss_percent
-                ? nblocks_stream_k_rounded
-                : nblocks_stream_k_raw;
+            int nblocks_stream_k = nblocks_stream_k_raw;
+            if (efficiency_loss_percent <= max_efficiency_loss_percent) {
+                nblocks_stream_k = nblocks_stream_k_rounded;
+            } else if (nblocks_stream_k_raw >= ntiles_dst) {
+                nblocks_stream_k = std::min(((nblocks_stream_k_raw + ntiles_dst/2) / ntiles_dst) * ntiles_dst, ntiles_KV*ntiles_dst);
+            }
```

With this change (same machine, 128K prefill t/s):

| | stock | patched |
|---|---:|---:|
| 5090 · 9B | 3951 | 5399 (+37%) |
| 5090 · 27B | 1224 | 1710 (+40%) |
| 5090 · 35B-A3B | 4542 | 4487 (within noise) |
| 4090 · 9B / 27B / 35B-A3B | 4412 / 1403 / 3762 | 4425 / 1401 / 3757 (unchanged) |

Short context (d 0–32K) on the 5090 is unchanged within ±2.5% (same session, stock vs. patched). `test-backend-ops -o FLASH_ATTN_EXT` passes (4004/4004) on the 5090 with the patch. In a real llama-server workload (Qwen3.8-27B Q6_K, ~98K-token prompt) the full prompt time went from 51.3 s to 44.7 s.

Not verified: other GPUs with SM counts that don't fit `ntiles_dst` (e.g. other Blackwell SKUs), head sizes other than 256, and why 35B-A3B (also 128 tiles) is not affected (no profiler run). Related: #29435 (whole-tile scheduling on DGX Spark; reported small/inconsistent changes on 5090 for other models).

### First Bad Commit

Not bisected (the 5% rounding rule has been in place for a while).

items.title: [AMD] CoalesceAsyncCopy produces a layout the direct-to-LDS lowering cannot coalesce when a warp spans more than the fastest shared dimension
items.author: bogdan-petkovic
items.body_excerpt:
### Describe the bug

### Describe the bug

`TritonAMDGPUCoalesceAsyncCopy` can rewrite an async copy into a src layout that the direct-to-LDS lowering then rejects on GFX9. It happens when the blocked order and the shared order differ and a warp has more lanes than the fastest shared dimension has elements.

For a swizzled shared encoding the pass distributes the lanes and warps along the shared order and then rebuilds the blocked encoding with the original blocked order (added in #10928). The order of a blocked encoding also decides how the lanes are linearized, so once the lanes span more than one dimension, the first lanes walk along the dimension that is strided in LDS and the writes are no longer coalesced. This only works while all lanes of a warp fall in the fastest shared dimension, like the 64x2 tile in the tests of #10928.

The existing test `async_copy_different_order` in `test/TritonGPU/amd/amd-coalesce-async-copy.mlir` already shows it. Its expected layout, `threadsPerWarp = [32, 2], warpsPerCTA = [1, 4], order = [1, 0]` for an `order = [0, 1]` shared layout, fails the same way when it is lowered.

### Reproducer

Triton main at 20d9d98fead78c2f65e1b3ba5a7881d86a836dad. No GPU needed, this is a compile failure.

`repro.mlir`, a 16x4 f32 copy with 2 warps on gfx950:

```mlir
#blocked = #ttg.blocked<{sizePerThread = [1, 1], threadsPerWarp = [16, 4], warpsPerCTA = [2, 1], order = [1, 0]}>
#shared = #ttg.swizzled_shared<{vec = 1, perPhase = 1, maxPhase = 1, order = [0, 1]}>
#smem = #ttg.shared_memory
module attributes {"ttg.num-ctas" = 1 : i32, "ttg.num-warps" = 2 : i32, "ttg.target" = "hip:gfx950", "ttg.threads-per-warp" = 64 : i32} {
  tt.func @copy(%input: tensor<16x4x!tt.ptr<f32>, #blocked> {tt.contiguity = dense<[1, 4]> : tensor<2xi32>, tt.divisibility = dense<[16, 16]> : tensor<2xi32>, tt.constancy = dense<[1, 1]> : tensor<2xi32>},
                %view: !ttg.memdesc<16x4xf32, #shared, #smem, mutable>) {
    %token = ttg.async_copy_global_to_local %input, %view : tensor<16x4x!tt.ptr<f32>, #blocked> -> <16x4xf32, #shared, #smem, mutable>
    tt.return
  }
}
```

```
triton-opt repro.mlir --tritonamdgpu-coalesce-async-copy=gfx-arch=gfx950 --allocate-shared-memory --convert-triton-amdgpu-to-llvm=gfx-arch=gfx950
```

```
repro.mlir:7:14: error: cannot lower 'ttg.async_copy_global_to_local' to a direct-to-LDS copy: the resulting writes into shared memory are not coalesced for a vectorization of 1 element(s). Adjust the blocked or shared encoding so each warp writes a contiguous range.
```

CoalesceAsyncCopy rewrites the src to `#ttg.blocked<{sizePerThread = [1, 1], threadsPerWarp = [16, 4], warpsPerCTA = [1, 2], order = [1, 0]}>`. Lanes 1 to 3 then take the next columns, 16 elements apart in LDS. The same tile with `order = [0, 1]` lowers to a single buffer load to LDS:

```
sed 's/warpsPerCTA = \[2, 1\], order = \[1, 0\]/warpsPerCTA = [1, 2], order = [0, 1]/' repro.mlir > shared-order.mlir
triton-opt shared-order.mlir --allocate-shared-memory --convert-triton-amdgpu-to-llvm=gfx-arch=gfx950
```

And the existing test case:

```
awk 'BEGIN{RS="// -----\n"} /async_copy_different_order/' test/TritonGPU/amd/amd-coalesce-async-copy.mlir > different-order.mlir
triton-opt different-order.mlir --tritonamdgpu-coalesce-async-copy=gfx-arch=gfx942 --allocate-shared-memory --convert-triton-amdgpu-to-llvm=gfx-arch=gfx942
```

fails with the same error.

### How we hit it

In rocmlirTriton (https://github.com/ROCm/rocmlirTriton) a non-power-of-two K tile is split into power-of-two segments, so a K tile of 36 has a last segment of 4. For f32 convolutions on gfx950 with an M tile of 16 or 32 the copy of that segment is a 16x4, 32x2 or 16x8 tile, which is exactly this case. Our weekly tuning ran into it on 677 configs. We disabled those tile sizes on gfx950 for now.

In our tree, falling back to the shared order when the rebuilt encoding cannot be lowered fixed all of them and left the code of every config that already compiled unchanged. We did not send that as a PR because it calls `canLoadDirectToLDS` from the pass, and a fix that builds the right layout up front seems preferable. Happy to test any fix.


### Environment details

Triton main at 20d9d98fead78c2f65e1b3ba5a7881d86a836dad, built from source with CMake (TritonRelBuildWithAsserts, nvidia and amd backends, only the triton-opt target) against the prebuilt LLVM from cmake/llvm-info.json (b010a18d2b648cab83c83967ff26b8fde11acdc6). Ubuntu 22.04.5 on x86_64, GCC 11.4.

No GPU is needed, this is a compile failure in triton-opt and the target comes from gfx-arch (gfx950 for the reproducer, gfx942 for the existing test case). We first hit it compiling f32 convolutions for gfx950 in rocmlirTriton, whose vendored Triton has the same CoalesceAsyncCopy code.

comments.author: he-yufeng
comments.body:
Picking this up. I read the pass and the mechanism checks out: the swizzled branch distributes lanes along the shared order and then stamps the original blocked order back on, which re-linearizes the lanes. Once a warp spans more than the fastest shared dimension, consecutive lanes walk a dim that is strided in LDS, and the rewritten copy is exactly what the direct-to-LDS lowering rejects.

Fix I am testing: after building the blocked-order candidate, check it with canLoadDirectToLDS (the same predicate the lowering uses, already called from this pass) and keep the shared-order distribution when the candidate would not lower. That matches what you validated in rocmlirTriton, and leaves every config whose rewritten layout already lowers byte-identical. Will add lit coverage for both the pass output and the end-to-end lowering of your 16x4 repro.

comments.author: he-yufeng
comments.body: PR up: #12159. The pass now checks the re-stamped encoding with `canLoadDirectToLDS` and keeps the shared-order distribution when the src order cannot lower. Your 16x4 reproducer lowers cleanly with it, and `async_copy_different_order` turned out to have the same latent problem, its expected layout changes to the shared order as well.
