items.title: [Bug]: EAGLE-3 latency penalty on Hopper with TensorRT-LLM 1.3.0rc29
items.author: dtemraz
items.body_excerpt:
### System Info


- **Primary hardware:** single H100 SXM 80 GB, same pod for the cross-engine tests
- **Runtime:** TensorRT-LLM `1.3.0rc29`, PyTorch backend; comparison with vLLM `0.31.0`
- **Serving:** `trtllm-serve --backend pytorch`, `--kv_cache_free_gpu_memory_fraction 0.85`
- **Environment:** CUDA toolkit 12.8; Python 3.12; TensorRT-LLM installed from NVIDIA PyPI wheels
- **Host controls:** 22.1-core cgroup CPU quota, with no additional CPU-throttling events observed during the load tests; `OMP_NUM_THREADS=8`, `MKL_NUM_THREADS=8`, `TOKENIZERS_PARALLELISM=false`


### Who can help?

_No response_

### Information

- [ ] The official example scripts
- [x] My own modified scripts

### Tasks

- [ ] An officially supported task in the `examples` folder (such as GLUE/SQuAD, ...)
- [x] My own task or dataset (give details below)

### Reproduction

- **Target:** `Qwen/Qwen3-4B` (BF16) or `Qwen/Qwen3-4B-FP8` (official block-scaled FP8 checkpoint)
- **Draft head:** `AngelSlim/Qwen3-4B_eagle3`, one-model EAGLE-3, `max_draft_len: 2`
- **Requests:** approximately 1,040 shared prefix tokens, ~50 request-specific tokens; outputs average 10.5 tokens (p95 18), max_tokens: 24, greedy sampling, thinking disabled
- **Traffic:** open-loop Poisson, 20 requests/sec, 400 requests per run
- **Measurement:** request arrival to completed response, p50/p95 in milliseconds; first run after boot discarded; reported measurements taken from warmed runs
- **Repeatability:** quoted latency cells were checked against a second consecutive warm run, typically agreeing within approximately 10%.

The workload used a shared, byte-stable prefix and a ~50 request-specific tokens. 
Requests were sent at open-loop Poisson arrival times. Latency was measured from scheduled arrival through response completion. The first benchmark run after each server restart was excluded.

EAGLE configuration:

```yaml
enable_in_graph_sampling: true
speculative_config:
  decoding_type: Eagle3
  max_draft_len: 2
  speculative_model: AngelSlim/Qwen3-4B_eagle3
```

The one-model EAGLE-3 path (`eagle3_one_model=True`) was confirmed in startup logs. The request-level comparisons were run without iteration performance statistics enabled.


### Expected behavior

Enabling EAGLE-3 with draft acceptance of ~2 output tokens per iteration (out of a maximum 3) should reduce, or at worst not increase, request latency. Just as it does in vLLM 0.31.0 on the same host and in TensorRT-LLM on RTX PRO 6000.


### actual behavior

On H100 SXM, enabling one-model EAGLE-3 in TensorRT-LLM 1.3.0rc29 increases request latency for our short-output workload, despite draft acceptance of ~2 output tokens per iteration out of a maximum 3. The same draft checkpoint improves latency in vLLM 0.31.0 on the same host, and EAGLE-3 also helps TensorRT-LLM on RTX PRO 6000 (−14% p50, −32% p95).

### H100 results: same FP8 checkpoint and EAGLE head

| Engine | FP8 without EAGLE (p50 / p95) | FP8 with EAGLE-3 (p50 / p95) |
|---|---:|---:|
| vLLM 0.31.0 | ~78 / 121 ms | **67.1 / 102.0 ms** |
| TensorRT-LLM 1.3.0rc29 | **68.6 / 98.7 ms** | 100.6 / 165.2 ms |

Within vLLM, EAGLE-3 improves p50 by about 14% and p95 by 16%. Within TensorRT-LLM, it worsens p50 by about 47% and p95 by 67%.

The TensorRT-LLM EAGLE configuration takes about **50% longer at p50** and **62% longer at p95** than vLLM's EAGLE configuration.

Both engines use the same target and draft checkpoint, GPU, traffic shape, and draft length.

### Draft acceptance

The draft head is producing useful predictions in both engines:

| Engine | Measured acceptance |
|---|---|
| TensorRT-LLM | `acceptanceLength` 2.03–2.04 output tokens per iteration; approximately 52.5% of drafted tokens accepted |
| vLLM | 1,984 / 4,168 drafted tokens accepted (47.6%); 59.6% at draft position 0 and 35.7% at position 1 |

The TensorRT-LLM acceptance metric was collected with `enable_iter_perf_stats`. That instrumentation affects latency on this workload, so we do **not** use instrumented runs for the end-to-end comparison above. 

### Fixed-batch experiment

To remove ongoing request admission from the test, we sent bursts of 1, 4, or 16 simultaneous requests, with no further arrivals until completion. The figures below are medians across five warmed bursts using the BF16 target, with iteration statistics disabled.

Each cell gives **median request latency / slowest request / burst makespan** in milliseconds.

| Simultaneous requests | BF16 without EAGLE | BF16 + EAGLE-3 |
|---|---:|---:|
| 1 | 66.4 / 66.4 / 66.6 | 75.5 / 75.5 / 75.6 |
| 4 | 105.9 / 139.2 / 143.5 | 133.6 / 138.1 / 142.5 |
| 16 | 150.5 / 213.6 / 217.9 | 186.5 / 205.4 / 211.1 |

EAGLE increases median request latency at every tested burst size, although the slowest-request latency and makespan are close between configurations at 4 and 16 requests. 

### Version comparison

Results from the same H100 pod, using BF16:

| TensorRT-LLM version | Without EAGLE (p50 / p95) | With EAGLE-3 (p50 / p95) |
|---|---:|---:|
| 1.2.1 | 143.8 / 261.7 ms | 137 / 248 ms |
| 1.3.0rc29 | 76.3 / 110.8 ms | 98.3 / 158.8 ms |

The non-speculative path improved far more between these releases than the EAGLE path. As a result, EAGLE moves from a small net benefit in 1.2.1 to a substantial regression in 1.3.0rc29. 

### Cross-GPU results

TensorRT-LLM 1.3.0rc29, BF16 target, same model family and draft head:

| GPU | Without EAGLE (p50 / p95) | With EAGLE-3 (p50 / p95) |
|---|---:|---:|
| RTX PRO 6000 (SM120) | 89.0 / 144.0 ms | **76.3 / 97.5 ms** |
| H100 (SM90) | **76.3 / 110.8 ms** | 98.3 / 158.8 ms |
| H200 (SM90) | **52.7 / ~80 ms** | 81 / 149 ms |

EAGLE helps on RTX PRO 6000 but hurts on both tested Hopper GPUs.


Please investigate why enabling one-model EAGLE-3 in TensorRT-LLM 1.3.0rc29 increases request latency on the tested Hopper systems despite comparable draft acceptance, while the same checkpoint improves latency in vLLM on H100 and in TensorRT-LLM on RTX PRO 6000.

items.title: [Performance]: MLA chunked prefill builds context K with a cat per loop and a fixed buffer batch size
items.author: lucifer1004
items.body_excerpt:
### Proposal to improve performance

MLA context attention with chunked prefill (`MLA.forward_context_with_chunked_prefill` and `forward_context_with_cached_kv` in `tensorrt_llm/_torch/attention/mla.py`) builds the FMHA K for every cached-KV loop and for the current chunk as `maybe_compiled_cat((k_nope, k_pe.expand(-1, H, -1)), -1)` after a `split` and two `view`s. For a long prompt this runs once per loop per MLA layer, and the cached KV is expanded in loops of `chunk_size * chunked_prefill_buffer_batch_size` tokens, where the batch size is fixed at the dataclass default 4 (no config entry).

Measured on Rubin single GPU, Kimi K3 MLA layer (12 heads per rank, 2K-token chunks), the deepest chunk of a 128K prompt (129024 cached tokens), one layer forward:

| | kernels / layer | host enqueue µs | GPU µs |
|---|---|---|---|
| cat, buffer batch 4 (16 loops) | 112 | 3175 | 3659 |
| one Triton pack kernel, buffer batch 4 | 112 | 2781 | 2765 |
| pack kernel, buffer batch 16 (4 loops) | 40 | 1217 | 2132 |

Over 24 MLA layers that is about 1730 fewer launches, 47 ms less host time and 37 ms less GPU time for the deepest chunk, about half of that on average over a 128K prompt. Separately, when the K packing is a Triton kernel specialized on the token count, the first chunk whose token count is not a multiple of 16 (typically a prompt's last chunk) compiles a second variant mid-request, about 0.1 s once per process.

Proposal: pack K with one Triton kernel (a pure copy, bitwise the cat; the cat stays as fallback for layouts the kernel does not take), without specializing on the token count, and make `chunked_prefill_buffer_batch_size` settable (`TLLM_MLA_CHUNKED_PREFILL_BUFFER_BATCH_SIZE`, default 4). The KV cache profiling run already sizes its cached prefix from that value. PR to follow.

items.title: [Feature]: b12x MoE: inline NVFP4-CSF scales for the micro W4A16 decode path (GB10)
items.author: zengjiajun0623
items.body_excerpt:
### Before submitting

- [x] I have searched existing issues and this request has not been filed yet.

### Problem

On DGX Spark (GB10, SM121), single-stream decode of `nvidia/GLM-5.3-Flash-FP4-Local` spends about 5.8% of GPU busy time in the standalone NVFP4-CSF scale expansion kernel (`nvfp4_csf` `Pair`), which runs before every routed-expert MoE layer and is not overlapped with other work.

Setup: 2x DGX Spark, TP=2, `eugr/spark-vllm-b12x:latest` (2026-10-15 build, flashinfer 0.7.1 with b12x), the published recipe (`--moe-backend b12x`, `VLLM_B12X_MOE_FP4_FORCE_A16=1`, MTP with 3 speculative tokens, CUDA graphs on). Decode therefore runs the `micro` implementation with `quant_mode == "w4a16"`.

What the torch profiler shows for a decode window (CUDA graphs, rank 0):

| | value |
|---|---|
| CSF expansion kernel time | 325.8 ms over 2562 launches (about 104 to 129 us per MoE layer per step) |
| of which overlapped with other kernels | 73.4 ms (23%) |
| exposed (serial) CSF time | 252.4 ms = **5.8% of GPU busy time** |
| launch stream | the main stream for 2478 of 2562 launches |

`VLLM_B12X_CSF_SCALE_PREFETCH` does not help here, since per its comment it applies to eager prefill calls only.

For context, the weight-streaming kernels in the same trace are already close to the memory roofline (device copy measured at 218 GB/s on GB10): the W4A16 fused MoE kernel reaches roughly 215 GB/s and the FP8 dense GEMMs 188 to 200 GB/s. That makes the scale expansion one of the few remaining overheads in the decode step that is not set by weight bandwidth.

In current `main`, `_impl.py` already has an inline path (`nvfp4_inline_scales` via `experts.nvfp4_csf.inline_scales`), but it is gated on `binding.implementation == "dynamic"` and `quant_mode == "nvfp4"`, so the `micro` / W4A16 decode path still calls `experts.nvfp4_csf.decode(...)` into scratch before the MoE kernel reads the expanded scales.

### Requested outcome

Let the `micro` W4A16 decode path read NVFP4-CSF scales inline (or fuse the routed expansion into the MoE kernel prologue), as the `dynamic` NVFP4 path already can, so the scale expansion no longer costs a separate serial kernel per MoE layer during decode. If that is not practical, overlapping the expansion with the preceding attention on a side stream in CUDA-graph decode (as `VLLM_B12X_CSF_SCALE_PREFETCH` does for eager prefill) would recover most of the same time.

Expected upper bound on GB10 for this model: about 5 to 6% faster single-stream decode, with no change in numerics (the format is lossless).

### Target hardware

SM121 (DGX Spark / GB10). Likely also SM120 (RTX PRO 6000 Blackwell, RTX 5090) with the same checkpoint.

### Additional context

- Model: https://huggingface.co/nvidia/GLM-5.3-Flash-FP4-Local
- Recipe: https://github.com/eugr/spark-vllm-docker (`recipes/glm-5.3-flash.yaml`)
- I have not built current `main` to re-measure; the gating above is from reading `flashinfer/experimental/b12x/moe/fused_moe/_impl.py` on `main`. Happy to re-run the profile against a newer build if that is useful.

### 🐛 Describe the bug

To reproduce:
```python
import torch.distributed as dist

tensor = torch.empty((5,),dtype=torch.bool)
if dist.get_rank() == 0:
    gather_list = [torch.empty((5,),dtype=torch.bool) for _ in range(dist.get_world_size())]
else:
    gather_list = None
dist.gather(tensor, gather_list)
```
This is also the case for `all_gather`, `reduce`, `all_reduce` and `broadcast`. Changing `dtype=torch.bool` to `dtype=torch.uint8` resolves the error, while `torch.bool == torch.uint8` evaluates to `True`.

items.title: [RLlib] Potential infinite Env Runer sampling loop with non default algorithm parameters
items.author: corentinlger
items.body_excerpt:
### What happened + What you expected to happen

Hi ! While investigating algo configs leading to silently discarded env runners results (https://github.com/ray-project/ray/issues/63302), I ran into a rare but weird case where RLlib training can hang forever without any error. It probably almost never happens, but it still seems a bit weird it's possible, so I'm still posting an issue in case it can help.

The issue: with a synchronous algo on the new API stack (e.g. PPO), if every `sample()` call takes longer than `sample_timeout_s`, each sampling round returns nothing. If `min_sample_timesteps_per_iteration > 0`, the iteration can never reach its minimum, so `train()` loops forever without crashing.

RLlib already warns while this happens and gives a useful advice to fix it, but can still keeps running the training indefinitely.

```
2026-10-01 12:54:33,281 WARNING rollout_ops.py:122 -- No samples returned from remote workers. If you have a slow environment or model, consider increasing the `sample_timeout_s` or decreasing the `rollout_fragment_length` in `AlgorithmConfig.env_runners().
2026-10-01 12:54:35,290 WARNING rollout_ops.py:122 -- No samples returned from remote workers. If you have a slow environment or model, consider increasing the `sample_timeout_s` or decreasing the `rollout_fragment_length` in `AlgorithmConfig.env_runners().
. . .
```

Do you think it would make sense to add a simple safeguard (e.g if no new samples are collected for N consecutive training steps, raise an error and crash the training) ? If so, I can open a quick PR for this (: (but idk if it's worth it as this bug is likely very rare)

### Versions / Dependencies

- Ray 2.58.0
- Python 3.11.13

### Reproduction script

```python
# Toy env whose episodes take ~10s (longer than sample_timeout_s)
class SlowEnv(gym.Env):
    def __init__(self, config=None):
        self.observation_space = spaces.Box(-1.0, 1.0, (2,), np.float32)
        self.action_space = spaces.Discrete(2)
        self._t = 0
        self.n_resets = 0

    def reset(self, *, seed=None, options=None):
        print(f"{self.n_resets = }")
        self.n_resets += 1
        super().reset(seed=seed)
        self._t = 0
        return self.observation_space.sample(), {}

    def step(self, action):
        time.sleep(0.2)          # 50 steps * 0.2s = ~10s per episode
        self._t += 1
        print(f"{self._t = }")
        done = self._t >= 50
        return self.observation_space.sample(), 0.0, done, False, {}

# algo config with low sample timeout + non null min_sample_timesteps_per_iteration
config = (
        PPOConfig()
        .environment(SlowEnv)
        .env_runners(
            num_env_runners=2,
            batch_mode="complete_episodes",
            sample_timeout_s=2.0,          # too low: episodes take ~10s
        )
        .reporting(min_sample_timesteps_per_iteration=100)  # the gate that causes the hang
    )

algo = config.build_algo()
result = algo.train()  # infinite env runner sampling loop
```

### Issue Severity

None

comments.author: lindicaphxag-tech
comments.body:
I put together a draft implementation in #66687 to explore the no-progress safeguard described here. It detects a successful training-step loop that repeatedly makes zero sampling progress while `min_sample_timesteps_per_iteration > 0` and `sample_timeout_s` is finite, and covers both the old counters path and the new lifetime-metrics path.

I have intentionally kept it draft because one design point deserves maintainer input: the current prototype uses `num_consecutive_env_runner_failures_tolerance` as the retry budget, which avoids a new config knob but couples EnvRunner failure tolerance to sampling-timeout/no-progress tolerance. If a separate internal/default budget or dedicated config is preferred, I can adjust before review.

Also happy to defer/close the draft if the original reporter would prefer to implement the fix.

comments.author: corentinlger
comments.body: Hi, I'd be happy in implementing a PR for this issue if needed , but before doing so it would be good to even know if RLlib maintainers think it's worth fixing (which is not sure)

comments.author: lindicaphxag-tech
comments.body: Update on my draft fix in [PR #66687](https://github.com/ray-project/ray/pull/66687): I rebased the change onto current `master` and separated the no-progress budget from `num_consecutive_env_runner_failures_tolerance`. The new `num_consecutive_sample_no_progress_tolerance` defaults to 100 and is independently configurable through `AlgorithmConfig.fault_tolerance(...)`. This avoids changing the worker-failure retry behavior when users tune the sampling-stall safeguard. Added tests for both independence directions, and retained coverage for old/new API stacks, env/agent counters, progress reset, finite vs blocking timeouts, NaN retired-agent metrics, and invalid infinite counters. Current-head CI is now the gate; I am not claiming merge-ready until the required Ray checks pass.

items.title: [Data] Improve planning for full Parquet schema inference
items.author: jiangxt2
items.body_excerpt:
### Description

With `read_parquet(..., merge_schema=True)`, DSV2 reads the footers of all eligible Parquet files during planning to infer the full schema. Execution also reads footer metadata to plan row-group work. For large or remote datasets, this can increase planning time and driver-side metadata usage.

As a follow-up to [PR #66522](https://github.com/ray-project/ray/pull/66522), distribute planning-time footer reads and reuse their metadata during execution where feasible. Keep default bounded schema inference unchanged, and use the same discovered candidate file set for full schema inference and execution. PR #66522 implements the opt-in behavior discussed in [issue #66444](https://github.com/ray-project/ray/issues/66444).

Spark provides a useful reference: its shared Parquet/ORC [`SchemaMergeUtils.mergeSchemasInParallel`](https://github.com/apache/spark/blob/v4.2.0/sql/core/src/main/scala/org/apache/spark/sql/execution/datasources/SchemaMergeUtils.scala) reads schemas on executors, merges them within each task partition, and returns at most one merged schema per partition for a final merge on the driver. This reduces the number of schema objects collected by the driver without prescribing the same implementation for Ray.

The proposed optimization should distinguish three concerns:

- **Partial schema merging:** Consider merging schemas within metadata tasks so the driver does not need to retain every file's schema. Any partial-merge approach needs validation against Ray's existing unifier for field order, metadata, type promotion, nullability, nested/extension types, and incompatibility detection. Distributed reads alone do not reduce this memory cost if every file's schema is still collected on the driver.

- **Metadata reuse:** Reusing footer metadata can reduce repeated I/O, but a merged schema alone does not provide all the row-group metadata required for execution planning. Metadata retention, transfer, and lifecycle costs need separate evaluation; reuse does not automatically reduce memory usage.

- **Candidate-file index:** Retaining the complete discovered candidate set still requires file metadata proportional to the number of files. Spark's ordinary directory reads also retain an [`InMemoryFileIndex`](https://github.com/apache/spark/blob/v4.2.0/sql/core/src/main/scala/org/apache/spark/sql/execution/datasources/InMemoryFileIndex.scala) on the driver. Parallel listing does not eliminate this O(N) file-index cost. This issue should improve planning overhead without promising constant-memory file discovery or changing the candidate-file contract from #66522.

### Use case

Users reading large or remote Parquet datasets may need fields that appear only in later files to be present in the Dataset schema before they build downstream filters and projections. They want to opt into full schema inference while keeping planning latency and driver memory usage manageable as the number of files grows.

items.title: [Bug] GroupRMSNorm kernels: shared-memory init race inflates outputs; one-warp large-batch path never normalises input 1
items.author: builtin-pb
items.body_excerpt:
**Summary.** Two bugs in the GroupRMSNorm kernels make `torch.ops.trtllm.group_rms_norm_base`, `group_rms_norm_heuristic` and `group_rms_norm_large_batch` write wrong outputs: a race on the shared-memory initialisation inflates outputs, and the large-batch kernel never normalises input 1 when it runs with one warp. We suggest a `__syncthreads()` after the initialisation in both kernels for the first; the second can be fixed in two ways, listed under additional notes.

### System Info

- TensorRT-LLM 1.2.1 wheel, torch 2.9.1+cu130, A100 80GB PCIe (driver 610.57).
- `cpp/tensorrt_llm/kernels/groupRmsNormKernels/groupRmsNormKernels.cu` is unchanged on main `b031dbe`. The two device kernels in the 1.2.1 release are identical to main's.

### Who can help?

_No response_

### Information

- [ ] The official example scripts
- [x] My own modified scripts

### Tasks

- [ ] An officially supported task in the `examples` folder (such as GLUE/SQuAD, ...)
- [x] My own task or dataset (give details below)

### Reproduction

A minimal script:

```python
import torch
import tensorrt_llm  # registers torch.ops.trtllm

def run(name, batch, dims, calls=1000):
    op = getattr(torch.ops.trtllm, name)
    xs = [(torch.randn(batch, d) * (1 + i)).bfloat16().cuda() for i, d in enumerate(dims)]
    ws = [(0.5 + torch.rand(d)).bfloat16().cuda() for d in dims]
    refs = []
    for x, w in zip(xs, ws):
        xd = x.double()
        refs.append(xd * torch.rsqrt(xd.square().mean(-1, keepdim=True) + 1e-6) * w.double())
    wrong = [0] * len(dims)
    for _ in range(calls):
        outs = [torch.empty_like(x) for x in xs]
        op(xs, outs, ws, 1e-6, 0.0)
        for i, (y, ref) in enumerate(zip(outs, refs)):
            wrong[i] += bool(((y.double() - ref).abs() > 1e-3 + 0.016 * ref.abs()).any())
    print(f"{name} {batch}x{dims}: wrong calls per input {wrong} of {calls}")

torch.manual_seed(0)
run("group_rms_norm_base", 64, (1536, 512))
run("group_rms_norm_large_batch", 2048, (256, 256))
```

On an A100 (SXM4 80GB) it printed:

```
group_rms_norm_base 64x(1536, 512): wrong calls per input [1000, 991] of 1000
group_rms_norm_large_batch 2048x(256, 256): wrong calls per input [0, 1000] of 1000
```

Results with the 1.2.1 wheel, from a longer harness: each op ran for 120 s, cycling three input sets.
- Input 0 is `randn` and input 1 is `2 * randn`, both rounded to bf16.
- Weights are `0.5 + rand`, rounded to bf16.
- `eps = 1e-6` and `weight_bias = 0`.
- The reference is float64 from the same bf16 inputs.
- A call counts as wrong if any element of an output differs by more than 1e-3 + 0.016 · |ref|.

| Operator | Inputs | Wrong calls |
|---|---|---|
| `group_rms_norm_base` | [64, 1536] + [64, 512] | 397748 / 397774 |
| `group_rms_norm_heuristic` (falls back to the base kernel on A100) | [64, 1536] + [64, 512] | 368411 / 368440 |
| `group_rms_norm_large_batch` | [2048, 256] + [2048, 256] | input 1 wrong in 401268 / 401268; input 0 correct in every call |

Examples of the wrong values:
- 0.0262 for 0.0187 (base): one of input 1's two warp sums was lost;
- 2448.0 for 1.19 (heuristic): both were lost, so the kernel used `rsqrt(eps)` = 1000;
- −47.25 for −0.018 (large batch): input 1 was multiplied by its sum of squares.

Each of these logged values equals exactly what the mechanism below predicts.

### Expected behavior

Each output row is `x * rsqrt(mean(x²) + eps) * (w + weight_bias)`.

### actual behavior

#### Cause

**1. Race on the shared-memory initialisation.** In `GroupRMSNormBaseKernel`, warp 0 initialises `smem_input_mask[lane]` and `smem_warp_sum_sqs[lane]` (lines 104–109). Lane 0 of every other warp `k` later writes its partial sum and input index to slot `k` of the same arrays (lines 179 and 188). No barrier separates the two; the first `__syncthreads()` is at line 191. If warp 0's initialising store lands after warp `k`'s write, warp `k`'s contribution to the sum of squares is lost. The row then comes out too large.

The `__syncwarp()` for `sm < 900` before line 188 ("needed to avoid race condition on smem_input_mask write") orders only within a warp. In a standalone copy of the kernel, Compute Sanitizer racecheck reports this race. A `__syncthreads()` after the initialisation removed both the report and the wrong outputs on A100 and A40. In an sm_80 build we compiled with CUDA 12.6, the initialising stores are scheduled after the loads. We have not run on Hopper or Blackwell.

`GroupRMSNormKernelLargeBatch` has the same pattern:
- warps 0 and 1 initialise rows 0 and 1 of `smem_rsqrts` (lines 286–289);
- lane 0 of each warp writes `smem_rsqrts[0][warp_idx]` and `smem_rsqrts[1][warp_idx]` (lines 388 and 429), before the first barrier (line 433).

Racecheck reports it as well, and the one launch we ran under racecheck gave inflated outputs. In about 9,000 normal launches each on A100 and A40, we saw no wrong output from it.

**2. Input 1 is never normalised when the large-batch kernel runs with one warp.** The large-batch kernel converts each input's sum of squares to a reciprocal RMS in a dedicated warp:

```cpp
if (warp_idx == 0) { ... smem_rsqrts[0][0] = rsqrtf(block_sum / input_dim_0 + params.eps); }
else if (warp_idx == 1) { ... smem_rsqrts[1][0] = rsqrtf(block_sum / input_dim_1 + params.eps); }
```

When each input has at most 256 bf16 or fp16 elements (128 fp32), `calculateNumWarpsLargeBatch` launches a single warp, and the `warp_idx == 1` branch never runs. `smem_rsqrts[1][0]` keeps the sum of squares of input 1's row that warp 0 stored at line 429, and input 1 is multiplied by it (lines 523 and 529). Input 1 is wrong in every call; input 0 is correct.

By our reading of the heuristic model in `groupRmsNormKernels.h`, `group_rms_norm_heuristic` also picks this one-warp kernel for two 256-wide inputs at batch sizes from about 1034 on SM90 and 1387 on SM100. We did not run it there.

### additional notes

#### Suggested fix for 1

```diff
@@ -108,6 +108,8 @@ __global__ void GroupRMSNormBaseKernel(GroupR

items.title: [Performance]: Kimi K3 KDA prefill persistent kernels (fused K123, K4) hard-code a 148-block grid
items.author: lucifer1004
items.body_excerpt:
### Proposal to improve performance

The Kimi K3 KDA prefill path launches two persistent CuTe DSL kernels whose grid is fixed at 148 blocks, the SM count of B200:

- fused K1+K2+K3 (`cute_dsl_kernels/blackwell/kimi_k3_kda/fused_k123.py`: `NUM_SMS = 148`, used for the grid and as the `for_generate` stride);
- persistent K4 (`custom_ops/cute_dsl_kimi_k3_custom_ops.py`: `_launch_k4_persistent(..., num_sm=148)`, the grid ceiling and the size of its workspace).

On a GPU with more SMs, the extra SMs stay idle during these kernels, and K4 needs an extra persistent round as soon as the work units (sequences x heads) exceed 148. `is_kda_optimized_supported()` admits SM100, SM103 and SM107, which do not all have 148 SMs.

Measured on Rubin single GPU (200-SM engineering sample), Kimi K3 KDA shapes (96 heads, head dim 128), comparing the 148-block grid with a grid of the device's SM count:

- fused K123, one 8192-token prefill chunk: 124.9 us -> 110.2 us; summed over the model's KDA layers about 1.0 ms per 8K chunk (about 10-15 ms of TTFT at 128K context);
- K4 with 13 or more context sequences per step: 41-46% faster (two persistent rounds become one).

Outputs and the state pool are bitwise identical to the 148-block grid in all tested shapes (14-15 shapes, eager and CUDA graph replay), since each work unit is computed by exactly one block wherever it lands.

Proposal: size both grids by the launch device's SM count (queried once per device), and key the compiled-function caches on it. PR to follow.

items.title: [QST] SM120 FP8 MMA with FP32 accumulate, plain form against block-scaled form with unit scales
items.author: emre570
items.body_excerpt:
**What is your question?**

On an RTX 5080, the plain FP8 MMA with FP32 accumulate runs at half the rate of the block-scaled FP8 MMA with FP32 accumulate. When all scale bytes are `0x7F` (UE8M0 1.0), the two forms give equal bits.

My FP8 attention kernel in CuTe DSL used `MmaFP8Op`. I changed it to `MmaMXF8Op` with constant unit scales and no other change. The kernel time went from 123.6 ms to 83.6 ms and the output is byte-equal (sgl-project/sglang#43390). So a user can do this today. My question is about the default.

1. Is there a reason to keep the plain form for E4M3 x E4M3 with FP32 accumulate on SM120?
2. If there is no reason, do you want `MmaFP8Op` and `rr_op_selector_sm120` to emit the block-scaled form with unit scales for this case? I can send a PR.

### Related report

The same behavior is reported in flashinfer-ai/flashinfer#5963 for the FlashInfer SM120 FP8 attention kernel, with RTX 5090 numbers and a bit-identity check. That issue also points to the MXFP8 attention work in flashinfer-ai/flashinfer#3628 and flashinfer-ai/flashinfer#4149. The numbers below add an RTX 5080 and a CUTLASS GEMM measurement to that report.

### Scope

E4M3 x E4M3, FP32 accumulate, one RTX 5080 (driver 595.99.02, CUDA 13.3, CUTLASS `ffa119a12`). I did not measure other types or other cards.

### Raw MMA rate

Independent MMA chains, no memory access, 84 SMs. The rate is the same from 4 to 32 warps per SM.

| instruction | TFLOP/s |
|---|---:|
| `kind::f8f6f4.m16n8k32 ... f32.e4m3.e4m3.f32` | 246 |
| `kind::mxf8f6f4.block_scale.scale_vec::1X.m16n8k32 ... f32.e4m3.e4m3.f32.ue8m0` | 489 |

### Bit equality

- Random finite inputs. 0 of 704,643,072 accumulator registers differ.
- Negative control with scale 2.0. 704,643,071 registers differ.
- Edge cases (subnormal, ±448, NaN bytes, accumulator start at zero, FLT_MAX, subnormal, infinity, NaN). 30 classes, 176,160,768 registers each, 0 bits differ.

### CUTLASS GEMM

I used the SM120 `CollectiveBuilder` with `OpClassTensorOp`, pingpong schedule, tile 128x128x128, FP32 output. Then I changed only the instruction in `SM120_16x8x32_TN<float_e4m3_t, float_e4m3_t, float>` to the block-scaled form. The scale `0x7F7F7F7F` stays in a register. There is no scale factor tensor and no additional load. The patch is 34 lines.

I measured 30 shapes from real models. All 30 give 0 different output words. Five examples:

| shape source | M x N x K | plain | patched | speedup |
|---|---|---:|---:|---:|
| Wan 2.2 14B, `to_q` | 32760 x 5120 x 5120 | 236.1 | 398.6 | 1.69x |
| Llama 3.3 70B, MLP up | 4096 x 28672 x 8192 | 234.7 | 398.1 | 1.70x |
| FLUX.1-dev, FFN up | 4608 x 12288 x 3072 | 231.8 | 393.3 | 1.70x |
| MiniMax-H3, FFN up | 30272 x 14336 x 5376 | 234.6 | 363.5 | 1.55x |
| Gemma 3 27B, MLP up | 128 x 21504 x 5376 | 195.8 | 203.4 | 1.04x |

TFLOP/s. The speedup is 1.55x to 1.72x for the 22 shapes with M of 4096 or more. It is 1.04x to 1.82x for the 8 shapes with M = 128, where the low end is DRAM-bound.

Nsight Compute on the stock plain kernel shows the tensor pipe 96% busy. The MMA instruction rate is 47.9% of the peak.

One caution. These numbers use `max_swizzle_size = 8`. With the default of 1, three large shapes become DRAM-bound and the patched kernel is slower than the plain kernel (0.88x). I can open a different issue for that with the data.

### Where the plain form is used

- CuTe DSL `MmaFP8Op`
- `rr_op_selector_sm120` in `sm120_mma_builder.inl`, `sm120_array_mma_builder.inl` and `sm120_blockwise_mma_builder.inl`

cuBLASLt on the same card uses `QMMA.SF.16832.F32.E4M3.E4M3.E8` in its FP8 GEMM kernel and no plain `QMMA`.

I can share the benchmark source, the patch and the raw results if they are useful.

items.title: [BUG] sm120 GEMM hangs when K = 0 (grouped and non-grouped) after can_implement(), initialize() and run() return success
items.author: vera-rubin
items.body_excerpt:
**Describe the bug**

On sm120, a CUTLASS 3.x GEMM with K = 0 passes `can_implement()`, and `initialize()` and `run()` return `kSuccess` in the tested release builds. The records show zero-K kernels not completing within 10, 15 or 60 seconds.

- **Grouped GEMM, where K = 0 is documented as supported.** With the sm120 ptr-array kernel, the recorded K = {128, 0, 256, 0} and {0, 0, 0, 0} groups do not complete within the recorded timeouts, while {128, 128, 128, 128} and {256, 512} pass. The mainloop source indicates that one K = 0 group is sufficient. CHANGELOG 4.3.0 says ([CHANGELOG.md L715](https://github.com/NVIDIA/cutlass/blob/0b55a2f691d69981583568fd9eb69687b1f0de8a/CHANGELOG.md?plain=1#L715)):

  > Enable GEMM_K = 0 in grouped gemm.

  The same case was fixed for Hopper in #2547 and for sm100 grouped GEMM in #2746.
- **Non-grouped GEMM, a validation gap.** The docs don't say whether K = 0 is supported, and a debug build stops at `assert(gmem_prob_shape[0] >= 1)` in `make_tma_copy_desc` ([copy_traits_sm90_tma.hpp L957](https://github.com/NVIDIA/cutlass/blob/0b55a2f691d69981583568fd9eb69687b1f0de8a/include/cute/atom/copy_traits_sm90_tma.hpp#L957)). A release build (`-DNDEBUG`, as the examples use) prints `Error: Failed to initialize the TMA descriptor 1` to stderr, `initialize()` still returns `kSuccess`, and the launched kernel does not complete before the recorded timeout. With M = 0 or N = 0, the same kernel's `run()` returns `Error Internal` instead. Upstream examples 79a (NVFP4) and 79c (MXFP8 x MXFP6) time out at `--k=0`. Our own tests time out the same way with FP8 (cooperative and pingpong) and NVFP4 cooperative kernels at 128x128, and with FP8 at 300x392 with L = 2 and with beta = 0. They use real (non-null) A/B buffers.

A caller whose K can be 0 at run time (for example a weight-gradient GEMM for an MoE expert that received no tokens) is an illustrative scenario. This makes reachability plausible, not demonstrated for a deployed SM120 framework, product, or protected workload.

The submitted computation does not complete within the recorded timeout. Software waiting for it can lose availability; recovery and impact on other GPU users were not assessed. No confidentiality or integrity failure was demonstrated.

**Cause (our reading):**

1. The producer issues TMA loads only inside `for ( ; k_tile_count > 0; --k_tile_count)` ([sm120_mma_tma.hpp L400](https://github.com/NVIDIA/cutlass/blob/0b55a2f691d69981583568fd9eb69687b1f0de8a/include/cutlass/gemm/collective/sm120_mma_tma.hpp#L400), [sm120_blockscaled_mma_tma.hpp L665](https://github.com/NVIDIA/cutlass/blob/0b55a2f691d69981583568fd9eb69687b1f0de8a/include/cutlass/gemm/collective/sm120_blockscaled_mma_tma.hpp#L665)), so at K = 0 it loads nothing.
2. The consumer `mma()` clears the accumulators and then calls `pipeline.consumer_wait(smem_pipe_read)` unconditionally ([sm120_mma_tma.hpp L526](https://github.com/NVIDIA/cutlass/blob/0b55a2f691d69981583568fd9eb69687b1f0de8a/include/cutlass/gemm/collective/sm120_mma_tma.hpp#L526), [sm120_blockscaled_mma_tma.hpp L848](https://github.com/NVIDIA/cutlass/blob/0b55a2f691d69981583568fd9eb69687b1f0de8a/include/cutlass/gemm/collective/sm120_blockscaled_mma_tma.hpp#L848)). No TMA transaction ever completes that barrier. The array mainloops have the same first wait ([sm120_mma_array_tma.hpp L516](https://github.com/NVIDIA/cutlass/blob/0b55a2f691d69981583568fd9eb69687b1f0de8a/include/cutlass/gemm/collective/sm120_mma_array_tma.hpp#L516), [sm120_blockscaled_mma_array_tma.hpp L934](https://github.com/NVIDIA/cutlass/blob/0b55a2f691d69981583568fd9eb69687b1f0de8a/include/cutlass/gemm/collective/sm120_blockscaled_mma_array_tma.hpp#L934)).
3. The collectives' `can_implement()` checks only TMA alignment ([sm120_mma_tma.hpp L278](https://github.com/NVIDIA/cutlass/blob/0b55a2f691d69981583568fd9eb69687b1f0de8a/include/cutlass/gemm/collective/sm120_mma_tma.hpp#L278), [sm120_blockscaled_mma_tma.hpp L399](https://github.com/NVIDIA/cutlass/blob/0b55a2f691d69981583568fd9eb69687b1f0de8a/include/cutlass/gemm/collective/sm120_blockscaled_mma_tma.hpp#L399)). When the descriptor encode fails, [copy_traits_sm90_tma.hpp L1066-L1080](https://github.com/NVIDIA/cutlass/blob/0b55a2f691d69981583568fd9eb69687b1f0de8a/include/cute/atom/copy_traits_sm90_tma.hpp#L1066-L1080) prints the error and calls `assert(false)`, which `NDEBUG` compiles out, so `initialize()` still reports success.

Other architectures, read, not run (we have no sm90 or sm100 GPU):

- Hopper's ptr-array mainloop guards the first wait with `if (k_tile_count > 0)` ([sm90_mma_array_tma_gmma_ss_warpspecialized.hpp L533](https://github.com/NVIDIA/cutlass/blob/0b55a2f691d69981583568fd9eb69687b1f0de8a/include/cutlass/gemm/collective/sm90_mma_array_tma_gmma_ss_warpspecialized.hpp#L533)). Hopper's non-grouped mainloop has only a debug `assert(k_tile_count >= 1)` before an unconditional `consumer_wait` ([sm90_mma_tma_gmma_ss_warpspecialized.hpp L481-L487](https://github.com/NVIDIA/cutlass/blob/0b55a2f691d69981583568fd9eb69687b1f0de8a/include/cutlass/gemm/collective/sm90_mma_tma_gmma_ss_warpspecialized.hpp#L481-L487)).
- The sm100 mainloops skip the first wait when `k_tile_count <= 0` ([sm100_mma_warpspecialized.hpp L670](https://github.com/NVIDIA/cutlass/blob/0b55a2f691d69981583568fd9eb69687b1f0de8a/include/cutlass/gemm/collective/sm100_mma_warpspecialized.hpp#L670), [sm100_blockscaled_mma_warpspecialized.hpp L991](https://github.com/NVIDIA/cutlass/blob/0b55a2f691d69981583568fd9eb69687b1f0de8a/include/cutlass/gemm/collective/sm100_blockscaled_mma_warpspecialized.hpp#L991)).

**What a one-line guard did.** We added `if (k_tile_count <= 0) { return; }` right after `clear(accum)` in `mma()` and rebuilt on the RTX 5090:

items.title: Expert Parallelism (EP) roadmap for SM12x b12x MoE kernel (b12x_fused_moe / B12xMoEWrapper)
items.author: ItamarTerem
items.body_excerpt:
Hi flashinfer team,
We're deploying a large MoE model (384 experts, top_k=8) on 8x RTX PRO 6000 (SM120/Blackwell workstation) using the b12x_fused_moe CuteDSL kernel via TensorRT-LLM's pytorch backend, and have hit the Expert Parallelism restriction:

b12x_fused_moe does not yet support Expert Parallelism
(num_local_experts={X} != num_experts={Y}).
Use a different MoE backend for EP configurations.

This comes from the explicit guard in flashinfer/fused_moe/cute_dsl/b12x_moe.py (both in the free function b12x_fused_moe and in B12xMoEWrapper.__init__), confirmed in flashinfer version 0.6.12.
Context on why this matters for us specifically: without EP, every GPU must retain workspace/routing capacity sized for the full state_E (all 384 experts), even though tensor parallelism already shards each expert's weights across GPUs. This is a meaningful, measured memory cost — in our case, the dynamic workspace's packed_input buffer alone accounts for roughly 7–11GB/GPU across a 60-MoE-layer model, purely from having to size for the worst-case "all experts active" scenario rather than a num_experts/ep_size subset.

What we're asking:

1. Is EP support for the SM12x b12x kernel family (static/dynamic/micro backends) on the roadmap, even at a preliminary stage?
2. Is there a rough timeline or tracking issue we could follow?
3. Are there known architectural blockers specific to SM120 (vs. SM100/SM103, where other kernels like MegaMoE already support EP) that make this a harder problem here?

We also note that vLLM's FlashInferB12xExperts (_supports_parallel_config) explicitly declines to use this backend when EP is requested, for the same underlying reason — so this appears to be a shared, cross-framework limitation rather than something specific to our integration.
Happy to provide more detail on our exact shapes/config if useful. Thanks for your work on this — the b12x kernel has otherwise been the only correctness-verified MoE path we've found for SM120 (CUTLASS produces silently incorrect output on this architecture in our testing).

Update `doc/source/ray-security/token-auth.md`, `doc/source/core/internals/token-authentication.md` and the VM, Kubernetes and on-prem deployment guides: token auth is on by default for every cluster from 2.61, how nodes and clients get the token, and the `RAY_AUTH_MODE=disabled` opt-out (which every node and client of an opted-out cluster must set).

In the VM deployment guide, note that existing `ray up` clusters update their worker nodes once after upgrading to a Ray version with the auth token file mount (#67050): each worker reruns its setup commands and restarts Ray, and in Docker mode its container restarts. Instances aren't relaunched.

Also document metrics scraping in `doc/source/cluster/metrics.md`: how an external Prometheus sends the token (`authorization` with `credentials_file`), and that `ray metrics launch-prometheus` needs the token in a file.

Also say in the docs and the release notes that an auth rejection now raises `AuthenticationError` at once, where `ray.init(address=...)` used to raise `ConnectionError` after retrying. `AuthenticationError` subclasses `ConnectionError`, so existing handlers still catch it.

Must land in the same release as #67055.

items.title: [RFC]: xDiT Video Generation API
items.author: happyandslow
items.body_excerpt: ### Summary The goal of this API is to expose a scalable, distributed video generation service for xDiT using models such as CogVideoX, ConsisID, and Latte. The API allows clients to submit text prompts with optional generation parameters and receive video outputs either as a file path or base64-encoded data. ### Motivation The API is designed to enhance AIBrix's ability to generate image and video, based on an example engine [xDiT](https://github.com/xdit-project/xDiT/tree/main) : - Support both disk-based and memory-based outputs. - Scale across multiple GPUs via Ray remote workers. - Provide a simple OpenAI-style endpoint for common video generation. - Allow future extensibility for multi-stage pipelines or DAG-based workflows. ### Proposed Change `POST /generatevideo` Description: Generates a video from a text prompt. Content-Type: application/json Authentication: TBD (future optional API key support) **Request Model** ``` { "prompt": "A fox running through a forest", "num_inference_steps": 50, "num_frames": 17, "seed": 42, "cfg": 7.5, "save_disk_path": "output/", "height": 1024, "width": 1024, "fps": 8 } ``` `curl` request example with disk output ``` curl -X POST http://127.0.0.1:6000/generatevideo \ -H "Content-Type: application/json" \ -d '{ "prompt": "A fox running through a forest", "num_frames": 17, "fps": 12, "save_disk_path": "output/" }' ``` `curl` request with base64 output ``` curl -X POST http://127.0.0.1:6000/generatevideo \ -H "Content-Type: application/json" \ -d '{ "prompt": "A fox running through a forest", "num_frames": 17, "fps": 12, "save_disk_path": "output/" }' ``` Field | Type | Default | Description -- | -- | -- | -- prompt | string | N/A | Text prompt describing the video content. Required. num_inference_steps | int | 50 | Number of denoising steps in the diffusion process. num_frames | int | 17 | Number of frames in the video. seed | int | 42 | RNG seed for reproducibility. cfg | float | 7.5 | Guidance scale for the diffusion model. save_disk_path | string | None | If provided, video will be saved to path; otherwise, returned as base64. height | int | 1024 | Video frame height in pixels. width | int | 1024 | Video frame width in pixels. fps | int | 8 | Frames per second of output video. **Response** - Synchronous Response 1. Response with path provided ``` { "message": "Video generated successfully", "elapsed_time": "12.34 sec", "output": "output/generated_video_20250922-141500.mp4", "save_to_disk": true } ``` 2. Response without path provided ``` { "message": "Video generated successfully", "elapsed_time": "12.34 sec", "output": "", "save_to_disk": false, "format": "mp4" } ``` - Asynchronous Response - TBD **Error Handling** HTTP Status | Condition | Response -- | -- | -- 400 | Missing or invalid prompt/parameters | {"detail": "Prompt cannot be empty"} 500 | Model execution error | {"detail": "Error generating video: "} ### Alternatives Considered ComfyUI style workflow request like: ``` POST /prompt Content-Type: application/json { "1": { "class_type": "TextPrompt", "inputs": { "text": "A fox running through a forest" } }, "2": { "class_type": "CogWidowXVideo", "inputs": { "prompt": ["1", 0], "duration": 5, "fps": 12, "width": 720, "height": 480, "seed": 123 } } } ``` This forces ComfyUI to be deployed along with AIBrix. **Deploying along with ComfyUI** ComfyUI could be used as a frontend client that connects to third-party/service API, see [link1](https://github.com/comfyanonymous/ComfyUI/tree/707b2638ecd82360c0a67e1d86cc4fdeae218d03/comfy_api_nodes) and [link2](https://docs.comfy.org/tutorials/api-nodes/overview). Currently, ComfyUI runs/manages model to run in a single instance and model management could be found [here](https://github.com/comfyanonymous/ComfyUI/blob/master/comfy/model_management.py). To make it support distributed environment, we either need to update ComfyUI so it supports distributed serving (through library like xfuser) or we let ComfyUI to call backend services through API (API node, see below) and the backend services could deploying large model distributedly, and/or have multiple replicas serving requests. I found one project that attempted to do distributed ComfyUI [here](https://github.com/robertvoy/ComfyUI-Distributed). items.title: [Performance]: Kimi K3 decode runs the MoE-tail additions as separate kernels before the next attention-residual
items.author: lucifer1004
items.body_excerpt:
### Proposal to improve performance

In Kimi K3 decode, every MoE layer ends with `prefix_sum + (routed_out + shared_out)` (`KimiK3MoERuntime.forward` returns `routed_out + shared_out`, then `KimiLinearDecoderLayer.forward` adds it to the prefix sum). These are two small elementwise kernels per MoE layer. Their result is read first by the next layer's pre-attention attention-residual + RMSNorm, or by the model's output attention-residual + norm. In the decode window, that consumer is already `trtllm::attn_res_add_rmsnorm_fwd`'s kernel family, which loads the prefix sum as its last candidate and can already fold one addend into it.

Proposal: give `trtllm::attn_res_add_rmsnorm_fwd` an optional second addend (`layer_residual_add2`) that computes `bf16(prefix + bf16(routed + shared))`, rounding exactly like the two BF16 tensor additions. Then add an opt-in path in which a MoE layer hands `(prefix, routed, shared)` to that consumer instead of adding them itself. Wherever the consumer would not take the fused per-token kernel (a hidden-state capture layer for speculative decoding, no snapshots yet, the persistent kernel, shapes outside the fused window), the addition is done first and the existing code runs unchanged.

Measured on Rubin, TP8 across 2 nodes (MNNVL), Kimi K3 with speculative decoding, CUDA graphs, single request, decode step time, same change on our integration branch: -0.106 / -0.117 / -0.121 / -0.126 / -0.107 / -0.107 ms at 2K / 32K / 64K / 96K / 128K / 393K context. Accuracy and needle checks unchanged; the materialized prefix sums are bitwise identical.

PR to follow (draft, opt-in via an environment variable).

items.title: [cake deslop] cake_minimax_h3 round 2: merge sm100a/sm103a copies (−13.4K), share SM120 FC1 FP8 GEMMs (−5.6K), fix AdaLN-row clamp
items.author: yyihuang
items.body_excerpt:
**Background.** This family covers the MiniMax-H3 diffusion operators behind `flashinfer.diffusion_ops`. It has five parts. First, six Cake-generated SM120 TUs (`csrc/cake_minimax_h3_sm120_*_sm120a.cu`, 55,601 lines) for FP8/NVFP4 varlen attention, quantized pre-attention, FC1+SwiGLU, MLP and out-proj. Second, two shared headers (857 lines). Third, the SM100/SM103 FC1+SwiGLU / MLP / out-proj operators, shipped as `_sm100a.cu`/`_sm103a.cu` file pairs (26,884 lines). Fourth, the SM103-only `flashinfer/experimental/nvfp4_attention` program behind `prefill.prepare_nvfp4_attention(backend="cake")` (2,698 lines). Fifth, the hand-written (not Cake) `csrc/nvfp4_attention_sm120` behind `flashinfer.nvfp4_attention_sm120_{quantize_qkv,fwd}` (952 lines, #3640). At 3184bbea the family has 63 files and 104,888 lines, including 10,392 lines of Python and 7,873 of tests. Every source compiles: 12 JIT-only modules, the experimental program and the AOT `nvfp4_attention_sm120` module. The first round was #5792 and #5781. #5905 closed #5792: it added the shared `cake_minimax_h3_sm120_host.cuh` and `cake_minimax_h3_sm120_norm_adaln_quant.cuh` and bounded the FP8 varlen caches. #5866 closed #5781: it regenerated the experimental SM103 program and made it accept strided inputs. Since then, #5660, #6060, #6068, #6169 (+22,050), #6176 (+15,455), #6196, #6314, #6474 and #6475 have added material. #6169 copied the FC1 FP8 GEMMs and the norm/quant kernels into the new MLP TU instead of sharing them. No sub-issue has covered the SM100/SM103 pairs (#5491, #5525, #6176). Out of scope: `include/flashinfer/attention/sm120/nvfp4_attention_sm120/` (5,829 lines) and the other MiniMax-H3 csrc that `diffusion_ops` dispatches to (mxfp8/nvfp4 pre-attention and QKV pack, see #5790/#5791; `cake_minimax_h3_dense_attention_sm120a.cu`).

**Findings**
- **SM100/SM103 copies.** `csrc/cake_minimax_h3_{mlp,fc1_swiglu,out_proj}_sm103a.cu` (6,796 + 3,586 + 3,060 = 13,442 lines) differ from their `_sm100a` twins in only 6/8/8 lines: the header comment and `TVM_FFI_CHECK(... properties.minor == 0` vs `== 3)` (mlp 6518, fc1 3404, out_proj 2878). The device code is byte-identical and already branches on `__CUDA_ARCH__`. The only consumers of the `_sm103a.cu` names are the `_TARGETS` dicts (lines 28-30) in `flashinfer/jit/minimax_h3_{mlp,fc1_swiglu,out_proj}.py`. The module names `minimax_h3_<op>_{target}_v1` already keep the JIT cache entries apart.
- **FC1 FP8 GEMMs copied into the MLP.** In `csrc/cake_minimax_h3_sm120_quant_mlp_sm120a.cu` (18,368 lines), `h3_mlp_fc1_fp8_sm120a` (599-3380) and `h3_mlp_fc1_fp8_mx_sm120a` (3397-6192) are 0.999 similar to `h3_fc1_swiglu_gemm_fp8_{legacy,mx}_sm120a` in the FC1 TU (5,578 lines). The only differences are the namespace and the INF macro. The mx copy also has a different kernel symbol with three extra parameters (`act_q_w`, `act_sf_w`, `y_global_scale`), which the MLP host documents as unused (18254-18258).
- **AdaLN table hard-coded to 9 rows.** `csrc/cake_minimax_h3_sm120_norm_adaln_quant.cuh` takes no row count. It checks `idx < 9` (157, 469), indexes the table with a 5376 stride, and zeroes the activation for an invalid index. The pre-attention host (7247-7251) and the FC1 host (7385-7389) accept any `adaln_scale.size(0) >= 1`. Only the FC1 wrapper pins `MINIMAX_H3_ADALN_ROWS = 9`; the pre-attention wrapper reads the row count from the shape (130). From the code, with fewer than 9 rows, an index in [rows, 9) reads past the table; with more than 9 rows, indices ≥ 9 silently get a zeroed activation. Not reproduced on GPU; the tests use 9 rows only. The MLP's private copy of this prologue (45-589, 0.795 similar) already takes `adaln_rows` and `adaln_row_stride`. FC1 and pre-attention still require dense tables.
- **FP8 legacy/mx instruction-form clones.** The `mma.sync ... e4m3` and `kind::mxf8f6f4` unit-scale forms are near-identical: FC1 0.951, MLP FC1 0.950, MLP FC2 0.896 (270 and 520 differing lines). FC1 picks a form per board with `strstr(properties.name, "GeForce")` (7353-7354); the MLP uses `ResolveFp8Form` / `fp8_mma_form` (18059-18064). The outputs are documented and tested as bit-identical, but the FC1 header (line 35) says the plain form keeps a lower register budget on RTX PRO 6000. Added in #6475 and #6169/#6196.

items.title: [cake deslop] cake_bgmv_moe: delete 30 never-launched kernels (36.5K lines), finish the #5787 hidden-size merge, gate per-arch forms
items.author: yyihuang
items.body_excerpt:
**Background.** `csrc/cake_bgmv_moe` contains the Cake-generated BGMV LoRA-MoE shrink and expand kernels. They sit behind `flashinfer.fused_moe.prepare_bgmv_moe(..., backend="cake")` on sm90a, sm100a, sm103a and sm107a. Unsupported capability, rank, hidden size or slice shapes fall back to the portable `BGMVMoEPortablePlan` (`csrc/bgmv_moe`, #5809), which this issue does not cover. The first round was #5787 ("one templated body instead of per-hidden-size clones", ~5.7K → ~1.7K lines). #5989 (+166/−320) closed it: that PR added the one-time `CheckCompiledArch` in `Configure` and the `y_accum` output stride. It changed each body by only +2/−19 lines and left the bodies untemplated. More code was added after that:
- #5850 (+15,266) added the 8 generic bodies (~1.5K lines each) and the route index.
- #6016 (+130,592/−4,478: pair-grouped pipeline, programmatic dependent launch, per-arch selectors) added 15–19 kernels to each generic body. Each body is now 11.7K–19.8K lines.
- #6238 added the sm107a target.

At 3184bbea the family's paths hold 22 files / 150,208 lines. `csrc/cake_bgmv_moe` accounts for 14 files / 144,815 lines: 4 specialized bodies `cake_bgmv_moe_{bf16,f16}_h{2688,3072}.cu` (1,759/1,759/1,825/1,825), 8 generic bodies `cake_bgmv_moe_generic_{bf16,f16}_r{8,16,32,64}.cu` and 2 binding headers (317 + 791). All 12 bodies are compiled once per arch, for 48 JIT/AOT modules. Grep doesn't find them by name because the loader (`flashinfer/jit/cake_bgmv_moe.py`, "loader" below) builds the names with f-strings at L467/L599.

**Findings**
- **30 never-launched kernels (36,466 lines).** Every module compiles them, but no path from `prepare_bgmv_moe` launches them:
  - **bf16 direct grouped shrink `shrink_grouped_bf16_r{8,16,32,64}`** (4 kernels, 11,346 lines). The loader sets `RING_SINGLE_TILE=1` on sm90a and `MIXED=1` for bf16 on Blackwell/Rubin (L828-837). That makes `GroupShrinkRing` true in every bf16 module (generic binding L150-153, L594-600).
  - **`shrink_grouped_single_*`, rank 16/32/64, both dtypes** (6 kernels, 17,316 lines). This form needs `!ring` and 1 rank tile per CTA. `GroupShrinkRankTilesPerCta` never yields 1 for rank >= 16 (2/4/8, L132-138). The f16 r8 direct kernel is launched through the r8 alias (loader L648-652) and stays.
  - **Generic decode shrink `*_p4_s3` / `*_p4_s3_pdl`** (16 kernels, 6,484 lines). `select_cake_bgmv_moe_generic_shrink` returns only form 2 or form 0 (L357-361). Its docstring says form 1 is never selected.
  - **Specialized `expand_token_t64`** (4 kernels, 1,320 lines). `select_cake_bgmv_moe_schedule` picks this kernel only when `num_tokens in (1, 4, 8)` (L733-734). The specialized variant requires 32–1024 tokens (`CAKE_BGMV_MOE_SPECIALIZED_TOKEN_WINDOW`, L504-512), so the two conditions never overlap.
  - **4 sm90a specialized AOT modules.** `flashinfer/aot.py` L849-861 prebuilds them, but the sm90a window is `None` (loader L507), so they are never selected.
- **Hidden-size clones (#5787 unfinished).** Each h2688/h3072 pair differs in 33 line pairs, and in 0 once the literal 2688/3072 is neutralised (bf16 and f16). The generated binding already `#define`s `CAKE_BGMV_MOE_HIDDEN` (loader L795). bf16 and f16 h2688 differ in 179 lines, all inline-asm conversion. The exact-token expand selector and the `BGMVMoEBlackwellPlan` alias (`bgmv_moe.py` L566), both flagged by #5787, are still in place.
- **Rank clones.** Once the `_r{N}` token is normalised, generic r16/r32/r64 differ in 219–305 of 19,756 lines (bf16) and 207–293 of 17,630 lines (f16). `kRank` is already a binding constexpr (generic binding L43). r8 differs by ~8.7K lines because it has no `*_single` forms. bf16 and f16 r16 differ by 3,894–4,432 lines because the mixed-precision forms exist only in bf16.
- **Expanded arch guards.** 3,808 `#if defined(__CUDA_ARCH__) && (__CUDA_ARCH__ >= 1000)` blocks take up 67,872 lines, 45% of the family. 3,584 of them are a 17-line pair FMA (`fma.rn.f32x2` / two `__fmaf_rn`). The other 224 are a 31-line 8-wide `fma.rn.f32.bf16` dot. About 21.8K of these lines sit in kernels that step 1 deletes, leaving 2,528 blocks / 46,112 lines after it.
- **Per-target dead forms.** All four targets share one body, so 32–70% of each generic module's compiled kernel lines can never launch on that module's target:

  | Module | Never-launched lines |
  | --- | --- |
  | Blackwell bf16 r16 | 13,926 of 19,757 (70%) |
  | sm90a bf16 r16/32/64 | 9,210 (47%) |
  | Blackwell f16 r16/32/64 | 5,676 of 17,631 (32%) |

  `cake_bgmv_moe_pdl_mode` never returns 0 on sm100a/sm103a/sm107a (L554-555). Mixed forms launch only on bf16 Blackwell/Rubin, and non-mixed ring forms launch only on sm90a. The generated `.cu` already `#define`s `CAKE_BGMV_MOE_CC_MAJOR/_MINOR` before it includes the body (loader L847-848), so `#if` gating needs no new plumbing. The remap/`order_build` kernels (~975 lines per body) are auto-selected only on sm90a (L272-274). The public `order_remap=True` kwarg can still force them on any arch (`bgmv_moe.py` L929-930), and `tests/moe/test_cake_bgmv_moe.py` L720/L778 do this.
- **Exact-shape routes.**
  - **Specialized tier.** It serves only hidden ∈ {2688, 3072} × rank 32 × 32–1024 tokens on sm100a/sm103a/sm107a. The loader records 1.08–1.5× wins on expert-sorted routes and 7–21% losses on contiguous top-k=2 routes (L494-503). Its sm107a rows "inherit the Blackwell window pending R200 measurement" (L510, L527).
  - **`token_owned_dual_col`** (4 kernels, 1,740 lines). It runs only for exactly (3072, 512|1024) or (2688, 1024). The selector docstring puts the three schedules within 1.2% of each other on B200 and 3.5% on H100. The `bench_cake_bgmv_moe.py` SHAPES (L36-40) are exactly the selector's token points.
  - **Specialized decode shrink `*_r32_p4_s3`** (1,316 lines). It runs only with <= 32 pairs at >= 32 tokens. No test passes `top_k=1`.
  - **sm90a plain `expand_generic_token_t64`** (8 kernels, 2,649 lines). It runs only at <= 8 tokens with hidden > 25,344 on a 13

items.title: [cake deslop] blackwell_msa/msa_nvfp4_decode (2): fold uniform-FP8 arch pair, drop xform2 exact-shape routes, template clones (~88K lines)
items.author: yyihuang

**Background.** The Cake-generated Blackwell MSA family serves `flashinfer.msa_ops.msa_sparse_attention`, `msa_sparse_decode_attention` and `msa_topk_select` on SM100/SM103 through `flashinfer/msa_ops/_blackwell_sm100.py`. Its 31 dense programs live in `csrc/blackwell_msa`, are registered in `flashinfer/jit/blackwell_msa.py` and are built by AOT. The family also includes the JIT-only NVFP4 sparse-decode backend behind `prepare_msa_nvfp4_sparse_decode` (`flashinfer/experimental/msa_nvfp4_decode`, also exported from `flashinfer.msa_ops`), with 14 programs and 32 (program, arch) specs including sm_107a. At 3184bbea the listed paths hold 157 files / 166,303 lines: `csrc/blackwell_msa` 70,845, `msa_nvfp4_decode` 64,147, Cake Python in `msa_ops` ~8,040, and the 1,866-line loader. The rest is tests, JSON manifests and ~10.3K lines of non-Cake SM12x CuTe-DSL code (`msa_ops/cute_dsl/`, `proxy_score.py`). Round one had two parts. #5778, closed by #5893, merged SM100/SM103 under `__CUDA_ARCH__`, removed the env-var switches and replaced the hash-lock tests, but kept the xform2 exact-shape routes and the `direct_group` alias. #5779, closed by #5875, left one source per NVFP4 program and removed the workspace, but kept the ABI carriers and the 212-SM literal. Several PRs added material back afterwards: #6315 regenerated the family (+11,082/−23,189), #6387 added 8 opt-in `use_cache_hit` union programs (+50,499/−10,185, the largest re-growth), #6397 split `decode_uniform_fp8` back into per-arch programs, and #6410 added `topk_select_keq`/`topk_select_q32` (+10,879/−2,362). #6443, #6459 and #6463 changed FP8 decode, streaming top-k and prefill. All 31 dense programs are routed and all 14 NVFP4 programs are registered, so there are no never-compiled sources.

**Findings**
- **Per-arch copy re-created by #6397.** `decode_uniform_fp8` is the only remaining pair: `cake_blackwell_msa_a126296d8aaae82459b7` (sm_100a) and `cake_blackwell_msa_2a38253c76cec86dc2cd` (sm_103a). They differ only in `NUM_DECODE_KV_STAGES` (4 vs 8) and its derived SMEM-offset/mbarrier/stage-wrap constants (82 normalized lines). `SMEM_TOTAL` (183296), the block [512,1,1], the flags and the 26-entry arg_plan are identical, and the bindings differ only in the host-shim namespace hash. #6443 regenerated the pair. Both kernels also define `SMEM_SMEM_NVFP4_*` constants and `smem_nvfp4_*` pointers that nothing uses. The other 29 programs are single-source with `__CUDA_ARCH__` guards.
- **Exact-coordinate routes kept by #5893.** `decode_fp8_q1:{q1_paged_xform2,q1_flat_xform2}` (`0d391c271a9e1dd7de1b`, `2949bc72ee78a52859c9`; 3,390 lines including their registry, dispatcher and test code; present since #4355). `_fp8_q1_schedule` (`_blackwell_sm100.py` l.964-1001) selects them only if all of these hold: `force_fused=True` (the public default is `None`), not under graph capture, causal, bf16 Q / FP8 K, `seqlen_q == 1`, heads 64/4, and exactly paged batch 128 / 4,096 K rows / 32 pages or flat batch 32 / 262,144 K rows. None of the 27 GPU test cases reaches them. Only two bench rows do: `decode_fp8_b128_q1_kv4096_h64` and `coverage_decode_mixed_fp8_b32_q1_kv8192_h64_hkv4_k16_flat`. `decode_m16:bfloat16:float8_e4m3fn:{paged,flat}` serves the same inputs. The module docstring (l.24-25) still says "no shape-exact routes".
- **Dead code and stale docs.**
  - The sm100a routes `long_bf16_reverse:paged:gqa16:direct_group:*` (`blackwell_msa.py` l.1723-1724, predicate `max_pages == 8192`) point at the same programs as the plain route. They change only the launch-signature string.

  - `_PERSISTENT_ABI_CARRIERS`/`_SHORT_ABI_CARRIERS` and the `carriers` branch of `_bind` (`cake_backend.py` l.102-114, l.417-440) match no `ARG_PLANS` name.
  - `_LONG_WORK_TAIL_SPLIT` and `_LONG_WORK_ORDER_Q_RESIDENT` are always `True`, which leaves a dead `else: work.sort(...)` (l.1658-1659).
  - `docs/api/sparse.rst` l.106-119 and `CLAUDE.md` l.785-786 still document `FLASHINFER_MSA_PREFILL_SCHEDULE`/`FLASHINFER_MSA_FP8_Q1_SCHEDULE`. #5893 removed both; the unit has no `os.environ`/`getenv` calls.

items.title: [Performance]: copyBatchBlockOffsetsToDeviceKernel walks each long block-offset row with one CTA
items.author: lucifer1004
items.body_excerpt:
### Proposal to improve performance

`KVCacheManagerV2.copy_batch_block_offsets` launches `copyBatchBlockOffsetsToDeviceKernel` (`cpp/tensorrt_llm/batch_manager/kvCacheManagerV2Utils.cu`) once per manager per step. Its grid is `(num_pools, num_seqs)`: a single 128-thread CTA walks each whole row of block offsets, two `cp.async` loads deep, reading the pinned host table. For long-context pools the rows are long; at 32772 blocks per sequence, each CTA runs 64 sequential load iterations. The kernel is then latency bound, with a handful of CTAs on the whole GPU.

Measured on Rubin, Kimi K3 decode (target manager with 2 pools, draft manager with 1, 32772 blocks per sequence, 1 sequence): 28-33 µs per call, about 60 µs per decode step on the critical path between steps.

Proposal: add a third grid dimension that splits each row into tiles of 1024 offsets, one CTA each, keeping the per-element arithmetic and the read-at-execution-time semantics unchanged. A Triton prototype of exactly this tiling (same reads, same integer arithmetic, bitwise-equal output) took the call from 27.7 µs to 4.0 µs (2 pools) and from 27.0 µs to 3.6 µs (1 pool) in a microbenchmark. End to end on Rubin, TP8 across 2 nodes (MNNVL), single request, it reduced decode step time by 0.014-0.043 ms depending on context length, and 128K TTFT by 0.043 s.

PR to follow (draft; the C++ version still needs a GPU build and microbenchmark).

items.title: [Bug] sm12x MoE CuTe-DSL kernels are never disk-cached — cute.compile hardcodes no_cache=True, so every fresh engine re-pays 15–40 s MLIR compiles per kernel shape
items.author: jhsmith409
items.body_excerpt:
## Summary

The Blackwell sm12x fused-MoE path compiles all of its CuTe-DSL kernels through explicit
`cute.compile(...)`, which unconditionally disables the DSL's file cache. The only caching
layer is three in-process Python dicts, so **every engine start re-pays the full MLIR JIT
cost for every kernel specialization it touches** — measured at **~40 s** for the dynamic
kernel's first hit and **~15–18 s per small-`m` micro-kernel specialization**. In a serving
context (vLLM `--moe-backend=flashinfer_b12x`) these compiles land mid-request and freeze
the whole engine (vllm#47458: ~17.5 s stop-the-world stalls, all in-flight requests frozen
including mid-decode).

`CUTE_DSL_CACHE_DIR` / `CUTE_DSL_DISABLE_FILE_CACHING` have no effect on this path — the
gate that would consult them is short-circuited before they are read.

## Environment

- flashinfer 0.6.12, 0.6.13, and **0.6.15.post1** (all verified; `moe_dispatch.py` cache
  structure unchanged across them)
- nvidia-cutlass-dsl 4.5.0 and **4.6.0** (both verified)
- SM120: RTX 5070 Ti (×2, TP/PP), RTX 5090 (unsharded), RTX PRO 6000 Blackwell — reproduced
  on all three in the vllm#47458 thread
- Model: `nvidia/Qwen3.6-35B-A3B-NVFP4` via vLLM `--moe-backend=flashinfer_b12x`

## Mechanism (exact code paths)

1. **The DSL hardcodes `no_cache=True` for explicit compiles.**
   `CompileCallable._compile` sets `kwargs["no_cache"] = True` unconditionally:
   - nvidia-cutlass-dsl 4.5.0: `base_dsl/compiler.py:604-605`
   - nvidia-cutlass-dsl 4.6.0: `base_dsl/compiler.py:1319`

2. **The file cache is gated behind `if not no_cache`** — both the load and the dump —
   so the env vars are never even consulted for explicit compiles:
   - 4.5.0: `base_dsl/dsl.py:1645` (load), `:1736` (dump)
   - 4.6.0: `base_dsl/dsl.py:2004` (load), `:2105` (dump); in-memory `jit_cache` lookups
     likewise skipped under `no_cache` at `:2012`, `:2293`

3. **The sm12x MoE dispatch only ever compiles through `cute.compile`,** with plain
   in-process dicts on top — nothing reaches disk:
   - 0.6.12/0.6.13: `blackwell_sm12x/moe_dispatch.py:676/912/1675` (compile sites);
     `_STATIC/_MICRO/_DYNAMIC_KERNEL_CACHE`
   - 0.6.15.post1: compile sites at `:697/:942/:1723`; caches at `:486/:733/:1524`

4. Compounding factor (tracked separately as #3836): the micro-kernel `cache_key`
   includes both `m` and `workspace.max_rows` (0.6.15.post1 `moe_dispatch.py:770-791`,
   fields at `:774`/`:778`), so workspace growth invalidates already-compiled small-batch
   entries even *within* a process lifetime. With no disk layer underneath, each
   invalidation is a full 15 s+ recompile, not a reload.

## Verification

Behavioral check from the vllm#47458 thread (credit @waynehacking8, on 0.6.12 / DSL 4.5.0):

- `cute.compile` of a trivial `@cute.jit` function leaves `CUTE_DSL_CACHE_DIR` **empty**.
- Calling the same jit function **directly** (implicit compile path) writes
  `cute_dsl_<hash>.mlir`, and a fresh process then logs `JIT cache hit IN-FILE`.
- Only the implicit direct-call path caches; flashinfer's MoE dispatch never uses it.

Source-level re-verification on 0.6.15.post1 / DSL 4.6.0 (2026-08-02, inside the
`vllm/vllm-openai` nightly image): every line cite in the Mechanism section above was
confirmed against the installed packages — the hardcoded `no_cache=True`, the
`if not no_cache` gates around both file-cache load and dump, the three `cute.compile`
sites, the three in-process dicts, and `m`/`max_rows` still present in the micro-kernel
cache key.

Measured first-hit compile costs (RTX PRO 6000, synthetic MoE E=32/topk=4 driving
`B12xMoEWrapper.run` exactly as vLLM's `FlashInferB12xExperts` does):

| kernel path | first hit | subsequent (same key) |
|---|---|---|
| dynamic (m-independent key) | ~40 s | 1–3 ms |
| micro m=1 | 14.9 s | ms |
| micro m=2 | 15.2 s | ms |
| micro m=64 | 18.3 s | ms |

Production symptom: vllm#47458 — py-spy captured 16 consecutive samples over 8.35 s pinned
in `b12x_fused_moe (flashinfer/fused_moe/cute_dsl/b12x_moe.py:166)` during a live
~17.5 s engine-wide stall; `perf` showed `_cutlass_ir.cpython-312.so` frames present only
during stalls.

## Why this deserves a disk layer even after #3836

#3836 stops *rekeying* (recompiles within one process). But serving engines restart —
deploys, config changes, crash recovery, autoscaling — and each fresh process re-pays the
entire compile set: ~40 s dynamic + 15–18 s per small-shape class. For a model like
Qwen3.6-35B-A3B this is 1–2 minutes of mid-serving stalls per engine lifetime that a
disk cache would reduce to milliseconds. The artifacts are deterministic products of
(kernel source, shape/config tuple, DSL version, arch) — exactly what file caches are for.

## Suggested fix directions

Either would resolve it; the first is contained entirely in flashinfer:

1. **flashinfer grows its own disk layer for sm12x MoE kernels**: serialize the compiled
   artifact keyed by the existing `cache_key` tuples + flashinfer version +
   nvidia-cutlass-dsl version + SM arch, under `FLASHINFER_WORKSPACE_DIR` (or a new env),
   loading into `_STATIC/_MICRO/_DYNAMIC_KERNEL_CACHE` on miss. The DSL's own
   `compile_and_cache` machinery demonstrates the artifact is serializable (the implicit
   path already writes/reads `.mlir` + compiled objects).
2. **Upstream: nvidia-cutlass-dsl honors its file cache under explicit `cute.compile`**
   (stop hardcoding `no_cache=True`, or add an opt-in kwarg flashinfer can pass).

A third, cheaper-but-partial option is an official warm-up API (the attempt in
vllm#47599 was closed unmerged): it moves the cost to boot but still re-pays it every
process start, and needs the largest-workspace-first ordering to avoid #3836 rekeying —
a disk cache composes with, rather than replaces, that.

## Cross-references

- vllm#47458 — serving-stall report this splits from (mechanism established in-thread by
  @waynehacking8; py-spy confirmation by me)

items.title: [CUDA] F.conv3d silently falls back to slow_conv_dilated3d for batched degenerate shapes (output 1×1×1) — ~5 orders of magnitude slower than the equivalent matmul
items.author: daojiancha
items.body_excerpt:
### 🐛 Describe the bug

### 🐛 Describe the bug

`F.conv3d` / `nn.Conv3d` on CUDA with a "batched degenerate" shape — kernel equals the
input's spatial dims and stride equals the kernel, so every output spatial dim is 1 —
does not go through cuDNN. The native stack shows it dispatches to
`at::native::slow_conv_dilated3d_cuda`, which is catastrophically slow for large batch:
~58 s for a single call that is mathematically a `(8192×1536) @ (1536×1152)` matmul
(~0.0002 s). **No warning is emitted**, so from user code it just looks like "the model
is slow".

This occurs in practice: `Qwen3VLPatchEmbed` (transformers 5.x, the text encoder of
Qwen-Image-2.x diffusion pipelines) applies exactly this conv to every image with
`N = num_patches` as the batch dim (4096 patches for a 1024×1024 image), making the
text-encoder forward take 25–60 s per image.

### Minimal code example to reproduce the bug

```python
import time, torch

N, C_in, T, P, C_out = 8192, 3, 2, 16, 1152
x = torch.randn(N, C_in, T, P, P, device="cuda", dtype=torch.bfloat16)
conv = torch.nn.Conv3d(C_in, C_out, (T, P, P), stride=(T, P, P)).to("cuda").to(torch.bfloat16)

torch.cuda.synchronize(); t0 = time.time()
out = conv(x)                                  # (N, C_out, 1, 1, 1)
torch.cuda.synchronize()
print(f"conv3d: {time.time()-t0:.2f}s")         # ~58 s

w, b = conv.weight, conv.bias
def mm():
    o = x.reshape(N, -1) @ w.reshape(C_out, -1).t()
    return (o + b).view(N, C_out, 1, 1, 1)

mm(); torch.cuda.synchronize(); t0 = time.time()
for _ in range(10): out_b = mm()
torch.cuda.synchronize()
print(f"matmul: {(time.time()-t0)/10:.6f}s")   # ~0.0002 s
print("max|diff|:", (out.float()-out_b.float()).abs().max().item())  # 0.0
```


### Versions

- PyTorch version: 2.9.1+cu128 (pip wheel)
- How installed: pip
- CUDA used to build PyTorch: 12.8
- cuDNN: 9.10.2 (91002)
- GPU: NVIDIA H800 (SM90), driver 535.261.03
- Python: 3.12.11
- OS: Linux

items.title: [Serve] [RFC] Computed Retry-After for backpressure rejections
items.author: vinay7373
items.body_excerpt:
## Motivation

PR #65193 added `BackpressureConfig`. Deployments can now reject backpressured requests with a 429 and a static `Retry-After` header. Each caller (proxy or `DeploymentHandle`) has its own request queue, and at the time of a backpressure rejection a static `Retry-After` value can be incorrect in both directions. If the queue is deep and the static value is too short, clients retry into another rejection, adding load exactly when the system is trying to shed it. If the queue drains fast and the value is too long, capacity sits idle while clients wait.

This proposal computes the `Retry-After` value from observed load. This makes the header a reliable estimate of when capacity will be available, instead of a number the operator guessed. This was the original shape of the production request behind #65193 and it fits the discussion there about making 429 the default at some point.

No OSS inference server does this today (TGI, Triton, NVIDIA Dynamo and TorchServe all reject without a retry hint). The closest prior art is cloud-side (Azure OpenAI's `retry-after-ms`, AWS's `x-amz-retry-after`) and per-client rate limiters, where the value can be exact because a rate window is a clock. Capacity recovery is not a clock, so here the value is an estimate at any layer.

## Goals

- An opt-in `BackpressureConfig` policy that computes `Retry-After` from load signals the rejecting component already has.
- Keep the rejection path as cheap as it is today. No RPCs, locks or extra work on reject-and-respond.
- Degrade gracefully: computed, else static, else no header. Never fail or delay a rejection.

## Non-goals

- Changing when requests are rejected. Admission control is a separate discussion.
- Guaranteeing admission at the suggested time. The header is a hint, not a reservation.
- Changing the default rejection status code. Tracked separately.
- Implementing any further policy, such as the cluster-informed one (see "Future policies").

## Proposed API

```python
from ray.serve.config import BackpressureConfig

@serve.deployment(
    max_queued_requests=64,
    backpressure_config=BackpressureConfig(
        status_code=429,
        retry_after_policy="queue_drain_rate",   # NEW: "static" (default) | "queue_drain_rate"
        retry_after_s=5,                         # static value; also the fallback for computed policies
    ),
)
```

`retry_after_policy` is a named policy instead of a bare `"auto"` so future strategies can be added without changing what existing configs mean.

## Proposed design

This design adds a new field to `BackpressureConfig` called `retry_after_policy`, and one new policy named `queue_drain_rate` that computes `Retry-After` from the rejecting component's observed queue depth and drain rate.

The overall mechanism has 3 basic aspects: (i) how to compute the `Retry-After` value (what the `queue_drain_rate` policy implements), (ii) where to compute it, and (iii) who stamps the header and emits it to the client.

These boil down to emission and estimation. Emission answers (iii) and is fixed: the rejecting component stamps the header. Estimation covers (i) and (ii): one shared implementation, invoked at the two places Serve rejects today, each feeding its own local signals.

### The `queue_drain_rate` policy (this proposal)

```
retry_after = ceil(observed_queue_depth / drain_rate)
```

- **The numerator is the depth observed at rejection.** It is at least `max_queued_requests`, since a rejection only fires once the queue has reached the cap, and occasionally a little above it: the router's check is not atomic, and replica-rejected requests re-enter the queue behind new arrivals. The raise site already holds this number (it is in the `BackPressureError` message today), so using the observed value costs nothing and is exact.
- **`drain_rate` is the live signal**: how fast the queue empties, updated at the end of every interval as `drain_rate = 0.3 * rate_over_last_interval + 0.7 * previous_drain_rate`. `rate_over_last_interval` is the fresh measurement: requests drained during the interval that just ended. `previous_drain_rate` is this same formula's output from the previous update, so it carries the whole history with older intervals fading out. The 70% weight on the trend keeps lumpy traffic from whipping the value around (completions land in bursts, so a single interval can read 0 or 3x the true rate), and the 30% on the fresh measurement keeps the estimate chasing real load changes within a few intervals. The split, the interval length and the warmup threshold are implementation constants with environment-variable overrides, like Serve's other internal tunables, not new `BackpressureConfig` fields. The update runs on a lightweight background timer in the component's existing metrics machinery (default 1s). An interval with zero completions counts as a real observation when work is in flight, since that is what slow drain looks like, but idle intervals (nothing running or queued) skip the update instead of decaying the rate. The rate counts as warm after a configurable minimum number of counted intervals; until then the fallback applies.
- **Two call sites, one implementation.** On the proxy path the router rejects; its drain rate is its own assignment throughput, from a monotonic counter added at the existing send event (the current per-replica counter is an in-flight gauge, so it can't provide a rate). The rate is fleet-blended: faster replicas take more assignments, so mixed hardware is priced in. On direct ingress the replica rejects; its drain rate is its own completion rate, and its queue is drained only by itself. Same formula, different local inputs, different values, each describing its own queue. A replica's value is a conservative upper bound, since a retry may be re-balanced to a replica that frees up sooner.
- **Clamp to [1, 60] seconds.** Common client SDKs ignore `Retry-After` above 60s.
- **Jitter (for example +/-20%) is applied in the shared heade
