shortlist.title: [Feature Request][MP] Concurrent multi-turn benchmark for memory-budget-aware KV offload and retrieval
shortlist.author: shivankur-code
shortlist.body_excerpt:
**Label**
new feature; multiprocess mode / benchmarking, if applicable.

**Is your feature request related to a problem? Please describe.**

I'd like to help evaluate memory-budget-aware KV offloading and retrieval for concurrent, multi-turn conversations. Before changing any policy, I'd like to agree on a small workload and the specific limitation it should test.

The concrete starting point is MP prefetch admission: the current controller limits in-flight requests by count, while their L1 footprints can differ a lot. Eight short-prefix loads and eight long-prefix loads are very different memory and transfer workloads. The existing [controller design](https://github.com/LMCache/LMCache/blob/dev/docs/design/v1/distributed/l2_adapters/overall.md#max-in-flight-limiting) already calls out memory-based admission as a possible improvement.

I found #4529, which addresses this directly with byte-aware admission and aging, so I'm not proposing another implementation of that queue. What I'd like to check is how the existing approach behaves when conversations grow over successive turns, compete with one another, and overlap stores with retrievals under a fixed budget. I haven't run this experiment yet, and I'm not reporting a reproduced serving failure or claiming this coverage is absent everywhere.

**Describe the solution you'd like**

Start with a focused benchmark/test extension using the existing engine-bench infrastructure from #5489, rather than a new scheduler. Initial scope would be one serving engine (vLLM), MP mode, one GPU and DRAM L1 plus local filesystem L2. No P2P or distributed placement changes.

The workload would:

- Interleave short and long conversations. Each conversation keeps its exact previous token prefix and appends subsequent turns, including generated output. Turns within one conversation remain ordered; different conversations run concurrently, with configurable think time.
- Use a deterministic seed and a working set large enough to produce actual tier pressure. Verify useful prefix hits and actual L2 reads, rather than assuming a large prompt exercises off-GPU retrieval.
- Sweep concurrency and context lengths at fixed GPU and host-cache budgets. Include an ample-capacity control and separate cold-start from warmed measurements.
- Compare no external offload, eager offload, and existing eviction-aware lazy offload. Evaluate #4529 separately on a pinned compatible revision, with its author's agreement. Deadline/fallback interactions from #5255 would be a follow-up, not a requirement to merge all pending work together.

The first deliverable would be a reproducible workload, a documented run matrix, and a report showing:

- p50/p95/p99 time to first token, inter-token latency, and requests meeting agreed latency targets;
- per-conversation queueing time and whether long conversations repeatedly lose admission;
- useful hit tokens, actual transfer bytes, allocation failures/fallbacks, and evictions;
- separate GPU KV-pool usage, GPU temporary/pinned-for-transfer usage, and host L1 allocated/staging bytes, identifying any unavailable measurements rather than estimating them as results.

If this exposes a reproducible problem that existing work doesn't cover, I'd bring back a narrowly scoped fix with regression tests. Fewer transferred bytes alone would not count as success if response latency or useful reuse gets worse. Any cancellation/timeout tests must keep buffers charged and protected until transfer completion or confirmed abort; returning a fallback result doesn't make outstanding I/O safe to forget.

**Describe alternatives you've considered**

- Just lower the current in-flight request count or increase L1 capacity. Both are useful controls, but neither tells us how mixed-size conversations behave at equal resource budgets.
- Contribute tests directly to #4529 instead of adding a benchmark workload. I'm happy to do this if that is the more useful boundary.
- Build a new global scheduler or cost model. I'd rather avoid that before there is evidence of a gap in the existing policies.
- Compress L2 storage. That's a separate experiment: smaller serialized objects don't automatically reduce the engine's GPU-resident KV pool, since data may be reconstructed on load. Copying KV off GPU also isn't proof that its GPU blocks have been reclaimed.

**Additional context**

Related work I want to coordinate with:

- #4847: merged eviction-aware lazy offload.
- #4529: byte-aware MP prefetch admission, including small-load ordering and aging.
- #5255: optional prefetch deadline and recompute fallback.
- #5837 / #5838: L1 allocated-byte eviction accounting.
- #5489: merged tier-pressure benchmark.
- #5780, particularly #5782 / #5783: cost-aware admission and serving qualification. This request should complement those experiments, not duplicate them.
- #4557: earlier shared-L2 QoS proposal, including in-flight byte limits; closed, but relevant prior discussion.

Would this mixed-size, growing-prefix workload be useful as a separate benchmark contribution, or should it live under one of the existing threads? In particular, I'd appreciate guidance from the prefetch/benchmark maintainers and the authors of #4529 and #5780 on the scope before starting implementation. The first step is agreeing on that boundary, not changing defaults or claiming a new policy.

shortlist.title: [good-first-issue] tests: make flaky vllm_bench throughput comparisons reproducible
shortlist.author: maobaolong
shortlist.body_excerpt:
Parent tracker: #5313 · Onboarding: #3372

## Confirmed flaky behavior

`k3-multiprocess-test / vllm / vllm_bench / zmq` changes its throughput verdict without a source update:

| Build #5340, September 29, 2026 (UTC) | Result |
| --- | --- |
| [Original job](https://buildkite.com/lmcache/k3-multiprocess-test/builds/5340#01a0eab1-a517-4a38-8163-b0ec7cfaff63) | LMCache throughput **7.34% slower** than baseline; fails the 5% limit |
| [Retry](https://buildkite.com/lmcache/k3-multiprocess-test/builds/5340#01a0eaba-4671-4f79-a910-4a02cfa0cadf) | LMCache throughput **0.62% faster** than baseline; passes |

Both are `dev` builds of **`9e8226dd49728769843bf6f586b00b33ab616125`**, with no PR-base merge, vLLM **`0.30.1rc1.dev244+g0da126676`**, and torch **`2.13.0+cu130`**. Both baseline and LMCache completed all 50 requests with 500400 input tokens. This is an intermittent benchmark verdict, not an installation failure.

The inputs are not reproducible across those attempts: the original uses seed `1790644335`, the retry `1790645482`. Each attempt uses the same seed for its own baseline/LMCache pair, but the default `RANDOM_SEED` comes from `date +%s`. The seed change is a confirmed confounder; it is **not proven to be the sole cause** of the throughput fluctuation.

## Bounded good-first task

Make this benchmark's inputs reproducible across retries, and make the comparison auditable. This is the first test-harness improvement for the confirmed flake, not a production performance optimization.

1. Replace the clock-derived default seed with a documented stable default; continue honoring an explicit `RANDOM_SEED` override.
2. Save a small comparison manifest next to `baseline.json` and `lmcache.json`: effective seed, model, request count and lengths, actual checkout SHA, installed vLLM/torch versions, and the two throughput values/verdict. Keep any new diagnostics local to this workload.
3. Preserve separate attempt results when used in CI. Follow the existing result-directory/cleanup conventions, and ensure the manifest is accessible in the job log or a public Buildkite artifact rather than merely naming a container-local file.
4. Add focused CPU-only regression coverage using stub benchmark commands: default seed is repeatable, both sides receive it, an override is honored, and success/failure summaries retain the actual numbers.

Keep the 5% throughput limit, request/token checks, and cache-retrieval validation. Do not add blanket retries, remove assertions, or present a fixed seed as proof of a resolved performance issue. #5227 already added retry mitigation; this task addresses reproducibility within the workload.

Starting points, checked at `42be9c7439a1eb0b17bf6b7565a894a9743fd052`:

- [Workload seed and result comparison](https://github.com/LMCache/LMCache/blob/42be9c7439a1eb0b17bf6b7565a894a9743fd052/.buildkite/k3_tests/multiprocess/scripts/workloads/vllm/vllm-bench.sh).
- [Result cleanup/copying](https://github.com/LMCache/LMCache/blob/42be9c7439a1eb0b17bf6b7565a894a9743fd052/.buildkite/k3_tests/multiprocess/scripts/cleanup.sh).
- [Buildkite step and existing retry policy](https://github.com/LMCache/LMCache/blob/42be9c7439a1eb0b17bf6b7565a894a9743fd052/.buildkite/k3_tests/multiprocess/pipeline.yml).

## Acceptance

- [ ] Default inputs are identical across attempts; explicit overrides still work.
- [ ] A reviewer can recover both results, the effective inputs, versions, and verdict from public job output/artifacts.
- [ ] Stubbed CPU coverage exercises default/override and passing/failing results.
- [ ] GPU validation reports first-attempt results with a fixed seed; remaining fluctuation is reported as unresolved rather than hidden.
- [ ] Existing behavioral assertions and thresholds remain effective.

## Reproduce the CI workload

The evidence below comes from CI; this issue does not claim a local GPU reproduction. Use a dedicated Linux x86_64 GPU test host with Docker and NVIDIA Container Toolkit, two available CUDA GPUs capable of running separate `Qwen/Qwen3-14B` servers, sufficient host RAM for the default 80 GiB LMCache buffer (plus the mock L2 storage for the L2 case), and disk/network access for the image, wheels, and model. CI uses CUDA 13.0, Python 3.12, and a 1 GiB `/dev/shm`. A maintainer can run the GPU validation for a contributor who only has a CPU machine.

These commands build the public CI image recipe, explicitly start Bash, and pin the historical LMCache and vLLM revisions. They are a reproduction recipe, not a fully locked copy of every historical dependency or GPU scheduling condition. Run from a fresh directory; make the actual PR against current `dev`.

```bash
git clone https://github.com/LMCache/LMCache.git
cd LMCache
git checkout 9e8226dd49728769843bf6f586b00b33ab616125
docker build -t lmcache-flake-ci \
  -f .buildkite/k3_harness/ci-base.Dockerfile .
docker run --rm --gpus '"device=0,1"' --shm-size=1g \
  --entrypoint bash \
  -v "$PWD:/workspace/LMCache" -w /workspace/LMCache \
  -e MAX_JOBS=1 \
  -e INFERENCE_ENGINE=vllm \
  -e LMCACHE_REQUEST_TRANSPORT=zmq \
  -e LMCACHE_PR_BASE_MERGE=never \
  -e PINNED_VLLM_VERSION=0.30.1rc1.dev244+g0da126676 \
  -e PINNED_VLLM_ARCHIVE_INDEX_URL=https://wheels.vllm.ai/0da126676e38f5dc1b02b2c4f48dc85f90f5a79f/cu130 \
  lmcache-flake-ci -c '
    set -e
    source /opt/venv/bin/activate
    command -v git uv python3 nvcc gcc g++
    nvidia-smi
    git config --global --add safe.directory /workspace/LMCache
    .buildkite/k3_tests/multiprocess/run.sh vllm_bench
  '
```

Use the linked failed and passed jobs as the initial reproduction pair. For subsequent GPU runs, record the actual checkout SHA, installed package versions, GPU model, input settings, and first-attempt result. A green retry alone does not show that the underlying fluctuation was fixed.

## Claim and contribution rules

This is primarily for a new contributor. Claim **one active sub-issue at a time** by commenting `/claim` here; check existing comments and ass

**Expected Outcome / Goal**

The five calls use `%s` placeholders, and `ruff check --select G004` reports no violations for this file. The rendered log text stays identical — f-string interpolation and `%s` both go through `str()`.

**Additional Context**

- Scope is this one file only, format style only, no behavior change. Whether the (currently uncalled) `debug_print_device` helper should exist at all is a separate question and out of scope here.

shortlist.title: [RFC / Feature] SPICY-KV: 28.6x–50x Pre-RoPE Algebraic Multigrid KV Compression for RadixAttention & Long-CoT (91.7%–100% RULER Recall & 100% Shared-Prefix Multi-Query Reuse)
shortlist.author: Yuge-Y
shortlist.body_excerpt:
### Checklist

- [ ] If this is not a feature request but a general question, please start a discussion at https://github.com/sgl-project/sglang/discussions. Otherwise, it will be closed.
- [ ] Please use English. Otherwise, it will be closed.

### Motivation

### Motivation: Compressing `RadixAttention` Shared Prefixes & Long-CoT (`<think>`) Traces by 28.6x–50x

Hi `SGLang` team! We evaluated our newly released Pre-RoPE Algebraic Multigrid KV compression framework (**SPICY-KV**: *SPectral Invariant Coarse-graining with dYadic KV renormalization*) across both the **NVIDIA `RULER` benchmark suite** (`28.6x` / `3.5%` KV and `50.0x` / `2.0%` KV on `DeepSeek-R1-Distill-Qwen-7B` & `1.5B`) and **4-Turn Shared-Prefix Multi-Query Reuse** (compressing a shared prefix once and answering 4 distinct sequential user queries without re-prefilling, directly mirroring `SGLang`'s **`RadixAttention`** tree nodes).

We wanted to share why existing eviction (`SnapKV`, `PyramidKV`, `H2O`, `StreamingLLM`) and post-RoPE token-merging (`KVMerger`, `CaM`) baselines break down on `RadixAttention` shared prefixes and extreme compression ratios, and discuss a 4-byte per-node kernel calibration hook for `FlashInfer` / `Triton` paged attention:

1. **Why Observation-Window Eviction (`SnapKV`, `H2O`) Fails on Shared `RadixAttention` Prefixes:** Eviction methods score prefix tokens using only the trailing observation window of the *first* prompt. When subsequent turns query different branches or facts in the cached prefix, evicted tokens are permanently gone (`62.5%` multi-query recall for `SnapKV`, `25.0%` for `PyramidKV`, `0.0%` for `H2O`).
2. **Why Post-RoPE Token Merging (`KVMerger`, `CaM`) Hits `0.0%` on `RULER`:** Linearly merging post-RoPE keys across positions $t_1 \neq t_2$ causes destructive trigonometric phase cancellation. `SPICY-KV` inverts RoPE ($R_{\Theta, t_i}^{-1}$, or taps pre-RoPE / MLA latent vectors $c_t^{KV}$) and applies **two-level moderated-step mean centering ($B_{\text{step}}=128$)** to strip `k_proj.bias` sink cones and cumulative causal drift.
3. **Hybrid Algebraic Multigrid ($C/F$) Splitting + 2nd-Order Subgrid Variance Closure:** Retains $C$-point landmarks (including cross-block bridge hubs and causally dilated bound-value spans) at exact $1\times$ resolution ($m_c=1, \sigma_c^2=0$) with exact positions $t_c$, coalesces $F$-point background bulk in unrotated space, and closes the **Softmax Jensen Inequality Gap** ($\mathbb{E}[e^{q^\top k}] > e^{q^\top \mathbb{E}[k]}$) by tracking intra-cluster subgrid key variance $\sigma_m^2$ via the Law of Total Variance:
   $$s_m = \frac{q_T^\top R_{\Theta, \bar{t}_m} \tilde{k}_m}{\sqrt{d_k}} + \log(m_m) + \frac{\lVert q_T \rVert_2^2 \sigma_m^2}{2 d_k}$$

---

### Headline Results: NVIDIA `RULER` (`7B` & `1.5B`) & 4-Turn Shared-Prefix Reuse

| Method | `1.5B` `RULER` @ **28.6×** (`3.5%` KV) | `1.5B` `RULER` @ **50.0×** (`2.0%` KV) | `7B` `RULER` @ **28.6×** (`3.5%` KV) | `7B` `RULER` @ **50.0×** (`2.0%` KV) | **4-Turn Shared-Prefix Reuse** |

### Proposed `SGLang` Integration Discussion
We'd love architectural feedback from the `SGLang` maintainers on:
1. **4-Byte Per-Slot Calibration Metadata in `Triton` / `FlashInfer` Paged Kernels:** Passing two FP16 scalars per cached node—log-mass $\log(m_m)$ and subgrid key variance $\sigma_m^2$ (4 bytes/node total, `< 0.4%` memory overhead)—into the online softmax loop (`score += log_m[j] + 0.5 * q_norm_sq * sigma_sq[j] / d_k`).
2. **`RadixAttention` Prefix Node Coarsening:** Compressing cold/shared `RadixCache` prefix blocks by $20\times\text{–}28.6\times$ via `SPICY-KV` single-pass hybrid $C/F$ restriction so `RadixCache` can hold $20\times+$ more concurrent prefix trees in GPU HBM without query-specific eviction blindness.

shortlist.title: Restart-proof KV cache for llama-server: 40K-token TTFT 155s to 6s after reboot
shortlist.author: qqkzlm
shortlist.body_excerpt:
Every restart wipes your prefill. Server crash, box reboot, model reload — a 40K-token agentic prompt pays the full ~155s prefill again before the first token.

I patched llama-server to persist KV-cache prefix checkpoints to disk and auto-restore the longest matching prefix on boot. Same prompt after a restart: **first token in ~6s instead of ~155s** (2.1s disk read once + decode). No client changes, no re-architecture — the server just remembers.

Measured on GTX 1080 8GB, Qwen3.6-35B-A3B, `-c 92160`:

- Cold: 151s prefill → first token at ~155s
- Warm (post-restart): 2.1s disk read (first request only) → first token at ~6s
- Checkpoints keyed by model + ctx + KV quant (wrong config = ignored, never corrupted); disk-budget eviction included

Single-commit patch (86KB): https://github.com/qqkzlm/llama-cpp-prompt-disk-cache — `git am` onto the PrismML `prism` branch, four flags (`--slot-save-path`, `--checkpoint-min-step`, `--ctx-checkpoints`, `--prompt-cache-disk-budget`).

One MoE lesson from the same box: keep experts on GPU, let KV follow the layers — pushing 20 MoE layers to CPU collapsed prefill 265→30 tok/s, which no cache can fix.

Happy to upstream behind a flag if maintainers are interested.

comments.author: qqkzlm
comments.body:
Update to the README since this went up — three things worth calling out for anyone trying it:

**1. Prebuilt CUDA binaries exist for both platforms.** The `v0.2.3` release ships `llama-server-win-cuda-v0.2.3.zip` and `llama-server-linux-cuda-v0.2.3.tar.gz`. The Linux package is built for `sm_61`/Pascal, so it also runs on GTX 10-series. No build needed:

```bash
./llama-server -m model.gguf -c 32768 --host 0.0.0.0 --port 8000 \
  --slot-save-path /var/tmp/kvstore/model \
  --prompt-cache-disk-budget 20 --checkpoint-min-step 2048 --ctx-checkpoints 64
```

**2. Only one flag is actually required.** `--slot-save-path` is the only one you must pass — `--prompt-cache-disk-budget` and `--prompt-cache-disk-path` are silently ignored without it, and entries land in `<slot-save-path>/pdcache`. `--prompt-cache-disk` is **enabled by default**, so passing it is optional; use `--no-prompt-cache-disk` to turn the cache off.

**3. Cache hits require a byte-identical prompt prefix.** Only the common prefix from token 0 onward is reused. If you prepend a timestamp or a random ID, everything after it misses and the cache is effectively unused. Put stable content first (system prompt, tool definitions, long docs) and per-turn content last — opencode / Claude Code already do this, so it works out of the box.

The README now has a "when does the cache hit / when does it miss" section covering this, a flag-duty table, and a Chinese-first three-step guide (the repo README is now Chinese-primary). A Windows `start-llama-server.bat` is included in the zip if you want a prompt-driven launcher instead of a command line.

Still happy to upstream this behind a flag if maintainers are interested — the whole feature is one commit touching `tools/server/server-prompt-disk.cpp` (~900 lines) plus slot/task integration.

shortlist.author: leepoly
shortlist.body_excerpt: ### Checklist - [x] 1. I have searched related issues but cannot get the expected help. - [x] 2. The bug has not been fixed in the latest version. - [x] 3. Please note that if the bug-related issue you submitted lacks corresponding environment info and a minimal reproducible demo, it will be challenging for us to reproduce and resolve the issue, reducing the likelihood of receiving feedback. - [x] 4. If the issue you raised is not a bug but a question, please raise a discussion at https://github.com/sgl-project/sglang/discussions/new/choose Otherwise, it will be closed. - [x] 5. Please use English, otherwise it will be closed. ### Describe the bug Hi, I encountered an inconsistency in decode throughput reporting. When benchmarking with the bench_serving script, the reported TPOT is **much lower** than the decode throughput logged by the engine. This gap is significant for **small models or high concurrency settings**. ### Reproduction #### start the server ``` python -m sglang.launch_server \ --model-path Qwen/Qwen2.5-0.5B \ --trust-remote-code \ --tp 1 \ --load-format dummy \ --port 30000 --host 127.0.0.1 ``` #### benchmark (seqlens 2048 concurrency 16) ``` python3 -m sglang.bench_serving \ --backend sglang \ --dataset-name random \ --random-range-ratio 1.0 \ --random-input-len 2048 \ --random-output-len 256 \ --num-prompts 16 \ --max-concurrency 16 \ --host 127.0.0.1 \ --port 30000 ``` Observed Results: - The bench_serving script reports a median TPOT of 4.45 ms, equating to a token throughput of 224 $\times$ 16 = 3584 tokens/second. - However, the engine logs show a decode throughput of 7026 tokens/second. The gap between these metrics is significant and raises concerns about potential discrepancies in throughput measurement. Please let me know if you need additional details or logs to assist in troubleshooting. ### Environment Python: 3.10.0 (default, Mar 3 2022, 09:58:08) [GCC 7.5.0] CUDA available: True NVIDIA H800 GPU CUDA_HOME: /usr/local/cuda NVCC: Cuda compilation tools, release 12.6, V12.6.85 CUDA Driver Version: 535.129.03 PyTorch: 2.5.1+cu124 sglang: 0.4.1.post5 flashinfer: 0.1.6+cu124torch2.4 triton: 3.1.0 transformers: 4.48.0 torchao: 0.7.0 numpy: 1.26.4

comments.author: YEXINGZHE54
comments.body: I think it's just a difference between  long-time metric and short-time peak metric. From the perspective of bench_serving, estimating token throughput using TPOT (Time Per Output Token) provides a comprehensive evaluation over the entire testing period. On the other hand, the throughput printed in the engine log refers to the number of tokens generated within a single logging interval (which can be understood as the time for 40 consecutive decodes) divided by the time taken. Clearly, the data in the engine log is influenced by various factors, including: the potential interleaving of the prefill phase between decodes, which extends the total time; additionally, the amount of remaining memory also affects the number of tokens output per decode. Of course, the core issue here is that the engine log records short-term peak throughput, and similar results might be obtained if using the P25 (25th percentile) of TPOT for estimation.

comments.author: Tshiyao
comments.body:
I think I've found the cause. In multiple tests, when the backend is specified as "sglang," the `flush_cache` function is called to clear the cache.

 If `flush_cache` is executed successfully, there will be an inconsistency in the Decode Throughput between `bench_serving` and `engine logs`, specifically, `bench_serving` will be lower than `engine logs`. 

If `flush_cache` fails, the difference in Throughput between the two is within an acceptable range.

I speculate that the time loss caused by the successful execution of `flush_cache` might be the reason. The Decode Throughput in `engine logs` is not affected by this, but `bench_serving` is. I'm still not sure how to fix it. Does anyone have any suggestions?

When the backend is specified as "sglang," the following code is called to flush the cache，code in [here](https://github.com/sgl-project/sglang/blob/9cf407729441a18561ee5a8b2c1e3e535ba817f9/python/sglang/bench_serving.py#L961):
```python
# Flush cache
if "sglang" in backend:
    requests.post(base_url + "/flush_cache")
```

The specific implementation of `flush_cache` can be found [here](https://github.com/sgl-project/sglang/blob/9cf407729441a18561ee5a8b2c1e3e535ba817f9/python/sglang/srt/managers/scheduler.py#L1677):
```python
def flush_cache(self):
    """Flush the memory pool and cache."""
    if len(self.waiting_queue) == 0 and (
        self.running_batch is None or len(self.running_batch.reqs) == 0
    ):
        self.tree_cache.reset()
        self.tree_cache_metrics = {"total": 0, "hit": 0}
        if self.grammar_backend:
            self.grammar_backend.reset()
        self.req_to_token_pool.clear()
        self.token_to_kv_pool.clear()

        if not self.spec_algorithm.is_none():
            self.draft_worker.model_runner.req_to_token_pool.clear()
            self.draft_worker.model_runner.token_to_kv_pool.clear()

        self.num_generated_tokens = 0
        self.forward_ct_decode = 0
        self.spec_num_total_accepted_tokens = 0
        self.spec_num_total_forward_ct = 0
        torch.cuda.empty_cache()
        logger.info("Cache flushed successfully!")
        if_success = True
    else:
        logging.warning(
            f"Cache not flushed because there are pending requests. "
            f"#queue-req: {len(self.waiting_queue)}, "
            f"#running-req: {0 if self.running_batch is None else len(self.running_batch.reqs)}"
        )
        if_success = False
    return if_success
```

comments.author: ptimizeroracle
comments.body:
I went through both sides of this with the current code (main @ 99b9109). Happy to turn any of it into a fix if wanted, but evidence first.

**The two numbers are different estimators, not two measurements of the same thing:**

| | bench_serving | engine log |
|---|---|---|
| definition | TPOT-derived, per request: `(latency − ttft)` over `output_len − 1`, averaged across the whole run, client-side | `num_generated_tokens / gap_latency` where `gap_latency` is the time since the previous log line (`scheduler_components/metrics_reporter.py:799,894`) |
| window | entire run: queueing, any cold start, `[DONE]` tail included | one reporting interval, near-instantaneous |

So bench < engine is expected whenever the run has any ramp-up: the engine line reads close to a short-window peak, the bench number is a whole-run average.

Three smaller things verified along the way (all `python/sglang/benchmark/serving.py` unless noted):

1. TPOT arithmetic is the standard upstream vLLM formula (`(latency − ttft)/(output_len − 1)`, `:1136`): sound.
2. `itl` is recorded per stream **event**, not per token (`:334-337`, `:466+`). Events carrying several tokens (stream-interval batching, speculative decoding) contribute one itl sample, so `len(itl) < output_len − 1` and ITL percentiles conflate event latency with token latency. A retokenized correction already exists, but only for the `sglang-oai` backends (`:1131-1135`, `:1145-1155`); the completions/chat paths don't get it. I wrote CPU unit tests pinning this behavior (sum(itl) + [DONE]-tail == latency − ttft exactly; mean(ITL) > TPOT for the same request from denominators alone). Happy to PR them.
3. `should_flush_cache` is `("sglang" in backend AND SGLANG_IS_IN_CI) or --flush-cache` (`:1467-1471`), not default-on, so the cold-start mechanism discussed earlier in this thread needs CI or the explicit flag to apply to a default run.

If it's useful, the options I see: (a) a note in the bench output clarifying the window difference vs engine logs, (b) an engine-side long-window average for apples-to-apples runs, (c) extending the retokenized ITL path to the other backends. Which, if any, would you want?

shortlist.title: [Bug] FP8 block-quantized checkpoint on SM86 (FP8 Marlin) intermittently gives wrong tokens with the overlap scheduler; exact without it
shortlist.author: DiaaAj
shortlist.body_excerpt:
## Summary
On an RTX 3090, SGLang 0.5.22 serves a 128×128 block-FP8 checkpoint through FP8 Marlin (weight-only; SM86 has
no FP8 tensor cores). In most runs of a 192-request workload, 1–5 requests produce wrong tokens, either
from their first token or from a later decode step. Rerunning gives different requests, and some runs are
clean. With `--disable-overlap-schedule` the same workload was exact in 5 of 5 runs.

The checkpoint's weights are exactly representable in FP8 with power-of-two block scales, and every output
token is known in advance, so these are not numerical differences:
- vLLM 0.31.0 is exact on the same checkpoint, also through FP8 Marlin;
- SGLang is exact on the bf16 checkpoint it was quantized from, with the same settings.

## Observed (probec probe twin of Qwen3-0.6B, 28 layers; greedy; 192 requests x 256 tokens)
| SGLang 0.5.22, RTX 3090, FP8 128×128 blocks | runs with wrong requests | wrong requests per run |
|---|---|---|
| default (FlashInfer attention, radix cache, overlap scheduler, CUDA graphs) | 5 of 7 | 0, 2, 0, 5, 1, 1 (+1 on another host) |
| `--attention-backend triton` | 1 of 1 | 3 |
| `--disable-radix-cache` | 1 of 5 | 1 |
| `--disable-cuda-graph` | 1 of 3 | 1 |
| **`--disable-overlap-schedule`** | **0 of 5** | 0 |
| bf16 checkpoint (control), default settings | 0 of 3 | 0 |

**What goes wrong.** In the probe, each layer looks one token up in the KV cache. A failing request's
output switches to the token the probe emits when a lookup finds nothing (the same token in every failing
request). So a layer's query, key or value for some tokens is wrong, or the attention read misses them.
Requests that share a prefix and were batched together fail at the same step, with the same tokens.

**The GEMM is exact in isolation.** [`tools/marlin_determinism.py`](https://github.com/DiaaAj/probec/blob/main/tools/marlin_determinism.py) calls SGLang's
`apply_fp8_marlin_linear` on the checkpoint's FP8 block weights (layers 0 and 27, all five projections). It
found no call that differed from the exact product:
- every M from 1 to 1024 plus nine larger sizes (10,330 calls);
- 20 repeats each of 12 sizes (no nondeterminism);
- two streams sharing a layer's lock workspace;
- input production, GEMM and readback on one side stream, as the overlap scheduler's forward stream does.

So the failure needs the engine, the overlap scheduler in particular.

## Repro
```
pip install "probec @ git+https://github.com/DiaaAj/probec" "sglang[all]==0.5.22"
probec compile --like Qwen/Qwen3-0.6B --no-scale-check -o dense
probec quantize dense --format fp8-block --device cuda -o dense-fp8-block
probec run dense-fp8-block --engine sglang --matrix quick --only flashinfer/default --out results.jsonl   # repeat a few times
probec report results.jsonl
```

## Environment
SGLang 0.5.22 (pip), RTX 3090 (SM86), driver 595.84, CUDA 13.0 image; two hosts.

shortlist.title: [RFC]: Parallelize long-running Mooncake Store unit tests
shortlist.author: Aionw
shortlist.body_excerpt:
## Status

Draft / implementation in review.

This RFC replaces the oversized prototype PR #2896 with six smaller draft PRs that have an explicit review and merge topology.

## Motivation

Several Mooncake Store unit-test executables contain many semantically unrelated cases and run for a long time as one scheduling unit. Splitting those cases by behavior gives CTest more useful parallel work and makes failures easier to locate, but creating one executable per source file increases compile/link overhead.

The proposal therefore separates two concerns:

1. Keep source files organized by semantic behavior.
2. Use a small CMake helper to combine compatible files into a bounded number of Unity-built test targets.

No hard-coded shard index or test-name routing table is introduced.

## Invariants

- Preserve all 296 source-defined GTest cases.
- Changes to test-only fixture behavior are acceptable when needed for isolation.
- Production behavior must not change.
- Each domain split must remain independently reviewable.
- The final target-balancing change must be isolated in its own commit/PR layer.

## PR topology

```text
                         +--> #2900 DummyClient + offload --------+
                         +--> #2901 SSD + snapshot SSD -----------+
RFC #2898 / main --------+--> #2902 promotion --------------------+--> #2905 Unity/target balance
                         +--> #2903 MasterService core -----------+
                         +--> #2904 snapshot MasterService -------+
```

The five domain PRs are all based directly on the same `main` commit and can be reviewed in parallel. #2905 contains those five commits plus one final CMake-only commit; review that final commit after the domain PRs, then let its diff shrink as #2900–#2904 merge.

## Tracking

| Order | PR | Scope | Source tests | Review dependency |
| --- | --- | --- | ---: | --- |
| 1 | #2900 | DummyClient + offload | 17 | RFC only |
| 2 | #2901 | SSD + snapshot SSD | 26 | RFC only |
| 3 | #2902 | Promotion | 40 | RFC only |
| 4 | #2903 | MasterService core | 144 | RFC only |
| 5 | #2904 | Snapshot MasterService | 69 | RFC only |
| 6 | #2905 | Unity build and target balancing | 296 total | #2900–#2904 |

## CMake design

`add_store_test()` remains the single registration primitive. The final PR adds `add_store_unity_test()`, which delegates to it and enables CMake `UNITY_BUILD` for compatible semantic source groups.

The result is:

- 30 independently registered targets in the five domain PRs, useful for isolated review and validation.
- 21 balanced targets in the final integrated layout.
- Semantic directories and filenames remain intact.
- No numeric shard constants or hard-coded test-case mapping in CMake.

## Validation

Five independent branches:

- All targeted builds passed.
- 30/30 CTest targets passed.
- Source-defined test count: 17 + 26 + 40 + 144 + 69 = 296.
- Four-way group wall times: 32.69s, 43.32s, 36.63s, 85.97s, and 89.85s.

Final integration branch:

- 21/21 targets built on current `main`.
- 21/21 CTest targets passed with `ctest -j4` in 204.53s.
- Isolated prototype measurement: 148.05s target build and 203.81s test time.
- A contended cold build measured 490.52s after four concurrent worktree builds; it is retained as a host-load datapoint and is not used as a regression comparison.

## Acceptance criteria

- [x] 296 source-defined tests preserved.
- [x] Semantic source layout replaces the long monoliths.
- [x] Final test wall time is at most 210s at four-way concurrency.
- [x] Isolated changed-target build is at most 160s.
- [x] Combined isolated build + test time is at most 360s.
- [x] Domain PRs can be reviewed in parallel.
- [x] Target balancing is isolated for focused review.

## Rollout

1. Review #2900–#2904 in parallel.
2. Merge accepted domain PRs in any order, resolving only localized CMake registration overlap if needed.
3. Rebase #2905 as those PRs land.
4. Review the final CMake-only target-balancing commit.
5. Mark the drafts ready only after human review of every changed line and successful CI.

## Superseded prototype

#2896 demonstrated the full approach but is too large to review effectively. It is superseded by this RFC and #2900–#2905.

shortlist.author: maobaolong
shortlist.body_excerpt:
Part of #3372. This is a community tracker for small, independently claimable improvements to flaky tests.

## The problem

Recent PR CI contains assertions that race background work and an intermittent hang that can occupy a runner for almost six hours. These failures consume contributor time and make unrelated PRs harder to validate.

The initial triage reviewed GitHub Actions `Test` runs from September 13-23, 2026 and recent `k3-unit-tests` failures. These are selected examples, not a complete inventory or a measured repository-wide flake rate. The test code was checked against `dev` at [21571dae80c6](https://github.com/LMCache/LMCache/commit/21571dae80c64ab4d141be571744494995270160).

The initial tasks cover:

- **Health-monitor exit:** a fixed 200 ms sleep precedes a thread-exit assertion; two PRs have same-checkout failed/passed attempts.
- **Health-monitor fallback/recovery:** a fixed 200 ms sleep precedes a state assertion; failure logs show fallback completing after the assertion.
- **RESP wait diagnostics:** a same-checkout rerun passes after an almost-six-hour hang near the RESP test boundary. The exact blocked operation remains unproven; this task adds bounded waits and diagnostics, not a speculative production fix.

## Initial tasks

- [x] #5314: Synchronize health-monitor exception-driven exit
- [ ] #5315: Synchronize health-monitor fallback/recovery phases
- [ ] #5316: Bound RESP waits and add stalled-operation diagnostics

## September 22–29 follow-up tasks

The follow-up scan covered **September 22, 2026 04:31 UTC through September 29, 2026 04:31 UTC**. It inspected 1,338 GitHub Actions run records across `Test`, `CPU Device Tests`, and `Operator: CI`, and 2,106 Buildkite build records across the active LMCache pipelines, then examined relevant failed jobs and retry logs. These inventory counts are not a repository-wide flake rate or a claim that every failed log was exhaustively analyzed.

Each new task below includes a failed/passed pair within the **same `dev` Buildkite build**, with the same LMCache checkout and vLLM/torch versions. PR-head-only matches with an unverified base merge, dependency/version changes between attempts, and one-off failures were not used as confirmation.

- [ ] #5402: Make `vllm_bench` inputs reproducible across retries and retain the comparison settings/results. Build #5340 changes from 7.34% slower than baseline to 0.62% faster without a source change.
- [ ] #5403: Preserve separate baseline/LMCache raw timings for `long_doc_qa`. Build #5294 changes from 50.3% TTFT improvement (fail) to 70.4% (pass); #5291 provides a second pair.
- [ ] #5404: Retain L2 data-flow diagnostics after `long_doc_qa_l2` performance failures. Build #5287 changes from 1.49x TTFT speedup (fail) to 1.54x (pass).

These are independently claimable **reproducibility and diagnostics improvements for confirmed intermittent test verdicts**. They deliberately keep the existing performance/data-flow assertions. Completing a diagnostic task does not establish that the underlying timing instability is fixed; report any remaining root-cause work separately.

Contributors can develop the scoped regression coverage with CPU-only command stubs. End-to-end validation uses two CUDA GPUs and the exact CI workload; each child provides a self-contained historical reproduction recipe. A maintainer can help with GPU validation. The CPU environment below applies to the initial #5314–#5316 tasks, not these GPU workload runs.

Existing health-monitor/RESP tasks and ongoing MQ, distributed-storage, and observability work were checked to avoid duplicate newcomer assignments. Intermittent model-output mismatches were not turned into generic timing-hardening tasks or described as harmless flakes.

## Claim one sub-issue

Use the native **Sub-issues** list below. Start with either health-monitor task if this is your first test contribution; the RESP task benefits from familiarity with Python futures and event loops.

These tasks are primarily meant to help new contributors learn the LMCache contribution workflow. Please claim **only one sub-issue at a time**. If you already have an assigned task or an open PR in this tracker, finish that one before taking another, and leave the remaining tasks for other new contributors.

1. Pick one unassigned sub-issue and check its comments for an existing claim.
2. Comment `/claim` or "I'd like to work on this" **on that sub-issue**, so a maintainer can coordinate assignment. Please do not claim the parent tracker itself.
3. Keep one task per PR, target `dev`, and follow [the onboarding guide](https://github.com/LMCache/LMCache/issues/3372) and [CONTRIBUTING.md](https://github.com/LMCache/LMCache/blob/dev/CONTRIBUTING.md).
4. Sign off every commit (`git commit -s`), run `pre-commit run --all-files`, and include exact test commands and results in the PR.

## Shared CPU test setup (initial tasks)

The initial #5314–#5316 tasks do not require a GPU, model download, or external Redis server. Use Linux x86_64 with Git, a C/C++ build toolchain, FFmpeg, and Python 3.12 with venv support. The RESP tests use an in-memory mocked client. Allow sufficient disk space for PyTorch/vLLM dependencies. The full pre-commit checks also need Rust/Cargo with rustfmt and clippy.

Run this in a fresh working directory. The explicit revision is the **triage reference**; make the actual PR against current `dev`.

NO_GPU_EXT=1 python -m pip install -e . --no-build-isolation
python -m pip install pre-commit
export PYTHONHASHSEED=0

```

shortlist.title: [Feature] Unified JIT / Precompilation Cache Directory
shortlist.author: whybeyoung
shortlist.body_excerpt:
### Checklist

- [ ] If this is not a feature request but a general question, please start a discussion at https://github.com/sgl-project/sglang/discussions. Otherwise, it will be closed.
- [ ] Please use English. Otherwise, it will be closed.

### Motivation


## Summary

**Request:** Unify all JIT and precompilation cache paths under a single configurable root so that users and operators can manage cache location, size, and persistence in one place. The current situation is fragmented across multiple env vars and default paths (including `/tmp`), which makes it hard to reason about where compiled artifacts live and to reuse caches across runs or machines.

## Current State (Fragmented)

### 1. Triton JIT cache

| What | Env var / source | Default / behavior |
|------|------------------|--------------------|
| Direct `@triton.jit` (e.g. allocator, MoE kernels) | `TRITON_CACHE_DIR` (Triton runtime) | Triton default: `~/.triton/cache`; often overwritten by Inductor to a path under `/tmp/torchinductor_*` |
| SGLang override | `SGLANG_TRITON_CACHE_DIR` (if implemented) | e.g. `~/.triton/cache` or `~/.cache/triton` |

- Set only in some entry paths (engine, gRPC launcher, scheduler process); custom/PD launchers may not set it.
- When PyTorch Inductor runs first, it can set `TRITON_CACHE_DIR` to its own subdir, so later Triton JIT (including allocator) writes under `/tmp`.

### 2. PyTorch Inductor (torch.compile)

| What | Env var / source | Default / behavior |
|------|------------------|--------------------|
| Inductor cache | `TORCHINDUCTOR_CACHE_DIR` (PyTorch) | `/tmp/torchinductor_<user>` (or similar) |
| SGLang override | `SGLANG_TORCHINDUCTOR_CACHE_DIR` (if implemented) | e.g. `~/.cache/sglang/inductor` |

- Default lives in `/tmp`, so cache is often non-persistent and can conflict with other users on shared nodes.

### 3. DeepGEMM JIT cache

| What | Env var / source | Default / behavior |
|------|------------------|--------------------|
| DeepGEMM cache | `SGLANG_DG_CACHE_DIR` / `DG_JIT_CACHE_DIR` | `~/.cache/deep_gemm` |

- Set in `layers/deep_gemm_wrapper/compile_utils.py`; separate from Triton/Inductor.
- 
## Problems

1. **No single root:** Triton, Inductor, SGLang torch_compile, and DeepGEMM each have their own env or default; some write to `/tmp`, others to `~/.cache/...`.

## Proposal

### 1. Introduce a single JIT cache root

- **New env var:** `SGLANG_JIT_CACHE_ROOT` (or `SGLANG_CACHE_ROOT` if we want to align with existing `SGLANG_CACHE_ROOT` in custom_all_reduce_utils).
- **Default:** `~/.cache/sglang` (or `$XDG_CACHE_HOME/sglang` when set).
- **Semantics:** All JIT/precompilation caches that SGLang controls should live under this root in fixed subdirs.

### 2. Standard layout under the root

Suggested subdirs (all under `SGLANG_JIT_CACHE_ROOT`):

| Subdir | Purpose | Maps from |
|--------|---------|-----------|
| `triton/` | Triton JIT (direct `@triton.jit` and, when possible, Triton used by Inductor) | `TRITON_CACHE_DIR` |
| `inductor/` | PyTorch Inductor (torch.compile) | `TORCHINDUCTOR_CACHE_DIR` |
| `torch_compile/` | SGLang torch.compile cache (hash-based, when using SGLangBackend) | `SGLANG_CACHE_DIR` + `torch_compile_cache` |
| `deep_gemm/` | DeepGEMM JIT | `SGLANG_DG_CACHE_DIR` / `DG_JIT_CACHE_DIR` |

- If we keep backward compatibility, existing env vars (`SGLANG_TRITON_CACHE_DIR`, `SGLANG_TORCHINDUCTOR_CACHE_DIR`, `SGLANG_CACHE_DIR`, `SGLANG_DG_CACHE_DIR`) could override the default subdir path when set; otherwise they are derived as `{SGLANG_JIT_CACHE_ROOT}/{subdir}`.

CC @Fridge003 @hnyls2002 

### Related resources

_No response_

shortlist.title: [Performance]: spec-decode boot-to-boot throughput dispersion on L4 (CV up to 13.92%), resolved in 0.30.0
shortlist.author: akshathtiwari
shortlist.body_excerpt:
### Proposal to improve performance

Not a proposal so much as a measurement suggestion. Speculative-decoding throughput on this stack is boot-dependent to a degree a single-boot benchmark cannot see: on 0.29.0 / L4, twelve boots of a byte-identical configuration gave CV 13.92% in one container and 3.73% in another. Anything comparing speculative configurations from one boot each is partly measuring which boot it got.

0.30.0 looks much better on this axis (0.99% and 1.61% across two containers on different physical cards), so this may already be resolved. I am reporting it mainly because the mechanism is not what I assumed, and the protocol seems worth having on record either way.

### Report of performance regression

Reporting this because 0.30.0 appears to resolve it, and the obvious explanation turns out to be wrong, so something else changed and I would like to know what.

**Setup.** Qwen3-4B target, `z-lab/Qwen3-4B-DFlash-b16` drafter, 5 speculative tokens, bf16 weights, `--kv-cache-dtype auto`, FlashInfer pinned. GSM8K, concurrency 1, one fixed prompt set replayed on every boot. 12 boots per arm inside a single container, one physical GPU per session (UUID recorded). The harness speaks HTTP only and never imports vLLM.

Throughput at concurrency 1, output tokens/s:

| card | engine | session | default | --enforce-eager | ratio | default CV |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| L4 (SM89) | 0.29.0 | A | 39.2 | 80.5 | **0.487** | **13.92%** |
| L4 (SM89) | 0.29.0 | B | 61.2 | 79.7 | **0.768** | **3.73%** |
| L4 (SM89) | 0.30.0 | C | 82.8 | 81.6 | **1.014** | 0.99% |
| L4 (SM89) | 0.30.0 | D | 78.2 | 77.0 | **1.017** | 1.61% |
| A10 (SM86) | 0.29.0 | E | 132.6 | 138.3 | 0.959 | 2.08% |

Each ratio is the default arm divided by the eager arm measured in the same container, so session and card effects cancel. On 0.29.0/L4 the CUDA-graph path runs at 49% and 77% of the eager path; on 0.30.0 it reaches parity. Acceptance length is flat throughout (tau 4.11-4.15), so this is throughput rather than a change in what the drafter gets accepted.

### Misc discussion on performance

Two observations, one related issue, and a question.

**1. The CUDA-graph fallback still fires on 0.30.0.** I had assumed the improvement was the speculative path gaining full graphs. It is not. The warning is byte-identical on both versions and capture proceeds under PIECEWISE in each:

> CUDAGraphMode.FULL_AND_PIECEWISE is not supported with spec-decode for attention backend FlashInferBackend (support: AttentionCGSupport.UNIFORM_SINGLE_TOKEN_DECODE); setting cudagraph_mode=PIECEWISE

Backend selection is unchanged too: both versions log FLASHINFER for the target and FLASH_ATTN for the second selection. So neither graph mode nor backend choice explains the difference.

**2. On 0.29.0 the dispersion magnitude is itself not reproducible.** Two twelve-boot measurements of the identical configuration gave CV 13.92% and 3.73%, with means 39.2 and 61.2 tok/s. The effect is present in both; its size is not a property of the configuration. The eager arm is stable across every session measured (80.5, 79.7, 81.6, 77.0 on L4; 138.3 on A10), which is what makes it usable as a control.

**Related, but I do not think it is the same thing: #58677.** That reports the draft model's torch.compile cache identity flipping between exactly two values across restarts with byte-identical argv, attributed to the shared VllmConfig being mutated in-place during the main model's warmup and CUDA-graph-capture phase, before the draft head compiles. Two differences: the symptom there is startup recompile cost rather than steady-state throughput, and it reports 0.27.1 affected with 0.29 appearing immune, whereas what I measure is on 0.29.0.

Still, the shape is close enough that I would rather ask than assume: **if VllmConfig is mutated in place during graph capture and that mutation reaches what the draft compiles to, could the same mechanism produce a steady-state throughput difference and not only a cache-key difference?** My measurements begin after the server reports healthy, so any recompilation has finished by then.


**The question.** What changed between 0.29.0 and 0.30.0 on this path, given the fallback and the backend selection are identical in both? If a specific PR is responsible I would rather cite it than guess. I looked at #53867, #51700, #54646 and #52228 and could not attribute it from the release notes alone.

**Possibly relevant.** The effect is much weaker on an A10 (ratio 0.959) than on an L4 (0.487 and 0.768) at the same engine version. The A10 has 24 GiB against the L4's 22.03 GiB usable, and this configuration sits close enough to the memory ceiling that --enforce-eager alone decides whether an fp8_e4m3-KV variant boots at all. So capacity pressure may matter more here than architecture. I have not separated the two.

**Reproduction.** Harness, raw append-only records, analysis scripts and the engine logs are at https://github.com/akshathtiwari/spec-fp8-study (archived at https://doi.org/10.5281/zenodo.23033168). The boot-variance runs are one command each and the per-session numbers regenerate from the stored records. Happy to run further configurations if a specific one would help; the full sweep is a couple of GPU-hours.

### Your current environment (if you think it is necessary)

Not `collect_env.py` output: the engine runs in an ephemeral container on a rented GPU, so this machine's environment is not the one under test. These are the fields the harness records per measurement, read from nvidia-smi and from the running server.

```text
GPU         NVIDIA L4 (SM89, 22.03 GiB usable) and NVIDIA A10 (SM86)
            one physical card per session, gpu_uuid recorded per record
driver      580.95.05
CUDA        13.0
torch       2.13.0+cu130
vLLM        0.29.0 and 0.30.0, pinned by image digest. Version is read from
            the server's /version endpoint and checked against the declared
            value before any measu

comments.author: akshathtiwari
comments.body:
Correction to the "possibly relevant" paragraph in my original post.

I wrote that the A10 has 24 GiB against the L4's 22.03 GiB usable, and offered memory capacity as the likelier of two readings for why the deficit is weak on the A10. **That is wrong.** Both cards report **22.5 GiB** in my own records, and I had never checked the field before writing it. Capacity is not the difference between them.

What does differ, from the same records:

| | VRAM | arch | max SM clock | power limit |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| L4 | 22.5 GiB | SM8.9 | 2040 MHz | **72 W** |
| A10 | 22.5 GiB | SM8.6 | 1695 MHz | **150 W** |

So the card showing the deficit has less than half the power budget. That is a better fit for the symptom than capacity ever was: CUDA graphs run the work faster, faster work draws more power, and a 72 W part can hit its cap and clamp — variably, depending on thermal history, which would also explain why the dispersion magnitude itself does not reproduce between sessions. The eager arm runs slower, stays under the cap, and is stable in every session measured.

I want to be clear that this is a hypothesis and **my data cannot test it.** I was recording `clocks.max.sm` and `power.limit`, which are what the card is permitted to do, not what it did. A throttling explanation is precisely what configured limits cannot see.

I have since added sampling of achieved SM clock, power draw and `clocks_throttle_reasons.*` across the measurement window, and a run is in flight. If `sw_power_cap` is active during the default arm and not during the eager arm, that is the driver answering the question directly rather than me inferring it from a clock curve. I will post the result either way, including if it kills the hypothesis.

The throughput numbers and the ratio table in the original post are unaffected by this — they are measured, and the correction is to an explanation I attached to them.

shortlist.title: [RFC]: [Store] Recoverable client liveness states and asynchronous offboarding
shortlist.author: Doube-Suzerain
shortlist.body_excerpt:
### Changes proposed

## Motivation

Mooncake Store currently treats one client heartbeat timeout as a permanent failure. Temporary network jitter, a client pause, or a delayed Master monitor loop can therefore irreversibly unmount recoverable resources and delete their metadata.

We propose adding a recovery window: after the first TTL expires, the Master retains the client's resources but stops routing new requests and work to them; a valid liveness signal makes them serving again. Terminal cleanup starts only if the client remains unavailable for a second TTL.

Resource availability checks are currently distributed across allocation, replica lookup, Copy/Move, task dispatch, drain, offload, and promotion. This proposal also centralizes that decision so the new liveness semantics are applied consistently.

## Changes proposed

- Introduce an **Active → Suspected → Offline** state machine for each client incarnation, with separate active and suspicion TTLs.
- Add a typed `ServingEligibility` seam for all client-owned resource routing, while retaining Suspected resources for possible recovery.
- Separate client liveness from remount readiness and segment lifecycle.
- Express terminal cleanup as a retryable `ClientOffboardingJob`; complete it synchronously first, then move the same job to an asynchronous executor.
- Preserve the existing Ping RPC schema and legacy TTL configuration.
- Rebuild process-local liveness records when restoring Master snapshots; keep NoF on its independent health model.

## Proposed design

### Client liveness

Each client incarnation has a `ClientLivenessRecord`:

```text
Active --active TTL--> Suspected --suspicion TTL--> Offline
   ^                       |
   +---- liveness signal --+
```

- **Active** resources may serve new requests.
- **Suspected** resources are retained but cannot receive new allocations, descriptors, or work. A valid liveness signal recovers the same incarnation.
- **Offline** is terminal for that incarnation and starts offboarding.

The suspicion TTL starts when the Master actually commits `Active -> Suspected`, so a delayed monitor does not shorten the recovery window. Ping and successful segment mounts are liveness signals; ordinary Put/Get traffic and task/offload/promotion heartbeats are not.

Ping remains wire-compatible: a ready Active client receives `OK`; an unknown or Offline client receives `NEED_REMOUNT`; Ping may recover a Suspected client before applying the existing remount-readiness check.

Client liveness, remount readiness (`ok_client_`), and segment lifecycle remain independent. In particular, `ok_client_` will no longer determine whether resources may serve or must be retained.

### `ServingEligibility`

Allocation, metadata reads, task routing, offload, promotion, and drain will use a small typed interface with the following common semantics:

```text
resource can serve
  = resource is intrinsically valid
  && segment lifecycle permits serving
  && owning ClientLivenessRecord is Active

ShouldRetainResources
  = ClientLivenessRecord is Active or Suspected
```

This supplements existing segment checks rather than replacing them. NoF resources continue to use their own probe and lifecycle rules.

While Suspected, the Master blocks new dependencies on the client, including allocations, descriptors, Copy/Move routing, task delivery, offload/promotion work, and drain selection. End, Revoke, failure, and completion callbacks for already-started work remain accepted so refcounts, quota, and task state can converge.

Memory allocator registrations and buffers retain the specific `ClientLivenessRecord` that created them, preventing a later incarnation from reactivating old memory resources.

### Offboarding

Terminal retirement uses one job interface:

```text
PrepareClientOffboarding(record) -> ClientOffboardingJob
CompleteClientOffboarding(job)
```

Prepare commits Offline and immediately isolates the incarnation. Complete performs the expensive work: metadata cleanup, memory segment unmount, LocalDisk/offload/promotion cleanup, quota convergence, and external metadata cleanup. The old record is removed only after all steps succeed; until then it acts as a Mount/ReMount barrier.

The first implementation calls Complete synchronously from the client monitor. A follow-up submits the same job to an asynchronous executor with batching, retry, shutdown draining, and queue observability. This keeps state and cleanup semantics unchanged when execution becomes asynchronous.

### HA restore and compatibility

After snapshot restore, each restored client starts as Active with a fresh active TTL, preserving the current recovery semantics. The Master rebuilds the liveness associations needed by restored resources, while readiness still follows the existing ReMount protocol.

Snapshot creation must not capture partially completed offboarding. The synchronous phase preserves the current exclusion behavior; asynchronous offboarding will add explicit snapshot/offboarding coordination.

New configuration:

```yaml
client_active_ttl_sec: 10
client_suspicion_ttl_sec: 20
```

`client_live_ttl_sec` and `--client_ttl` remain deprecated aliases for the active TTL. If an active/legacy TTL is explicitly configured but suspicion TTL is omitted, suspicion inherits the resolved active TTL. No RPC schema change is required.

LocalDisk and task metadata currently identify ownership by client ID. Initially, complete cleanup plus the Offline remount barrier prevents old resources from overlapping a new incarnation. An explicit incarnation token would provide stricter isolation for artificially reused client IDs, but requires a wire/schema change and is outside the initial scope.

## Development plan

1. Add `ClientLivenessRecord`, dual-TTL configuration, Ping/Mount integration, and the three-state monitor.
2. Introduce `ServingEligibility` across allocation, descriptors, Copy/Move, task/drain, LocalDisk/offload, and promotion.
3. Add synchronous `ClientO

- [x] AiterMLA

@Etelis @VedantMadane @gshtras @Mohit-Gaur thank you for your PRs! I will respond here with thoughts so I don't repeat myself:

  I'm working on extracting the KV-cache update for FlashAttnMLA as discussed in this issue.

  I saw your note about providing a default do_kv_cache_update in a base class (using reshape_and_cache_flash) that backends can override if needed — and @Etelis already did this for standard

  - MLA has different inputs (k_c_normed, k_pe) vs. standard attention (key, value)

  This would cover FlashAttnMLA / FlashMLA / FlashInferMLA, while special MLA backends (e.g., sparse/fp8 variants) could still override as needed.

  Or do you prefer each MLA backend to implement do_kv_cache_update separately?

  Thanks for your guidance!

comments.author: Kare0638
comments.body:
Hi @ProExpertProg,

  I’m working on FlashAttnMLA. Since all MLA backends share MLACommonImpl.forward(), removing the KV-cache update there now would break other MLA backends that haven’t
  migrated yet.

  Would you prefer one of these concrete options?

  Option 1 (two-phase, safest now):

  - In MLACommonImpl: add do_kv_cache_update() (using concat_and_cache_mla)
  - Keep the existing KV update inside MLACommonImpl.forward() for now
  - Do not flip behavior until MLA caller-side changes land
  - Later: add caller-side update, remove in-forward update, set forward_includes_kv_cache_update=False

  Option 2 (gate inside forward):

  - Add a conditional gate in MLACommonImpl.forward():
      - If forward_includes_kv_cache_update=True → keep current in-forward update
      - If False → skip in-forward update
  - Then FlashAttnMLA can set forward_includes_kv_cache_update=False once the MLA caller is updated to call do_kv_cache_update().

  Also, if MLA caller-side changes are needed (e.g., MLAAttention.forward / unified_mla_attention), who will handle those?

  Thanks for the guidance!

shortlist.title: [RFC]: Add GDS offload for mooncake-store based on existing TENT gds transport
shortlist.author: tong1heng
shortlist.body_excerpt:
### Changes proposed

## Summary

Add opt-in GDS SSD offloading to mooncake store by reusing the existing TENT GDS transport.

The implementation adds:

1. A client-local, fixed-size GDS backing file exposed as a TENT `file://` segment and managed by an aligned extent allocator.
2. A first-class `ReplicaType::GDS` with storage identity, generation, offset, value size, and allocation size in store metadata and wire serialization.
3. Required dual-write behavior for enabled `BatchPut`: memory/NoF writes and GDS writes are submitted in parallel and waited on before finalization.
4. A GDS-only creation fallback when memory replica allocation fails because of capacity or tenant quota.
5. Memory-first `BatchGet` selection, followed by a local matching GDS replica, while retaining existing NoF, local-disk, and disk fallbacks.
6. TENT/Transfer Engine capability checks and GDS buffer-registration tracking needed for sub-slice cuFile requests.

The feature is enabled through environment variables and requires no changes to upstream vLLM, so existing deployments remain unchanged when it is disabled.

## Motivation

Mooncake store currently supports POSIX and `io_uring` file offloading. Its existing data path is as follows:

1. **Write path:** when memory usage in a global segment (CPU memory) reaches the configured eviction watermark, mooncake master selects objects for offloading and places them in the background offload queue. The client then reads the objects from the global segment and writes them to the configured file backend through POSIX or `io_uring`. After the file write completes, the master records the file-backed replica and may release the corresponding memory replica.
2. **Read path:** the client first queries the master for the object's replica metadata and prefers an available memory replica. If the object is no longer present in memory, the client loads it from the file backend through POSIX or `io_uring` and returns the data to the caller.

This data path becomes a bottleneck when host memory is constrained. GPU-to-CPU and CPU-to-SSD bandwidths are not matched: GPU data must first be copied into CPU memory and then written to SSD. **When GPU production outpaces this two-step pipeline, CPU memory and CPU-side file I/O cannot drain the global segment fast enough. Some KV cache is consequently discarded before it can be completely offloaded, preventing more valid KV cache from being offloaded to the SSD even when sufficient SSD capacity remains.**

GPUDirect Storage (GDS) addresses this mismatch by supporting GPU-to-SSD DMA, so the data can bypass the CPU staging path. The GDS transport has already been integrated into TENT, **but the data path between TENT and mooncake store has not yet been connected.** An earlier draft PR (#2731) attempted to add GDS offload at the mooncake store layer by introducing a separate GDS context. This approach would duplicate cuFile resource management and make mooncake store responsible for transport-specific details that already belong to TENT.

Therefore, the central design goal of this change is to preserve the existing separation of mooncake store and TENT while connecting the two components: TENT owns all GDS cuFile operations, transport selection, and buffer registration, while mooncake store owns only object and replica metadata, allocation/lifecycle decisions, and transfer-request submission. Mooncake store should reuse the existing Transfer Engine and TENT GDS transport instead of introducing another GDS/cuFile implementation. This keeps the GDS data path composable with store's replica semantics and avoids a second, divergent GDS context in mooncake store.

## Non-goals

- Replacing the existing `enable_ssd_offload`/`LOCAL_DISK` POSIX or `io_uring` path.
- Providing remote reads from another client's local GDS file. A remote GDS descriptor falls back to the existing memory, NoF, local-disk, or disk paths.
- Recovering a client's GDS index after restart or promising crash/durability semantics for the local file.

## Architecture

```text
RealClient (env opt-in)
  +-- client
      +-- GdsStorageManager
      |    +-- aligned extent allocator
      |    +-- file:// backing segment handle
      |    `-- storage_id + generation + read leases
      +-- TransferSubmitter::submitFile
      |    `-- TransferEngine / TENT GDS / cuFile
      `-- MasterClient RPCs
           `-- MasterService: GDS storage identities and replicas

BatchPut:
  reserve local extent
    +-- BatchPutStart -> MEMORY/NoF PROCESSING replicas
    +-- BatchAddGdsReplicaStart -> GDS PROCESSING replica
    `-- submit both write paths -> wait -> commit + BatchPutEnd

BatchGet:
  local MEMORY -> any MEMORY -> matching local GDS -> NoF/disk fallbacks
```

### Local GDS storage

`GdsStorageManager` creates/truncates and preallocates the configured backing file, opens it once through `openSegment("file://...")`, and allocates raw value extents aligned to 4 KiB. Reservations are move-only and automatically aborted unless committed or explicitly preserved after an uncertain RPC. A reference-counted read lease keeps an extent alive until all GDS read futures finish.

Each client registers a `storage_id` and `storage_generation` with the master. The generation changes when the file is recreated, preventing an old metadata descriptor from addressing the same offset in a new file.

### Store metadata and RPCs

`ReplicaType::GDS` is an independent replica type rather than an alias for `LOCAL_DISK`:

```text
GdsDescriptor {
  owner_client_id
  storage_id
  storage_generation
  value_offset
  value_size
  allocated_size
}
```

The master exposes storage registration/unregistration, `BatchAddGdsReplicaStart`, and `BatchCreateGdsOnlyObjects`. GDS replicas use the existing `PROCESSING` -> `COMPLETE` lifecycle, participate in `BatchPutEnd` / `BatchPutRevoke`, and are removed during stale-client cleanup. MessagePack serialization uses a stable explicit replica type value and validates the six-field G

comments.author: RuixiangMa
comments.body:
@tong1heng Great work! The design  is clean and well-motivated. A few points I'd like to understand better:
1. submitFile splits at 16 MiB and batches at 128 entries, but GdsTransport::submitTransferTasks already does the same splitting (kMaxSliceSize) and batch checking (io_batch_depth_, user-configurable). If a user sets io_batch_depth=32, submitFile still batches 128 — only 32 get accepted per TENT batch. Is this intentional double-protection, and if so, should the batch limit be read from TENT config rather than hardcoded?
2. Main has added some TENT infrastructure since this RFC was written. Transport::tracksLocalBuffer() seems like a natural fit for GDS's cuFileBufRegister (local-only, shouldn't be advertised via desc.transports). Transport::quiesce() could settle cuFile I/O before buffer deregister. And the all-or-nothing submitTransferTasks contract means partial failure needs rollback of pushed params. Would it make sense to reference these in the RFC?
3. Main recently refactored lease (shared_ptr<Lease>, group-shared) and group eviction (GroupDomain, all-or-none). How do GDS-only objects interact — do they get an independent or group-shared lease? Could UnregisterGdsStorage stale cleanup break all-or-none eviction by removing one GDS replica from a group?
4. Preserve creates finalized=false entries that are never auto-cleaned. If finalize RPCs fail repeatedly (network jitter, master restart), the backing file could be exhausted silently. The Roadmap mentions eviction policy as future work — should the gap be acknowledged in the main body with a short-term mitigation (metric, max count, or TTL)?
5. storage_generation algorithm and collision risk aren't specified. The PR uses steady_clock XOR client_id — steady_clock resets on reboot, so if client_id is reused (e.g. vLLM config), a timestamp collision (low but non-zero) could cause stale descriptors to be accepted. Would it be worth specifying the algorithm and confirming generation=0 as an invalid sentinel?

comments.author: tong1heng
comments.body:
Thanks for the thoughtful review! These points identify several implementation gaps and areas where the RFC needs clarification.

1. The two layers serve different purposes: `submitFile` bounds store-level submissions and manages their futures, while `GdsTransport::submitTransferTasks` enforces cuFile limits. However, the hardcoded batch limit of 128 is inconsistent with the configurable `io_batch_depth`. One clarification: an over-capacity submission returns `TooManyRequests`; it does not accept only the first 32 entries. We will expose the effective GDS batch depth through TENT and use it in `submitFile`, counting capacity in terms of entries after splitting. We will also align the splitting limits and add tests for different batch depths and submissions spanning multiple batches.

2. Agreed. We will reference these interfaces in the RFC and adapt the implementation accordingly. GDS will implement `tracksLocalBuffer()` using its local registration registry and stop advertising cuFile registrations through `desc.transports`. We will implement `quiesce()` to stop new submissions and settle outstanding I/O before teardown releases buffers and batch resources. For the all-or-nothing submission contract, we will validate all requests before modifying the sub-batch and restore appended state on failure. We will also verify cuFile’s submission-failure semantics to ensure potentially accepted I/O cannot be treated as a clean rejection and retried through another transport.

3. The PR currently uses the older group-registration path and needs to be adapted to main’s `shared_ptr<Lease>` and `GroupDomain` implementation. GDS-only objects should follow the same semantics as other objects: ungrouped objects have an independent lease, while grouped objects share the group’s lease. The local GDS `ReadLease` separately protects an extent during an in-flight read. `UnregisterGdsStorage` removes matching GDS replicas and deletes an object only when no valid replica remains. We will preserve group bookkeeping through the common metadata-removal path and add mixed MEMORY/GDS group tests. We will also clarify that invalid-storage cleanup is distinct from policy-driven eviction; current main tests permit safe members to be evicted while unsafe members remain, so strict all-or-none wording needs qualification.

4. Yes, we will acknowledge this limitation explicitly in the main body. `Preserve()` retains an allocation because an RPC failure does not establish whether the master applied the operation, but these uncertain entries currently have no reconciliation or automatic reclamation path. The issue also includes entries committed locally before a finalize RPC fails, so tracking only `finalized=false` is insufficient. As a short-term mitigation, we will track uncertain-entry counts, bytes, age, and allocation failures, and introduce a configurable admission limit. A TTL may trigger reconciliation, but it must not directly reclaim an extent without confirming that the master no longer references it and that local I/O has completed.

5. Agreed. `steady_clock` XOR the client ID does not provide a reliable cross-restart uniqueness guarantee when the client ID is reused. We will replace it with a fresh, randomly generated nonzero 64-bit storage-incarnation token whenever the backing file is recreated, preserving the current wire format. The RFC will specify the algorithm and its probabilistic collision properties. `generation=0` is already invalid: initialization avoids it, and `RegisterGdsStorage()` rejects it. We will document this invariant and add tests for zero-generation rejection and stale descriptors after storage recreation with a reused client ID.

shortlist.title: [Onboarding 2026] Good first issues — start contributing to LMCache in one PR
shortlist.author: maobaolong
shortlist.body_excerpt:
👋 Welcome to join lmcache slack channel. https://join.slack.com/t/lmcacheworkspace/shared_invite/zt-4d1c2uk6t-55YZVvOQnJFNeAJK32U~Gg 

👋 Welcome to LMCache! This umbrella issue is the **single entry point** for first-time
contributors. If you've never sent a PR to LMCache before, start here.

> If you're looking for the older onboarding thread, see #627. This 2026 version
> focuses on smaller, well-scoped tasks with a friendly step-by-step PR workflow.

---

## 0. Before you start

- Read [`CONTRIBUTING.md`](../blob/dev/CONTRIBUTING.md). The most important parts:
  - Base branch is `dev`. Open PRs against `dev`, not `main`.
  - Every Python file starts with `# SPDX-License-Identifier: Apache-2.0`.
  - Imports are grouped as `# Standard / # Third Party / # First Party / # Local`.
  - Line length is **88**, formatter is `ruff format`, lint is `ruff check`.
  - Never access `_private` members of other classes (SLF rule).
  - Public functions/methods need **type hints** + **docstring**.
- Set up the environment:
  ```bash
  uv venv --python 3.12 && source .venv/bin/activate
  uv pip install -e . --no-build-isolation
  uv pip install -r requirements/test.txt
  pre-commit install
  ```

## 1. How to claim a task

These tasks are mainly for new contributors to learn the LMCache issue-to-PR workflow. Please claim **only one good-first issue at a time**. If you already have an assigned good-first issue or an open good-first PR, finish that work before taking another one, and leave the remaining tasks for other newcomers.

1. Pick **one** sub-issue below that has no assignee and no `🔒 claimed` comment.
2. Comment exactly: `/claim` (or `I'd like to work on this 🙋`).
   A maintainer will assign it to you within ~2 business days.
3. If you go silent for 7 days we'll un-assign so others can pick it up — totally fine,
   just leave a comment if you need more time.

## 2. Branch & commit

```bash
git checkout dev && git pull
git checkout -b gfi/<issue-number>-short-slug
# ... do the work ...
git commit -s -m "short imperative summary"   # -s is required (DCO)
```

- **Sign-off is required** (`-s`). PRs without DCO sign-off cannot be merged.
- Keep the PR small: one issue = one PR.

## 3. Local checks (must pass before pushing)

```bash
pre-commit run --all-files
pytest -xvs tests/<the_file_you_touched>.py    # if applicable
```

## 4. Open the PR

**PR title format** (please follow):

```
[good-first-issue] <area>: <imperative summary>  (#<sub-issue-number>)
```

Examples:
- `[good-first-issue] docs: fix broken link in quickstart (#1801)`
- `[good-first-issue] tests: add unit test for FooBar.flush (#1802)`
- `[good-first-issue] lint: add SPDX header to scripts/foo.py (#1803)`

**PR description** — please use this template (the repo's PR template already
gives you the skeleton; just fill it in):

```markdown
**What this PR does / why we need it**:
Closes #<sub-issue-number>
Refs #<this umbrella issue number>

<one or two sentences describing the change>

**Special notes for your reviewers**:
- This is my first PR to LMCache 🙇 please be gentle.
- I ran `pre-commit run --all-files` locally — all green.
- I ran `pytest -xvs tests/...` — all green.

**If applicable**:
- [ ] this PR contains user facing changes - docs added
- [ ] this PR contains unit tests
```

> Tip: writing `Closes #1234` in the description auto-closes the sub-issue when the
> PR is merged. Keep `Refs #<umbrella>` so the umbrella stays linked.

## 5. Finding a reviewer

You don't need to find one yourself — `.github/CODEOWNERS` will auto-request
the right people based on the files you changed. If the PR sits idle for **3 working
days**, leave a polite comment like:

> Friendly ping — PTAL when you have a moment 🙏 cc @<one CODEOWNER from the file you changed>

If you really can't tell who to ping, default to:
- Tests / CI / packaging → @hickeyma @sammshen @ApostaC @deng451e
- Docs / examples → @sammshen @deng451e
- Storage backends → @maobaolong @sammshen @chunxiaozheng
- Core engine / memory → @ApostaC @YaoJiayi @sammshen
- Multiprocess → @ApostaC @OasisGit @hlin99

(See [`.github/CODEOWNERS`](../blob/dev/.github/CODEOWNERS) for the full map.)

## 6. Responding to review comments

This is the part most newcomers miss — please follow it, it makes everyone happier:

1. **Address every comment.** For each thread:
   - If you agree → push a fix and reply `Done in <commit-sha>`.
   - If you disagree → explain politely, propose an alternative.
   - If you don't understand → ask! Reviewers expect questions.
2. **Don't force-push** during review (it loses inline-comment context). Just add
   commits; we'll squash on merge.
3. **Re-request review explicitly** once all threads are resolved:
   > Addressed all comments, PTAL again 🙏 @reviewer1 @reviewer2

   `PTAL` = "Please Take Another Look". Tag every reviewer who left comments.
4. If CI is red, fix it before pinging — reviewers will skip red PRs.


---

## 7. How to create and claim a sub-issues

- You can extend the new cli commend line tools, ref to https://github.com/LMCache/LMCache/pull/3719 and https://github.com/LMCache/LMCache/pull/3678

---

Stuck? Drop a message in the `#contributors` channel of our
[Slack](https://join.slack.com/t/lmcacheworkspace/shared_invite/zt-3g8e6xzz8-KzS_HI8bPERGFK5PTB~MYg)
or comment here. We're happy to help. 🙌


**Maintainers**: please update this checklist as sub-issues are filed.

---

## Next step: Good second issues

Finished your first PR? Head over to **#5751 — [Good second issues — next step after your first PR](https://github.com/LMCache/LMCache/issues/5751)** for your next small, well-scoped task.
